modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A quantitative backtest transforms discrete mathematical signals into simulated portfolio equity through strict chronological execution rules. The Market sandbox enforces a deterministic 1-bar execution delay: a signal calculated using data available at the close of Bar $t$ executes at the opening price of Bar $t+1$. This delay mirrors institutional reality, where market participants cannot act upon a closing price until that closing auction has concluded.

The account operates on a long-or-cash basis, deploying 100% of available cash into fractional shares upon a buy signal. The execution model accounts for bid-ask friction and brokerage costs: - **Buy Fill Price**: $P_t^{\text{buy}} = O_t (1 + s)$, where $O_t$ is the opening price and $s$ is slippage (default $3\text{ bps} = 0.0003$). Commission $c$ (default $5\text{ bps} = 0.0005$) is charged on the total purchase value, determining share quantity:

$$
q = \frac{\text{Cash}}{P_t^{\text{buy}} (1 + c)}
$$

 - **Sale Fill Price**: $P_{t'}^{\text{sell}} = O_{t'} (1 - s)$. Commission is deducted from gross proceeds:

$$
\text{Net Proceeds} = q \cdot P_{t'}^{\text{sell}} (1 - c)
$$

Every realized trade recorded in the trade log reflects net proceeds after both transaction costs. If a position remains open at the conclusion of the backtest, it is marked to market at the final bar's close ($P_T^{\text{close}}$) to calculate ending equity, but is excluded from closed-trade statistics (such as Win Rate and Profit Factor).

The reference benchmark—**Buy & hold**—executes a single purchase at the opening price of Bar 1, incurs entry friction once, and holds the position perpetually. This represents the ultimate hurdle for any active timing strategy: if a quantitative rule cannot outperform buy-and-hold net of transaction friction, its active trading is destroying capital.

## A worked example

To trace order execution step by step, follow a complete round-trip trade starting with $E_0 = \$100{,}000$ cash, slippage $s = 3\text{ bps}$ ($0.0003$), and commission $c = 5\text{ bps}$ ($0.0005$).

A buy signal triggers at the close of Bar $t$ where price is $100.00$. Bar $t+1$ opens at $O_{t+1} = 101.00$. The executed buy price after slippage is:

$$
P^{\text{buy}} = 101.00 \times (1 + 0.0003) = 101.00 \times 1.0003 = \$101.0303
$$

 Accounting for the $5\text{ bps}$ commission, the total cash outlay per share is $101.0303 \times 1.0005 \approx \$101.0808$. The allocated share quantity is:

$$
q = \frac{\$100{,}000.00}{101.0303 \times 1.0005} = \frac{\$100{,}000.00}{101.080815} \approx 989.3074\text{ shares}
$$

Several bars later, an exit signal triggers. The subsequent bar opens at $O_{t'} = 104.00$. The executed sell price after slippage is:

$$
P^{\text{sell}} = 104.00 \times (1 - 0.0003) = 104.00 \times 0.9997 = \$103.9688
$$

 Gross sale proceeds equal:

$$
\text{Gross Proceeds} = 989.3074 \times 103.9688 \approx \$102{,}857.06
$$

 Deducting the $5\text{ bps}$ commission ($102{,}857.06 \times 0.0005 \approx \$51.43$):

$$
\text{Net Proceeds} = \$102{,}857.06 \times (1 - 0.0005) \approx \$102{,}805.63
$$

 The net realized gain is:

$$
\text{Net Gain} = \frac{\$102{,}805.63 - \$100{,}000.00}{\$100{,}000.00} = +2.8056\% \approx +2.81\%
$$

 Notice that while the raw asset price rose from $101.00 \to 104.00$ ($+2.9703\%$), execution slippage and commissions absorbed $16.5\text{ bps}$ of performance.

Now consider the **Multi-Horizon Look-Ahead Audit**. Under Geometric Brownian Motion, running a 1-year backtest (252 bars) and a 3-year backtest (756 bars) using the same random seed (seed 42) produces the exact same first 252 price bars. Any causal, backwards-looking trading rule must therefore execute the exact same trades during that first year. When we test the valid 50-day trend rule, it executes exactly 28 trades during year one on both horizons. However, when we test the look-ahead rule (`close > 0.9 * max(close)`), it executes 22 trades during year one on the 1-year horizon, but only 10 trades during that identical period on the 3-year horizon. Adding future bars shifted the global historical maximum, altering past trading signals. Divergent trade executions on identical historical data are definitive mathematical proof of look-ahead bias.

## Put the idea into practice

**Execute the baseline strategy.** In the **Market sandbox**, activate the **Trend following** chip and click **Run experiment**. The **Console** log confirms: "756 bars · 59 fills · final equity $76,598.46".

**Audit an individual execution.** Open the **Trades** tab to inspect the chronological trade blotter, which lists Date, Side, Quantity, Price, Fee, and P&L. Select the very first BUY trade and record its Date and Price. Switch to the **Market** chart tab, locate the corresponding bar, and inspect its Open. Verify that the recorded execution price matches Open $\times (1 + 0.0003)$ to the penny.

**Compare equity against the benchmark.** Open the **Equity curve** chart tab. The visualization plots active Strategy equity against the passive Buy & hold curve. Select the **Buy & hold** quick-strategy chip and execute: verify that the final equity in **All metrics** aligns with the terminal value of the dashed benchmark line.

**Stress-test transaction friction.** Click the gear icon (**Execution settings**). Set both **Commission (bps)** and **Slippage (bps)** to 0. Restore the **Trend following** chip and execute: note that final equity rises from $\$76{,}598.46$ to $\$80{,}271.18$ ($R \approx -19.73\%$), while fill counts remain unchanged at 59. Next, set commission and slippage to $20\text{ bps}$ each: final equity plunges to $\$62{,}538.12$ ($R \approx -37.46\%$), while fills remain at 59. Frictional costs degrade returns without altering underlying signal states.

**Conduct the multi-horizon look-ahead audit.** Set **Horizon** to **1 year** on the **Parameters** tab. In `strategy.py`, enter the look-ahead rule: `return data["close"] > max(data["close"]) * 0.9`. Execute the run and count the recorded trades on the **Trades** tab (22 trades). Now change **Horizon** to **3 years** and execute again: filter the **Trades** blotter to only include trades dated within the first calendar year (2020). Exactly 10 trades appear. The fact that adding future data in 2021 and 2022 altered trades executed in 2020 exposes look-ahead bias. Repeat this test with the baseline trend rule to confirm it executes identical trades across both horizons.

### Practise in the lab

Open the [Market sandbox](/lab?tool=market) and rerun the default rule with costs at 0, at the defaults and at 20 bps each, then run the one-year versus three-year look-ahead test on two rules and record what changes. The worksheet on this page is an interactive arithmetic verification aid: it remains strictly in cash and does not execute your trading strategy, so you should record all substantive findings and performance figures directly from the lab itself.

Because the lab's default market data is synthetically generated from stochastic models, a profitable run demonstrates that your execution logic and risk parameters function properly under those specific assumptions—it is never empirical evidence of a tradable real-market edge. Complete your session by documenting what you modified, the empirical outputs you observed, and the next falsification test you plan to run in [My notebook](/notebook).

cash = 100000.0
slippage = 3.0 / 10000.0
commission = 5.0 / 10000.0
open_buy = 101.00
buy_price = open_buy * (1.0 + slippage)
shares = cash / (buy_price * (1.0 + commission))
open_sell = 104.00
sell_price = open_sell * (1.0 - slippage)
gross_proceeds = shares * sell_price
net_proceeds = gross_proceeds * (1.0 - commission)
print("Executed buy price:", round(buy_price, 4), "Shares purchased:", round(shares, 4))
print("Executed sell price:", round(sell_price, 4), "Net proceeds:", round(net_proceeds, 2))
net_gain_pct = (net_proceeds / cash - 1.0) * 100.0
raw_price_pct = (open_sell / open_buy - 1.0) * 100.0
print("Net portfolio gain:", round(net_gain_pct, 2), "% vs raw price change:", round(raw_price_pct, 2), "%")
friction_drag_bps = (raw_price_pct - net_gain_pct) * 100.0
print("Friction drag in basis points:", round(friction_drag_bps, 1))
print("Look-ahead audit trade counts (1-yr vs 3-yr):", 22, "vs", 10)

assignment.solution: Across all three cost environments, total fills remain constant at 59 because transaction friction modifies cash balances without altering underlying indicator comparisons. On seed 42, zero friction yields final equity of ~$80,271 (-19.73%), default friction yields ~$76,598 (-23.40%), and adverse friction (20 bps each) yields ~$62,538 (-37.46%), demonstrating how transaction drag compounds over time. In the multi-horizon look-ahead audit, the causal 50-day trend rule executes exactly 28 trades during year one across both 1-year and 3-year runs. In contrast, the rule referencing max(data['close']) executes 22 trades on the 1-year run but only 10 trades during that same period on the 3-year run. When future data alters historical decisions, the backtest has leaked the future and is scientifically invalid.

modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Evaluating a quantitative backtest requires looking far beyond simple cumulative return. A trading strategy can generate an impressive final equity curve while carrying uncompensated tail risks, unbearable drawdown periods, or extreme vulnerability to transaction friction. The Strategy lab equips researchers with a rigorous 14-metric analytical suite to evaluate strategy risk, reward, and execution efficiency.

Following a backtest run, the **EXPERIMENT OUTPUT** panel surfaces four primary performance cards: - **CAGR (Compound Annual Growth Rate)**: Compounds the total geometric return over the standard 252 trading bars per year:

$$
\text{CAGR} = (1 + R)^{252 / N} - 1
$$

 - **SHARPE (Annualized Sharpe Ratio)**: Measures excess return per unit of total risk relative to a 3% annual risk-free hurdle ($r_f = 0.03$):

$$
\text{Sharpe} = \frac{\bar{r} - r_f}{s_r} \sqrt{252}
$$

 - **MAX DRAWDOWN (MDD)**: Measures the maximum peak-to-trough percentage decline in portfolio equity:

$$
\text{MDD} = \min_{t} \left(\frac{E_t - \max_{\tau \le t} E_{\tau}}{\max_{\tau \le t} E_{\tau}}\right)
$$

 - **WIN RATE**: Percentage of closed round-trip trades that achieved a positive net P&L after all commissions and slippage.

Expanding **All metrics** reveals ten additional statistical indicators: total return, profit factor (gross winning dollar volume divided by gross losing dollar volume), total trade executions, final equity, capital asset pricing alpha and beta relative to buy-and-hold, Sortino ratio (dividing excess return by downside semi-deviation), Calmar ratio ($\text{CAGR} / |\text{MDD}|$), Value at Risk (VaR 95%), and Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR / Expected Shortfall 95%).

The lab handles undefined metrics with scientific honesty. If a strategy remains 100% in cash, its daily return variance is zero; the Sharpe ratio denominator vanishes, so the interface displays an em-dash ("—") on cards and "Undefined" in tables rather than a misleading zero. Furthermore, if you modify any parameter slider or code expression after a run, the timestamp displays "· inputs changed" to warn you that visible outputs no longer reflect active controls.

## A worked example

To master performance evaluation, examine the baseline 50-day trend run on seed 42 ($N = 756\text{ bars}$, 3 years). The strategy yields a cumulative return of $R = -23.40\%$. Calculating CAGR:

$$
\text{CAGR} = (1 - 0.2340)^{252 / 756} - 1 = (0.7660)^{1/3} - 1 \approx 0.91498 - 1 = -8.50\%
$$

 The maximum peak-to-trough drawdown reached $\text{MDD} = -27.07\%$. The Calmar ratio scales annual growth by maximum drawdown:

$$
\text{Calmar} = \frac{\text{CAGR}}{|\text{MDD}|} = \frac{-0.0850}{|-0.2707|} = \frac{-0.0850}{0.2707} \approx -0.314
$$

 The backtest recorded 59 fills: 30 buys and 29 sales, completing 29 full round-trip trades. A win rate of $17.24\%$ indicates that exactly 5 trades were profitable, while 24 were unprofitable. The profit factor of $0.32$ confirms that total dollar gains from those 5 winners amounted to only one-third of the losses incurred by the 24 losers.

Now examine the **High-Win-Rate Paradox**. In the sandbox, select the **Mean reversion** quick-strategy chip on seed 42. The performance cards display a stunning **WIN RATE of 76.7%** (23 winners out of 30 closed trades). Yet the strategy's total return is $-2.37\%$ and its CAGR is $-0.80\%$!

How can a strategy that wins three-quarters of its trades lose money overall? Mathematical expectancy depends on both probability and payoff magnitude:

$$
\mathbb{E}[\text{Trade}] = (p_{\text{win}} \times \overline{\text{Win}}) - (p_{\text{loss}} \times \overline{\text{Loss}})
$$

 The mean-reversion rule captures dozens of tiny $0.3\%$ profits, but occasionally holds onto deteriorating positions that crash for $-4.5\%$ losses before closing. A high win rate is completely meaningless in isolation—it frequently masks an asymmetric distribution of small wins wiped out by catastrophic left-tail losses.

## Put the idea into practice

**Inspect the primary metric cards.** Execute the **Trend following** baseline chip with default parameters. Read the four output cards: CAGR ($\approx -8.5\%$), SHARPE ($\approx -0.92$), MAX DRAWDOWN ($\approx -27.1\%$), and WIN RATE ($\approx 17.2\%$).

**Audit comprehensive metrics in the drawer.** Click **All metrics** to expand the full statistical readout. Record the 14 reported metrics: Total return ($-0.2340$), CAGR ($-0.0850$), Sharpe ($-0.9200$), Sortino ($-1.1400$), Max drawdown ($-0.2707$), Calmar ($-0.3140$), Win rate ($0.1724$), Profit factor ($0.3200$), Total trades ($59.0000$), Final equity ($\$76{,}598.46$), Alpha ($-0.0750$), Beta ($0.4500$), VaR 95% ($-0.0185$), and CVaR 95% ($-0.0270$).

**Verify mathematical relationships by hand.** Open the lesson worksheet. Confirm that your manual calculations of CAGR from total return ($756\text{ bars}$) and Calmar ratio from CAGR and maximum drawdown match the reported figures to the fourth decimal place.

**Navigate performance visualizations.** - Switch to the **Drawdown** chart tab ("Drawdown from peak"): trace the underwater curve and identify the exact calendar date of the deepest valley ($-27.07\%$). - Open the **Returns** tab: inspect the monthly returns heatmap. Observe which calendar months suffered the steepest losses and which generated gains. - Open the **Trades** tab: filter the trade blotter by positive P&L to confirm that exactly 5 closed trades produced gains.

**Expose the high-win-rate paradox.** Click **Parameters**, select the **Mean reversion** quick-strategy chip, and execute. Write down the 14 metrics alongside the trend rule. Observe the striking divergence: win rate surges to $76.7\%$, yet total return remains negative ($-2.37\%$).

**Trigger the input staleness alert.** Move the **Annual volatility** slider from $20\%$ to $25\%$ without clicking Run. Observe the label "· inputs changed" appear beside the execution timestamp, indicating that the displayed equity curve belongs to the previous parameter state.

### Practise in the lab

Open the [Market sandbox](/lab?tool=market) and run the Trend following and Mean reversion chips on the same seed and compare all fourteen metrics side by side. The worksheet on this page is an interactive arithmetic verification aid: it remains strictly in cash and does not execute your trading strategy, so you should record all substantive findings and performance figures directly from the lab itself.

Because the lab's default market data is synthetically generated from stochastic models, a profitable run demonstrates that your execution logic and risk parameters function properly under those specific assumptions—it is never empirical evidence of a tradable real-market edge. Complete your session by documenting what you modified, the empirical outputs you observed, and the next falsification test you plan to run in [My notebook](/notebook).

modules.title: The valuation tool: net current assets, haircuts and Graham value
modules.subtitle: Compute unadjusted and adjusted Net Current Asset Value (NCAV) per share, apply liquidation haircuts, test Benjamin Graham's two-thirds screen, and evaluate valuation sensitivity to recovery and growth assumptions.
modules.objective: Compute unadjusted and adjusted Net Current Asset Value (NCAV) per share, apply liquidation haircuts, test Benjamin Graham's two-thirds screen, and evaluate valuation sensitivity to recovery and growth assumptions.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes studying deep-value liquidation models and haircut theory, 10 minutes working through the adjusted NCAV and break-even recovery arithmetic, and 12 minutes stress-testing balance sheet assumptions in the Valuation tab; all corporate balance sheets in the tool are educational models.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Quantitative research extends beyond price-series momentum to fundamental business valuation. The **Valuation** tool implements classic deep-value liquidation models pioneered by Benjamin Graham in *Security Analysis*. Graham's central insight was that an investor could establish an impregnable margin of safety by purchasing a company's common stock at a steep discount to its net liquid assets—treating property, plant, equipment (PP&E), and intangible goodwill as having zero residual value.

The model computes **Unadjusted Net Current Asset Value (NCAV)** per share:

$$
\text{NCAV}_{\text{unadj}} = \frac{C + R + I - L}{N}
$$

 where $C$ is cash and cash equivalents, $R$ is accounts receivable, $I$ is inventory, $L$ is total liabilities (short-term and long-term obligations), and $N$ is diluted common shares outstanding.

Graham established a demanding investment rule known as the **two-thirds NCAV screen**: purchase shares only if the market price $P$ trades at or below two-thirds of unadjusted NCAV per share:

$$
P \le \frac{2}{3} \text{NCAV}_{\text{unadj}}
$$

However, unadjusted book values assume full liquidation recovery. In distressed bankruptcies or forced asset sales, customers dispute invoices and inventories sell for scrap. The tool models **Adjusted NCAV** by applying recovery rate haircuts:

$$
\text{NCAV}_{\text{adj}} = \frac{C + \rho_R R + \rho_I I - L}{N}
$$

 where cash recovers $100\%$ ($1.0$), receivables recover at rate $\rho_R$ (default $85\% = 0.85$), and inventory recovers at rate $\rho_I$ (default $60\% = 0.60$). The fundamental **Margin of Safety (MoS)** is:

$$
\text{MoS} = 1 - \frac{P}{\text{NCAV}_{\text{adj}}}
$$

The tool also incorporates Graham's valuation heuristic for operating earnings:

$$
V_{\text{Graham}} = \frac{\text{EPS} \times (8.5 + 2g) \times 4.4}{Y}
$$

 where $\text{EPS}$ is trailing earnings per share, $8.5$ represents the P/E of a no-growth company, $g$ is the expected multi-year earnings growth rate (in percent), $4.4$ represents the historical yield on AAA corporate bonds, and $Y$ is the prevailing corporate bond yield (in percent). While widely cited, this growth formula is highly speculative and serves as a sensitivity test rather than an asset-backed valuation.

## A worked example

To evaluate balance sheet valuation mechanics, examine the default corporate balance sheet in the tool: Cash $C = \$40\text{m}$, Receivables $R = \$60\text{m}$, Inventory $I = \$80\text{m}$, Total Liabilities $L = \$70\text{m}$, Diluted Shares $N = 10\text{m}$, and Market Price $P = \$6.00$. (All financial figures are in millions except per-share values).

First, compute **Unadjusted NCAV per share**:

$$
\text{NCAV}_{\text{unadj}} = \frac{\$40\text{m} + \$60\text{m} + \$80\text{m} - \$70\text{m}}{10\text{m}} = \frac{\$110\text{m}}{10\text{m}} = \$11.00\text{ per share}
$$

 Graham's two-thirds screen threshold is:

$$
P_{\text{screen}} = \frac{2}{3} \times \$11.00 \approx \$7.33\text{ per share}
$$

 Because the active market price is $P = \$6.00 \le \$7.33$, the stock successfully passes Graham's unadjusted two-thirds screen.

Next, apply realistic liquidation recovery haircuts ($\rho_R = 0.85$, $\rho_I = 0.60$):

$$
\text{Recoverable Assets} = \$40\text{m} + (0.85 \times \$60\text{m}) + (0.60 \times \$80\text{m}) = \$40\text{m} + \$51\text{m} + \$48\text{m} = \$139\text{m}
$$

 Deducting total liabilities:

$$
\text{Adjusted Net Liquid Assets} = \$139\text{m} - \$70\text{m} = \$69\text{m}
$$

$$
\text{NCAV}_{\text{adj}} = \frac{\$69\text{m}}{10\text{m}} = \$6.90\text{ per share}
$$

 The margin of safety relative to adjusted asset backing is:

$$
\text{MoS} = 1 - \frac{\$6.00}{\$6.90} \approx +13.04\%
$$

Now stress-test inventory recovery. If market conditions deteriorate and inventory realizes only $\rho_I = 40\%$ ($0.40$):

$$
\text{Recoverable Assets} = \$40\text{m} + \$51\text{m} + (0.40 \times \$80\text{m}) = \$40\text{m} + \$51\text{m} + \$32\text{m} = \$123\text{m}
$$

$$
\text{NCAV}_{\text{adj}} = \frac{\$123\text{m} - \$70\text{m}}{10\text{m}} = \frac{\$53\text{m}}{10\text{m}} = \$5.30\text{ per share}
$$

 At $\$5.30$, the active market price of $\$6.00$ trades at a premium over liquid asset backing ($\text{MoS} = 1 - 6.00 / 5.30 = -13.2\%$).

We can solve algebraically for the exact break-even inventory recovery rate $\rho_I^*$ where adjusted NCAV equals the $\$6.00$ price:

$$
\frac{40 + 51 + 80\rho_I^* - 70}{10} = 6.00 \implies 21 + 80\rho_I^* = 60 \implies 80\rho_I^* = 39 \implies \rho_I^* = \frac{39}{80} = 48.75\%
$$

 If inventory recovers less than $48.75\%$, the investment thesis loses its asset-backed protection.

Finally, examine the Graham heuristic: with $\text{EPS} = \$4.00$, growth $g = 5\%$, and bond yield $Y = 4.4\%$:

$$
V_{\text{Graham}} = \frac{4.00 \times (8.5 + 2 \times 5) \times 4.4}{4.4} = 4.00 \times 18.5 = \$74.00
$$

 If bond yields rise to $Y = 6.0\%$, valuation falls sharply to $4.00 \times 18.5 \times (4.4 / 6.0) \approx \$54.27$.

## Put the idea into practice

**Navigate to the Valuation workbench.** Click the **Valuation** tab in the top navigation bar. Under **BALANCE SHEET INPUTS**, inspect the baseline figures: **Cash & equivalents** ($40$), **Accounts receivable** ($60$), **Inventory** ($80$), **Total liabilities** ($70$), **Diluted shares** ($10$), and **Market price / share** ($6$).

**Audit the Valuation Worksheet.** The right-hand panel **VALUATION WORKSHEET** displays: - **ADJUSTED NCAV / SHARE**: $\$6.90$ - Comparison progress bar: Market price ($\$6.00$) vs Adjusted asset value ($\$6.90$) - **Unadjusted NCAV**: $\$11.00$ - **Two-thirds screen price**: $\$7.33$ - **Margin of safety · adjusted NCAV**: $+13.0\%$ - **Graham heuristic value**: $\$74.00$ - Screen verdict badge: "Passes the unadjusted two-thirds NCAV screen."

**Stress-test liquidation recovery rates.** In the **Liquidation assumptions** section, drag **Inventory recovered** from $60\%$ down to $40\%$. Watch the status indicator "· UPDATING" appear momentarily. Adjusted NCAV per share drops to $\$5.30$, and Margin of safety turns negative ($-13.2\%$). Notice that the verdict badge still reads "Passes the unadjusted two-thirds NCAV screen." because the screen evaluates unadjusted accounting book values.

**Find the exact break-even recovery.** Adjust the inventory slider until the Margin of Safety reads $0.0\%$. Confirm that the recovery rate settles at approximately $48.75\%$.

**Evaluate the Graham growth heuristic.** Under **Graham formula inputs**, change **Bond yield (%)** from $4.4\%$ to $6.0\%$. Watch the heuristic valuation contract from $\$74.00$ down to $\$54.27$. Next, change **Growth (%)** from $5\%$ to $10\%$: the valuation jumps to $\$83.60$. Observe how volatile growth assumptions are compared to tangible balance-sheet asset liquidation values.

### Practise in the lab

Open the [Valuation](/lab?tool=valuation) and move the two recovery sliders until the margin of safety reaches zero, and record the recovery rates at which the price equals the adjusted asset value. The worksheet on this page is an interactive arithmetic verification aid: it remains strictly in cash and does not execute your trading strategy, so you should record all substantive findings and performance figures directly from the lab itself.

Because the lab's default market data is synthetically generated from stochastic models, a profitable run demonstrates that your execution logic and risk parameters function properly under those specific assumptions—it is never empirical evidence of a tradable real-market edge. Complete your session by documenting what you modified, the empirical outputs you observed, and the next falsification test you plan to run in [My notebook](/notebook).

assignment.solution: With default balance sheet inputs ($40m cash, $60m receivables at 85% recovery, $80m inventory, $70m liabilities, 10m shares), adjusted NCAV equals the $6.00 market price when (40 + 51 + 80*r - 70)/10 = 6.00, yielding 21 + 80*r = 60, or r = 39/80 = 48.75%. Below 48.75% inventory recovery, the margin of safety becomes negative. The Graham growth heuristic produces $34.00 at 0% growth, $74.00 at 5% growth, and $114.00 at 10% growth under a 4.4% bond yield. Adjusted NCAV warrants substantially greater quantitative confidence because it is anchored in verifiable, audited balance-sheet liquid assets, whereas the Graham growth formula swings wildly ($+$40 per 5 percentage points of growth) based on subjective, unprovable future growth assumptions.

modules.title: The factor studio: models, coefficients and robust errors
modules.subtitle: Estimate CAPM and Fama-French multi-factor regressions on synthetic asset returns, interpret factor betas with Newey-West HAC standard errors, and evaluate alpha estimates through the lens of statistical significance.
modules.objective: Estimate CAPM and Fama-French multi-factor regressions on synthetic asset returns, interpret factor betas with Newey-West HAC standard errors, and evaluate alpha estimates through the lens of statistical significance.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading empirical factor asset pricing theory, 10 minutes calculating standard error distances and alpha significance by hand, and 12 minutes fitting factor specifications in the Factor studio; all observations are generated from known synthetic DGPs.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Modern quantitative portfolio management relies on linear asset pricing models to decompose an asset's returns into systematic factor risk exposures and idiosyncratic residual performance. Instead of asking whether a manager made money, factor analysis asks *how* that money was made—separating passive market beta, small-cap tilts, and value premiums from genuine investment skill.

The **Factor studio** estimates multi-factor regressions via Ordinary Least Squares (OLS):

$$
r_{i,t} - r_{f,t} = \alpha_i + \beta_{\text{MKT}} f_{\text{MKT},t} + \beta_{\text{SMB}} f_{\text{SMB},t} + \beta_{\text{HML}} f_{\text{HML},t} + \varepsilon_{i,t}
$$

 where $r_{i,t} - r_{f,t}$ is the asset's excess return, $f_{\text{MKT},t}$ is the excess market return, $f_{\text{SMB},t}$ is the Small-Minus-Big size factor, $f_{\text{HML},t}$ is the High-Minus-Low value factor, $\alpha_i$ represents abnormal risk-adjusted performance (alpha), and $\varepsilon_{i,t}$ is the residual disturbance.

In financial econometric regressions, standard OLS standard errors are notoriously unreliable because residuals exhibit time-varying heteroskedasticity and serial autocorrelation. If uncorrected, conventional standard errors appear artificially narrow, producing falsely inflated $t$-statistics and spurious discoveries. The Factor studio resolves this by reporting **Newey–West HAC (Heteroskedasticity and Autocorrelation Consistent)** standard errors:

$$
t_{\hat\beta} = \frac{\hat\beta - \beta_0}{\operatorname{SE}_{\text{HAC}}(\hat\beta)}
$$

Crucially, the Factor studio provides something impossible in real-world finance: **a known ground truth**. The data is generated from a known Data-Generating Process (DGP) with pre-set factor exposures, displayed in the panel **KNOWN DATA-GENERATING PROCESS**. This allows you to evaluate econometric precision by measuring the exact distance between OLS estimates and planted truth in standard error units.

The tool also reports **TEST R² · RIDGE**: a cross-validation test that trains a regularized ridge regression on the first $75\%$ of observations ($567\text{ bars}$) and scores it out-of-sample on the remaining $25\%$ ($189\text{ bars}$). This out-of-sample test protects against overfitting.

## A worked example

To evaluate factor regression mechanics, examine the baseline configuration: Fama–French three-factor model, $N = 756$ observations, random seed 42, and $1.0\%$ daily idiosyncratic volatility.

The planted ground-truth parameters are:

$$
\beta_{\text{MKT}} = 1.10, \quad \beta_{\text{SMB}} = 0.25, \quad \beta_{\text{HML}} = 0.40, \quad \alpha_{\text{daily}} = 0.0001\text{ (1 bp/day)}
$$

Executing the OLS fit yields the following parameter estimates: - **Market Beta**: $\hat{\beta}_{\text{MKT}} = 1.0907$ with $\operatorname{SE}_{\text{HAC}} = 0.0393$. Measuring distance from ground truth:

$$
t_{\text{diff}} = \frac{\hat{\beta}_{\text{MKT}} - \beta_{\text{MKT}}}{\operatorname{SE}_{\text{HAC}}} = \frac{1.0907 - 1.1000}{0.0393} = \frac{-0.0093}{0.0393} \approx -0.237\text{ standard errors}
$$

 - **SMB Beta**: $\hat{\beta}_{\text{SMB}} = 0.2256$ with $\operatorname{SE}_{\text{HAC}} = 0.0385$.

$$
t_{\text{diff}} = \frac{0.2256 - 0.2500}{0.0385} = \frac{-0.0244}{0.0385} \approx -0.634\text{ standard errors}
$$

 - **HML Beta**: $\hat{\beta}_{\text{HML}} = 0.3662$ with $\operatorname{SE}_{\text{HAC}} = 0.0371$.

$$
t_{\text{diff}} = \frac{0.3662 - 0.4000}{0.0371} = \frac{-0.0338}{0.0371} \approx -0.911\text{ standard errors}
$$

 All three systematic factor estimates land within $1.0$ standard error of ground truth, reflecting excellent econometric recovery. In-sample $R^2$ reaches $0.564$, and out-of-sample Ridge Test $R^2$ confirms stability at $0.496$.

Now examine the estimated daily alpha:

$$
\hat{\alpha}_{\text{daily}} = 0.000586\text{ with } \operatorname{SE}_{\text{HAC}} = 0.000381, \quad t = 1.54, \quad p = 0.124
$$

 Annualizing this daily alpha yields an apparently massive return:

$$
\text{Annualized Alpha} \approx 0.000586 \times 252 \approx +14.77\%
$$

An unsophisticated investor would celebrate a $+14.8\%$ annualized alpha. But the econometrician checks the $p$-value: at $p = 0.124 > 0.05$, the estimate is statistically indistinguishable from zero! In fact, the true planted alpha was only $0.0001$ ($2.5\%$ annually). The estimated $+14.8\%$ was largely an artifact of random sampling noise. Precise factor loadings alongside noisy, statistically insignificant alpha estimates are the norm in empirical asset pricing.

## Put the idea into practice

**Open the Factor studio.** Click the **Factor studio** tab. Leave the default settings: **Factor specification** set to "Fama–French · three factors", **Observations** at 756, **Random seed** at 42, and **Idiosyncratic daily volatility** at 1.0%. Click **Fit factor model**.

**Audit model diagnostics.** Under **MODEL DIAGNOSTICS**, inspect the summary cards: - **R² · OLS**: $0.564$ - **ADJUSTED R²**: $0.562$ - **TEST R² · RIDGE**: $0.496$ Read the explanatory footnote: "756 observations · 6 HAC lags · ridge training/test split 567/189."

**Audit the coefficient table.** Review the regression results table: - Alpha (daily): $\beta = 0.000586$, $\operatorname{SE} = 0.000381$, $p = 0.124$ - Market: $\beta = 1.0907$, $\operatorname{SE} = 0.0393$, $p < 0.001$ - SMB: $\beta = 0.2256$, $\operatorname{SE} = 0.0385$, $p < 0.001$ - HML: $\beta = 0.3662$, $\operatorname{SE} = 0.0371$, $p < 0.001$

**Verify estimation accuracy against ground truth.** Compare the estimated betas against the **KNOWN DATA-GENERATING PROCESS** box (Market $1.10$, SMB $0.25$, HML $0.40$). Divide each difference by its reported SE · HAC: confirm that all three estimates land within $\pm 1.0$ standard errors of truth.

**Evaluate model misspecification.** Switch **Factor specification** to **CAPM · market only** and click **Fit factor model**. Observe how the Market beta shifts to $1.1235$: omitting the SMB and HML factors forces their correlated risk exposures to load onto the market term. Next, test **Carhart · four factors** and **Fama–French · five factors** to observe how additional factors modify $R^2$.

**Scale idiosyncratic noise.** Increase **Idiosyncratic daily volatility** from $1.0\%$ to $3.0\%$ and re-fit. Notice that OLS $R^2$ collapses to $\approx 0.14$, standard errors triple in width, and parameter estimates wander further from ground truth, illustrating how unmodeled noise obscures systematic signals.

### Practise in the lab

Open the [Factor studio](/lab?tool=factors) and fit the three-factor model at seeds 42, 43 and 44 and record how far each estimated exposure lands from its planted value, measured in standard errors. The worksheet on this page is an interactive arithmetic verification aid: it remains strictly in cash and does not execute your trading strategy, so you should record all substantive findings and performance figures directly from the lab itself.

Because the lab's default market data is synthetically generated from stochastic models, a profitable run demonstrates that your execution logic and risk parameters function properly under those specific assumptions—it is never empirical evidence of a tradable real-market edge. Complete your session by documenting what you modified, the empirical outputs you observed, and the next falsification test you plan to run in [My notebook](/notebook).

assignment.prompt: Fit the Fama–French three-factor model on seeds 42, 43, and 44 with default parameters. For each seed, record each estimated beta, its HAC standard error, its distance from ground truth in standard errors, and the daily alpha's p-value. Explain what remains stable across seeds versus what varies.
assignment.solution: Across seeds 42, 43, and 44, the estimated systematic factor loadings consistently cluster near the true planted exposures (Market ~ 1.09-1.12 vs 1.10; SMB ~ 0.21-0.26 vs 0.25; HML ~ 0.36-0.42 vs 0.40), with nearly all estimates remaining within 1.5 HAC standard errors of truth. This stability confirms that linear OLS regressions reliably recover systematic risk loadings from 756 observations. In contrast, the daily alpha estimate fluctuates wildly across seeds, shifting in magnitude and sign with p-values consistently above 0.05. Because a tiny planted alpha (~0.0001/day) is easily drowned out by 1.0% idiosyncratic noise, an annualized alpha of ~15% cannot be distinguished from zero. Quantitative researchers must report HAC standard errors and treat statistically insignificant alpha as unproven noise rather than investment skill.

modules.title: Robustness in the sandbox: costs, seeds and scenarios
modules.subtitle: Conduct comprehensive robustness evaluations across random seeds, escalating transaction cost structures, and exogenous stress scenarios, and account for multiple testing bias in strategy evaluation.
modules.objective: Conduct comprehensive robustness evaluations across random seeds, escalating transaction cost structures, and exogenous stress scenarios, and account for multiple testing bias in strategy evaluation.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 6 minutes studying multiple-testing bias and Monte Carlo dispersion theory, 8 minutes analyzing cross-seed statistics, and 16 minutes executing parameter and scenario sweeps in the Market sandbox; all scenarios represent synthetic models rather than historical replays.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A quantitative backtest evaluated on a single dataset or random seed represents only a single realization of a stochastic process. A trading rule that demonstrates spectacular returns on seed 42 may incur devastating losses on seed 43 simply due to the timing luck of local peaks and troughs. Scientifically rigorous research requires multidimensional robustness sweeps to determine whether a strategy possesses a genuine structural edge or is merely overfitted to historical noise.

Robustness testing in the Market sandbox spans three orthogonal testing dimensions: 1. **Seed Dispersion Sweeps**: Run the identical strategy across multiple independent random seeds ($S = 5$) holding all market parameters constant. Calculate the ensemble mean $\bar{R}$ and sample standard deviation $\hat{\sigma}_R$:

$$
\bar{R} = \frac{1}{S} \sum_{s=1}^{S} R_s, \qquad \hat{\sigma}_R = \sqrt{\frac{1}{S - 1} \sum_{s=1}^{S} (R_s - \bar{R})^2}
$$

 A wide standard deviation relative to the mean signals that performance is heavily path-dependent. 2. **Transaction Cost Escalation**: Evaluate strategy viability as transaction friction scales from frictionless conditions ($0\text{ bps}$), to standard institutional costs ($8\text{ bps}$ total), to stressed retail friction ($40\text{ bps}$ total). If a strategy's profitability collapses under standard costs, it has no viable commercial future. 3. **Exogenous Stress Scenarios**: Subject the rule to five distinct historical-inspired market stress regimes: - **Pure random walk**: Zero drift ($\mu = 0$), pure diffusion. - **Deflationary crash · 1929-inspired**: Jump diffusion with $-15\%$ annual decline and $38\%$ volatility. - **Stagflation · 1970s-inspired**: Low drift ($+1.5\%$) with severe volatility ($32\%$). - **Liquidity crisis · 2008-inspired**: Heston stochastic volatility with $-18\%$ annual collapse and $55\%$ volatility. - **Crypto flash crash · −50%**: Injects a sudden 1-day $-50\%$ liquidity hole at the midpoint bar.

Crucially, every parameter tweak or seed you execute represents an experimental trial. Testing 40 variations and reporting only the single best Sharpe ratio introduces severe **multiple-testing selection bias**. Quantitative researchers must log total trial counts and apply Deflated Sharpe Ratio adjustments.

## A worked example

To quantify robustness, evaluate the baseline 50-day trend rule across five consecutive seeds (seeds 42 through 46) under default parameters ($T = 3\text{ years}$, $5\text{ bps}$ commission, $3\text{ bps}$ slippage):

- **Seed 42**: Strategy $R = -23.40\%$, Buy & Hold $R = -18.46\%$, Strategy $\text{MDD} = -27.07\%$ vs Hold $\text{MDD} = -34.18\%$ - **Seed 43**: Strategy $R = +4.90\%$, Buy & Hold $R = +5.10\%$, Strategy $\text{MDD} = -21.40\%$ vs Hold $\text{MDD} = -28.90\%$ - **Seed 44**: Strategy $R = +19.60\%$, Buy & Hold $R = +88.40\%$, Strategy $\text{MDD} = -18.30\%$ vs Hold $\text{MDD} = -26.10\%$ - **Seed 45**: Strategy $R = +2.30\%$, Buy & Hold $R = +30.70\%$, Strategy $\text{MDD} = -22.10\%$ vs Hold $\text{MDD} = -31.50\%$ - **Seed 46**: Strategy $R = -5.80\%$, Buy & Hold $R = +0.40\%$, Strategy $\text{MDD} = -29.50\%$ vs Hold $\text{MDD} = -25.20\%$

Computing the ensemble statistics across the 5 seeds:

$$
\bar{R}_{\text{rule}} = \frac{-23.40 + 4.90 + 19.60 + 2.30 - 5.80}{5} = \frac{-2.40}{5} = -0.48\%
$$

$$
\hat{\sigma}_{R} \approx 15.82\text{ percentage points}
$$

The active strategy lagged the passive Buy & Hold benchmark on all five seeds! However, the trend rule achieved a shallower maximum drawdown on 4 out of the 5 seeds (averaging $\text{MDD} \approx -23.7\%$ compared to $-29.2\%$ for buy-and-hold). If an unethical marketer reported only seed 44 ($+19.60\%$), they would present a completely distorted picture of performance.

Next, examine the **Cost Sensitivity** on seed 42: - Zero costs ($0\text{ bps}$ commission, $0\text{ bps}$ slippage): $R = -19.73\%$ - Default costs ($5\text{ bps}$ commission, $3\text{ bps}$ slippage): $R = -23.40\%$ - Adverse costs ($20\text{ bps}$ commission, $20\text{ bps}$ slippage): $R = -37.46\%$

Finally, examine the **Stress Scenarios** on seed 42: - Pure random walk: Strategy $-26.6\%$ vs Buy & Hold $-35.8\%$ - 1929 Deflationary crash: Strategy $-75.4\%$ vs Buy & Hold $-92.0\%$ - 1970s Stagflation: Strategy $-36.8\%$ vs Buy & Hold $-51.4\%$ - 2008 Liquidity crisis: Strategy $-37.3\%$ vs Buy & Hold $-64.1\%$ - Crypto flash crash: Strategy $-57.5\%$ vs Buy & Hold $-59.2\%$ In severe market crashes, trend following significantly mitigates losses by stepping aside into cash as prices cross beneath the moving average. However, in the flash crash, the $-50\%$ gap occurs in a single bar before signals can exit.

## Put the idea into practice

**Prepare the experimental baseline.** In the **Market sandbox**, select the **Trend following** chip and confirm default parameters ($T = 3$, $5\text{ bps}$ commission, $3\text{ bps}$ slippage). Click the gear icon (**Execution settings**) to access the **Seed** input.

**Execute the 5-seed sweep.** Run seeds 42, 43, 44, 45, and 46 in succession. For each run, record Total return and Max drawdown from **All metrics**, and record the benchmark Buy & Hold return from the terminal point of the dashed curve on the **Equity curve** chart. Compute the sample mean and standard deviation.

**Execute the transaction friction sweep.** Set the seed back to 42. In **Execution settings**, set **Commission (bps)** and **Slippage (bps)** to 0 and execute. Record final equity ($\$80{,}271$). Set both to defaults ($5$ and $3$) and record ($\$76{,}598$). Set both to $20\text{ bps}$ each and record ($\$62{,}538$).

**Execute the scenario stress sweep.** Keep seed 42 and default costs. Open the **Parameters** tab. Select each scenario from the **SCENARIO** dropdown in turn: 1. Pure random walk 2. Deflationary crash · 1929-inspired 3. Stagflation · 1970s-inspired 4. Liquidity crisis · 2008-inspired 5. Crypto flash crash · −50% Execute each run and record the comparative strategy and benchmark returns. Notice the note: "Named stress scenarios override selected process defaults."

**Log total experimental trials.** Count every run executed during this lesson: 5 seed trials $+ 3$ cost trials $+ 5$ scenario trials $= 13$ total trials. Document all 13 trials in your research notebook. Acknowledge that the best-performing run cannot be cited in isolation without disclosing the full trial ledger.

### Practise in the lab

Open the [Market sandbox](/lab?tool=market) and run the default rule on five seeds and on the five named scenarios with every other setting fixed, and tabulate total return against buy and hold for all ten runs. The worksheet on this page is an interactive arithmetic verification aid: it remains strictly in cash and does not execute your trading strategy, so you should record all substantive findings and performance figures directly from the lab itself.

Because the lab's default market data is synthetically generated from stochastic models, a profitable run demonstrates that your execution logic and risk parameters function properly under those specific assumptions—it is never empirical evidence of a tradable real-market edge. Complete your session by documenting what you modified, the empirical outputs you observed, and the next falsification test you plan to run in [My notebook](/notebook).

modules.title: Paper trading: liquidity, stale-data, spread and drawdown guards
modules.subtitle: Operate the mock broker simulation, calculate execution prices with bid-ask spread, slippage, and volume participation caps, and trigger deterministic pre-trade risk guards and circuit breakers.
modules.objective: Operate the mock broker simulation, calculate execution prices with bid-ask spread, slippage, and volume participation caps, and trigger deterministic pre-trade risk guards and circuit breakers.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 7 minutes studying broker execution architecture and risk controls, 9 minutes calculating fill friction and circuit breaker equity thresholds, and 14 minutes triggering pre-trade guards in the Paper trading tab; the mock broker never connects to real exchanges.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Moving from backtesting to order execution introduces the harsh realities of market microstructure. In a backtest, orders are assumed to execute smoothly; in live markets, liquidity vanishes, quotes become stale, spreads blow out during panic, and flawed algorithms can bankrupt a firm in minutes. The **Paper trading** tool provides a deterministic single-session mock broker engineered to demonstrate the pre-trade risk controls and safety guards required by institutional market-access regulations (such as SEC Rule 15c3-5).

The paper account starts with $\$100{,}000$ in simulated cash and operates on a long-only basis. When an order is submitted, the broker models three market frictions: 1. **Bid-Ask Spread & Slippage**: The executed fill price moves away from the reference price by the full slippage plus one-half of the bid-ask spread:

$$
P_{\text{fill}} = P_{\text{ref}} \left(1 \pm \frac{s + \frac{1}{2}\text{spread}}{10{,}000}\right)
$$

 (Plus for purchases, minus for sales, where $s$ and $\text{spread}$ are specified in basis points). 2. **Brokerage Commission**: A commission fee ($c\text{ bps}$, default $5\text{ bps}$) is charged on the total executed dollar value. 3. **Volume Participation Cap**: To prevent the illusion that arbitrary order size can trade at a single price, the broker caps fill quantity at $10\%$ of available bar volume:

$$
q_{\text{fill}} = \min(q_{\text{order}}, \, 0.10 \times V_{\text{bar}})
$$

 If an order exceeds this limit, it executes partially up to the cap, and the remaining shares are immediately discarded as unfilled.

Before executing any order, the broker evaluates a deterministic six-stage **Pre-Trade Guard Pipeline**: 1. **Halted State Check**: If the account is halted, all order submissions are rejected. 2. **Drawdown Circuit Breaker**: If marked equity falls below $97.5\%$ of starting capital ($\$97{,}500$), the circuit breaker trips, halting the account to prevent catastrophic runaway loss. 3. **Stale Data Guard**: If the reference price quote is older than 60 seconds, the order is rejected ("Price data is stale."). 4. **Excessive Spread Guard**: If the bid-ask spread exceeds $100\text{ bps}$, the order is rejected ("Spread exceeds the 100 bps guard."). 5. **Liquidity Guard**: If available bar volume is zero, the order is rejected ("No available liquidity."). 6. **Balance Sufficiency Guard**: The account must hold sufficient cash for purchases (including fees) or sufficient shares for sales.

This deterministic guard architecture illustrates the vital safeguard that Knight Capital infamously lacked in 2012 when an unconstrained algorithmic loop lost $\$440$ million in 45 minutes.

## A worked example

To trace execution mechanics and safety guards, examine a standard purchase: Order quantity $q = 10\text{ shares}$, reference price $P_{\text{ref}} = \$100.00$, available bar volume $V = 1{,}000\text{ shares}$, spread $= 5\text{ bps}$, slippage $s = 3\text{ bps}$, and commission $c = 5\text{ bps}$.

The executed fill price is:

$$
P_{\text{fill}} = 100.00 \times \left(1 + \frac{3 + \frac{5}{2}}{10{,}000}\right) = 100.00 \times \left(1 + \frac{5.5}{10{,}000}\right) = 100.00 \times 1.00055 = \$100.055
$$

 The total cost for 10 shares is $10 \times 100.055 = \$1{,}000.55$. The $5\text{ bps}$ commission is:

$$
\text{Fee} = \$1{,}000.55 \times 0.0005 = \$0.500275 \approx \$0.50
$$

 Total cash outlay is $\$1{,}000.55 + \$0.50 = \$1{,}001.05$, leaving $\$98{,}998.95$ in available cash.

Now observe the **Volume Participation Cap**: Submit an order for 150 shares against the same $1{,}000$ shares of bar volume. The broker enforces the $10\%$ participation limit:

$$
q_{\text{fill}} = \min(150, \, 0.10 \times 1{,}000) = \min(150, 100) = 100\text{ shares}
$$

 The order executes 100 shares, and the **ORDER AUDIT LOG** flags the status as "partially filled". The remaining 50 shares are not queued.

Finally, examine the **Drawdown Circuit Breaker**: Reset the account and set bar volume to $100{,}000$ shares. Place an aggressive buy order for 990 shares at $P_{\text{ref}} = \$100.00$. The purchase cost is $990 \times 100.055 = \$99{,}054.45$, plus commission of $\$49.53$, totaling $\$99{,}103.98$. Remaining cash is:

$$
\text{Cash} = \$100{,}000.00 - \$99{,}103.98 = \$896.02
$$

Now simulate a market drop: change the reference price to $\$97.00$ and attempt any order. The broker marks active portfolio equity to market before processing the order:

$$
\text{Marked Equity} = \text{Cash} + (\text{Shares} \times P_{\text{ref}}) = \$896.02 + (990 \times \$97.00) = \$896.02 + \$96{,}030.00 = \$96{,}926.02
$$

 Expressing marked equity as a percentage of initial capital:

$$
\text{Equity Ratio} = \frac{\$96{,}926.02}{\$100{,}000.00} = 96.93\%
$$

 Because $96.93\% < 97.50\%$, the drawdown circuit breaker trips immediately. The order is rejected, the account risk state switches to "Halted", and all future submissions are blocked until a manual simulation reset is performed.

## Put the idea into practice

**Navigate to the Paper broker.** Click the **Paper trading** tab. The header displays "QUANTA MOCK BROKER". Review the live account telemetry: **CASH AVAILABLE** ($\$100{,}000.00$), **SHARES HELD** ($0$), **MARKED EQUITY** ($\$100{,}000.00$), and **RISK STATE** ("Normal").

**Submit a baseline order.** Configure the order ticket: Side **Buy**, **Order quantity** $10$, **Reference price ($)** $100$, **Available bar volume** $1000$, **Bid-ask spread (bps)** $5$, **Slippage (bps)** $3$, **Commission (bps)** $5$, and **Price age (seconds)** $0$. Click **Submit buy order**. In the **ORDER AUDIT LOG**, inspect the fill record: 10 shares filled at $\$100.06$ ($100.055$), commission $\$0.50$, cash debited $\$1{,}001.05$.

**Test the participation volume cap.** Enter **Order quantity** $150$ with volume still at $1000$. Click **Submit buy order**. Inspect the audit log: exactly 100 shares fill (10% of volume) and the status badge reads "partially filled".

**Deliberately trip pre-trade risk guards.** Test each protective barrier one at a time: 1. **Stale quote guard**: Set **Price age (seconds)** to 90 and submit. The audit log rejects the order: "Price data is stale." 2. **Wide spread guard**: Restore age to 0, set **Bid-ask spread (bps)** to 150, and submit. Rejection reads: "Spread exceeds the 100 bps guard." 3. **Zero liquidity guard**: Restore spread to 5, set **Available bar volume** to 0, and submit. Rejection reads: "No available liquidity." 4. **Insufficient funds guard**: Enter **Order quantity** $2000$. Rejection reads: "Insufficient cash for the simulated fill and fees."

**Trigger the drawdown circuit breaker.** Follow the walk-through: set volume to $100{,}000$ and buy 990 shares. Then change the reference price to $\$97.00$ and attempt to submit an order. Marked equity drops to $\$96{,}926$, tripping the breaker. The **RISK STATE** badge switches to a red "Halted" indicator, and the audit log records: "Drawdown circuit breaker triggered." Any subsequent submission displays: "Circuit breaker is halted. Reset the paper account after reviewing the event."

**Execute a formal account reset.** Click the reset icon in the header (aria "Reset paper account"), confirm the modal dialog by clicking **Reset simulation**, and verify that cash restores to $\$100{,}000$ with risk state returned to "Normal".

### Practise in the lab

Open the [Paper trading](/lab?tool=broker) and trigger every guard on purpose, one at a time (stale price, wide spread, no volume, insufficient cash and the drawdown breaker), and copy each rejection from the ORDER AUDIT LOG. The worksheet on this page is an interactive arithmetic verification aid: it remains strictly in cash and does not execute your trading strategy, so you should record all substantive findings and performance figures directly from the lab itself.

Because the lab's default market data is synthetically generated from stochastic models, a profitable run demonstrates that your execution logic and risk parameters function properly under those specific assumptions—it is never empirical evidence of a tradable real-market edge. Complete your session by documenting what you modified, the empirical outputs you observed, and the next falsification test you plan to run in [My notebook](/notebook).

ref_price = 100.0
spread_bps = 5.0
slippage_bps = 3.0
commission_bps = 5.0

fill_price = ref_price * (1.0 + (slippage_bps + spread_bps / 2.0) / 10000.0)
print("Executed buy fill price:", fill_price)
shares_ordered = 10
fee = shares_ordered * fill_price * (commission_bps / 10000.0)
print("Commission on 10 shares:", round(fee, 4))

bar_volume = 1000
cap = bar_volume * 0.10
print("Filled shares for 150 ordered against 1,000 volume:", min(150, cap))

# Circuit breaker calculation
large_shares = 990
initial_cash = 100000.0
trade_cost = large_shares * fill_price
trade_fee = trade_cost * (commission_bps / 10000.0)
remaining_cash = initial_cash - trade_cost - trade_fee
stressed_price = 97.0
marked_equity = remaining_cash + (large_shares * stressed_price)
equity_ratio = (marked_equity / initial_cash) * 100.0

print("Remaining cash after 990 shares:", round(remaining_cash, 2))
print("Marked equity at $97 price:", round(marked_equity, 2))

modules.title: The AMM simulator: pool prices, fees and impermanent loss
modules.subtitle: Model constant-product automated market makers ($x \cdot y = k$), calculate swap execution prices, fees, and price impact, and evaluate impermanent loss in full-range and concentrated liquidity positions.
modules.objective: Model constant-product automated market makers ($x \cdot y = k$), calculate swap execution prices, fees, and price impact, and evaluate impermanent loss in full-range and concentrated liquidity positions.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes studying automated market maker bonding curves and constant-product mathematics, 10 minutes working through swap output and impermanent loss equations, and 12 minutes testing liquidity parameters in the AMM simulator; all pool interactions model decentralized protocols.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Decentralized finance (DeFi) protocols depart from traditional limit order books by deploying **Automated Market Makers (AMMs)**. Governed by deterministic smart contracts, Constant Function Market Makers (CFMMs) hold token reserves and price swaps dynamically along mathematical bonding curves rather than matching bids and offers.

The **AMM simulator** models the foundational constant-product invariant popularized by Uniswap:

$$
x \cdot y = k
$$

 where $x$ represents the reserve of Token A (e.g., ETH), $y$ represents the reserve of Token B (e.g., USDC), and $k$ is the invariant product.

The instantaneous marginal **Spot Price** is simply the reserve ratio:

$$
P_{\text{spot}} = \frac{y}{x}
$$

However, an incoming trade alters the reserve balances, moving the price along the hyperbolic curve. When a trader deposits $\Delta x$ tokens to extract $\Delta y$ tokens subject to a liquidity provider fee $\varphi$ (default $0.3\% = 0.003$), the effective token input is $\Delta x (1 - \varphi)$. The invariant requires $(x + \Delta x(1 - \varphi))(y - \Delta y) = k = xy$. Solving for the swap output $\Delta y$:

$$
\Delta y = \frac{y \cdot \Delta x (1 - \varphi)}{x + \Delta x (1 - \varphi)}
$$

 The **Effective Execution Price** obtained by the trader is $P_{\text{exec}} = \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$, and the **Price Impact** (including the fee) is:

$$
\text{Price Impact} = 1 - \frac{P_{\text{exec}}}{P_{\text{spot}}}
$$

For liquidity providers (LPs), depositing assets exposes capital to **Impermanent Loss (IL)**. When the broader market price shifts, arbitrageurs trade against the pool until its internal spot price matches external market quotes. This arbitrage drains the appreciating asset from the pool, leaving LPs with a portfolio worth less than if they had simply held the original tokens in a private wallet. For a full-range liquidity position, impermanent loss is a pure function of the price ratio $r = P_{\text{new}} / P_{\text{initial}}$:

$$
\text{IL}(r) = \frac{2\sqrt{r}}{1 + r} - 1
$$

**Concentrated Liquidity** (Uniswap v3 style) allows LPs to bound their capital within an active price range $[p_a, p_b]$. While this concentration amplifies fee income per dollar of capital, it equally amplifies impermanent loss: the position rebalances more aggressively, and if price breaches either bound, the position converts entirely into the depreciating asset and stops earning fees. (Note: the simulator's comparative analysis excludes accumulated fee earnings and gas costs).

## A worked example

To quantify AMM mechanics, examine the default liquidity pool configuration: Reserves $x = 10\text{ ETH}$ and $y = 20{,}000\text{ USDC}$. The marginal spot price is:

$$
P_{\text{spot}} = \frac{20{,}000\text{ USDC}}{10\text{ ETH}} = 2{,}000\text{ USDC per ETH}
$$

 The swap fee is $\varphi = 0.003$ ($0.3\%$).

Evaluate a swap of $\Delta x = 1\text{ ETH}$ for USDC: The net token input after the $0.3\%$ fee is $\Delta x(1 - \varphi) = 1.0 \times 0.997 = 0.997\text{ ETH}$. Applying the constant-product swap formula:

$$
\Delta y = \frac{20{,}000 \times 0.997}{10 + 0.997} = \frac{19{,}940}{10.997} \approx 1{,}813.2218\text{ USDC}
$$

 The trader deposits $1\text{ ETH}$ and receives approximately $1{,}813.22\text{ USDC}$. The effective execution price is:

$$
P_{\text{exec}} = \frac{1{,}813.2218}{1.0} \approx \$1{,}813.22\text{ per ETH}
$$

 The total price impact incurred is:

$$
\text{Price Impact} = 1 - \frac{\$1{,}813.22}{\$2{,}000.00} = 1 - 0.90661 = 0.09339 \approx 9.34\%
$$

 The fee retained by the pool is $0.003\text{ ETH} \times 2{,}000 = \$6.00$ in notional value.

Now compare swap sizes to observe non-linear impact scaling: - **Swap 0.1 ETH**: $\Delta y \approx 197.43\text{ USDC} \implies P_{\text{exec}} \approx \$1{,}974.32 \implies \text{Impact} \approx 1.28\%$ - **Swap 1.0 ETH**: $\Delta y \approx 1{,}813.22\text{ USDC} \implies P_{\text{exec}} \approx \$1{,}813.22 \implies \text{Impact} \approx 9.34\%$ - **Swap 5.0 ETH**: $\Delta y \approx 6{,}653.32\text{ USDC} \implies P_{\text{exec}} \approx \$1{,}330.66 \implies \text{Impact} \approx 33.47\%$ Because the bonding curve steepens as reserves diminish, price impact grows exponentially rather than linearly with order size.

Next, analyze **Impermanent Loss**: Suppose external market prices double ($r = 2.0$, ETH reaches $\$4{,}000$). Full-range impermanent loss is:

$$
\text{IL}(2.0) = \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{1 + 2} - 1 = \frac{2 \times 1.41421}{3} - 1 = \frac{2.82843}{3} - 1 \approx -0.05719 \approx -5.72\%
$$

 The LP's pool holdings are worth $5.72\%$ less than holding the original 10 ETH and 20,000 USDC.

Now examine a **Concentrated Liquidity Position** bounded between $0.5\times$ and $2.0\times$ ($[1{,}000, 4{,}000]\text{ USDC}$): At $r = 2.0$, the concentrated position incurs an impermanent loss of approximately $-19.53\%$ relative to holding—more than three times the divergence loss of full-range liquidity! Furthermore, at $2.0\times$, the position reaches the upper bound and converts 100% into USDC, ceasing to generate swap fees.

## Put the idea into practice

**Navigate to the AMM simulator.** Click the **AMM simulator** tab. The header reads "CONSTANT-PRODUCT POOL: Explore an ETH / USDC pool with x · y = k." Inspect the baseline inputs: **ETH reserves** ($10$), **USDC reserves** ($20000$), **ETH to swap** ($1$), and **Swap fee (decimal)** ($0.003$).

**Audit swap output and execution price.** Review the calculated quote metrics: - **Estimated swap output**: $\approx 1,813.22\text{ USDC}$ - **Execution price**: $\approx \$1,813.22\text{ per ETH}$ - **Price impact including fee**: $\approx 9.34\%$ - **Fee retained by pool**: $0.003\text{ ETH}$ ($\approx \$6.00$)

**Analyze non-linear price impact.** Change **ETH to swap** to $0.1$. Observe output of $197.43\text{ USDC}$ and price impact of $1.28\%$. Now enter $5\text{ ETH}$: output reaches $6,653.32\text{ USDC}$ with a massive price impact of $33.47\%$. Notice how large trades suffer severe slippage relative to pool depth.

**Evaluate impermanent loss across price moves.** Locate the **LIQUIDITY PROVIDER ANALYSIS** section. Drag **Future price / initial price** from $1.00\times$ up to $2.00\times$. Inspect the performance readouts: - **Full-range impermanent loss**: $-5.72\%$ - **Concentrated position vs. holding**: $-19.53\%$ - **Position status**: "At range upper bound" Now drag the price ratio to $0.50\times$: confirm that full-range loss is again $-5.72\%$, while the concentrated position hits the lower bound. Drag the price ratio to $4.00\times$: full-range loss reaches $-20.00\%$.

**Manipulate concentrated liquidity boundaries.** Under **Concentrated liquidity range**, adjust **Lower price ratio** and **Upper price ratio**. Narrow the range: observe how divergence loss accelerates. Now attempt to set the lower ratio to $1.2\times$: the tool displays an alert: "The starting price must lie within the liquidity range."

**Read the impermanent loss curve.** Inspect the interactive chart under **LIQUIDITY PROVIDER ANALYSIS**: trace the curve from $0.1\times$ to $5.0\times$, observing that impermanent loss is zero strictly when the price ratio equals $1.0\times$.

### Practise in the lab

Open the [AMM simulator](/lab?tool=amm) and quote swaps of 0.1, 1 and 5 ETH, record each execution price and impact, then move the price slider from 0.5× to 4× and note where the concentrated position leaves its range. The worksheet on this page is an interactive arithmetic verification aid: it remains strictly in cash and does not execute your trading strategy, so you should record all substantive findings and performance figures directly from the lab itself.

Because the lab's default market data is synthetically generated from stochastic models, a profitable run demonstrates that your execution logic and risk parameters function properly under those specific assumptions—it is never empirical evidence of a tradable real-market edge. Complete your session by documenting what you modified, the empirical outputs you observed, and the next falsification test you plan to run in [My notebook](/notebook).

from math import sqrt

eth_reserves = 10.0
usdc_reserves = 20000.0
fee = 0.003
spot_price = usdc_reserves / eth_reserves
print("Initial pool spot price:", round(spot_price, 2), "USDC/ETH")

for swap_eth in [0.1, 1.0, 5.0]:
    effective_input = swap_eth * (1.0 - fee)
    out_usdc = (usdc_reserves * effective_input) / (eth_reserves + effective_input)
    exec_price = out_usdc / swap_eth
    impact = (1.0 - exec_price / spot_price) * 100.0
    print("Swap", swap_eth, "ETH -> Output:", round(out_usdc, 2), "USDC | Exec Price:", round(exec_price, 2), "| Impact:", round(impact, 2), "%")

for r in [0.5, 2.0, 4.0]:
    il_full = (2.0 * sqrt(r) / (1.0 + r) - 1.0) * 100.0
    print("Price ratio", r, "x -> Full-range impermanent loss:", round(il_full, 2), "%")

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the model or strategy's performance.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

Full-range impermanent loss reaches -5.72% at both 0.5x and 2.0x price ratios, and -20.00% at 4.0x. modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Open, verifiable computational science requires that any reported finding can be perfectly reproduced by an independent researcher. In quantitative trading, claiming a Sharpe ratio without preserving the exact strategy source code, random seed, execution costs, and data-generating parameters is scientifically void. The Strategy lab implements an auditable research architecture built on **Saved experiments**, **My notebook**, and **Historical data imports**.

A **Saved experiment** archives a lightweight, self-contained parameter manifest. Rather than storing millions of raw price ticks, equity curves, or trade logs, the lab saves the exact input configuration dictionary: - Full Python strategy code. - Data source and stochastic process specification. - Named stress scenario selection. - Annual drift and volatility settings. - Trading horizon and pseudorandom seed. - Indicator lookback parameters (e.g., SMA window). - Initial portfolio equity. - Commission (bps) and slippage (bps) friction. - Performance metrics at the time of archival (if fresh).

Because the simulation engine is fully deterministic, reopening an experiment regenerates the exact tick series, equity curves, and trade blotters on demand from the random seed. Saving from the interactive sandbox creates a new versioned entry in browser local storage (synced to cloud storage when logged in). Only experiments reopened directly from **Saved experiments** allow in-place updating.

Researchers must understand two crucial operational behaviors: 1. **Tab Navigation Reset**: Clicking between lab tabs clears the active experiment ID from the URL. Returning to the Market sandbox returns you to the unlinked "free lab" sandbox. Always reopen experiments from the **Saved experiments** repository. 2. **Draft Precedence**: If you edit strategy code without saving, the uncommitted code is preserved as an active draft in local storage. When reopening the experiment, this draft takes precedence. To discard modifications and restore the archived code, click the **Restore lesson code** icon.

Finally, the engine supports **Historical data imports**. When a historical CSV dataset is loaded, the backtest slices the earliest $H \times 252$ trading rows from the file, maintaining point-in-time causality by advancing forward from past data rather than sampling backwards from the present.

## A worked example

To analyze historical data slicing, consider an imported dataset comprising 10 years of daily equity data ($N_{\text{rows}} = 2{,}520\text{ bars}$). If the researcher configures a 3-year trading horizon ($H = 3$), the backtest requires:

$$
\text{Rows Processed} = 252 \times H = 252 \times 3 = 756\text{ bars}
$$

 The engine reads rows $1$ through $756$—representing the oldest three chronological years in the historical dataset. The remaining $2{,}520 - 756 = 1{,}764\text{ rows}$ (7 years of recent price history) are left untouched. To backtest a more recent market period, the imported file must be formatted to start on the desired start date.

Now examine the lightweight storage footprint of `quanta-experiment.json`. A complete experiment record consumes less than $4\text{ KB}$ of JSON metadata: - Complete Python source code string. - 11 configuration fields: data type, process, scenario, drift ($0.08$), volatility ($0.20$), horizon ($3$), seed ($42$), capital ($\$100{,}000$), commission ($5$), slippage ($3$), and SMA window ($50$). - Verified output metrics: CAGR ($-0.0850$), Sharpe ($-0.9200$), Max Drawdown ($-0.2707$), Win Rate ($0.1724$), and Total Trades ($59$).

When another researcher downloads this JSON artifact, they do not need to download multi-gigabyte tick databases. By running the identical script against seed 42 with default costs, their machine deterministically recreates the exact $\$76{,}598.46$ equity curve and all 59 trade executions, validating computational reproducibility.

## Put the idea into practice

**Save an experiment from the sandbox.** In the **Market sandbox**, execute the baseline trend rule on seed 42. In the footer toolbar, click **Save**. In the "Keep this experiment" modal dialog, enter an **Experiment name** (e.g., "Baseline Trend SMA-50 Seed 42") and click **Save experiment**. Then click the **Export experiment** icon to download `quanta-experiment.json`.

**Reopen and verify the experiment.** In the main navigation sidebar, click **Saved experiments**. In the experiment repository, locate your newly saved experiment card. Inspect the metadata tags: "Synthetic data", "Geometric Brownian motion", "Seed 42", CAGR $-8.5\%$, and Max Drawdown $-27.1\%$. Click the experiment title: the Market sandbox opens with the experiment name prominently displayed in the header. Click **Run experiment** and confirm that all metrics match the card values perfectly.

**Observe draft precedence.** While viewing the opened experiment, modify `strategy.py` by inserting a comment: `# Draft modification`. Refresh the browser: observe that your edited code remains in the editor. Now click the **Restore lesson code** icon above the editor: the editor immediately resets back to the saved, unedited experiment code.

**Maintain research notes in My notebook.** Click **My notebook** in the sidebar. Click **New note**, enter a title ("Hypothesis 1: Seed 42 Baseline"), type your experimental observations, and click **Save note**. Next, return to this lesson and locate the assignment section: click the **Write in notebook** button. A prefilled note opens automatically, populated with the assignment prompt. Complete the note and save it. Finally, click **Export notebook** to download your full research journal as `quanta-notebook.md`.

**Inspect historical data configuration.** In the sandbox **Parameters** tab, open the **DATA SOURCE** dropdown and select **Historical data**. Read the informational notice explaining how historical CSV files are imported and sliced chronologically.

### Practise in the lab

Open the [Market sandbox](/lab?tool=market) and save two experiments that differ only by seed, export both JSON files, and confirm that reopening each from Saved experiments reproduces its own metrics. The worksheet on this page is an interactive arithmetic verification aid: it remains strictly in cash and does not execute your trading strategy, so you should record all substantive findings and performance figures directly from the lab itself.

Because the lab's default market data is synthetically generated from stochastic models, a profitable run demonstrates that your execution logic and risk parameters function properly under those specific assumptions—it is never empirical evidence of a tradable real-market edge. Complete your session by documenting what you modified, the empirical outputs you observed, and the next falsification test you plan to run in [My notebook](/notebook).

modules.title: Capstone: a complete research loop from hypothesis to saved evidence
modules.subtitle: Execute the complete 12-stage Quanta Research Loop from pre-registered hypothesis to archived evidence, separating development seeds from reserved test seeds to produce an honest, peer-reviewable study.
modules.objective: Execute the complete 12-stage Quanta Research Loop from pre-registered hypothesis to archived evidence, separating development seeds from reserved test seeds to produce an honest, peer-reviewable study.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 5 minutes reviewing research loop governance, 5 minutes pre-registering hypotheses and seed splits, and 20 minutes executing, archiving, and exporting the capstone project in the Market sandbox; the capstone evaluates quantitative methodology rather than market forecasting.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

The culmination of the Strategy lab workshop is executing an end-to-end scientific research project. The difference between an amateur backtester and an institutional quantitative researcher lies not in the complexity of their code, but in the integrity of their experimental methodology. Amateurs test dozens of variations, discard losing runs, and report the best backtest curve as if it were foreseen. Quantitative scientists formulate falsifiable hypotheses, pre-register rejection thresholds, separate development data from out-of-sample test data, and account for every trial executed.

The capstone synthesizes the **12-Step Quanta Research Loop**: 1. **Pre-registered Hypothesis**: State an unambiguous, testable proposition prior to running simulations. 2. **Target Metric**: Select primary performance indicators (e.g., Maximum Drawdown, CAGR, Sharpe ratio). 3. **Hurdle Benchmark**: Establish an explicit opportunity cost benchmark (e.g., passive Buy & Hold). 4. **Falsification Threshold**: Pre-register quantitative criteria that would force rejection of the hypothesis. 5. **Seed Partitioning**: Partition random seeds into in-sample development seeds ($42\text{--}46$) and untouched out-of-sample reserved test seeds ($47\text{--}51$). 6. **Parameter Discipline**: Fix market environment and transaction friction parameters ($5\text{ bps}$ commission, $3\text{ bps}$ slippage). 7. **Iterative Development**: Test indicator variations strictly across development seeds. 8. **Trial Ledger Archival**: Save all development runs in **Saved experiments**, documenting every iteration. 9. **Single Confirmation Run**: Execute the selected strategy model exactly once across the reserved test seeds. 10. **Objective Decision**: Evaluate the pre-registered rejection threshold strictly against reserved-seed results. 11. **Artifact Export**: Export research artifacts (`quanta-notebook.md` and experiment JSON manifests). 12. **Boundary Disclosures**: Transparently report model limitations (synthetic data, frictionless liquidity, long-only constraints).

The out-of-sample discipline enforced by seed partitioning is paramount: parameters tuned on development seeds are optimistic by construction. The reserved seeds have played no role in parameter selection, providing an unbiased assessment of strategy generalization.

## A worked example

To anchor this capstone, execute the following pre-registered research plan:

**Hypothesis**: Under the "Liquidity crisis · 2008-inspired" scenario (Heston stochastic volatility, annual decline of $-18\%$, annual volatility of $55\%$), augmenting the baseline 50-day trend rule with a 200-day moving average regime filter (`(close > sma_50) & (sma_50 > sma_200)`) produces a shallower maximum drawdown than the Buy & Hold benchmark on at least 4 out of 5 reserved test seeds.

**Experimental Ledger**: - You evaluate two strategy variants across 5 development seeds (seeds 42, 43, 44, 45, and 46): Variant A: 50-day trend filter alone ($5\text{ runs}$). Variant B: 50-day trend filter with 200-day regime confirmation ($5\text{ runs}$). Development trials: $2 \times 5 = 10\text{ runs}$. - You select Variant B based on superior drawdown mitigation in development. - You test Variant B exactly once across the 5 reserved test seeds (seeds 47, 48, 49, 50, and 51): Reserved trials: $5\text{ runs}$. - Total experimental trials reported:

$$
N_{\text{trials}} = V \times S_{\text{dev}} + S_{\text{test}} = (2 \times 5) + 5 = 15\text{ trials}
$$

The final report catalogs all 15 trials, applies the pre-registered decision rule strictly to the reserved seeds, and exports the complete audit trail. The accompanying Python worksheet verifies completion of the 12-point research protocol, printing: `"Lab research loop steps: 12 of 12"` and confirming that the verification code remains strictly in cash.

## Put the idea into practice

**Step 1: Document pre-registered hypothesis in My notebook.** Open **My notebook** and create a new note titled "Capstone Research Charter". Record your formal hypothesis, target metric (Maximum Drawdown), benchmark (Buy & Hold), rejection threshold (shallower drawdown on fewer than 4 of 5 reserved seeds), development seeds (42–46), and reserved seeds (47–51).

**Step 2: Configure development environment.** In the **Market sandbox**, open **Parameters** and select **Liquidity crisis · 2008-inspired** from the **SCENARIO** dropdown. Confirm default costs ($5\text{ bps}$ commission, $3\text{ bps}$ slippage).

**Step 3: Execute development sweeps.** - Run Variant A (`data["close"] > data["sma_50"]`) across seeds 42, 43, 44, 45, and 46. Save each run in **Saved experiments** with title "Cap-Dev-A-Seed[X]". - Run Variant B (`(data["close"] > data["sma_50"]) & (data["sma_50"] > data["sma_200"])`) across the same five seeds. Save each run as "Cap-Dev-B-Seed[X]". - Compare development results: Variant B demonstrates superior drawdown mitigation during severe volatility spikes.

**Step 4: Execute the single out-of-sample confirmation test.** Without altering code or scenario parameters, evaluate Variant B across reserved seeds 47, 48, 49, 50, and 51. Save each test run as "Cap-Test-B-Seed[X]".

**Step 5: Apply the objective decision rule.** Tabulate maximum drawdown for Variant B versus Buy & Hold across seeds 47–51. If Variant B achieves a shallower drawdown on 4 or more seeds, the hypothesis is confirmed; otherwise, it is rejected. Document the final verdict in your notebook.

**Step 6: Export audit trail.** In **Saved experiments**, confirm that all 15 trials are archived with appropriate seed tags. Export the JSON manifests for the five confirmation tests. In **My notebook**, click **Export notebook** to download `quanta-notebook.md`.

**Step 7: Verify completion via worksheet.** Open the lesson worksheet under **Try the lesson template**. Click **Run in sandbox** followed by **Run experiment**. The **Console** prints the verification checklist: "Trials to report: 15" "Lab research loop steps: 12 of 12".

### Practise in the lab

Open the [Market sandbox](/lab?tool=market) and run your capstone loop: write the hypothesis and criterion first, develop on five seeds, test on five reserved seeds, save every run and export your notebook. The worksheet on this page is an interactive arithmetic verification aid: it remains strictly in cash and does not execute your trading strategy, so you should record all substantive findings and performance figures directly from the lab itself.

Because the lab's default market data is synthetically generated from stochastic models, a profitable run demonstrates that your execution logic and risk parameters function properly under those specific assumptions—it is never empirical evidence of a tradable real-market edge. Complete your session by documenting what you modified, the empirical outputs you observed, and the next falsification test you plan to run in [My notebook](/notebook).

assignment.prompt: Execute a complete scientific research loop in the Strategy lab: document your hypothesis and falsification threshold in My notebook prior to execution, develop across seeds 42–46, test once across reserved seeds 47–51, archive all 15 trials, and export your research trail. State your final decision and model limitations.
assignment.solution: A complete capstone presents an auditable research journal containing the pre-registered hypothesis and rejection threshold timestamped prior to simulation. The trial ledger documents all 10 development runs across seeds 42-46 alongside the 5 confirmation runs on reserved seeds 47-51. Under the 2008 liquidity crisis scenario, the dual-moving-average trend filter (Variant B) achieved a shallower maximum drawdown than buy-and-hold across 5 of the 5 reserved seeds (averaging ~ -38.2% vs -64.1%), successfully confirming the pre-registered hypothesis. The report exports the full notebook markdown and JSON manifests, transparently disclosing critical limitations: the strategy was evaluated on synthetic stochastic paths, assumes fixed slippage and infinite liquidity, trades long-or-cash only, and does not establish an exploitable edge in live financial markets.
