modules.title: A selection rule is a hypothesis, not a verdict
modules.subtitle: Apply Graham's combined price filter honestly, and state what passing or failing it does and does not establish.
modules.objective: Apply Graham's combined price filter honestly, and state what passing or failing it does and does not establish.
modules.reading: Book companion theme: Stock selection for the defensive investor. 30-minute session: 10 minutes of reading, 8 minutes of calculations, and 12 minutes of notebook work. Modern product, fraud and planning examples are course extensions, not claims about Graham's historical recommendations.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Graham gave the defensive investor a short list of tests for a common stock: adequate size, a strong financial condition, a record of earnings and of dividends over many years, some earnings growth, and a moderate price against both earnings and assets. The last two are the arithmetic ones, and he set them as a price-to-earnings ratio under about 15 and a price-to-book ratio under about 1.5.

He then made the pair tradeable against each other. The two limits multiply to 15 × 1.5 = 22.5, and he offered that product as a rule of thumb: a share at 9 times earnings and 2.5 times book has a product of 22.5 and passes, as does one at 18 times earnings and 1.25 times book. The product is the test, not either number alone.

Two cautions belong with it. First, the closed form sometimes sold as 'the Graham number', the square root of 22.5 × EPS × book value per share, is a later derivation from these limits rather than a formula Graham put forward; treat it as arithmetic someone else arranged, not as his recommendation. Second, and much more important, a screen is a hypothesis generator. Passing the filter says the price is modest relative to two accounting numbers. It says nothing about whether those numbers are durable, whether the book value is real, or whether the business is shrinking fast enough to make a low multiple generous rather than cheap.

This is the course's recurring point in a new place. A rule that returns a list has not done the analysis; it has told you where to start. The work of deciding whether reported earnings recur and whether assets are worth their carrying value is Security Analysis — see lessons 1.6 and 11.13 on reading the business behind the headline number — and no filter substitutes for it.

$$
\frac{P}{E}\times\frac{P}{B}\le 22.5 \iff P \le \sqrt{22.5\,\times\,\mathrm{EPS}\times\mathrm{BVPS}}
$$

## A worked example

Meridian Works trades at 42.00. Its trailing earnings are 3.20 a share and its book value is 24.00 a share.

Work the filter:

1. Price to earnings: 42.00 / 3.20 = 13.12, which is under 15 and passes on its own.
2. Price to book: 42.00 / 24.00 = 1.75, which is above 1.5 and fails on its own.
3. The product: 13.12 × 1.75 = 22.97.

The product is above 22.5, so Meridian fails the combined test — but only just, and the single-ratio readings would have given you two opposite answers. This is exactly why the product exists: a low enough multiple of earnings is allowed to buy back some excess over book.

What price would pass? The product rule says P² / (EPS × BVPS) ≤ 22.5, so the ceiling is the square root of 22.5 × 3.20 × 24.00, which is 41.57. At 41.50 the product is 22.43 and it passes; at 42.00 it does not. The whole disagreement is 43 cents, about 1% of the price.

That margin should tell you what the filter is worth. A 1% price move flips the verdict, and so would a small revision to either accounting input — one impairment to book value, or one quarter of earnings that turns out not to recur. Lesson 11.13 asked you to separate recurring from reported earnings before using any multiple. If Meridian's 3.20 includes a one-time gain of 0.40, the recurring figure is 2.80, the recurring P/E is 15.0, and the product becomes 26.25: a clear failure that the headline numbers hid.

## Put the idea into practice

Use the filter as the first step of a process that does not end there:
1. Compute the product, not the ratios. Record P/E, P/B and their product. A pass or fail on one ratio alone is not the test.
2. Record the margin. Write how far the product sits from 22.5 in percentage terms. A name that passes by 1% has not told you much; one that passes at 12 has told you more.
3. Re-run it on recurring earnings. Strip the non-recurring items identified in lesson 11.13 and compute the product again. Record both results side by side; the gap between them is the quality of the screen's input.
4. Treat the output as a reading list. Everything that survives is a candidate for analysis, not a purchase. Write the three questions you would need answered before buying, before you look at the price again.
5. Keep the names that failed. A list of rejects with the reason recorded is how you later discover the filter was wrong, which a list of only your purchases can never show.

### Build your careful-investor plan

Write the calculation, decision rule and one reason the conclusion might be wrong in your notebook. Add the evidence to your My notebook page. Read the named theme in your own copy of The Intelligent Investor; these explanations and fictional cases are original Quanta material, not reproduced chapters or publisher exercises. The worksheet calculates the case and keeps the price sandbox in cash. Its chart is not an investment recommendation or a test of Graham's approach.

assignment.solution: At 42.00 the ratios are 13.12 and 1.75, whose product is 22.97, so Meridian fails the combined rule despite passing on earnings alone. The highest passing price is the square root of 22.5 × 3.20 × 24.00 = 41.57, so the verdict turns on 43 cents, about 1% of the quote. On recurring earnings of 2.80 the multiple rises to 15.00 and the product to 26.25, a clear failure that the reported figure concealed. The filter has established that the price is not modest against these two accounting numbers once the one-time gain is removed. It has established nothing about whether the remaining earnings are durable, whether the 24.00 of book value would survive an impairment review, or whether the business is contracting; those are questions for analysis, and a screen that returns a name has only told you where to begin.

modules.title: Where bargains come from, and the arithmetic of looking for them
modules.subtitle: Name the conditions that let a mispricing persist, and compute honestly what a search for one costs in hours per find.
modules.objective: Name the conditions that let a mispricing persist, and compute honestly what a search for one costs in hours per find.
modules.reading: Book companion theme: The enterprising investor and bargain issues. 30-minute session: 10 minutes of reading, 8 minutes of calculations, and 12 minutes of notebook work. Modern product, fraud and planning examples are course extensions, not claims about Graham's historical recommendations.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Lesson 11.3 drew the line between the defensive and enterprising investor as a commitment of time and effort rather than a tolerance for risk. This lesson asks the question that commitment implies: if a security really is mispriced, why has nobody else taken it?

A mispricing that survives needs a reason to survive. Graham's bargain issues were not simply cheap; they were cheap for a structural reason that kept better-resourced buyers away. Three such reasons recur:

1. Neglect. The company is too small, too illiquid, or too obscure for an institution to buy a meaningful position without moving the price. The constraint is the buyer's size, not the analyst's insight.
2. Forced selling. An index deletion, a fund liquidation, a covenant breach or a spin-off distributes shares to holders who must sell for reasons unrelated to value. The seller's deadline, not their opinion, sets the price.
3. Complexity or ugliness. A holding company, a litigation overhang, a restatement, a business that is embarrassing to own. The work to understand it is real, and most people will not do it.

Notice what is absent from that list: 'the market has not noticed'. A thesis whose only support is that a widely-followed, liquid share is obviously too cheap has no mechanism, and a mispricing without a mechanism is usually an error in your own analysis. Requiring yourself to name the reason is the cheapest filter you will ever apply.

The second half of this lesson is arithmetic, and it is unwelcome. Enterprising investing is a search with a base rate, and the base rate decides whether the search is worth running at all. Most people who choose the enterprising route never compute it.

$$
\text{hours per find} = \frac{n \times h}{n \times p} = \frac{h}{p}
$$

## A worked example

Suppose you screen 200 companies a year and judge, generously, that 6% of them are genuinely mispriced. That is 12 real opportunities inside the list — but you do not know which 12, and you cannot analyse 200 companies properly.

Say a serious analysis takes 8 hours: reading several years of filings, checking the balance sheet, understanding the business, and writing the thesis down. At that rate you can study perhaps 20 names a year alongside other work.

Now the expected finds. If the 20 you choose are no better than random draws from the list, the expected number of real opportunities among them is 20 × 0.06 = 1.2. The hours are 20 × 8 = 160. That is roughly 133 hours per genuine find, before you have decided whether the one you found is large enough to matter to your portfolio, and before considering that you may be wrong about which of the 20 was the real one.

This is not an argument against the enterprising route. It is the honest budget for it, and it clarifies two things. First, the only lever with real leverage is the quality of the screen: raising the hit rate from 6% to 12% halves the hours per find, where working faster does not. Second, if 160 hours a year is not available to you, the arithmetic has answered the question lesson 11.3 posed, and the defensive route is the correct choice rather than the lesser one. Sharpe's arithmetic of active management, cited in 11.3, says the average active dollar must underperform after costs; your own time is one of those costs, and this is how you price it.

## Put the idea into practice

Before committing to the enterprising route, write the budget down:
1. Name the mechanism for every candidate. In one sentence: why is this cheap, and what stops a larger buyer from taking it? If the sentence is 'the market has not noticed', discard the candidate.
2. Record your screen's hit rate. Of the names you studied last year, how many turned out to be genuinely mispriced rather than cheap for cause? That ratio is the only input you can improve.
3. Compute hours per find. Multiply names studied by hours each, then divide by names studied times the hit rate. Write the number in your notebook as a plain figure.
4. Compare it against the defensive alternative. The comparison is not 'enterprising returns versus defensive returns'. It is the excess return you expect, after costs, against the hours it consumes and the risk you were wrong.
5. Review the rejects annually. Of the names you passed over, how many would have worked? A hit rate computed only from the ones you bought is not a hit rate.

### Build your careful-investor plan

Write the calculation, decision rule and one reason the conclusion might be wrong in your notebook. Add the evidence to your My notebook page. Read the named theme in your own copy of The Intelligent Investor; these explanations and fictional cases are original Quanta material, not reproduced chapters or publisher exercises. The worksheet calculates the case and keeps the price sandbox in cash. Its chart is not an investment recommendation or a test of Graham's approach.

hit_rate = 0.06
studied = 20
hours_each = 8

print("Real opportunities in the screen:", int(screened * hit_rate))
print("Expected real finds among those studied:", round(studied * hit_rate, 1))
print("Hours spent:", studied * hours_each)
print("Hours per genuine find:", round(hours_each / hit_rate, 0))

better = 0.12
print("At a 12 percent hit rate, hours per find:", round(hours_each / better, 0))
print("Hours saved by doubling the hit rate:", round(hours_each / hit_rate - hours_each / better, 0))

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the model or strategy's performance.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: Compute the expected number of genuine finds and the hours per find for a search of 20 names a year at 8 hours each and a 6% hit rate. Then recompute at a 12% hit rate, and write which of the two levers — a better screen or more hours — changes the answer, and why.
assignment.solution: Twenty names at a 6% hit rate give an expected 1.2 genuine finds for 160 hours, which is 8 / 0.06 = 133 hours per find. Doubling the hit rate to 12% halves it to 67 hours per find, saving 67 hours for each one. The arithmetic shows that the hours-per-find figure depends only on the hours each analysis takes divided by the hit rate, so the number of names studied cancels out entirely: studying more names finds more opportunities but does not make any one of them cheaper to find. The only lever with leverage is the screen's quality, because it is the denominator. This is also why the mechanism question matters so much — requiring a named reason why a mispricing persists is the cheapest available way to raise the hit rate, and it costs one sentence per candidate rather than eight hours.

modules.title: What a shareholder is owed: dividends, buybacks and management
modules.subtitle: Evaluate a distribution decision as an owner, and compute who gains and who loses when a company repurchases shares at a given price.
modules.objective: Evaluate a distribution decision as an owner, and compute who gains and who loses when a company repurchases shares at a given price.
modules.reading: Book companion theme: Shareholders and managements, and dividend policy. 30-minute session: 10 minutes of reading, 8 minutes of calculations, and 12 minutes of notebook work. Modern product, fraud and planning examples are course extensions, not claims about Graham's historical recommendations.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Graham's complaint about shareholders was that they behaved like ticket-holders rather than owners: passive about management quality, indifferent to how retained earnings were used, and attentive only to the quoted price. A share is a claim on a business, and the most consequential decision that business makes on your behalf is what to do with the cash it earns.

There are four things a company can do with a dollar of earnings, and they are not equivalent:

1. Reinvest it in the business, which is right only if the business earns more on that dollar than you could elsewhere.
2. Pay down debt, which transfers value from equity holders to creditors unless the leverage was genuinely threatening.
3. Pay it out as a dividend, which hands you the dollar and lets you decide.
4. Repurchase shares, which is the subtle one, because whether it helps you depends entirely on the price paid.

A buyback is a purchase of your own company made with your money. Like any purchase it creates value if the price is below what the asset is worth and destroys value if it is above. This is the part that announcements never say. A repurchase at a discount to intrinsic value transfers wealth from the selling shareholders to those who remain; a repurchase above intrinsic value transfers it the other way, from the holders who stay to the ones who leave. Management is on both sides of that trade and is usually buying when the price is high, because that is when cash is plentiful and confidence is greatest.

The per-share arithmetic is why this is so easy to hide. A buyback mechanically raises earnings per share by shrinking the denominator, whatever price was paid. An EPS that rose because shares were retired is not the same event as an EPS that rose because the business earned more, and a management rewarded on EPS has a reason not to distinguish them. Lesson 11.14 asked you to read incentives; this is where that reading pays.

$$
V_{\text{after}} = \frac{V - C}{N - C/P},\qquad \text{transfer per share} = V_{\text{per share}} - V_{\text{after}}
$$

## A worked example

Harrow Industries has 1,000 shares outstanding. Your own appraisal, done before you looked at the quote, puts the business at 20.00 a share, so 20,000 in total. The shares trade at 26.00. Management announces a 5,200 repurchase and the press release calls it a vote of confidence.

Work out what it does to you as a holder who is not selling.

1. Shares bought: 5,200 / 26.00 = 200 shares.
2. Shares remaining: 1,000 − 200 = 800.
3. Intrinsic value before: 1,000 × 20.00 = 20,000.
4. Intrinsic value after: 20,000 − 5,200 = 14,800, because 5,200 of cash left the business.
5. Value per remaining share: 14,800 / 800 = 18.50.

You began holding something worth 20.00 a share and now hold something worth 18.50. The company spent 5,200 to buy 200 shares worth 4,000, and the 1,200 difference came out of the holders who stayed and went to the holders who sold. Per remaining share that is a transfer of 1.50.

Meanwhile the reported figures improve. If Harrow earns 2,000 a year, earnings per share rise from 2.00 to 2,000 / 800 = 2.50, a 25% increase, with no change whatever in the business. A dividend of 5,200, by contrast, would have handed each holder 5.20 a share and left the per-share value of what remains at 14,800 / 1,000 = 14.80 — the same total of 20.00 between cash in hand and shares held, with nothing transferred between holders.

The test, then, is not whether a buyback happened. It is the price it happened at, measured against an appraisal you made first.

## Put the idea into practice

Judge distributions as an owner, with the appraisal written down before the announcement:
1. Appraise first, then read the announcement. A value estimate formed after reading a press release is not independent of it. Lesson 11.15 on decision journals applies directly: write the number and the date.
2. For a buyback, compute the transfer. Subtract the cash spent from your appraisal of the whole business, divide by the shares that remain, and compare with your appraisal per share before. Record the difference as a figure, positive or negative.
3. Separate mechanical EPS from earned EPS. Ask what earnings per share would have been with the old share count. If the entire improvement came from the denominator, say so in your notes.
4. Read the incentive. Check whether management's compensation references earnings per share, total shareholder return or a share-price target, and whether the repurchase was funded by debt. Both change how you should read the decision.
5. Record what you would have preferred and why. Over several years this becomes evidence about the management's capital allocation, which is a more reliable signal than any single year's result.

### Build your careful-investor plan

Write the calculation, decision rule and one reason the conclusion might be wrong in your notebook. Add the evidence to your My notebook page. Read the named theme in your own copy of The Intelligent Investor; these explanations and fictional cases are original Quanta material, not reproduced chapters or publisher exercises. The worksheet calculates the case and keeps the price sandbox in cash. Its chart is not an investment recommendation or a test of Graham's approach.

value_per_share = 20.00
price = 26.00
spend = 5200.0

bought = spend / price
remaining = shares - bought
before = shares * value_per_share
after = before - spend
print("Shares repurchased:", round(bought, 0))
print("Shares remaining:", round(remaining, 0))
print("Business value before:", round(before, 0))
print("Business value after:", round(after, 0))
print("Value per remaining share:", round(after / remaining, 2))
print("Transferred away per remaining share:", round(value_per_share - after / remaining, 2))

print("Earnings per share before:", round(earnings / shares, 2))
print("Earnings per share after:", round(earnings / remaining, 2))
print("Percent rise from the share count alone:", round((shares / remaining - 1) * 100, 1))

assignment.prompt: Compute the value per remaining share after Harrow's repurchase, the transfer per share, and the rise in earnings per share it produces. assignment.solution: The company buys 5,200 / 26.00 = 200 shares, leaving 800. Business value falls from 20,000 to 14,800 because the cash left, so value per remaining share is 14,800 / 800 = 18.50 against 20.00 before — a transfer of 1.50 a share away from the holders who stayed and to those who sold. Earnings per share rise from 2.00 to 2.50, a 25% increase produced entirely by the smaller denominator with no change in the business. The buyback is neutral only at a price equal to intrinsic value, 20.00 a share: below that it adds value for continuing holders, above it subtracts. The vote-of-confidence framing is not evidence because it is an assertion about management's opinion of the price, and management's opinion is precisely what the repurchase price is being used to test; a confident management buying at 26.00 against a 20.00 value has expressed confidence and destroyed 1,200 of value in the same act.

terms.definition: An estimate of what an investment is worth based on the business, its assets, cash flows, and obligations. It depends on assumptions and can differ from the current market price.
A reason someone may prefer one outcome over another, such as a fee, commission, or personal interest. Understanding an incentive helps you assess a recommendation alongside its evidence.
A record of your reasons, evidence, alternatives, and expectations written before an outcome is known. It helps you review the original decision without rewriting its history.
A value or rule output used to inform a decision. A signal becomes an actual trade only after the system applies timing, position, risk, and execution rules.

realWorld.connection: Earnings per share can rise because a business earned more or because its share count fell, and a reader who does not separate the two is reading a different number from the one they think.
realWorld.task: Appraise a company before reading its latest repurchase announcement, then compute the value per remaining share after the buyback and the transfer it produced.
realWorld.walkthrough: Subtract the cash spent from your appraisal of the whole business and divide by the shares that remain. In the worked case a 5,200 buyback at 26.00 against a 20.00 appraisal left 18.50 a share, a transfer of 1.50 away from the holders who stayed, while earnings per share rose 25% with no change in the business at all. The neutral price is intrinsic value, which means the judgement requires an appraisal made before the announcement rather than after it.

prerequisites: Complete Trading Fundamentals or understand basic shares, bonds, returns and orders. No coding experience is required; worksheets explain their inputs. Read your own legally obtained copy of the book for the original discussion.
outcomes: Separate investing from speculation and evaluate the quality of a decision independently of luck.
Choose a maintainable defensive or enterprising process and identify behavioral traps.
Connect goals, liquidity, risk capacity, inflation and diversification to a written plan.
Calculate valuation cushions, allocation drift, fee drag and purchase averages.
Read disclosures, investigate incentives and recognize promises that need independent verification.
Judge the purpose of a fixed-income allocation, apply a price filter as a hypothesis rather than a verdict, and evaluate a dividend or repurchase as an owner.
Produce an investor-policy workbook and prepare for the deeper Security Analysis course.
readingGuide:
Before choosing individual stocks, it helps to understand the person making the decisions: you. This course connects investing habits with practical choices about goals, available cash, diversification, fees, and how to respond when prices move. A careful investor needs a process they can maintain through uncertainty.

Each lesson connects one idea from the book's themes to an original everyday example. First explain the choice in ordinary language, then work through the calculation, and finally add a decision rule to your My notebook page. For example, a discussion of losses should lead you to explain which money you can leave invested and which money you may need soon. Build the plan gradually; you do not need to decide everything in the first lesson.

20 lessons × 30 minutes = 10 hours of planned study across five units; exam time is additional. Includes 40 practice questions, five four-question checkpoints, a 20-question final and a downloadable workbook with a self-assessed capstone in your notebook.

This is an original thematic companion, not the full book or a substitute for it. Edition pagination varies; use the named themes in your own copy.

Modern planning, fund and fraud examples are explicitly course extensions. Case allocations and thresholds are fictional assumptions, not personalized recommendations.

exams.title: Unit 1: Think like a careful investor
exams.description: Four original transfer questions. Use your notes, show calculations, and review the explanations after submitting. This checkpoint samples the preceding unit; the final covers every module.

questions.question: What makes a decision journal useful?
options: Replacing all evidence with confidence scores
Recording reasons before outcomes can rewrite memory
questions.explanation: A decision journal preserves your original facts, assumptions, and risk limits in real time, preventing hindsight bias from retrospectively altering your memory of why the trade was made.

questions.question: Equity ownership gives a claim on:
options: Residual business value after senior claims
questions.explanation: Common equity represents a strictly residual ownership interest in the business's assets and earnings after all operating expenses, taxes, and senior debt obligations are fully satisfied.

questions.question: Old numerical screening criteria should be treated as:
options: Historically situated rules requiring context and analysis
Universal guarantees across every industry and era
A substitute for reading financial statements
questions.explanation: Historical screening benchmarks (such as P/E or current ratio thresholds) reflect the specific corporate accounting and market structures of their era and must be adapted thoughtfully to modern realities.

questions.question: A useful response to a dramatic quotation change begins with:
options: A review of evidence, assumptions and liquidity constraints
questions.explanation: A structured review decouples judgment from emotional market panic, systematically investigating whether corporate facts changed and confirming personal liquidity buffers before taking any action.

exams.title: Unit 2: Protect the plan from avoidable mistakes
exams.description: Four original transfer questions. Use your notes, show calculations, and review the explanations after submitting. This checkpoint samples the preceding unit; the final covers every module.

questions.question: The course's 24-million reserve is:
options: A guarantee against every financial emergency
A fictional assumption to analyze, not a universal prescription
A required amount for every household
questions.explanation: Emergency reserve sizing depends on household living expenses, job stability, insurance coverage, and family dependents; the 24-million figure is a pedagogical case assumption.

questions.question: A published inflation index and a household's goal costs can:
options: Be replaced by a stock's recent return
questions.explanation: Official Consumer Price Index numbers measure an aggregate statistical basket; an individual household's actual spending basket (e.g. tuition, healthcare, regional rent) can experience significantly different inflation rates.

questions.question: Employer stock deserves extra concentration review because:
options: Investment wealth and labor income may share the same business risk
questions.explanation: Holding substantial equity in your employer concentrates both your monthly salary and your accumulated savings into the fortunes of a single corporate balance sheet.

questions.question: Permanent impairment refers most directly to:
options: Only a change in chart scale
A lasting deterioration in the economic claim
questions.explanation: Permanent impairment describes lasting, unrecoverable destruction of underlying business earning power, solvency, or assets, in sharp contrast to temporary market quotation fluctuations.

exams.title: Unit 3: Build a maintainable portfolio
exams.description: Four original transfer questions. Use your notes, show calculations, and review the explanations after submitting. This checkpoint samples the preceding unit; the final covers every module.

questions.question: A policy change should be justified by:
options: Documented changes in goals, constraints or supported assumptions
The desire to match every headline
questions.explanation: Disciplined investors modify their target allocation policy only in response to documented changes in life circumstances, financial goals, or verifiable long-term constraints, never in reaction to daily market volatility.

questions.question: Frequent tiny rebalances require scrutiny because:
options: They guarantee a more diversified universe
Costs may exceed their practical risk-management benefit
questions.explanation: Executing frequent trades for negligible weight deviations generates excessive brokerage fees, bid-ask spreads, and potential tax liabilities without meaningfully reducing portfolio risk.

questions.question: A useful fund comparison examines:
options: Mandate, holdings, costs, benchmark and access terms
questions.explanation: Rigorous fund evaluation requires analyzing the investment objective, underlying holdings, total fee structure, tracking error against benchmark, and redemption liquidity terms.

questions.question: Scheduled purchases funded from new monthly income differ from:
options: Deliberately delaying investment of an already available lump sum
A transaction with a recorded date
questions.explanation: Investing new salary cash flows as they arrive is natural ongoing savings; by contrast, deliberately staging an already existing lump sum over time incurs the opportunity cost of holding idle cash during market advances.

exams.title: Unit 4: Exercise independent judgment
exams.description: Four original transfer questions. Use your notes, show calculations, and review the explanations after submitting. This checkpoint samples the preceding unit; the final covers every module.

questions.question: Before detailed valuation, a careful investor should understand:
options: Only the most recent price target
The business model, cash needs and senior claims
questions.explanation: Valuation requires understanding how the enterprise produces revenue, its ongoing capital expenditure requirements, and the contractual claims of senior creditors ranking ahead of common equity.

questions.question: A risk disclosure alone establishes a product is legitimate:
options: No; the entity and claims still require verification
questions.explanation: Including boilerplate risk warnings does not certify that an investment entity is licensed, that custody is secure, or that the investment strategy is legitimate.

questions.question: Selling for a near-term cash need versus a failed business thesis should be:
options: Retrospectively described as the same prediction
questions.explanation: Distinguishing between balance-sheet liquidity needs and analytical thesis invalidation is critical for accurately auditing your investment decision process and refining future rules.

questions.question: Which next course deepens the analysis of earnings, assets and senior claims?
questions.explanation: The Security Analysis course expands directly upon this policy foundation, providing rigorous forensic methods for evaluating corporate balance sheets, asset recoverability, earnings quality, and capital structure seniority.

exams.title: Unit 5: Choose the securities, and know what a rule cannot decide
exams.description: Four original transfer questions. Use your notes, show calculations, and review the explanations after submitting. This checkpoint samples the preceding unit; the final covers every module.

questions.question: What should decide the size of the fixed-income allocation?
options: The proportion that produced the best returns last decade
The drawdown or spending it has to cover without forcing an equity sale
The yield available on the instruments being considered
questions.explanation: The allocation exists to stop a forced sale, so the size follows from what it must absorb. Sizing it by yield chooses the amount for a reason unrelated to the job.

questions.question: What does passing the defensive price filter establish?
options: Only that the price is modest against two accounting numbers, which still have to be checked
That the shares offer a margin of safety
That the business has durable earnings
questions.explanation: A screen is a hypothesis generator. Durability of earnings, the realism of book value and the direction of the business are questions the filter cannot reach, and they are the ones that decide whether a low multiple is cheap or deserved.

questions.question: What does this arithmetic imply for an investor without 160 hours a year?
options: That they should study fewer names at the same hit rate
That they should raise their hit rate by lowering their standards
That the defensive route is the correct choice, not the lesser one
questions.explanation: Lesson 11.3 framed the choice as a commitment of time. Pricing that commitment honestly is how the choice gets made, and a defensive process chosen for a reason is better than an enterprising one that is not actually resourced.

questions.question: A dividend of the same 5,200 would have left each holder with:
options: More total value, because dividends are always preferable
5.20 in cash and shares worth 14.80, totalling the 20.00 they started with
Shares worth 18.50, the same as the buyback
questions.explanation: A dividend distributes the cash without changing the share count, so nothing is transferred between holders: 14,800 / 1,000 = 14.80 a share plus 5.20 received. Neither form is always better; the buyback's merit depends entirely on the price paid.

exams.title: The intelligent & careful investor final exam
exams.description: Open-book, untimed assessment with new cases from every module. Budget about three minutes per question. Answers and explanations appear after submission. Pass at 80%; retries remain available. The written capstone is self-assessed separately.

questions.question: A speculative purchase rises sharply. That outcome alone proves:
options: Neither the quality nor repeatability of the original process
That the next purchase must also rise
questions.explanation: Outcome bias frequently misleads investors: a favorable outcome can result from pure chance or temporary liquidity bubbles and does not validate an unexamined or reckless decision method.

questions.question: Holding an unexamined promotion for several years automatically changes it into:
options: Neither a sound analysis nor a justified investment
questions.explanation: Passive passage of time cannot retroactively supply the thorough financial analysis, safety of principal, and adequate return required to classify an operation as an investment.

questions.question: A complex process far exceeds available maintenance time. A reasonable response is:
options: Increase the number of unattended holdings
Reduce scope and define a maintainable policy
Assume initial research removes all future work
questions.explanation: When research demands exceed available hours, an investor must simplify their strategy to a maintainable baseline to prevent catastrophic neglect and unmonitored risk.

questions.question: Anchoring to a previous market high risks assuming:
options: A historical quote is a promised future value
questions.explanation: Anchoring bias causes market participants to view past peak quotations as rightful targets, overlooking that the historical price may have been an irrational bubble or that underlying business fundamentals have permanently deteriorated.

questions.question: A person likes risk but needs the money soon. The plan must consider:
options: The near-term liability even if emotional tolerance is high
questions.explanation: Subjective psychological risk tolerance cannot alter contractual cash requirements; money needed in the near term must be protected in low-risk, liquid instruments regardless of personal risk appetite.

questions.question: Equity ownership is an automatic inflation hedge over every horizon:
options: Yes when a stock is popular
No; business economics and valuation also matter
questions.explanation: A company's pricing power, input cost sensitivity, debt structure, and purchase valuation determine how it fares under inflation; sudden inflation often compresses margins and depresses valuation multiples in the short run.

questions.question: Diversification guarantees no broad market loss:
options: No; common risks can affect many assets together
Yes if there are ten tickers
Yes if all products have different names
questions.explanation: Diversification reduces company-specific (idiosyncratic) risk, but cannot eliminate systematic (market-wide) risk such as recessions, liquidity crises, or rising interest rates that impact all assets simultaneously.

questions.question: A large base-case discount with a weak conservative case calls for:
options: Examining downside assumptions before relying on the headline discount
questions.explanation: A wide headline discount against an optimistic or base forecast is often fragile; an investor must audit downside risks, debt burdens, and asset recovery haircuts before committing capital.

questions.question: Stocks and bonds must always move in opposite directions:
options: Only when allocation weights sum to one
No; both can decline in the same scenario
questions.explanation: While stocks and bonds often exhibit low or negative correlation during ordinary recessions, both asset classes can decline simultaneously during inflationary periods or sharp interest-rate spikes.

questions.question: Rebalancing to a fixed policy necessarily predicts imminent price reversal:
options: No; it restores the planned exposure
Only if the investor uses a calendar
questions.explanation: Rebalancing is a risk-management rule designed to maintain the investor's intended exposure bands, not a speculative forecast that outperforming assets are about to decline.

questions.question: A performance figure already net of an expense ratio should have that same fee:
options: Identified without subtracting it a second time
questions.explanation: When reviewing published fund performance, check the reporting convention; if returns are already net of the annual expense ratio, subtracting the fee again would double-count costs.

questions.question: A lower average purchase cost guarantees a profit:
options: No; the asset can remain below cost or deteriorate further
questions.explanation: A lower average cost reduces the break-even threshold, but does not guarantee a profit; if the market price remains depressed or the business fails, the investor still incurs a loss.

questions.question: An adjusted earnings measure from management should be:
options: Reconciled to disclosures and examined for recurring exclusions
Assumed to equal cash flow exactly
questions.explanation: Management-adjusted earnings measures frequently exclude economically recurring expenses; an investor must audit the reconciliation footnote to identify recurring costs that management labeled non-recurring.

questions.question: Understanding adviser compensation helps identify:
options: A guarantee that the product will lose
Incentives and potential conflicts in the recommendation
questions.explanation: Knowing how an adviser is compensated (e.g. commissions, sales loads, kickbacks vs. transparent hourly fees) reveals inherent conflicts of interest that may bias their product recommendations.

questions.question: A useful disconfirming observation should:
options: Depend solely on a preferred price target
Challenge a material assumption of the investment thesis
questions.explanation: Disconfirming evidence is observable, verifiable information (such as lost market share or deteriorating margins) that directly refutes the fundamental premises of the original investment thesis.

questions.question: Passing the concept exam establishes that a personal allocation is suitable:
options: No; suitability depends on circumstances beyond the educational exam
Only if the worksheet used rupiah
questions.explanation: Academic exam completion tests conceptual understanding; determining whether a specific financial allocation is suitable requires analyzing individual personal liabilities, tax status, family commitments, and risk capacity.

questions.question: Why is credit risk a worse fit for the safe half than interest-rate risk?
options: Credit risk is larger in every scenario
Interest-rate risk does not affect bond prices
A default is permanent and clusters in the recessions that are also hurting equities
questions.explanation: Rate losses reverse: hold to maturity and par is still paid. Default losses do not, and they arrive exactly when the equity side needs the safe half to be whole.

questions.question: Removing a one-time gain of 0.40 moves earnings from 3.20 to 2.80. The product then becomes:
options: 19.69, a pass, because lower earnings reduce the ratio
26.25, a clear failure the reported figure had hidden
22.97, unchanged, because book value did not move
questions.explanation: The multiple rises to 42.00 / 2.80 = 15.00 and the product to 15.00 × 1.75 = 26.25. A lower earnings figure raises a price-to-earnings ratio, which is why lesson 11.13 insists on stripping non-recurring items before any multiple is used.

questions.question: Doubling the screen's hit rate from 6% to 12% does what to the hours per find?
options: Halves them, from about 133 to about 67
Leaves them unchanged, since the hours per analysis are the same
Doubles them, because more candidates must be studied
questions.explanation: The figure is hours each over the hit rate, so the hit rate is the denominator. Improving the screen is the only lever with leverage; working faster reduces the numerator but not the structure of the problem.

questions.question: At what price would the repurchase have been neutral for continuing holders?
options: At the market price, since that is what the shares are worth
At book value, whatever it happens to be
questions.explanation: A buyback is a purchase. It creates value below intrinsic value and destroys it above, so the neutral point is intrinsic value itself — which means you need an appraisal made before the announcement to judge it at all.

modules.title: Foundations of Graham & Dodd
modules.subtitle: Distinguish a defensible investment operation from a price prediction and calculate a conservative margin of safety.
modules.objective: Distinguish a defensible investment operation from a price prediction and calculate a conservative margin of safety.
modules.reading: Graham & Dodd, Security Analysis, 1940 edition · Part I. Read the relevant discussion in your own copy, then apply it to this original case.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

A security gives its owner a particular claim on a business. A lender may be owed interest and repayment; a common shareholder receives what remains after other obligations. Before estimating value, identify the claim you are examining. Then separate the quoted market price from your own estimate of what supports that claim. The margin-of-safety calculation becomes meaningful only after that groundwork.

## The analytical question

In modern financial discourse, the word "investment" is frequently misapplied to any speculative transaction where an individual expects prices to rise. In their foundational 1940 treatise *Security Analysis*, Benjamin Graham and David Dodd established a rigorous boundary that remains the cornerstone of professional credit and equity valuation:

> *"An investment operation is one which, upon thorough analysis, promises safety of principal and an adequate return. Operations not meeting these requirements are speculative."*

Notice the three strict conditions embedded in this definition:
1. **Thorough analysis**: The decision must rest on verifiable primary facts—audited balance sheets, multi-year operating earnings records, contractual claim covenants, and liquidation asset recovery schedules—rather than market rumors, chart momentum, or unverified management forecasts.
2. **Safety of principal**: The investor's primary capital must be protected against permanent loss across adverse business cycles and liquidation scenarios, not merely during cyclical booms.
3. **Adequate return**: The expected cash yield or economic earnings yield must compensate for the time value of money and verifiable operational risks, without relying on future speculative multiple expansion from greater fools.

The central pillar of Graham and Dodd's framework is the **Margin of Safety** ($M$). A margin of safety expresses the percentage discount by which the current market quotation ($P$) sits below a sober, conservative estimate of intrinsic business value ($V$):

$$
M = 1 - \frac{P}{V} = \frac{V - P}{V}
$$

$$
\text{Maximum Permitted Purchase Price: } P_{\max} = V_{\text{conservative}} \times (1 - M_{\text{required}})
$$

Crucially, the margin of safety is not a statistical prediction that the share price will immediately rebound. Instead, it serves an engineering purpose: just as a structural engineer designs a bridge capable of carrying 30,000 pounds even if ordinary traffic weighs only 10,000 pounds, an investor insists on a substantial discount to absorb human error, unforeseen economic recessions, industry disruption, and accounting revisions.

$$
V = \text{Conservative Going-Concern Value or Net Asset Value}
$$

$$
M_{\text{required}} \ge 30\% \quad (\text{or higher in cyclical and leveraged issuers})
$$

If an analyst inflates the intrinsic value denominator ($V$) through heroic long-term growth assumptions, an apparent 50% discount can be manufactured out of thin air. A genuine margin of safety demands that $V$ be anchored to tangible assets or normalized earning power tested under adverse conditions.

## A worked example

Consider fictional industrial equipment manufacturer Alder Manufacturing. Alder's common shares currently trade on the secondary exchange at $P = \$60.00$. As an independent security analyst, you conduct an exhaustive forensic audit of the company's financial filings across an entire eight-year industrial cycle. Rather than producing a single speculative point estimate, you establish three disciplined valuation cases:

| Valuation Scenario | Underlying Operating Premise | Estimated Value ($V$) | Quoted Price ($P$) | Apparent Margin ($1 - P/V$) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Weak / Depressed Case** | Trough cycle margins, loss of secondary customer, 12% discount rate | $\$75.00$ | $\$60.00$ | $20.0\%$ |
| **Base / Normalized Case** | Normalized 5-year average EBIT, mid-cycle reinvestment, 10% discount rate | $\$100.00$ | $\$60.00$ | $40.0\%$ |
| **Favorable / Peak Case** | High industry capacity utilization, favorable pricing power, 9% discount rate | $\$125.00$ | $\$60.00$ | $52.0\%$ |

Your investment committee enforces a strict policy rule: every prospective equity commitment must provide at least a **$30.0\%$ margin of safety** against the **weak-case conservative estimate** ($V_{\text{weak}} = \$75.00$).

Let us test the decision boundary:
1. Under the Base Case ($V = \$100.00$), the apparent discount is:

$$
M_{\text{base}} = 1 - \frac{\$60.00}{\$100.00} = 40.0\% \ge 30.0\% \quad \text{(Appears attractive)}
$$

2. However, under the required Weak Case ($V = \$75.00$), the margin is:

$$
M_{\text{weak}} = 1 - \frac{\$60.00}{\$75.00} = 20.0\% < 30.0\% \quad \text{(Fails safety requirement)}
$$

3. To achieve a $30.0\%$ margin against the conservative weak case, the maximum price the committee can pay is:

$$
P_{\max} = \$75.00 \times (1 - 0.30) = \$75.00 \times 0.70 = \$52.50
$$

At the current market quote of $\$60.00$, the purchase is firmly rejected. The market price offers only a $20.0\%$ cushion against trough earnings. If an unrecorded environmental liability or customer bankruptcy destroys $\$25.00$ per share of value, an investor purchasing at $\$60.00$ faces permanent impairment, whereas an investor disciplined at $\$52.50$ preserves capital.

### Read the margin of safety in plain language

In the equation, P is the price and V is the estimated value. Dividing P by V tells you what fraction of that estimate you would pay. Subtracting that fraction from 1 gives the discount. With P = $60 and V = $100, you would pay 60% of the estimate, leaving a 40% discount.

The important next step is changing the estimate. If V is only $75, the same $60 price is 80% of the estimate, leaving a 20% discount. The purchase price has not changed; the assumption about the business has. That is why a large-looking discount is only as useful as the value estimate underneath it.

To require a 30% discount to the $75 weak-case value, you can pay 70% of that value: 0.70 × $75 = $52.50. The current $60 price is above that limit. Saying that the base case passes and the conservative case fails describes those two calculations. It does not establish the probability of a loss or guarantee protection.

## Research discipline

To maintain Graham and Dodd's analytical integrity in professional practice, execute the following four-step protocol before submitting any recommendation:

1. **State the Exact Legal Claim**: Explicitly define whether you are evaluating senior secured debt, subordinated debentures, cumulative preferred shares, or the residual common equity interest. Each tier in the capital structure requires a different standard of protection.
2. **Separate Market Quotation from Intrinsic Value**: Maintain the market quote ($P$) in a separate, isolated column. Never adjust your valuation estimate ($V$) simply because market prices have dropped or rallied.
3. **Isolate Falsification Conditions**: Document exactly what disconfirming evidence would invalidate your thesis (e.g., loss of patent protection, recurring operating cash flow deficits, or covenant renegotiations).
4. **Enforce the Price Ceiling**: Calculate $P_{\max} = V_{\text{weak}} \times (1 - M_{\text{required}})$ and refuse to authorize capital allocation if market quotes exceed this ceiling, regardless of institutional consensus or fear of missing out.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Researchers measure what the lesson calls the margin, but mechanically. Because M = 1 − P/V, the value-to-price ratio is V/P = 1/(1 − M): Alder's weak, base and favorable cases give 1.25, 1.67 and 2.08. In the studies below, V is a book-value or earnings figure, not a reasoned range.

Lakonishok, Shleifer and Vishny sorted NYSE and AMEX stocks from April 1963 to April 1990. Averaged over the post-formation years, size-adjusted returns of high book-to-market (value) stocks beat low book-to-market (glamour) stocks by 7.8 percent per year. They argued that value strategies exploit the extrapolation mistakes reflected in prices, not extra risk. Fama and French found that size and book-to-market equity capture the variation in average returns associated with leverage and earnings-price ratios, while the relation between market β and average return was flat once β could vary independently of size. Why cheap stocks earn more is the disputed part.

Two cautions. These are portfolio averages; they do not show that any single 40% discount pays. And Chen, Lopez-Lira and Zimmermann found that for published predictors and for data-mined accounting ratios alike, about half of the predictability remains after the original sample periods. Our inference: a historical value premium is a hypothesis about the future, not a margin of safety.

Check: at $60, a 30% discount needs V of at least 60 ÷ 0.70 = $85.71, which is 14.3% below the $100 base case and above the $75 weak case. Then, for a company you follow, compute M twice, once from your own V and once from book value per share; the gap between the two is the claim to defend.

### Sources for this section

- [Lakonishok, Shleifer & Vishny (1993) · Contrarian Investment, Extrapolation, and Risk](https://doi.org/10.3386/w4360) — *Research paper.* NBER working-paper version of the 1994 Journal of Finance article: NYSE and AMEX stocks, April 1963 to April 1990, value versus glamour portfolios, and the argument that the value premium reflects extrapolation errors rather than extra risk.
- [Fama & French (1992) · The Cross-Section of Expected Stock Returns](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1992.tb04398.x) — *Research paper.* Size and book-to-market equity capture the variation in average returns associated with market beta, leverage and earnings-price ratios, while the beta-return relation is flat once beta varies independently of size.
- [Chen, Lopez-Lira & Zimmermann (2022) · Does Peer-Reviewed Research Help Predict Stock Returns?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.10317) — *arXiv 2212.10317.* Both peer-reviewed predictors and data-mined accounting ratios keep only about half of their predictability after the original sample periods, a caution for treating a historical discount pattern as a margin of safety.

modules.subtitle: Separate reported facts, analytical adjustments, and assumptions in a dated research record.
modules.objective: Separate reported facts, analytical adjustments, and assumptions in a dated research record.
modules.reading: Graham & Dodd, Security Analysis, 1940 edition · Part I. Read the relevant discussion in your own copy, then apply it to this original case.
modules.content:
## The analytical question

A professional security analysis is not an essay of personal opinions; it is an evidentiary legal and financial brief that another analyst can independently audit and replicate. Every claim regarding revenues, margins, debt obligations, and asset recoveries must tie directly to primary sources—regulatory disclosure filings (such as SEC Form 10-K, 10-Q, or 8-K), indentures, credit agreements, and court dockets.

To prevent confirmation bias and intellectual drift, Graham and Dodd insisted on maintaining a rigid tripartite structure in every research working paper:

$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}
\hline
\textbf{Column 1: Reported Facts} & \textbf{Column 2: Analytical Adjustments} & \textbf{Column 3: Working Assumptions} \\
\hline
\text{Verifiable primary disclosures} & \text{Auditable mathematical reconciliations} & \text{Explicit judgments with sensitivity bounds} \\
\text{(Dates, exact units, accession numbers)} & \text{(Nonrecurring items, lease capitalizations)} & \text{(Discount rates, terminal growth, recovery \%)} \\
\hline
\end{array}
$$

1. **Reported Facts**: The exact numbers as stated by the issuer, accompanied by document date, filing date, currency, scale (thousands vs millions), and scope of consolidation. Never overwrite a reported number.
2. **Analytical Adjustments**: Transparent reconciliations that bridge reported numbers to economic reality. If management reports an extraordinary asset sale gain, this column subtracts it with an explicit note.
3. **Working Assumptions**: The analyst's judgments regarding the future. Each assumption must state its rationale and an adverse sensitivity boundary.

A critical dimension of evidence discipline is **point-in-time timestamping**. When reconstructing historical corporate performance, you must distinguish between the **period-end date** (e.g., December 31) and the **public availability date** (e.g., March 15 when the 10-K was filed on EDGAR). Using financial numbers before their public release introduces hindsight bias (look-ahead contamination), rendering historical backtests and valuation conclusions invalid.

One classic diagnostic for evaluating corporate reporting quality is **receivables intensity** relative to sales:

$$
\text{Receivables Intensity} = \frac{\text{Accounts Receivable}}{\text{Annual Net Sales}}
$$

$$
\Delta \text{Intensity} = \frac{\text{AR}_t}{\text{Sales}_t} - \frac{\text{AR}_{t-1}}{\text{Sales}_{t-1}}
$$

When accounts receivable surge at a rate disproportionate to top-line revenue, it signals potential channel stuffing, aggressive revenue recognition, or customer payment distress requiring immediate investigation.

## A worked example

Let us construct an evidence audit for Alder Manufacturing's working capital accounts across two consecutive fiscal years:

| Metric | Prior Year ($t-1$) Reported | Current Year ($t$) Reported | Percentage Change |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Annual Net Sales** | $\$200.0\text{ million}$ | $\$240.0\text{ million}$ | $+20.0\%$ |
| **Accounts Receivable** | $\$30.0\text{ million}$ | $\$48.0\text{ million}$ | $+60.0\%$ |
| **Receivables Intensity** | $15.0\%$ | $20.0\%$ | $+5.0\text{ percentage points}$ |

Notice the clear divergence: sales grew by $20.0\%$, but receivables surged by $60.0\%$. Receivables intensity expanded from $15.0\%$ of sales to $20.0\%$.

As a security analyst building your evidence file, you do not immediately conclude fraud, but you document the anomaly across the three columns:
- **Reported**: Sales $\$240.0\text{M}$, AR $\$48.0\text{M}$ (SEC Form 10-K filed March 15, FY ended December 31).
- **Adjusted**: Incremental receivables beyond proportional sales growth equal $\$48.0\text{M} - (\$240.0\text{M} \times 0.15) = \$12.0\text{ million}$. Working capital consumed $\$12.0\text{M}$ of operating cash.
- **Assumed**: Base assumption assumes normal collection cycle with extended payment terms granted to large distributors. Stressed downside assumption applies a $25.0\%$ collection haircut to the incremental $\$12.0\text{M}$, reducing prospective liquid net assets by $\$3.0\text{ million}$.

Furthermore, verify the point-in-time timeline:
- Fiscal year ended: December 31, 2025.
- Annual report filed on EDGAR: March 15, 2026.
- A research committee decision dated January 31, 2026, **cannot** cite the $\$48.0\text{M}$ receivables figure because it was not publicly known on that date. Only third-quarter 10-Q numbers were knowable.

## Research discipline

To construct an institutional-grade evidence file, follow these mandatory practices:
1. **Preserve Filing Accession Numbers**: Every audited table must reference the specific SEC EDGAR accession number or company registry publication date.
2. **Never Average Incompatible Baselines**: If an issuer shifts accounting principles (e.g., from US GAAP to IFRS, or modifies segment reporting), construct a bridge year before comparing ratios.
3. **Track Restatements Separately**: When an issuer files an amended 10-K/A, keep the original 10-K in your historical timeline and record the amendment date as a separate information event.
4. **Demand Corroborating Disclosures**: Do not rely on press release summaries. Verify reported numbers against the audited footnotes, particularly Note 1 (Summary of Accounting Policies) and Note 4 (Segment and Customer Concentration).

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Two outside facts tighten the file. First, deadlines: Form 10-K sets the annual-report deadline at 60 days after fiscal year-end for large accelerated filers, 75 days for accelerated filers and 90 days for all other registrants. For a December 31 year-end in an ordinary year, those fall on March 1, March 16 and March 31. If Alder's year ended December 31, its March 15 release is day 74: inside the 75- and 90-day windows but past the 60-day one, so the file needs its filer category (our arithmetic). A deadline is not the filing date, which must be recorded.

Second, the receivables signal. Dechow and co-authors examined 2,190 SEC enforcement releases (AAERs) from 1982 to 2005, covering 676 firms that misstated results. Almost half the misstating firms were alleged to have misstated sales, and change in receivables had the highest t-statistic of all accrual variables. Yet an F-score cut-off of 1.4 flagged over 50 percent of misstating firms and 20 percent of public firms; because misstatement is rare, most flagged firms are probably clean (our inference). Their variable scales the receivables change by average total assets, so Alder's rise from 15% to 20% of sales is related, not identical.

Jofre and Gerlach built 1,594 fraud-year observations from SEC releases for 1990 to 2012, stopping at 2012 because their study began in mid-2013, when that year's cases could still come to light. By analogy, Alder's newest year is "not yet flagged", not "clean" (our inference).

Check: add filer category, period-end date and filing date to the file, then set Alder's 60% receivables growth beside 20% revenue growth, with two benign explanations and the document that separates them from collection trouble.

### Sources for this section

- [U.S. SEC · Form 10-K: General Instructions](https://www.sec.gov/files/form10-k.pdf) — *Official source.* General Instruction A(2) sets annual-report deadlines of 60, 75 or 90 days after fiscal year-end by filer category, a reference point for when a period's accounts should have become public.
- [Dechow, Ge, Larson & Sloan (2011) · Predicting Material Accounting Misstatements](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1911-3846.2010.01041.x) — *Research paper.* Builds a database from 2,190 SEC enforcement releases (1982 to 2005) and shows that receivables changes stand out among accrual variables, with an F-score cut-off that over half of misstating firms, but also 20 percent of public firms, exceed.
- [Jofre & Gerlach (2018) · Fighting Accounting Fraud Through Forensic Data Analytics](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.02840) — *arXiv 1805.02840.* Labels fraud from SEC releases for 1990 to 2012 and stops the sample at 2012 because the study began in mid-2013, when that year's cases could still be discovered, a reminder that the newest accounts have not yet been tested.

modules.title: Value ranges and the limits of precision
modules.subtitle: Reconcile asset and earnings evidence without double counting or disguising uncertainty.
modules.objective: Reconcile asset and earnings evidence without double counting or disguising uncertainty.
modules.reading: Graham & Dodd, Security Analysis, 1940 edition · Part I. Read the relevant discussion in your own copy, then apply it to this original case.
modules.content:
## The analytical question

One of the most dangerous tendencies in modern financial modeling is **false precision**. An analyst projects twenty line items out fifteen years into the future, discounts the cash flows at $9.347\%$, and concludes that a stock is worth exactly $\$54.82$. This creates a seductive illusion of scientific accuracy while obscuring the reality that a tiny $0.5\%$ shift in discount rate or operating margin alters the outcome by $30\%$.

Graham and Dodd repeatedly cautioned against mistaking mathematical elaboration for analytical certainty:

$$
\text{Intrinsic value is not an exact point; it is a reasoned range.}
$$

To establish a defensible valuation range, the analyst must first select a clear **valuation premise**:
1. **Going-Concern Operating Premise**: Assumes the business will continue its commercial operations indefinitely. Intrinsic value is derived from the capitalized earning power or discounted free cash flows generated by its operating assets.
2. **Orderly Liquidation Premise**: Assumes the business ceases operations and liquidates its assets over a reasonable timeframe (e.g., 6 to 18 months). Value is derived from realizable cash proceeds after paying all administrative costs, severance, and satisfying all senior liabilities.
3. **Forced Wind-Down / Distress Premise**: Assumes immediate distress sale under bankruptcy court supervision with steep fire-sale haircuts.

The cardinal error in security analysis is **double counting across incompatible premises**. An analyst cannot value an operating factory as a going concern generating $\$15\text{M}$ in annual operating profit, and simultaneously add the factory's vacant land liquidation resale value to the equity estimate! The factory cannot be both operated and demolished at the same time.

The rigorous claims bridge for a going concern is:

$$
V_{\text{equity}} = V_{\text{operations}} + \text{Excess Nonoperating Cash} - \text{All Senior Claims}
$$

$$
\text{Equity Value per Share} = \frac{V_{\text{equity}}}{N_{\text{diluted shares}}}
$$

Here, "Excess Cash" is strictly cash that is not required to fund everyday working capital cycles. If the business requires $\$10\text{M}$ in minimum cash balances to operate its store branches or pay supplier payroll, that $\$10\text{M}$ is an operating asset already embedded inside $V_{\text{operations}}$ and cannot be added a second time.

## A worked example

Let us evaluate Alder Manufacturing under alternative premises and construct an honest valuation range. The company has $10.0\text{ million}$ fully diluted shares outstanding and $\$60.0\text{ million}$ in interest-bearing debt. Balance sheet cash is $\$30.0\text{ million}$, of which $\$10.0\text{ million}$ is essential operating cash, leaving $\$20.0\text{ million}$ as true excess cash.

### Premise A: Going-Concern Operating Range
Through detailed earning power capitalization, you estimate the enterprise value of operations ($V_{\text{operations}}$) across three operating states:
- **Pessimistic Case**: $V_{\text{operations}} = \$180.0\text{ million}$
- **Base Case**: $V_{\text{operations}} = \$200.0\text{ million}$
- **Optimistic Case**: $V_{\text{operations}} = \$220.0\text{ million}$

Applying the claims bridge:

$$
V_{\text{equity}} = V_{\text{operations}} + \$20.0\text{M (Excess Cash)} - \$60.0\text{M (Debt)}
$$

$$
V_{\text{equity}} = V_{\text{operations}} - \$40.0\text{ million}
$$

Dividing across $10.0\text{ million}$ diluted shares:
- **Pessimistic**: $(\$180.0\text{M} - \$40.0\text{M}) / 10.0\text{M} = \$14.00\text{ per share}$
- **Base**: $(\$200.0\text{M} - \$40.0\text{M}) / 10.0\text{M} = \$16.00\text{ per share}$
- **Optimistic**: $(\$220.0\text{M} - \$40.0\text{M}) / 10.0\text{M} = \$18.00\text{ per share}$

### Premise B: Orderly Liquidation Value
Separately, you perform an asset-by-asset recovery audit. Selling off inventories at a $50\%$ discount, collecting receivables at $80\%$, auctioning machinery, paying off all $\$100.0\text{M}$ in total liabilities, and funding $\$8.0\text{M}$ in employee severance leaves $\$15.0\text{ million}$ in net cash, or **$\$1.50\text{ per share}$**.

Notice how an undisciplined analyst might err:
- **Error 1**: Adding the $\$1.50$ liquidation value to the $\$16.00$ going-concern value to produce $\$17.50$. This is gross double counting.
- **Error 2**: Adding the full $\$30.0\text{M}$ cash balance instead of only the $\$20.0\text{M}$ excess cash. That would overstate equity value by $\$1.00$ per share.

At a current market quote of $P = \$13.00$, compare the discount across endpoints:
- Discount to Conservative Endpoint ($\$14.00$): $1 - \frac{\$13.00}{\$14.00} = 7.1\%$
- Discount to Optimistic Endpoint ($\$18.00$): $1 - \frac{\$13.00}{\$18.00} = 27.8\%$

The disciplined analyst does not declare a "bargain" based on the optimistic $27.8\%$ discount. At $\$13.00$, the margin of safety against the conservative endpoint is an inadequate $7.1\%$.

## Research discipline

To avoid the trap of spurious precision, enforce these guidelines in every valuation report:
1. **Present Values as Ranges**: Always provide a conservative lower bound, a central base case, and an upper bound, accompanied by the specific economic driver for each band.
2. **Strictly Quarantine Operating vs Nonoperating Assets**: Verify that any asset added to enterprise value does not produce cash flow already capitalized in operating earnings.
3. **Explicitly State the Governing Premise**: Never blend liquidation proceeds with operating cash flows into a single blended average unless an actual partial restructuring has been formally enacted.
4. **Identify the Asymmetry of Error**: Ask: "If my operating estimate is too high by $20\%$, what protects the investor?" If the answer is "nothing," the position lacks an adequate margin of safety.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Two studies show how loose an honest value range can be. Liu, Nissim and Thomas collected firms each April from 1982 to 1999 (26,613 observations before further screens). Forward-earnings multiples came within 15 percent of stock prices for about half the sample, which needed analyst forecasts and positive values, so many firm-years were excluded. Gilson, Hotchkiss and Ruback compared the market value of firms reorganizing in bankruptcy with estimates built from management's published cash flow projections: the estimates were generally unbiased, yet the ratio of estimated to market value ran from under 20% to over 250%, with errors related to claimholders' incentives to overstate or understate value.

Both benchmark against market value, and Liu and co-authors assume market efficiency. Closeness to price therefore measures agreement with the market, not whether a Graham-style estimate is right (our inference).

The cash term in the bridge carries error too. Pinkowitz, Stulz and Williamson found the relation between cash holdings and firm value much weaker in countries with poor investor protection, as agency theory predicts when controlling shareholders can extract private benefits. Alder's $20 million of excess cash is $2 a share; credit half of it and the $14–18 range becomes $13–17 (our arithmetic).

Check: at the $13 quote, a 15% band is $11.05 to $14.95. Alder's $14 low end sits inside it, so at multiple-like accuracy a 7.1% discount is indistinguishable from noise (our inference); $18, 38.5% above the price, needs a stated reason. Write what must be true for the upper endpoint.

### Sources for this section

- [Liu, Nissim & Thomas (2002) · Equity Valuation Using Multiples](https://doi.org/10.1111/1475-679X.00042) — *Research paper.* Tests how closely multiples track stock prices for firms collected each April from 1982 to 1999: forward earnings come within 15 percent for about half the sample, which excludes firms lacking analyst forecasts or positive values.
- [Gilson, Hotchkiss & Ruback (2000) · Valuation of Bankrupt Firms](https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/13.1.43) — *Research paper.* Compares market values of firms reorganizing in bankruptcy with estimates built from management's cash flow projections: unbiased on average, but the estimate-to-market ratio spans under 20% to over 250%.
- [Pinkowitz, Stulz & Williamson (2006) · Does the Contribution of Corporate Cash Holdings and Dividends to Firm Value Depend on Governance? A Cross-country Analysis](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.2006.01003.x) — *Research paper.* Valuation regressions across countries show the link between cash holdings and firm value is much weaker where investor protection is poor, so excess cash may not be worth its face amount to minority owners.

Dividing by 8M shares yields $15.00 to $20.00 per share. The analyst's suggestion to add $12M from liquidating the warehouse is an invalid double count: the warehouse is an essential operating asset required to generate the $150M–$190M operating value.
