modules.title: Supply chains, tariffs, and pass-through
modules.subtitle: Trace a policy or logistics shock through unit economics and customer behavior.
modules.objective: Trace a policy or logistics shock through unit economics and customer behavior.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A supply-chain shock changes more than a purchase price. Lead times, alternative suppliers, certification, inventory, working capital, and customer delivery commitments can all matter. Identify the exact product, jurisdiction, timing, and scope in the original announcement. A proposal, enacted measure, exemption, and implemented charge are distinct states; do not model them as interchangeable.

Pass-through is a behavioral and contractual assumption. A firm may raise prices but lose volume, absorb costs but preserve share, or redesign its supply chain at an upfront cost. A supplier's country of headquarters does not by itself determine the treatment of every shipment. For a live case, verify applicable terms through official material; the worksheet below is a fictional cost shock, not a statement of tariff law.

$$
\mathrm{Contribution}=Q\left(P-C_{\mathrm{import}}(1+\tau)-C_{\mathrm{other}}\right)
$$

## A worked example

Nusa sells 100 units at 100 each. Its per-unit imported cost is 60 and other variable cost is 20, leaving contribution of 2,000. A fictional 10% charge on the imported-cost base raises unit cost by 6. With no response, contribution falls to 1,400. Raising price by 3 while volume falls to 95 gives contribution of (103 - 66 - 20) × 95 = 1,615. Partial pass-through does not restore the original economics.

## Put the idea into practice

Build a cost bridge with the explicitly assumed charge base. Model at least no pass-through, partial pass-through with lost volume, and a supplier-switch scenario with upfront costs. Add inventory and financing needs where lead times increase. Separate the policy's announced effective date from the date the firm's income statement first reflects it. Keep uncertain scope as an open question, not a silently chosen input.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

A tariff reaches a company in stages, and studies of recent U.S. tariffs measure different stages. Cavallo and co-authors found that tariff pass-through at the border far exceeded exchange-rate pass-through, and that Chinese exporters trimmed their dollar prices only slightly. Prices in stores rose by less, which suggests that retail margins were squeezed and that the burden had so far landed largely on U.S. firms. Alviarez and co-authors, using U.S. customs data on continuing buyer-supplier relationships, estimated that suppliers take on roughly 30 percent of the 2018 tariffs, and their model implies that prices fall as a buyer accounts for more of its supplier's output. Our inference: the same charge may be shared differently by a large buyer and a small one.

Nusa's worksheet starts after the border: the supplier price stays at 60, the tariff adds 6 to unit cost, and a price rise of 3 passes on 3/6 = 50% of it. Treat the 30 percent supplier absorption as a scenario input, not a forecast: unit cost then rises 4.2 instead of 6, and contribution at a price of 103 and volume of 95 is 1,786 rather than 1,615.

Supplier switches have limits. Flaaen, Hortaçsu and Tintelnot found that earlier antidumping duties on South Korean and Chinese washers brought falling or small price changes and moved production to other export platforms. The 2018 tariffs hit nearly all source countries, and washer prices rose nearly 12 percent while dryer prices, which were not tariffed, climbed by an equivalent amount. Our inference: relocation helps mainly when the charge is country-specific, and rivals' price moves belong in the volume assumption.

Check: before choosing any scenario, write the charge's scope in one line, covering the products, the origins and the date it first reaches the income statement.

### Sources for this section

- [Cavallo, Gopinath, Neiman & Tang (2021) · Tariff Pass-Through at the Border and at the Store: Evidence from US Trade Policy](https://doi.org/10.1257/aeri.20190536) — *Research paper.* Compares tariff pass-through in import prices at the border with prices in stores and concludes retail margins absorbed part of the charge.
- [Flaaen, Hortaçsu & Tintelnot (2020) · The Production Relocation and Price Effects of US Trade Policy: The Case of Washing Machines](https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.20190611) — *Research paper.* Washing-machine evidence on relocation after country-specific duties and on price rises, including for untariffed dryers, after broad tariffs.
- [Alviarez, Fioretti, Kikkawa & Morlacco (2025) · Two-Sided Market Power in Firm-to-Firm Trade](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.12848) — *arXiv 2507.12848.* Estimates that suppliers absorb about 30 percent of the 2018 tariffs within continuing relationships, with bargaining power depending on buyer share.

modules.title: Regulation, litigation, and event-stage uncertainty
modules.subtitle: Separate allegations, proposals, decisions, appeals, and economic consequences.
modules.objective: Separate allegations, proposals, decisions, appeals, and economic consequences.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Read the status of an event before assigning a cash-flow impact. An allegation is not a judgment; an investigation is not a quantified liability; an announced rule may have implementation conditions. Identify the issuing authority, affected entity, procedural stage, stated effective date, and the source's actual claims. Do not turn legal vocabulary into a probability without a documented basis.

The economic impact can exceed an explicit fine through remediation, restricted operations, lost customers, or capital requirements. It can also be smaller if a remedy is limited or reversible. Keep a decision tree with mutually exclusive outcomes and show ranges when probabilities are uncertain. This is an analysis framework; live legal interpretation requires the current primary documents and appropriate expertise.

$$
E[C]=\sum_s p_s C_s,\qquad \sum_s p_s=1
$$

## A worked example

A fictional licensing dispute has analyst-assigned teaching scenarios: 50% no operating restriction with cost 2, 35% remediation with cost 10, and 15% closure with cost 50, all in millions and discounted to the same date. Expected cost is 12. A separate 8 of remediation spending already included in a chosen scenario must not be deducted again. The 12 is a scenario-weighted input, not a prediction that a court will order that amount.

## Put the idea into practice

Create a status timeline and a matrix of direct payments, operational restrictions, and timing. Label which facts are documented and which estimates belong to the analyst. Stress the probability of the adverse branch and the liquidity available to survive it. A small expected cost can hide an unacceptable tail outcome. Update the scenario tree when the event's stage changes, keeping the previous version for review.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Two ideas sharpen the lesson's scenario tree. The first is what the accounts already recognise. IAS 37 draws the line: an entity recognises a provision if an outflow is probable, and otherwise the item is a contingent liability. The IFRS summary gives litigation as an example of the latter when it is uncertain whether the entity committed wrongdoing and settlement is not probable. A provision is also discounted to present value. Our inference: a balance sheet without a provision does not mean zero risk, and a provision already booked should be reconciled with the scenario cost so the same amount is not deducted twice, as in the lesson's remediation warning.

The second is how large the swings can be. Cutler and Summers studied the Texaco-Pennzoil dispute over the Getty Oil takeover and found that it cost the two companies' claimants, taken together, more than $3 billion of wealth. Over the case, the gain to Pennzoil's shareholders was only one-sixth of the loss to Texaco's, and at settlement about two-thirds of the lost wealth came back. The swings exceeded most estimates of direct litigation costs and may reflect disruption of Texaco's operations. That is a single case; our inference is that the operating-restriction branch deserves its own cost line.

Probabilities deserve humility. Katz, Bommarito and Blackman built a model to predict U.S. Supreme Court outcomes using only data available before each decision. Over nearly two centuries it reached 70.2% accuracy at the case level and beat null models, and across the past century it edged out a null model optimized in-sample, by nearly 5%. Our inference: even a documented out-of-sample model with two centuries of data errs in nearly three cases in ten, so the lesson's 50/35/15 weights should be shown as ranges.

Check: move 10 points of weight from the no-restriction branch to closure. Expected cost rises from 12 to 16.8, which you can set against the liquidity available to survive the adverse branch.

### Sources for this section

- [IFRS Foundation · IAS 37 Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets](https://www.ifrs.org/issued-standards/list-of-standards/ias-37-provisions-contingent-liabilities-and-contingent-assets/) — *Official source.* Official summary of when a legal exposure becomes a recognised provision, a disclosed contingent liability, and how provisions are measured.
- [Cutler & Summers (1988) · The Costs of Conflict Resolution and Financial Distress: Evidence from the Texaco-Pennzoil Litigation](https://doi.org/10.2307/2555697) — *Research paper.* Uses market values around a landmark corporate lawsuit to show that the wealth swings exceeded most estimates of direct litigation costs.
- [Katz, Bommarito & Blackman (2016) · A General Approach for Predicting the Behavior of the Supreme Court of the United States](https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.03473) — *arXiv 1612.03473.* Out-of-sample legal-outcome model reaching 70.2% case-level accuracy, a benchmark for how reliable any outcome probability can be.

modules.title: Build a sector and company transmission map
modules.subtitle: Translate the same news into different business-model sensitivities instead of trading sector labels.
modules.objective: Translate the same news into different business-model sensitivities instead of trading sector labels.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Sector membership is a starting point, not an exposure measurement. Two banks can have different deposit mixes and loan repricing schedules; two retailers can sell necessities or discretionary goods; two software companies can differ in renewals, usage pricing, and customer concentration. Read segment economics and funding structure before generalizing from an industry headline.

Build a causal map with measurable links: news → relevant demand or cost driver → company KPI → revenue or margin → cash flow → valuation. Identify the time lag at every step and a counteracting channel. Correlated share-price moves can result from shared ownership or index flows even when near-term operating exposures differ. Distinguish that market linkage from a business linkage.

$$
\mathrm{Net\ interest\ income}=A y_A-F c_F
$$

## A worked example

A fictional bank has 1,000 of earning assets yielding 8% and 900 of funding costing 4%, for net interest income of 44 before credit losses and operating costs. In a rate-cut scenario, asset yield falls 100 basis points while funding cost falls only 50 basis points; income becomes 70 - 31.5 = 38.5. Lower borrower defaults could offset part of that decline. A retailer could instead benefit through consumer financing, while a software vendor may respond mainly through enterprise budgets and valuation rates.

## Put the idea into practice

For three firms, create an exposure table with one primary metric, one lag, one offset, and one disconfirming observation. Score evidence completeness rather than inventing a universal stock signal. Separate effects on this quarter's earnings from effects on long-run competitive position. Rank research priorities by exposure and uncertainty, then open the relevant filings to refine them.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

A transmission map separates two kinds of link. A business link is a customer, supplier or funding relationship that carries news into cash flows. Cohen and Frazzini identified related firms from each firm's principal customers and showed that stock prices are slow to reflect news about them, so a strategy built on the effect yielded monthly alphas of over 150 basis points. Pinchuk's later replication confirmed customer momentum but found that in the post-discovery sample it was smaller and lost statistical significance, consistent with exploitation by investors. Our inference: a map can show where news should travel, but a once-visible lag may no longer pay, so use the map to explain exposure rather than to manufacture signals.

A market link is different. Anton and Polk linked stocks that share the same active mutual fund owners and found that shared ownership forecasts return correlation after controls for factor exposure, style and sector similarity. They argue from the 2003 mutual fund trading scandal that shared ownership causes the excess comovement. Two stocks can move together with no operating connection, so a correlation alone should not become an arrow on the map.

The lesson's bank adds a measurable link inside one firm. Drechsler, Savov and Schnabl argue that the deposit franchise lets banks keep deposit rates low and slow to follow market rates, and show that banks closely match the rate sensitivities of interest income and expense, which insulates their equity from rate shocks. In the lesson's rate cut, income falls by 10 and expense by 4.5, so net interest income drops from 44 to 38.5. Our inference: that is an unmatched bank, and the question for a real one is where it sits.

Check: label every arrow on your map as business or market, and for each business arrow name the filing line that measures it.

### Sources for this section

- [Cohen & Frazzini (2008) · Economic Links and Predictable Returns](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.2008.01379.x) — *Research paper.* Shows that customer-supplier links carry news with a delay, so related firms' returns are predictable; a business link, not a sector label.
- [Anton & Polk (2014) · Connected Stocks](https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.12149) — *Research paper.* Shows that shared mutual fund owners create return comovement independent of sector and style, a market link without a business link.
- [Pinchuk (2023) · Customer Momentum](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.11394) — *arXiv 2301.11394.* Replicates the customer-momentum effect and finds it weaker and insignificant after its discovery, a caution on using links as signals.
- [Drechsler, Savov & Schnabl (2021) · Banking on Deposits: Maturity Transformation without Interest Rate Risk](https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.13013) — *Research paper.* Shows that banks match the rate sensitivities of interest income and expense through the deposit franchise, the measurable link behind the lesson's bank.

modules.title: Update valuation and reverse the market's assumptions
modules.subtitle: Distinguish better business prospects from an attractive price after the announcement.
modules.objective: Distinguish better business prospects from an attractive price after the announcement.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

Once you understand a business effect, you still need to connect it to value and price. An improvement may already have been expected, and a price move may include other influences. Keep three questions separate: what changed in the business, what changed in your estimate, and what changed in the market. The lessons show how to examine each with an appropriate comparison.

## Understand the idea

A sound news interpretation changes specific valuation assumptions rather than adding a vague premium for a positive story. Update cash-flow level, growth duration, reinvestment, financing claims, or the required return. Keep cash flows and discount rates matched by currency, inflation basis, and claim: equity cash flows use an equity rate, while operating cash flows require the corresponding firm-wide treatment.

Reverse valuation asks what the current price requires before deciding whether your new estimate differs meaningfully. A price increase can exceed the estimated business improvement; a good company development may leave less margin of safety. A simple perpetuity is useful for sensitivity training but requires stable distributable cash flows and a discount rate greater than growth. It cannot represent every growth stage or financing change.

$$
V=\frac{CF_1}{r-g},\qquad CF_{1,\mathrm{implied}}=P(r-g),\quad r>g
$$

## A worked example

A fictional mature firm is expected to distribute next-year equity cash flow of 6 per share, growing 2% with a 10% required return. The toy value is 75. News raises the cash flow estimate to 6.3, giving 78.75 at unchanged rates. If the stock moves from 70 to 85, the new price requires cash flow of 6.8 under those same assumptions. The business estimate improved 5%, yet the market price now exceeds the analyst's updated value.

## Put the idea into practice

Show the old model, each changed input, and the new value range. Reverse one uncertain assumption at a time rather than claiming a unique implied growth rate when several inputs can vary. Stress the required return and terminal growth together with reinvestment needs. Relate the conclusion back to Security Analysis: a narrative does not replace a conservative value range and the evidence that could invalidate it.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Reverse valuation has a research record, and it comes with warnings. Easton and Monahan examined seven accounting-based proxies for expected returns, each imputed from prices and analysts' earnings forecasts, which solves the lesson's pricing equation for the discount rate instead of for cash flow. For the entire cross-section they found the proxies unreliable: none had a positive association with realized returns, although some looked reliable when consensus long-term growth forecasts were low or analysts' forecast accuracy was high. An implied number inherits the forecasts put into it.

Li and Wang, in a preprint, apply the same arithmetic to the whole market. Dividing total market value by next-year dividends gives a valuation duration. When the tech bubble peaked, just 0.57% of market value came from the following year's dividends, a duration of 175 years; with the global financial crisis at its height, more than 2.2% did, a duration of 46 years. They report that investors know little about cash flow more than a year out, so a higher duration reflects a falling discount rate, not better news on long-run growth. At the lesson's prices, the toy firm's CF1/P moves from 6/70 = 8.57%, about 11.7 years, to 6.3/85 = 7.41%, about 13.5 years.

Which input moved? Vuolteenaho split firm-level returns into cash-flow news and expected-return news and found cash flows dominant, with a variance more than double that of expected-return news for a typical stock. Expected-return news, however, was highly correlated across firms. Our inference: if the stock's rise from 70 to 85 came with its peers, give the discount rate more weight than the cash-flow estimate.

Check: at 85 with CF1 of 6.3, r − g must be 7.41%. Holding g at 2%, r is 9.41%; holding r at 10%, g is 2.59%. State which change you can defend.

### Sources for this section

- [Easton & Monahan (2005) · An Evaluation of Accounting-Based Measures of Expected Returns](https://doi.org/10.2308/accr.2005.80.2.501) — *Research paper.* Tests implied-return proxies built from prices and analyst forecasts and finds them unreliable except where growth forecasts are low or analysts accurate.
- [Vuolteenaho (2002) · What Drives Firm-Level Stock Returns?](https://doi.org/10.1111/1540-6261.00421) — *Research paper.* Splits firm-level returns into cash-flow news and discount-rate news, the two things a price reversal cannot tell apart.
- [Li & Wang (2023) · Valuation Duration of the Stock Market](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.07110) — *arXiv 2310.07110.* Preprint measuring market value divided by next-year dividends, the lesson's 1/(r - g) multiple, and linking its swings to discount rates.

modules.title: Read the price reaction with an event-study baseline
modules.subtitle: Measure abnormal returns while separating description from causal attribution.
modules.objective: Measure abnormal returns while separating description from causal attribution.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

An event return mixes company information with market and industry movements. Start with a defined event timestamp, a predeclared return window, consistent price adjustments, and a benchmark. A market-adjusted return subtracts the benchmark; a market-model residual subtracts a return predicted using parameters estimated before the event. Neither automatically isolates the causal effect of one headline.

Confounding announcements, after-hours trading, thin liquidity, anticipatory moves, and benchmark choice complicate interpretation. Summing daily abnormal returns is a short-window CAR convention, distinct from compounding wealth. A single company's short-window residual is descriptive evidence; statistical claims need an appropriate design, uncertainty estimates, and attention to dependence across events.

$$
AR_t=R_{i,t}-R_{m,t},\qquad CAR=\sum_{t\in W}AR_t
$$

## A worked example

Across three fictional event-window days, Cedar returns 1%, -3%, and 2%, while the chosen market returns 0.5%, -1%, and 0.5%. Simple market-adjusted abnormal returns are 0.5%, -2%, and 1.5%, summing to zero. A sensational -3% middle-day headline misses both the market decline and the rebound. Zero CAR does not prove the event was irrelevant; other news or an unsuitable benchmark may mask its effect.

## Put the idea into practice

Write the event window before inspecting the reaction and record competing announcements. Compare more than one defensible benchmark without choosing the one that supports your thesis. If fitting beta, use only pre-event observations and check stability. Report raw and abnormal returns, adjustment method, and limitations together. Do not assume the release price was an executable fill for someone who only read the news afterward.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Cedar's zero CAR hides a benchmark choice. A market-adjusted return assumes a beta of 1, while a market-model residual is Cedar's return minus α minus β times the market return. Cedar's three returns sum to zero and so do the market's, so the three-day sum equals −3α whatever β is. Only the daily path shows the choice. With β = 1.5 the abnormal returns are 0.25%, −1.5% and 1.25%; with β = 0.5 they are 0.75%, −2.5% and 1.75%. The middle day stays negative, but how much of its −3% belongs to Cedar depends on a beta that must come from pre-event data.

Goldsmith-Pinkham and Lyu, in a 2025 preprint, show why such choices matter. Standard event studies assume a linear factor model whose factors are known; if that model is wrong, which the authors treat as nearly certain, the estimated effects are inconsistent. The distortion grows in turbulent markets, in long-horizon windows, and when the date of the news is tied to market conditions. For short windows with randomly timed events they say the conventional approach holds up, and as an alternative they propose synthetic controls assembled from comparison securities. Firms often pick their own release times, so a short window helps without settling the question (our inference).

Dependence is a second trap. Kolari and Pynnönen show that when events share a date, even modest correlation among firms' abnormal returns leads standard tests to reject a zero average effect too often. If one tariff headline moves five suppliers on the same day, treat it as one cluster, not five independent observations.

Check: re-run Cedar with β = 0.5, 1 and 1.5, and state which conclusion survives all three.

### Sources for this section

- [Kolari & Pynnönen (2010) · Event Study Testing with Cross-sectional Correlation of Abnormal Returns](https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhq072) — *Research paper.* Shows that event-date clustering with even low cross-correlation makes standard tests over-reject, so same-day sector headlines are not independent observations.
- [Goldsmith-Pinkham & Lyu (2025) · Causal Inference in Financial Event Studies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.15123) — *arXiv 2511.15123.* Explains how a misspecified factor model biases abnormal returns, most in volatile periods and long horizons, and why short windows are safer.

modules.title: Liquidity, positioning, and second-order effects
modules.subtitle: Interpret rapid market reactions without mistaking a price mechanism for a business change.
modules.objective: Interpret rapid market reactions without mistaking a price mechanism for a business change.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

News can move prices through order flow before an analyst can update a business model. Wide spreads, limited depth, forced selling, short covering, and index-related trades can amplify a move. These are possible mechanisms to investigate, not explanations to assert from a candle alone. A one-day rally need not mean estimated intrinsic value rose by the same amount.

Second-order effects follow responses: a competitor may gain customers after a rival's disruption, but capacity limits or shared suppliers can reduce that benefit. Ask who must act, over what horizon, and with which constraints. Positioning data, where available, often has lags and incomplete coverage. Keep sourced positioning facts separate from speculation about what 'everyone' owns.

$$
\mathrm{Quoted\ spread}=Ask-Bid,\qquad \mathrm{Midpoint}=\frac{Ask+Bid}{2}
$$

## A worked example

A fictional stock was quoted 100.00/100.10 before news and 98.00/102.00 after it. The midpoint remains 100, while the quoted spread widens from 0.10 to 4.00. A market buy of 100 shares at the offered price would cost 200 more than the midpoint reference, assuming enough shares at that offer and excluding fees. The midpoint alone conceals a large execution cost; a limit price controls a bound but may leave the order unfilled.

## Put the idea into practice

Record bid, ask, timestamp, market status, and available depth when studying execution. Separate a mark-to-market observation from a realizable return. In a second-order company map, identify capacity, contract, and input constraints before assigning a rival's lost sales to a beneficiary. A clear decision can be to wait for reliable prices and source confirmation while preserving the research thesis.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

The lesson's quote moves from 100.00/100.10 to 98.00/102.00 while the midpoint stays put, so the quote carries a liquidity message, not a valuation one. Lee and co-authors studied NYSE firms and found that wide spreads go with thin depth, and that ahead of earnings releases spreads widen and depth shrinks, more so when the eventual price change is large. They read this as liquidity providers managing information-asymmetry risk with both spreads and depths. A quote of 98.00/102.00 may therefore be dealers protecting themselves, and the quoted size matters as much as the quoted price.

Forced trading is a second mechanism. Coval and Stafford examined fund trades driven by capital flows between 1980 and 2003. Funds hit by large outflows tended to shrink their holdings, which put price pressure on the stocks these funds held in common, and investors who traded against such constrained funds earned highly significant returns for supplying liquidity. Our inference: a drop that reverses without new facts fits price pressure better than a lasting change in value, though one case cannot prove which.

News may also explain less than expected. Joulin and co-authors cross-correlated high-frequency stock returns with several news feeds. Neither company-specific nor market-wide news accounted for how often prices jump or how large the jumps are, and the authors suspect that most jumps come from swings in order flow when liquidity nearly vanishes.

Check: the post-news half-spread of 2.00 is 2% of the 100 midpoint, against 0.05% before it. For the next jump you study, record the quoted size at the bid and the offer, then see whether the price level held a week later.

### Sources for this section

- [Lee, Mucklow & Ready (1993) · Spreads, Depths, and the Impact of Earnings Information: An Intraday Analysis](https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/6.2.345) — *Research paper.* Shows that spreads widen and depths fall around earnings news, so a wide quote signals dealers' information risk as well as a trading cost.
- [Coval & Stafford (2007) · Asset fire sales (and purchases) in equity markets](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2006.09.007) — *Research paper.* Documents price pressure from fund outflows and the returns earned by liquidity providers, a flow mechanism separate from a business change.
- [Joulin et al. (2008) · Stock price jumps: news and volume play a minor role](https://arxiv.org/abs/0803.1769) — *arXiv 0803.1769.* Cross-correlates high-frequency returns with news feeds and finds that news does not explain the frequency or size of price jumps.

modules.title: Scenarios, Bayesian updates, and correlated evidence
modules.subtitle: Update conviction proportionally while avoiding false precision and duplicate evidence.
modules.objective: Update conviction proportionally while avoiding false precision and duplicate evidence.

modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A news item should update a prior assessment rather than automatically replacing it. For a binary teaching case, Bayes' rule combines a prior probability with the likelihood of seeing the evidence under each state. The likelihood ratio measures discrimination; it is not the probability that the source is correct. Real investment states and observation processes are usually more complex than this binary model.

Do not multiply evidence weights as though dependent reports were independent. Several articles derived from the same company release can repeat one signal. Subjective probabilities need ranges and sensitivity checks, particularly when the evidence's reliability is uncertain. Confidence should describe what the evidence supports, while position or research decisions also consider costs, downside, liquidity, and model error.

$$
P(H\mid E)=\frac{P(E\mid H)P(H)}{P(E\mid H)P(H)+P(E\mid\neg H)(1-P(H))}
$$

## A worked example

Suppose an analyst assigns a fictional 20% prior probability to a lasting margin recovery. A specific independently verified operational signal has probability 60% if recovery is real and 20% otherwise. The posterior is 0.12 / (0.12 + 0.16), or about 42.86%. The evidence raises the probability but does not establish certainty. Reprinting that same operational report in two newspapers is not a second independent signal.

## Put the idea into practice

Write the prior, event definition, likelihood assumptions, and source independence assessment before calculating. Test weaker signal reliability and alternative base rates. Use scenario-weighted values only when outcomes and their units are compatible, and show downside separately. In a memo, state 'conviction increases under these likelihood assumptions' rather than presenting a subjective posterior as a measured natural constant.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

The lesson's 42.86% posterior counts the verified operational report once. Enke and Zimmermann show why that discipline matters. In their experiments many people neglected the correlation between signals and treated correlated information as independent, so beliefs reacted too strongly to widely connected sources, a pattern the authors call overshooting. In an experimental asset market, the confidence swings this caused produced predictable bubbles and crashes. Apply the same slip to the lesson. Prior odds are 0.25 and the likelihood ratio is 3 (60% over 20%). Counting the report and one newspaper reprint as two signals gives odds of 0.25 × 3 × 3 = 2.25, a posterior of about 69.2%; two reprints would give about 87.1%, and no new fact has arrived.

A vivid report can mislead even when it is counted once. Griffin and Tversky separate the strength of evidence, meaning how extreme it looks, from its weight, meaning the credibility of the source or how large the sample is. People, they argue, attend mostly to strength, which breeds overconfidence when evidence is striking but thin. Augenblick and co-authors add that the error depends on signal size: in experiments, sports betting and financial markets alike, people drew too much from weak signals and too little from strong ones. Our inference: expect your gut to overshoot the Bayes arithmetic on a minor datum and to undershoot on a decisive one.

Check: give each report two ratings, how extreme it is and how much weight its source can bear, then recompute the posterior with every shared-origin report counted once.

### Sources for this section

- [Enke & Zimmermann (2017) · Correlation Neglect in Belief Formation](https://doi.org/10.1093/restud/rdx081) — *Research paper.* Experiments showing that people treat correlated signals as independent, which inflates beliefs and, in an asset market, produces bubbles and crashes.
- [Griffin & Tversky (1992) · The weighing of evidence and the determinants of confidence](https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285%2892%2990013-R) — *Research paper.* Separates the strength of evidence from its weight and explains when confidence runs ahead of what the source can support.
- [Augenblick, Lazarus & Thaler (2021) · Overinference from Weak Signals and Underinference from Strong Signals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.09871) — *arXiv 2109.09871.* Finds in experiments, betting markets and financial markets that people overreact to weak signals and underreact to strong ones.

modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

A research memo should let someone retrace your reasoning. Begin with the question and the dated sources, then show the calculation, alternatives, and conclusion. In this unit, you will bring the earlier steps together and review where AI can assist. Every important claim should remain connected to evidence that a reader can inspect.

## Understand the idea

A useful news memo lets another person retrace the reasoning without trusting your tone. Start with the question, decision time, and source ledger. Keep the sourced facts separate from the company's interpretation and your own forecast. Connect each modeled change to a specific driver, assumption, and follow-up test. A list of links without a causal explanation is not yet analysis.

Use an original short summary with publisher, title, link, date, and relevant location. Credit the source of figures and distinguish licensed data from your calculations. A reference does not itself grant permission to republish an article, chart, photograph, or dataset. The course's fictional packet is supplied for practice; for live research use material you may access and reuse appropriately, without fabricating quotations or sources.

$$
\mathrm{Evidence\ coverage}=\frac{\mathrm{Claims\ with\ verified\ support}}{\mathrm{Claims\ requiring\ support}}
$$

## A worked example

Your fictional packet contains an issuer release, an older annual report, a central-bank summary, and a derivative commentary article. Six claims appear in the draft memo, but only four have verified source locations. Evidence coverage is 4/6, or 66.67%; that is a workflow measure, not a probability that the investment thesis is right. Two unsupported claims about customer losses must be marked as hypotheses or removed.

## Put the idea into practice

Use the downloadable memo template: question; source timeline; facts; expectation baseline; business bridge; valuation range; alternative explanations; decision; next review. Link the note to the lesson in Quanta's notebook. For every conclusion write what would change your mind. Preserve previous memo versions so you can distinguish information improvements from hindsight rewriting.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

The lesson's evidence coverage of 4/6 is a recall-type measure. Liu and co-authors, auditing four generative search engines, paired two such measures: citation recall, meaning statements fully backed by their citations, and citation precision, meaning citations that genuinely support the statement they are attached to. On average only 51.5% of generated sentences were fully supported and only 74.5% of citations supported their sentence. Our inference: a memo needs both ratios, because a link beside a claim does not prove the page backs it.

The CIA-hosted Tradecraft Primer of 2009 supplies a ledger and a method. Its quality-of-information check suggests a database that sorts information by source type and date, with notes on each source's strengths and weaknesses, and it cautions that several sources do not replace information that has been properly vetted. That describes the packet's derivative commentary article: another link, not another fact. For the alternative-explanations section, the primer describes analysis of competing hypotheses: list hypotheses as columns and evidence as rows, mark each item consistent, inconsistent or not applicable, and treat evidence that fits every hypothesis as unimportant for choosing among them.

Do not oversell the method. Dhami and co-authors randomly assigned fifty intelligence analysts to use it or not. The trained analysts skipped some of its steps, the evidence that it curbs confirmation bias was mixed, and it may even raise inconsistency and error in judgement. Our inference: use the matrix as a transparency device, not as proof.

Check: mark each of the six claims as having a verified source location or not, mark each citation as supporting its claim or not, and report both ratios.

### Sources for this section

- [Liu, Zhang & Liang (2023) · Evaluating Verifiability in Generative Search Engines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.09848) — *arXiv 2304.09848.* Defines citation recall and precision and measures how often AI-generated answers are actually supported by their cited sources.
- [U.S. Government · CIA Center for the Study of Intelligence (2009) · A Tradecraft Primer: Structured Analytic Techniques for Improving Intelligence Analysis](https://www.cia.gov/resources/csi/static/Tradecraft-Primer-apr09.pdf) — *Official source.* Describes a source-quality check and the analysis of competing hypotheses matrix, which map onto the memo's source ledger and alternative explanations.
- [Dhami, Belton & Mandel (2019) · The “analysis of competing hypotheses” in intelligence analysis](https://doi.org/10.1002/acp.3550) — *Research paper.* A randomized test with intelligence analysts that found mixed evidence for the technique, a caution against treating a matrix as proof.

## Understand the idea

An AI summary can omit qualifiers, confuse an issuer with a subsidiary, mix reporting periods, or invent a citation. Use a fixed extraction schema: entity, event, event time, publication time, numeric claim, unit, source location, confidence, and unresolved ambiguity. Require the tool to distinguish an unsupported field from an empty value. Verify consequential claims against the original material.

Sentiment labels describe language under a labeling rule, not cash flow or expected returns. Positive wording can accompany an earnings miss. Evaluate on a labeled sample with duplicates grouped and time-based separation; a random split can leak repeated press releases across training and evaluation. Document false positives, false negatives, class balance, and the human review burden. Do not paste restricted articles into a service without checking permitted use.

$$
\mathrm{Precision}=\frac{TP}{TP+FP},\qquad\mathrm{Recall}=\frac{TP}{TP+FN}
$$

## A worked example

A fictional material-event classifier flags 20 items: 12 are true material events and 8 are false alarms. It misses another 6 true events. Precision is 12/20 = 60%; recall is 12/18 = 66.67%. Those metrics assess the declared labels, not trading profitability. If repeated versions of one release appear in both evaluation and training, even those scores may be overstated.

## Put the idea into practice

Compare tool output with a manually checked source ledger. Create a small failure log containing negation mistakes, wrong units, stale guidance, duplicate stories, and mismatched entities. Use a held-out date interval and deduplicated event groups. Set a human verification gate for source links and business-impact calculations. Connect further model work to the Machine learning for stocks course rather than treating this classifier worksheet as a complete trained model.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

The lesson's 60% precision and 66.67% recall measure agreement with a declared label, so the labeling rule deserves scrutiny too. Loughran and McDonald found that, across a large set of 10-Ks from 1994 to 2008, nearly three quarters of the words that the Harvard Dictionary tags as negative do not usually carry a negative meaning in financial writing. They built finance-specific word lists and linked them to returns around filings, trading volume, volatility, fraud, material weaknesses and earnings surprises. Record which lexicon or model version produced each label.

Extraction needs its own audit. Islam and co-authors tested 16 model configurations on a sample of 150 cases and manually reviewed 2,400 answers. GPT-4-Turbo paired with a retrieval system gave a wrong answer or declined to answer for 81% of questions, and every model showed weaknesses such as hallucinations. Those were 2023-era systems, so treat 81% as a snapshot, not a current error rate (our inference); the lesson is the verification gate.

Dates need care with language models. Lopez-Lira and co-authors argue that a model's forecasts about periods inside its training data deserve no trust: once it has seen the outcome, good output could be skill or memory, and the two cannot be separated. Telling the model to respect historical boundaries did not prevent accurate recall, and masking did not help because models rebuild entities and dates from small clues. For events after the cutoff they found no recall. Our inference: a held-out date interval must start after the model's training cutoff, not merely after your own training sample.

Check: run the classifier only on events dated after the tool's stated cutoff, and count wrong, refused and unsupported extractions separately.

### Sources for this section

- [Loughran & McDonald (2011) · When Is a Liability Not a Liability? Textual Analysis, Dictionaries, and 10-Ks](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.2010.01625.x) — *Research paper.* Shows that a general-purpose negative-word list misclassifies financial text, so a sentiment label depends on the dictionary behind it.
- [Islam et al. (2023) · FinanceBench: A New Benchmark for Financial Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.11944) — *arXiv 2311.11944.* Manually reviews thousands of model answers about public companies and reports high rates of wrong or refused answers and hallucinations.
- [Lopez-Lira, Tang & Zhu (2025) · The Memorization Problem: Can We Trust LLMs' Economic Forecasts?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.14765) — *arXiv 2504.14765.* Shows that language models recall data from their training period, which undermines tests run on dates the model has already seen.

modules.title: Review decisions, avoid hindsight, and know when to wait
modules.subtitle: Evaluate the quality of the reasoning separately from the next price move.
modules.objective: Evaluate the quality of the reasoning separately from the next price move.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A good decision can lose money, and a weak process can get lucky. Preserve the prediction, probability, horizon, source set, and invalidation condition before observing the outcome. Review both the accuracy of factual extraction and the appropriateness of the business mechanism. Do not rewrite the original thesis after prices move.

Use a decision log to distinguish 'evidence was wrong', 'mechanism was incomplete', 'timing differed', and 'outcome was within the stated downside distribution'. Probability scores can evaluate calibration over a suitable set of resolved events, but tiny, selected, or dependent samples do not support broad claims. A decision to wait is substantive when it specifies what information or price condition would justify reopening the case.

$$
\mathrm{Brier\ score}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_i(p_i-y_i)^2
$$

## A worked example

Three fictional binary forecasts assign probabilities 0.8, 0.6, and 0.3 to precisely defined events. Outcomes are 1, 0, and 1. Their mean squared probability error is (0.04 + 0.36 + 0.49)/3 = 0.2967. A constant 0.5 forecast scores 0.25 on these same three cases, which is better for this loss on this sample. The result is not enough to conclude the analyst has no skill across all news events.

## Put the idea into practice

Schedule a review date and outcome-resolution rule at memo creation. Record changes as new versions with new evidence. Compare with a declared baseline, keep unsuccessful and no-action cases, and avoid choosing the scoring window after the fact. Note unresolved events separately. For paper execution, include delay, spreads, fees, and the possibility of no fill; a research signal does not grant access to a past price.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Hindsight bias is why the lesson fixes the log before the outcome. Biais and Weber model agents who, once they have seen information, forget how little they knew beforehand. In an experiment with 66 students, hindsight bias reduced volatility estimates, and in another with 85 investment bankers working in London and Frankfurt, the more biased agents had lower performance. Roese and Vohs add that prompting people to weigh other causal stories for an outcome can weaken the bias. Our inference: the lesson's log categories (evidence wrong, mechanism incomplete, timing differed, within the downside) work partly because they force alternatives.

Scoring has its own hindsight trap. Murphy partitioned the Brier score into the uncertainty built into the events, the reliability of the forecasts and their resolution, and defined the uncertainty term as the score of the sample's relative frequencies. For the lesson's outcomes 1, 0 and 1 that frequency is 2/3, and a constant forecast of 2/3 scores 0.2222, better than the analyst's 0.2967 and better than the 0.25 of a constant 0.5. That baseline uses the outcomes, so nobody could have declared it in advance; write the baseline, such as a base rate from earlier events, into the memo.

Three cases cannot show calibration either. Dimitriadis and co-authors note that the usual way of binning forecasts for reliability diagrams gives unstable pictures because it hangs on arbitrary implementation choices, and their CORP method lets you attach uncertainty estimates. Pool resolved events before reading any calibration plot.

Check: at memo creation write the baseline, review date and resolution rule, then score every resolved event, including no-action cases, against that baseline.

### Sources for this section

- [Biais & Weber (2009) · Hindsight Bias, Risk Perception, and Investment Performance](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.1090.1000) — *Research paper.* Experiments with students and investment bankers linking hindsight bias to lower volatility estimates and lower performance.
- [Roese & Vohs (2012) · Hindsight Bias](https://doi.org/10.1177/1745691612454303) — *Research paper.* Review of what hindsight bias is, where it comes from and why considering alternative causal explanations can reduce it.
- [Murphy (1973) · A New Vector Partition of the Probability Score](https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0450%281973%29012%3C0595%3AANVPOT%3E2.0.CO%3B2) — *Research paper.* Splits the Brier score into uncertainty, reliability and resolution, with uncertainty defined by the sample's own relative frequencies.
- [Dimitriadis, Gneiting & Jordan (2020) · Evaluating probabilistic classifiers: Reliability diagrams and score decompositions revisited](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.03033) — *arXiv 2008.03033.* Shows why binned reliability diagrams are unstable and offers a method that attaches uncertainty to calibration checks.

modules.subtitle: Defend a complete evidence-to-cash-flow-to-price interpretation, including an alternative case.
modules.objective: Defend a complete evidence-to-cash-flow-to-price interpretation, including an alternative case.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Combine the course into one dated investment-research memo. Your deliverable is a reasoning chain with traceable inputs, a range of outcomes, and a revision rule. Separate what changed in the business from what changed in market expectations. A final exam checks concepts; it cannot certify the quality of a written memo or turn a fictional exercise into a live recommendation.

Use the supplied fictional Banyu Industrials packet and the reusable memo template. Each release has an availability time so you can reconstruct two information sets. Show revenue, costs, operating profit, cash conversion, financing claims, and diluted shares before assigning a value. The valuation cases deliberately simplify taxes and stable growth; discuss what a real multi-period model would require.

$$
FCFF=EBIT(1-T)+D\&A-Capex-\Delta NWC,\qquad V_{share}=\frac{FCFF_1/(WACC-g)-NetDebt}{Shares}
$$

## A worked example

Before the news, Banyu has sales of 1,000, variable cost of 600, and fixed operating cost of 200, so EBIT is 200. A confirmed input shock raises variable cost by 30, a conditional contract adds 20 of sales at 40% contribution, and efficiency saves 12. Base-case EBIT becomes 190. At 25% tax, depreciation 30, capex 40, and working-capital investment 20, illustrative next-year FCFF is 112.5. A 10% firm-wide discount rate and 2% perpetual growth imply operating value 1,406.25; subtract net debt of 300 and divide by 100 shares to get 11.0625 per share. At price 12, this base case offers no discount.

## Put the idea into practice

Build a downside case that removes the conditional contract, uses working-capital investment of 35, and raises the discount rate to 11%. EBIT is 182, FCFF is 91.5, and value per share is about 7.1667. Apply a hypothetical 25% required margin to that downside estimate to obtain a research price threshold of 5.375. Do not call this a recommended order: the threshold is conditional on a crude fictional model. Explain debt maturity, reinvestment, growth, and event-probability omissions, then write what evidence would justify a model update.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Banyu's one forecast year capitalized forever is a crude model, so ask how well even careful discounted cash flow does. Kaplan and Ruback compared the discounted value of cash flow forecasts with the market values of 51 highly leveraged transactions from 1983 to 1989. The valuations landed within 10 percent on average and did no worse than approaches built on comparable companies and deals. Our inference: the sample is narrow, and an average can hide larger single-case misses.

Horizon matters too. Penman and Sougiannis note that standard formulas need payoffs forecast to infinity, while practical analysis uses a finite horizon and needs troublesome terminal-value calculations. They valued firms from average realized payoffs across several horizons, with or without a terminal value, and compared the results with market prices. Errors were lower for accrual-earnings techniques than for cash-flow and dividend discounting. Banyu's whole value capitalizes one year, including its capex and working-capital investment.

Inputs swing the answer. With FCFF₁ held at 112.5, an 11% discount rate gives 9.50 per share and 3% growth gives about 13.07, against 11.0625 in the base case and a price of 12 (the growth case is crude, since faster growth usually needs more reinvestment). Either change exceeds the 0.9375 gap between value and price, and net debt magnifies it. Yee notes that DCF, comparables and fundamental analysis usually produce conflicting estimates that also tend to differ from the market price, and his Bayesian framework supports averaging them. Our inference: report the base case, the downside case and the market price as a range.

Check: re-run the base case at 9%, 10% and 11% and write the three per-share values beside the price of 12.

### Sources for this section

- [Kaplan & Ruback (1995) · The Valuation of Cash Flow Forecasts: An Empirical Analysis](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1995.tb04050.x) — *Research paper.* Tests discounted cash flow against transaction values in 51 deals and finds it within 10 percent on average, a benchmark for how far a model can be trusted.
- [Penman & Sougiannis (1998) · A Comparison of Dividend, Cash Flow, and Earnings Approaches to Equity Valuation](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1911-3846.1998.tb00564.x) — *Research paper.* Compares valuation techniques over finite horizons and finds lower errors for accrual earnings than for cash-flow discounting.
- [Yee (2007) · A Bayesian Framework for Combining Valuation Estimates](https://arxiv.org/abs/0707.3482) — *arXiv 0707.3482.* Argues that discounted cash flow, comparables and market price disagree and justifies combining them instead of trusting one.

readingGuide:
A headline can describe an important event without telling you what it means for a particular company. This course slows down the reasoning between reading the news and forming an investment view. You will check the source, understand the size and timing of the change, and follow its possible effects on sales, costs, cash flow, and value.

Work through each case in three passes. First write what the source actually establishes. Next calculate the possible business effect using clearly stated assumptions. Finally explain what remains uncertain and what investors may already have expected. Indonesian inflation, interest-rate, and rupiah examples help you practise the same method in a familiar setting. Keep your evidence and your interpretation in separate parts of the research memo.

24 lessons × 30 minutes = 12 hours of guided study across six units. Each session includes 8 minutes of lesson and primary-source reading, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation.

This estimate includes assignments; exam time is additional. There are 48 practice questions, six four-question checkpoints, and a 24-question final.

The capstone memo is self-assessed separately. All company names, releases, estimates, probabilities, and prices in the cases are fictional; the course contains no live news feed or stock recommendations.

modules.title: Time value of money
modules.subtitle: Put cash flows on a timeline and use a discount rate consistent with their timing and units.
modules.objective: Put cash flows on a timeline and use a discount rate consistent with their timing and units.
modules.reading: CFA Institute, Quantitative Investment Analysis, fourth edition · Chapter 1. Pair the book reading with this original application; course lesson numbers are independent of book chapter numbers.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

Receiving money today and receiving the same amount later are different because money available now can be put to use. Present value translates future payments into an equivalent amount today under a chosen rate. Begin by drawing a timeline. Place each payment on its own date before using the equation; the timing explains the exponent in the calculation.

## The analytical question

The foundational premise of financial mathematics is that a unit of currency received today is worth more than the same unit of currency received in the future. This divergence arises from three economic forces:
1. **The Opportunity Cost of Capital**: Capital available today can be invested to earn a productive return.
2. **Purchasing Power Depletion (Inflation)**: Future prices are generally higher, reducing the real goods and services a fixed nominal payment can purchase.
3. **Credit and Uncertainty Risk**: A promised future payment carries the risk that the payer may default or experience financial distress.

To evaluate any investment security, all projected future cash receipts and disbursements must be translated onto a single, synchronized date. This operation is governed by the **Present Value (PV)** equation:

$$
PV = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{CF_t}{(1 + r)^t}
$$

Where:
- $CF_t$ represents the expected net cash flow occurring at the end of period $t$.
- $r$ is the periodic discount rate (the required hurdle rate of return) reflecting opportunity cost and risk.
- $t$ is the exact time index (measured in consistent periods: years, semi-annual periods, or months).

A pervasive analytical error is mixing **cash flow units and discount rate conventions**:
- **Nominal vs Real**: A nominal cash flow forecast (which includes expected inflation) must be discounted at a **nominal discount rate**. Discounting nominal cash flows at a real interest rate produces an artificially inflated present value!
- **Matching Compounding Frequency**: If cash flows arrive quarterly, the discount rate must be expressed as an effective quarterly rate ($r_{\text{quarterly}} = (1 + r_{\text{annual}})^{1/4} - 1$), not an annual rate divided haphazardly.

When valuing perpetual cash flows, we encounter two classical asymptotic forms:
1. **Constant Flat Perpetuity**:

$$
PV = \frac{C}{r} \quad (\text{for constant periodic payment } C)
$$

2. **Growing Perpetuity (Gordon Model)**:

$$
PV = \frac{CF_1}{r - g} \quad (\text{requires } r > g)
$$

Notice the strict mathematical boundary: if the perpetual growth rate $g$ equals or exceeds the discount rate $r$, the denominator becomes zero or negative, rendering the finite-value formula completely undefined.

## A worked example

Consider a specialized mezzanine debt claim that promises two contractual cash payments:
- $CF_1 = \$110.00$ to be received exactly 1 year from today.
- $CF_2 = \$121.00$ to be received exactly 2 years from today.
- The investor's required opportunity cost of capital for this risk class is $r = 10.0\%\text{ per year}$ ($0.10$).

Let us compute the present value step-by-step:
1. Discount Year 1 Cash Flow:

$$
PV_1 = \frac{\$110.00}{(1.10)^1} = \frac{\$110.00}{1.10} = \$100.00
$$

2. Discount Year 2 Cash Flow:

$$
PV_2 = \frac{\$121.00}{(1.10)^2} = \frac{\$121.00}{1.21} = \$100.00
$$

3. Total Contractual Present Value:

$$
PV = PV_1 + PV_2 = \$100.00 + \$100.00 = \$200.00
$$

Observe the common arithmetic blunder:
An unsophisticated analyst sums the nominal cash flows ($\$110 + \$121 = \$231$) and simply divides by $1.10$, arriving at $\$210.00$. This error under-discounts the second payment by treating a two-year obligation as if it matured in one year!

Now examine a perpetual equity royalty stream:
The royalty promises $CF_1 = \$5.00$ next year, with cash flows projected to grow perpetually at $g = 2.0\%$ per year. The required rate of return is $r = 7.0\%$:

$$
PV = \frac{\$5.00}{0.07 - 0.02} = \frac{\$5.00}{0.05} = \$100.00
$$

If an analyst aggressively raises the growth assumption from $2.0\%$ to $5.0\%$, the denominator shrinks from $0.05$ to $0.02$, causing the estimated value to explode from $\$100.00$ to $\$250.00$ ($+150\%$). Sensitivity to long-term growth dominates the valuation.

### Move each payment back to today

At a 10% annual rate, $100 today grows to $110 after one year. To reverse that step, divide the one-year payment of $110 by 1.10. The result is $100 today.

The second payment is two years away. Reverse two periods of growth by dividing $121 by 1.10 twice, or by 1.10 squared. That also gives $100. Only after placing both payments on the same date should you add them: $100 + $100 = $200. Dividing $231 by 1.10 only once would treat both payments as arriving in one year.

The perpetuity calculation describes a different payment pattern that continues indefinitely under the stated growth assumption. Subtract 2% growth from the 7% required return to get 5%, or 0.05. Dividing next year's $5 payment by 0.05 gives $100. The result depends on that continuing pattern and on the required return remaining above the growth rate.

## Research discipline

To ensure institutional rigor in time-value-of-money models:
1. **Draw the Explicit Cash Flow Timeline**: Before writing code or entering numbers, plot every payment on a numbered time grid ($t=0, 1, 2, \dots, T$). Verify whether payments occur at period-end (ordinary annuity) or period-beginning (annuity due).
2. **Audit Nominal vs Real Consistency**: In corporate filings, check whether management's capital project projections are in constant purchasing-power dollars or nominal inflation-adjusted dollars.
3. **Conduct Terminal Value Decomposition**:

$$
\text{Terminal Value Percentage} = \frac{PV(\text{Terminal Value})}{PV(\text{Total Asset})}
$$

   If more than $75\%$ of an asset's present value resides in cash flows occurring beyond Year 10, recognize that the thesis is primarily a speculation on terminal growth.
4. **Never Rely on Blind Spreadsheet Formulas**: Always verify that the built-in function conventions (e.g., Excel `NPV` assumes period 1 discounting, whereas Python array indexing starts at 0) match your intended timeline.

assignment.prompt: Discount cash flows of $105.00 at Year 1 and $110.25 at Year 2 at a 5.0% annual discount rate. Then calculate the present value if both payments are shifted one year earlier (Year 0 and Year 1). Explain the economic difference.
assignment.solution: For payments at Year 1 and 2: PV = $105 / (1.05)^1 + $110.25 / (1.05)^2 = $100.00 + $100.00 = $200.00. If shifted one year earlier (Year 0 and 1): PV = $105 / (1.05)^0 + $110.25 / (1.05)^1 = $105.00 + $105.00 = $210.00. Shifting cash flows one year earlier eliminates one period of discounting, multiplying total present value by exactly (1 + r) = 1.05 ($200 × 1.05 = $210). Receiving money sooner increases economic value by avoiding delay.

modules.title: Compounding, annuities, NPV, and IRR
modules.subtitle: Distinguish nominal from effective rates, value annuities, and evaluate capital projects using NPV and IRR.
modules.objective: Distinguish nominal from effective rates, value annuities, and evaluate capital projects using NPV and IRR.
modules.reading: CFA Institute, Quantitative Investment Analysis, fourth edition · Chapter 1. Pair the book reading with this original application; course lesson numbers are independent of book chapter numbers.
modules.content:
## The analytical question

When evaluating investments across different financing agreements, interest rates are quoted under varying compounding frequencies (annual, semi-annual, monthly, continuous). A stated nominal annual rate does not reflect the true economic return earned over a full year due to intra-year interest reinvestment.

To compare rates on a uniform footing, the analyst must compute the **Effective Annual Rate (EAR)**:

$$
\text{EAR} = \left(1 + \frac{r_{\text{stated}}}{m}\right)^m - 1
$$

Where $r_{\text{stated}}$ is the stated annual percentage rate, and $m$ is the number of compounding periods per year. Under the mathematical limit of **continuous compounding** ($m \to \infty$):

$$
\text{EAR}_{\text{continuous}} = e^{r_{\text{stated}}} - 1
$$

In project finance and capital budgeting, two primary criteria govern resource allocation:
1. **Net Present Value (NPV)**: The present value of all expected future cash inflows minus the initial cash outlay:

$$
NPV = \sum_{t=1}^T \frac{CF_t}{(1 + k)^t} - C_0
$$

   Where $k$ is the project's cost of capital. A project creates economic value if and only if $NPV > 0$.
2. **Internal Rate of Return (IRR)**: The discount rate that equates the present value of future cash inflows with the initial investment, forcing $NPV = 0$:

$$
\sum_{t=1}^T \frac{CF_t}{(1 + \text{IRR})^t} - C_0 = 0
$$

Graham, Dodd, and modern CFA quantitative standards establish strict warnings regarding **IRR pitfalls**:
- **The Reinvestment Rate Fallacy**: IRR implicitly assumes all intermediate cash flows can be reinvested at the IRR itself (which may be an unrealistically high $40\%$), whereas NPV correctly assumes reinvestment at the actual cost of capital ($k$).
- **Multiple IRRs and Non-Normal Cash Flows**: If a project involves cash outflows in later years (e.g., environmental decommissioning), Descartes' Rule of Signs dictates that there may be multiple positive IRRs, making the IRR metric completely unreliable.
- **Scale and Mutually Exclusive Projects**: A small project earning a $50\%$ IRR on a $\$1,000$ investment generates less economic wealth than a large project earning a $20\%$ IRR on a $\$1,000,000$ investment. In all mutually exclusive project decisions, **NPV strictly dominates IRR**.

## A worked example

Let us evaluate the effective compounding rate and capital budgeting decisions for Alder Manufacturing:

### 1. Compounding Frequency Audit
A commercial lender offers Alder two financing structures:
- **Loan A**: Stated rate $6.0\%$ compounded semi-annually ($m = 2$).

$$
\text{EAR}_A = \left(1 + \frac{0.06}{2}\right)^2 - 1 = (1.03)^2 - 1 = 6.09\%
$$

- **Loan B**: Stated rate $5.95\%$ compounded monthly ($m = 12$).

$$
\text{EAR}_B = \left(1 + \frac{0.0595}{12}\right)^{12} - 1 = (1.004958)^{12} - 1 = 6.115\%
$$

Although Loan B advertised a lower stated nominal rate ($5.95\%$ vs $6.0\%$), Loan A is actually cheaper on an effective annual economic basis ($6.09\%$ vs $6.12\%$).

### 2. Capital Project NPV vs IRR Evaluation
Alder's engineering division proposes purchasing an automated robotic welding cell:
- Initial capital expenditure: $C_0 = \$20.0\text{ million}$
- Projected cash savings: $CF_1 = \$12.0\text{ million}$, $CF_2 = \$12.0\text{ million}$
- Cost of capital: $k = 10.0\%$

Let us compute NPV:

$$
NPV = \frac{\$12.0\text{M}}{1.10} + \frac{\$12.0\text{M}}{(1.10)^2} - \$20.0\text{M} = \$10.909\text{M} + \$9.917\text{M} - \$20.0\text{M} = +\$0.826\text{ million}
$$

Now solve for the project's IRR:

$$
\frac{\$12.0\text{M}}{1 + \text{IRR}} + \frac{\$12.0\text{M}}{(1 + \text{IRR})^2} = \$20.0\text{M}
$$

Setting $x = \frac{1}{1 + \text{IRR}}$, we have the quadratic equation:

$$
12x + 12x^2 = 20 \implies 3x^2 + 3x - 5 = 0
$$

Using the quadratic formula:

$$
x = \frac{-3 + \sqrt{9 - 4(3)(-5)}}{6} = \frac{-3 + \sqrt{69}}{6} \approx \frac{-3 + 8.3066}{6} \approx 0.8844
$$

$$
1 + \text{IRR} = \frac{1}{0.8844} \approx 1.1307 \implies \text{IRR} \approx 13.07\%
$$

Since $\text{IRR} = 13.07\% > k = 10.0\%$ and $NPV = +\$0.826\text{M} > 0$, the project is approved.

## Research discipline

When evaluating interest rates and capital projects:
1. **Always Convert Quoted Rates to EAR**: In credit agreements, inspect whether interest compounds daily, monthly, or quarterly. Never compare stated nominal APRs directly.
2. **Never Rely on IRR Alone for Mutually Exclusive Decisions**: Always rank mutually exclusive investment proposals by NPV in currency units.
3. **Verify the Reinvestment Assumption**: If a strategy claims an annualized internal rate of return of $60\%$, verify whether realized cash gains can actually be redeployed at that same $60\%$ rate in real markets.
4. **Audit Terminal Decommissioning Outlays**: If a project requires cash outflows at the end of its life (e.g., mine reclamation, lease restoration), plot the NPV profile across multiple discount rates to detect multiple IRR cross-over points.

modules.objective: Distinguish arithmetic from geometric compounding and normalize prices for corporate actions.
modules.reading: CFA Institute, Quantitative Investment Analysis, fourth edition · Chapter 2. Pair the book reading with this original application; course lesson numbers are independent of book chapter numbers.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

Before fitting a model, make sure the observations mean what you think they mean. A price, a return, and a cash payment are different kinds of data. This unit asks you to label dates, units, and calculation choices, then inspect the distribution. Those simple habits prevent a sophisticated calculation from answering the wrong question.

## The analytical question

In empirical finance and investment research, raw market prices cannot be analyzed directly without rigorous normalization. Corporate actions (such as stock splits, reverse splits, cash dividends, and rights offerings) alter the number of shares and nominal price levels without altering the underlying economic wealth of the investor:
- In a 5-for-1 stock split, the share price drops by $80\%$ overnight, but each shareholder receives five times as many shares. Treating this as an $80\%$ loss is a catastrophic data-engineering failure.

When summarizing historical investment returns over time, the analyst must distinguish between two fundamentally different averages:
1. **Arithmetic Mean Return ($\bar{R}_A$)**:

$$
\bar{R}_A = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T R_t
$$

   The arithmetic mean is the best unbiased estimate of the expected single-period return for the next period.
2. **Geometric Mean Return ($\bar{R}_G$, Compound Annual Growth Rate / CAGR)**:

$$
\bar{R}_G = \left[ \prod_{t=1}^T (1 + R_t) \right]^{1/T} - 1
$$

   The geometric mean measures the true compounded rate of wealth accumulation over multiple sequential periods.

The mathematical relationship between the arithmetic and geometric mean is governed by volatility:

$$
\bar{R}_G \approx \bar{R}_A - \frac{1}{2} \sigma^2
$$

$$
\text{The Arithmetic Mean is strictly greater than the Geometric Mean whenever returns fluctuate } (\sigma > 0).
$$

Consider the classic volatility drag example:
- Period 1: $+50.0\%$ return.
- Period 2: $-50.0\%$ return.
- Arithmetic Mean: $\frac{+50\% - 50\%}{2} = 0.0\%$.
- An investor who starts with $\$100$ reaches $\$150$ in Period 1, and drops to $\$75$ in Period 2—a severe **$-25.0\%$ net loss**!
- True Geometric Return: $\bar{R}_G = \sqrt{1.50 \times 0.50} - 1 = \sqrt{0.75} - 1 = 0.866 - 1 = -13.4\%\text{ per period}$.

The arithmetic mean paints an entirely false picture of capital preservation, while the geometric mean reflects real wealth in the bank.

## A worked example

Let us examine the corporate action adjustment and return measurement for an investor holding shares in Bank Central Asia (BBCA):
- Initial position: $100\text{ shares}$ purchased at $P_0 = \text{Rp } 50.00\text{ per share}$ (Total portfolio value = $\text{Rp } 5,000$).
- The company executes a **5-for-1 stock split**.
- The investor's share count expands to $100 \times 5 = 500\text{ shares}$.
- In the subsequent trading session, the stock closes at $P_1 = \text{Rp } 10.20\text{ per share}$.

Let us calculate the true investment return:
1. True Total Portfolio Value after split:

$$
V_1 = 500\text{ shares} \times \text{Rp } 10.20 = \text{Rp } 5,100
$$

2. True Holding Period Return:

$$
R = \frac{V_1 - V_0}{V_0} = \frac{\text{Rp } 5,100 - \text{Rp } 5,000}{\text{Rp } 5,000} = \frac{\text{Rp } 100}{\text{Rp } 5,000} = +2.0\%
$$

Look at the error of an unadjusted raw price calculation:
If an automated script simply looked at the raw price change:

$$
R_{\text{naive}} = \frac{\text{Rp } 10.20 - \text{Rp } 50.00}{\text{Rp } 50.00} = -79.6\%
$$

The script would report a phantom $-79.6\%$ crash and trigger false stop-loss liquidations!

Now evaluate multi-period compounding:
An asset produces returns of $+10.0\%$ in Year 1 followed by $+10.0\%$ in Year 2:

$$
\text{Wealth Factor} = (1 + 0.10) \times (1 + 0.10) = 1.10 \times 1.10 = 1.21
$$

$$
\text{Compounded Cumulative Return} = 1.21 - 1 = +21.0\%
$$

The extra $1.0\%$ represents the return earned on the first year's reinvested gain (**compound interest**).

## Research discipline

When managing financial return data:
1. **Maintain Separate Split and Dividend Adjustment Factors**: Store raw closing prices alongside the corporate action multiplier. Never overwrite historical raw price records permanently.
2. **Use Geometric Means for Multi-Year Performance Reporting**: When reporting historical performance to investors or regulators (GIPS standards), always display the geometric CAGR. Never use the arithmetic mean to report multi-year historical wealth growth.
3. **Use Arithmetic Means for Single-Period Forward Projections**: In portfolio optimization (Markowitz mean-variance models), the expected return vector must use the arithmetic mean of single-period returns.
4. **Audit Survivorship Bias in Index Constituents**: When calculating the average return of an industry over ten years, ensure that companies that went bankrupt or were delisted are included in the sample.
