modules.title: Catalysts, value traps and thesis invalidation
modules.subtitle: Distinguish a valuation gap from a timed mechanism for closing it.
modules.objective: Distinguish a valuation gap from a timed mechanism for closing it.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 10 minutes of original explanation and primary-source reading, 8 minutes of calculations, and 12 minutes of research notebook or project work. Longer independent experiments and exam time are additional.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A cheap security may stay cheap because value is uncertain, inaccessible or declining. A catalyst is a proposed event that could change cash flows, capital allocation or investor information; it is not a substitute for valuation. State the expected event window, the evidence needed to recognize it and the observation that would invalidate the thesis. Avoid labeling every price increase as confirmation after the fact.

Translate new information into the accounts before changing the portfolio. Inventory write-downs reduce recoverable assets, cash burn shortens the runway, and dilution changes the per-share claim. An event-driven screen needs timestamped event data and realistic reaction delays. A scheduled earnings date alone does not reveal its outcome. Use the news-to-markets course to build an evidence chain from a release to the company and its valuation.

$$
\mathrm{remaining\ asset\ cushion}=\mathrm{NCAV}_0-BT-P
$$

## A worked example

A company has adjusted NCAV of 8 per share and trades at 5.5. Four quarters of 0.5 per-share cash burn reduce the simple asset cushion to 6 before other changes, leaving only 0.5 above price. An expected asset sale is relevant only after considering proceeds, taxes, debt repayment and the probability that it occurs.

## Put the idea into practice

Write a thesis-monitoring table with one confirming event, one disconfirming event and one noninformative price move. Connect your entry to [Financial news to company & stock analysis](/curriculum/news-to-markets) and label any event-based extension as unimplemented until its timestamps and cash effects are tested.

### Research notebook evidence

Reproduce the worksheet, change the stated assumption, and save your calculation and interpretation with the assignment. Record what information was available, what was estimated, and what would invalidate the conclusion. The browser worksheet stays in cash: its price chart does not backtest this lesson's strategy. Use the downloadable Strategy Lab project for multi-asset simulations, trade ledgers and report exports. All supplied companies, prices and results are fictional teaching cases.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

A catalyst deserves explicit modelling because anomaly returns cluster around news. Across 97 anomalies, Engelberg and co-authors found returns six times higher on earnings announcement days and 50% higher on days with corporate news; their tests favored biased expectations, at least in part corrected once news appears, over dynamic risk and data mining. Our reading: the same event can also disconfirm the thesis, so an earnings date is a test rather than a confirmation.

Cheapness and failure risk are entangled, and the evidence has a real tension. Campbell and co-authors estimated each firm's failure probability from accounting and market data and found that since 1981 the stocks with high estimates earned unusually low returns while showing much greater volatility, market betas and exposure to value and small-cap factors. Griffin and Lemmon, proxying distress with Ohlson's O-score, found that in the most distressed group the return spread between high and low book-to-market stocks was over twice that of other firms, and that these firms also had the sharpest reversals at earnings announcements. Both can hold: within a distressed group cheap stocks may beat expensive ones even though the group lags. A cash-burning net-net sits in exactly that corner, where payoff and failure risk coexist (both points are our inference).

Turn the lesson's cushion into a clock. With adjusted NCAV 8, price 5.5 and burn of 0.5 a quarter, the cushion is 8 − 5.5 − 0.5n, which reaches zero after (8 − 5.5) / 0.5 = 5 quarters. Exercise: for each candidate, compute the quarters of burn until the cushion is gone, and write the exit rule as a number before the next earnings date.

### Sources for this section

- [Engelberg, McLean & Pontiff (2018) · Anomalies and News](https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.12718) — *Research paper.* Across 97 anomalies, returns concentrate on corporate news and earnings announcement days, evidence that mispricing is corrected when information arrives, which is what a catalyst must supply.
- [Campbell, Hilscher & Szilagyi (2008) · In Search of Distress Risk](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.2008.01416.x) — *Research paper.* Builds a failure probability and shows that distressed stocks since 1981 delivered low, not high, returns, so cheapness caused by distress is not automatically rewarded.
- [Griffin & Lemmon (2002) · Book-to-Market Equity, Distress Risk, and Stock Returns](https://doi.org/10.1111/1540-6261.00497) — *Research paper.* Finds the book-to-market return spread is largest among the most distressed firms, with the biggest reversals at earnings announcements, locating value payoffs and traps in the same group.

modules.title: Fundamental strategy research from screen to holdings
modules.subtitle: Evaluate a complete fundamental allocation and audit its exclusions and concentration.
modules.objective: Evaluate a complete fundamental allocation and audit its exclusions and concentration.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 10 minutes of original explanation and primary-source reading, 8 minutes of calculations, and 12 minutes of research notebook or project work. Longer independent experiments and exam time are additional.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A screen does not define a portfolio until entry, exit, weighting, rebalance and missing-data policies are specified. A monthly value screen may hold companies between publications, while a daily rerank may create turnover with little new accounting information. Distinguish an eligibility exit from a small rank change and measure how each contributes to trading.

Write a waterfall from the historical universe to usable filings, valid denominators, financial gates, ranked candidates and final constrained holdings. A strategy holding only one name after filters should not silently invest all capital if its mandate caps single-name exposure. Retain cash when too few candidates qualify. Compare the full rule against equal-weight eligible stocks and against simpler value-only and quality-only variants with matching timing and costs.

$$
w_i=\min(1/N_{\mathrm{selected}},w_{\max}),\qquad w_{\mathrm{cash}}=1-\sum_iw_i
$$

## A worked example

Six stocks enter the universe; one lacks available accounts, one fails coverage, and one fails the NCAV gate. Three candidates remain. A two-name portfolio with a 40% single-name cap invests at most 80%, leaving 20% in cash. If only one qualifies, the same cap leaves 60% cash rather than creating a new concentration rule.

## Put the idea into practice

Run value-quality in the local project and trace a signal through signals.csv to trades.csv and equity.csv. Reconcile rejected candidates and unused cash. Design a slower rebalance extension and compare the number of changed positions before interpreting its return.

### Research notebook evidence

Reproduce the worksheet, change the stated assumption, and save your calculation and interpretation with the assignment. Record what information was available, what was estimated, and what would invalidate the conclusion. The browser worksheet stays in cash: its price chart does not backtest this lesson's strategy. Use the downloadable Strategy Lab project for multi-asset simulations, trade ledgers and report exports. All supplied companies, prices and results are fictional teaching cases.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Piotroski's work shows how much a screen's average return can hide. He documented that less than 44% of high book-to-market firms earn positive market-adjusted returns in the two years after formation, so a value-only rule leans on a minority of winners. A financial-strength screen then produced a long-short return of 23% a year between 1976 and 1996, with the benefit concentrated in small and medium-sized firms, firms with low share turnover and firms with no analyst following.

Novy-Marx found that adding a profitability control sharply improves value strategies, most of all among the largest, most liquid stocks. The signals differ, so this is a contrast, not a contradiction, but a coverage or liquidity gate can remove the stocks where Piotroski's gains sat while keeping those where Novy-Marx's did. Our inference: log names and return contribution removed at every gate, and run value-only, quality-only and combined variants inside size buckets.

French's size and book-to-market portfolios show what full specification looks like: constructed at the end of each June, with NYSE breakpoints (30th and 70th percentiles for book-to-market), admitting a stock only with December and June market equity and positive prior-year book equity. State your own timing and missing-data rules as plainly.

Cattaneo and co-authors treat sorting as a nonparametric estimator and find that the optimal number of portfolios may be much larger than the usual 5 or 10. Our inference: how many names a screen keeps is the same kind of tuning choice, so report neighboring values of N and the cash each implies. Check the cap rule w = min(1/N, 0.4): N = 3 gives 33.3% each and no cash, N = 2 invests 80%, N = 1 invests 40%, and the cap binds only below N = 2.5. Count rebalance dates in each state before reading any return.

### Sources for this section

- [Piotroski (2000) · Value Investing: The Use of Historical Financial Statement Information to Separate Winners from Losers](https://doi.org/10.2307/2672906) — *Research paper.* Shows that a value portfolio's average return hides wide dispersion, and that the gains from a financial-strength screen sit in small, thinly covered, low-turnover firms.
- [Novy-Marx (2013) · The other side of value: The gross profitability premium](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2013.01.003) — *Research paper.* Combines value with gross profitability and finds the improvement largest among big, liquid stocks, a useful contrast when comparing value-only, quality-only and combined variants.
- [Kenneth R. French · Detail for 6 Portfolios Formed on Size and Book-to-Market](https://mba.tuck.dartmouth.edu/pages/faculty/ken.french/Data_Library/six_portfolios.html) — *Dataset documentation.* Official documentation of a published sort: June formation, NYSE breakpoints and the data a stock needs to enter. A model for stating a screen's timing and missing-data rules.
- [Cattaneo, Crump, Farrell & Schaumburg (2018) · Characteristic-Sorted Portfolios: Estimation and Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.03584) — *arXiv 1809.03584.* Treats portfolio sorting as a nonparametric estimator whose number of portfolios is a tuning choice, a useful lens for how many names a screen keeps.

modules.title: Time-series trend following
modules.subtitle: Build a causal directional trend rule and identify its regime-dependent losses.
modules.objective: Build a causal directional trend rule and identify its regime-dependent losses.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 10 minutes of original explanation and primary-source reading, 8 minutes of calculations, and 12 minutes of research notebook or project work. Longer independent experiments and exam time are additional.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

Trend and momentum strategies use past price behavior to form a rule. The timing and measurement choices determine what that rule actually does. Start with one asset and one decision date, calculate the signal by hand, and identify the earliest possible trade. Then compare how ranking assets, skipping recent periods, and rebalancing change the resulting portfolio.

## Understand the idea

A time-series trend rule compares an asset with its own history. Examples include price above a moving average or positive trailing return. These are hypotheses about persistence, not valuation estimates. Specify whether the latest completed close is included, how the warm-up period works, how often the rule updates and whether the allocation is long/cash or allows short exposure.

The rule can lose repeatedly in a sideways market when small reversals trigger entries and exits. A lagged indicator may also exit well after a sudden gap. Parameter choice changes the trade-off between responsiveness and turnover; there is no universally best lookback. Evaluate performance across windows and regimes under the same execution convention, and compare with an always-invested baseline so cash exposure is visible.

$$
s_t=\mathbf{1}\{P_t>L^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{L-1}P_{t-j}\}
$$

## A worked example

Completed closes of 98, 100, 101 and 105 have a four-close mean of 101. The 105 close is above that mean and queues a long instruction for the next open. If the next open gaps to 110, the strategy does not obtain the earlier 105 close. A close equal to the average remains cash under a strictly-greater rule.

## Put the idea into practice

Reproduce the moving average and list signals for a rising path and an alternating path. Compare entry counts under two windows before comparing profits. The project implements cross-sectional momentum; a time-series filter is a separate extension with its own tests.

### Research notebook evidence

Reproduce the worksheet, change the stated assumption, and save your calculation and interpretation with the assignment. Record what information was available, what was estimated, and what would invalidate the conclusion. The browser worksheet stays in cash: its price chart does not backtest this lesson's strategy. Use the downloadable Strategy Lab project for multi-asset simulations, trade ledgers and report exports. All supplied companies, prices and results are fictional teaching cases.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

The published evidence for trend following is wide, but it comes from a different setting than the lesson's rule. Moskowitz and co-authors studied 58 liquid instruments and found persistence in returns for one to 12 months that partially reverses at longer horizons, with the best performance in extreme markets. Hurst and co-authors pushed the record back to 1880: positive average returns in each decade and good results in 8 of the 10 largest crisis periods for a 60/40 portfolio, which by implication leaves two where it did not do well. Both use diversified portfolios across many markets, so our inference is that they say little about a single-asset long/cash average rule, and that the lesson's four-close window, far shorter than one to 12 months, is a timing exercise rather than evidence of a premium.

Lempérière and co-authors add three points for your design. They report a t-statistic of about 5 since 1960 and about 10 since 1800 for excess returns after accounting for the upward drift of these markets. In our view a long/cash rule needs the same correction, because part of its return is simply being invested. They also find a saturation effect for large signals, which in our reading favors a bounded indicator like the lesson's over a position that grows with distance from the average. Finally, they find no statistical degradation of long trends, while shorter trends have significantly withered.

Check this on a longer fixture: run the four-close rule beside much longer windows. For each, report entries, the share of days invested and the excess return over the always-invested baseline under the same next-open execution, then split the sample in halves to see whether the short window's edge survives in both.

modules.title: Cross-sectional momentum and skip periods
modules.subtitle: Rank assets by past performance with an explicit formation and holding calendar.
modules.objective: Rank assets by past performance with an explicit formation and holding calendar.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 10 minutes of original explanation and primary-source reading, 8 minutes of calculations, and 12 minutes of research notebook or project work. Longer independent experiments and exam time are additional.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Cross-sectional momentum compares assets with each other, while time-series momentum asks whether an asset's own trailing return is positive. Ranking can select relative winners even when every asset has fallen. Decide whether the mandate holds those winners or adds a positive-return gate; those are different strategies with different market exposures.

Define formation, skip and holding periods in actual timestamps. The French momentum factor uses prior months 2–12; it is a specific long-short research construction, not the same as a small long-only top-two portfolio. A skip period avoids using the most recent segment in the ranking but does not eliminate all reversal, crash or liquidity risk. The supplied daily fixture uses a short declared lookback and one-observation skip to make indexing inspectable, not to replicate a published factor.

$$
M_{i,t}=\frac{P_{i,t-s}}{P_{i,t-s-L}}-1
$$

## A worked example

At decision index 6 with lookback 3 and skip 1, the score uses close[5]/close[2] − 1. Values 110 and 100 give 10%. The current close[6] is not part of that score. Candidate B with 8% ranks below A; a separate positive-score gate determines what happens if both scores are negative.

## Put the idea into practice

Make an index table and manually check the first non-cash formation date in signals.csv. Mutate the current skipped close and verify its rank effect is absent while the decision's position-sizing price can still change. Keep ranking logic separate from sizing logic.

### Research notebook evidence

Reproduce the worksheet, change the stated assumption, and save your calculation and interpretation with the assignment. Record what information was available, what was estimated, and what would invalidate the conclusion. The browser worksheet stays in cash: its price chart does not backtest this lesson's strategy. Use the downloadable Strategy Lab project for multi-asset simulations, trade ledgers and report exports. All supplied companies, prices and results are fictional teaching cases.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Jegadeesh and Titman tested a skip in the original design. Using NYSE and AMEX stocks from 1965 to 1989, they ranked on returns over the past one to four quarters and held for one to four quarters, which gives 16 strategies. They then repeated all 16 with a one-week gap, to avoid some of the bid-ask spread, price-pressure and lagged-reaction effects. Their most successful long-short strategy, ranked on 12 months and held for 3, earned 1.31% a month with no gap and 1.49% with a one-week gap. In that sample the skip changed the return itself, so declare it before you test.

Which part of the lookback does the work? Novy-Marx found that momentum is driven mainly by performance 12 to seven months before formation, and that strategies built on the recent past are less profitable than those built on the intermediate past, especially among the largest, most liquid stocks. Split your formation window into an older and a newer segment and report each.

Falck and co-authors study factor momentum rather than stock ranking, but their spanning test, which controls for stock momentum, leaves significant Sharpe ratios only for implementations that include the last month of returns. Their stylized model has stock-level mean reversion at short lags and momentum at longer lags. Our inference is that the treatment of the most recent segment can decide whether a result exists.

A skip does not remove crash risk. Daniel and Moskowitz found infrequent, persistent strings of losses that occur in panic states, after market declines and when volatility is high, and coincide with market rebounds. Before trusting a top-two portfolio, line up its worst months against that pattern.

### Sources for this section

- [Jegadeesh & Titman (1993) · Returns to Buying Winners and Selling Losers: Implications for Stock Market Efficiency](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1993.tb04702.x) — *Research paper.* Original formation-by-holding grid for relative-strength strategies, run with and without a one-week gap, with the gap's stated purpose and its effect on the best strategy's return.
- [Novy-Marx (2012) · Is momentum really momentum?](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2011.05.003) — *Research paper.* Shows that the older part of the formation window carries more of the momentum signal than the recent past, which matters when choosing lookback and skip.
- [Daniel & Moskowitz (2016) · Momentum crashes](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2015.12.002) — *Research paper.* Documents momentum crashes in panic states after market declines and shows a dynamic strategy that roughly doubles alpha and Sharpe ratio, so a skip month is no crash protection.
- [Falck, Rej & Thesmar (2020) · Is Factor Momentum More than Stock Momentum?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.04824) — *arXiv 2009.04824.* A spanning test of factor momentum against stock momentum in which only implementations that include the last month of returns stand out, plus a model with short-lag mean reversion.

modules.title: Short-horizon reversal and microstructure effects
modules.subtitle: Distinguish a tradable reversal hypothesis from bid–ask bounce and execution artifacts.
modules.objective: Distinguish a tradable reversal hypothesis from bid–ask bounce and execution artifacts.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 10 minutes of original explanation and primary-source reading, 8 minutes of calculations, and 12 minutes of research notebook or project work. Longer independent experiments and exam time are additional.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A reversal rule expects a recent deviation to move back toward a reference level. It requires a reason: temporary liquidity pressure is different from a permanent earnings shock. A negative return by itself does not establish mispricing. Define the horizon, entry threshold, exit threshold and maximum holding time, and state which information would invalidate the reference level.

At short horizons, a last-trade price can alternate between bid and ask even while the midpoint is unchanged. Apparent negative autocorrelation then comes from measurement and spread crossing rather than an exploitable price pattern. Use quote-aware data when the claim depends on microstructure, include both entry and exit costs, and test slower execution. Daily bars cannot establish queue position or intraday fill probability.

$$
\mathrm{round\ trip\ edge/share}=\mathrm{gross\ edge}-(\mathrm{ask}-\mathrm{bid})-\mathrm{fees/share}
$$

## A worked example

A stable quote has bid 99.9 and ask 100.1. Alternating prints suggest reversals, but buying at the ask and immediately selling at the bid loses 0.2 per share before fees. A supposed 0.15 gross edge cannot cover that 0.2 round-trip spread cost under this simple model.

## Put the idea into practice

Compare a midpoint series and alternating last trades, then subtract a round-trip spread estimate from the proposed edge. Identify what additional data would be required before adapting the strategy to a short-horizon execution engine.

### Research notebook evidence

Reproduce the worksheet, change the stated assumption, and save your calculation and interpretation with the assignment. Record what information was available, what was estimated, and what would invalidate the conclusion. The browser worksheet stays in cash: its price chart does not backtest this lesson's strategy. Use the downloadable Strategy Lab project for multi-asset simulations, trade ledgers and report exports. All supplied companies, prices and results are fictional teaching cases.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Start with the bounce itself. Roll showed that when fundamental value fluctuates randomly, trading costs still induce negative serial dependence in successive observed price changes, and that the effective spread can be inferred from the first-order serial covariance of price changes. In our reading, a negative covariance in trade prices is therefore a reason to suspect the spread before suspecting a signal. For the lesson's prints, alternating between 99.9 and 100.1 gives changes of +0.2, −0.2, +0.2 and so on, so consecutive changes multiply to −0.04, while the midpoint stays at 100.0 and never changes.

Tradable reversal is a separate claim, tied to a horizon. Lehmann studied weeks and found that one week's winners and losers reverse sizeably the next week, with apparent arbitrage profits that persisted after corrections for bid-ask spreads and plausible transaction costs. He read this as probably reflecting inefficiency in the market for liquidity around large price changes. Within the day, Heston and co-authors report that short-term reversal is driven by temporary liquidity imbalances lasting less than an hour as well as bounce. Our inference: a daily-close rule can capture multi-day effects like Lehmann's, not the sub-hour one.

The cost side is not constant either. Zawadowski and co-authors examined liquid stocks after large intraday price changes and found significant reversals after both falls and rises. On the NYSE, though, a large widening of the bid-ask spread eliminated most of the contrarian profits, while on NASDAQ the spread stayed almost constant and profits survived. Use the quote at the signal time, subtract both legs of the round trip, and rerun with a delayed entry.

### Sources for this section

- [Roll (1984) · A Simple Implicit Measure of the Effective Bid-Ask Spread in an Efficient Market](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1984.tb03897.x) — *Research paper.* Classic result that trading costs create negative serial dependence in observed price changes even when value is a random walk, so apparent reversal in trade prices measures spread.
- [Lehmann (1990) · Fads, Martingales, and Market Efficiency](https://doi.org/10.2307/2937816) — *Research paper.* Weekly winner-loser reversals whose apparent profits survive corrections for bid-ask spreads and plausible transaction costs, interpreted as a liquidity effect around large price changes.
- [Heston, Korajczyk & Sadka (2010) · Intraday Patterns in the Cross-section of Stock Returns](https://arxiv.org/abs/1005.3535) — *arXiv 1005.3535.* Attributes short-term reversal to temporary liquidity imbalances lasting under an hour plus bid-ask bounce, which limits what daily bars can reveal.
- [Zawadowski, Andor & Kertész (2004) · Short-term market reaction after extreme price changes of liquid stocks](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0406696) — *arXiv cond-mat/0406696.* After large intraday moves in liquid stocks, reversals are significant, but a widening NYSE spread removed most contrarian profit while a steady NASDAQ spread did not.

modules.title: Rebalance buffers and parameter stability
modules.subtitle: Reduce unnecessary turnover and compare neighboring rules without selecting on the final sample.
modules.objective: Reduce unnecessary turnover and compare neighboring rules without selecting on the final sample.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 10 minutes of original explanation and primary-source reading, 8 minutes of calculations, and 12 minutes of research notebook or project work. Longer independent experiments and exam time are additional.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A ranking rule can oscillate around a cutoff, replacing nearly identical candidates every rebalance. A buffer or hysteresis rule enters at a stronger threshold and exits only after a weaker threshold is crossed. This can reduce trading but also delays response. It changes the strategy and must be specified before final evaluation. Record whether retained positions can exceed a cap because of price drift and when they are resized.

Inspect a parameter surface rather than only its maximum. A broad region of similar validation results is more encouraging than one isolated spike, but it is still selected evidence. Evaluate costs, turnover, concentration and drawdown across nearby settings. Do not repeatedly inspect the holdout while searching for an attractive plateau. The final choice should follow a declared tie-break, such as lower turnover among candidates meeting the validation requirement.

$$
\mathrm{approximate\ cost\ drag}=c\sum_t\mathrm{traded\ notional}_t/E_t
$$

## A worked example

A top-ten rule with an exit buffer at rank fifteen retains an existing holding at rank twelve but does not admit a new candidate at rank twelve. If modeled traded notional falls from 2.0 to 1.2 times equity, a 20-basis-point per-side proportional cost falls from 0.004 to 0.0024 of equity under a fixed notional approximation.

## Put the idea into practice

Hand-run entry and exit decisions for ranks 9, 12 and 16. Record neighboring lookbacks and their net result, turnover and worst period in the notebook. Label a buffer extension separately from the downloadable engine's unbuffered daily target rule.

### Research notebook evidence

Reproduce the worksheet, change the stated assumption, and save your calculation and interpretation with the assignment. Record what information was available, what was estimated, and what would invalidate the conclusion. The browser worksheet stays in cash: its price chart does not backtest this lesson's strategy. Use the downloadable Strategy Lab project for multi-asset simulations, trade ledgers and report exports. All supplied companies, prices and results are fictional teaching cases.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Your buffer has a name in the literature: a buy/hold spread. Novy-Marx and Velikov found it the most effective cost-mitigation technique they tested. Most anomalies with turnover below 50% a month kept significant net spreads when designed to cut costs, while few with higher turnover did. Their working paper gives the rule's shape: a 10%/20% rule buys only stocks entering the top 10% and sells only those leaving the top 20%, the same structure as admitting a top-ten name and holding it until rank fifteen. The same paper puts average round-trip costs for typical value-weighted strategies above 50 bps, though they have fallen over the last decade.

Why does a band make sense? Rej and co-authors show that with linear costs the optimal trading speed is zero inside a band, and that adding small quadratic costs narrows the band and lets speed grow with the distance outside it. Gârleanu and Pedersen derive a related partial-adjustment policy: the new portfolio blends the existing one with an aim portfolio, and slower-decaying signals get more weight in the aim. Our inference is that a buffer's width should depend on cost size and signal decay, so it is a design choice you can reason about before touching the holdout.

Rerun the lesson's cost arithmetic at a harsher level. Splitting 50 bps evenly gives 25 bps per side, so 1.2 times equity of traded notional costs 0.003 instead of 0.0024. Then compare exit ranks of 10 (no buffer), 12, 16 and 20 on turnover, net result and worst period, and choose with the tie-break you declared in advance.

### Sources for this section

- [Novy-Marx & Velikov (2016) · A Taxonomy of Anomalies and Their Trading Costs](https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhv063) — *Research paper.* Finds that a buy/hold spread, stricter to enter than to keep, is the most effective trading-cost mitigation, and that net spreads survive mainly for low-turnover strategies.
- [Gârleanu & Pedersen (2013) · Dynamic Trading with Predictable Returns and Transaction Costs](https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.12080) — *Research paper.* Closed-form optimal policy that trades partially toward an aim portfolio, weighting slower-decaying signals more, a counterpart to hard buffers.
- [Rej et al. (2015) · Optimal Trading with Linear and (small) Non-Linear Costs](https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.07359) — *arXiv 1511.07359.* Derives a no-trade band under linear costs and shows how small quadratic costs narrow it and make trading speed grow outside it.

modules.title: Statistical arbitrage pairs
modules.subtitle: Construct a spread with an explicit hedge definition and interpretable entry signal.
modules.objective: Construct a spread with an explicit hedge definition and interpretable entry signal.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 10 minutes of original explanation and primary-source reading, 8 minutes of calculations, and 12 minutes of research notebook or project work. Longer independent experiments and exam time are additional.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

A pairs strategy studies the relationship between two assets and may trade their relative movement. Similar-looking charts do not by themselves establish a reliable relationship. Begin with the economic connection, the statistical assumptions, and the costs of trading both sides. The following lessons show why borrowing, timing, and a broken relationship can matter as much as the initial signal.

## Understand the idea

A pairs hypothesis proposes that a relationship between two assets is sufficiently stable to support a spread trade. Start with an economic connection, then define whether the spread uses price levels, log prices or returns. The units of the hedge coefficient depend on that choice. A coefficient estimated in log prices is not automatically the number of shares to short.

Estimate the hedge ratio and reference distribution from information available before the trade. Define the formation window, re-estimation schedule, entry, exit, stop and maximum holding period. Standardizing a spread makes its deviation interpretable but does not make convergence certain. Hedging notional, market beta and statistical spread exposure are different objectives; identify which one the proposed trade targets.

$$
s_t=A_t-\beta B_t,\qquad z_t=(s_t-\mu_{\mathrm{past}})/\sigma_{\mathrm{past}}
$$

## A worked example

A price-level spread is A − 2B. With A at 108 and B at 50, the spread is 8. A prior mean of 2 and standard deviation of 3 give z = 2. A short-spread trade sells one A and buys two B before sizing; its notionals are 108 short and 100 long, so it is not exactly dollar-neutral.

## Put the idea into practice

Write both share legs and their signs beside every z-score. Compare the same pair under a dollar-neutral hedge and explain why the statistical spread changes. This lesson's worksheet calculates the case; a real two-leg engine is an extension beyond the supplied long-only project.

### Research notebook evidence

Reproduce the worksheet, change the stated assumption, and save your calculation and interpretation with the assignment. Record what information was available, what was estimated, and what would invalidate the conclusion. The browser worksheet stays in cash: its price chart does not backtest this lesson's strategy. Use the downloadable Strategy Lab project for multi-asset simulations, trade ledgers and report exports. All supplied companies, prices and results are fictional teaching cases.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Published pair strategies hedge in different ways, which is the lesson's notional-versus-beta-versus-spread distinction in practice. Gatev and co-authors matched stocks by minimum distance between normalized historical prices, with no fitted coefficient in our reading. A simple rule on daily data over 1962–2002 earned average annualized excess returns of up to 11% for self-financing portfolios of pairs, typically above conservative cost estimates, and they link the profit to a common factor in returns that differs from conventional risk measures.

Avellaneda and Lee regress each stock on PCA factors or sector ETFs and treat the residual as mean-reverting, so the hedge targets factor exposure rather than one partner. They standardize the residual's distance from equilibrium (their s-score), open at 1.25 standard deviations, close within 0.5 and estimate on a 60-day window, which corresponds roughly to one earnings cycle. They chose the cutoffs empirically from simulations over 2000 to 2004, inside a backtest running from 1997 to 2007, so part of the reported period also shaped the thresholds (our reading). After an assumed 5 basis points per trade, PCA strategies averaged a Sharpe ratio of 1.44 over 1997 to 2007 but only 0.9 in 2003–2007, and ETF strategies degraded similarly since 2002.

Guijarro-Ordonez and co-authors generalize the idea by building arbitrage portfolios as residuals from conditional latent factors; a pair is then the single-partner special case (our inference).

For the lesson's trade, 108 short against 100 long leaves 8 net short, 3.8% of 208 gross. Re-estimate the z-score on a 60-observation window, compare entry at 1.25 and 2 standard deviations, and report each half of the sample separately.

- [Guijarro-Ordonez, Pelger & Zanotti (2021) · Deep Learning Statistical Arbitrage](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.04028) — *arXiv 2106.04028.* Frames statistical arbitrage as residual portfolios from conditional latent factors, a generalization of single-partner pairs.

modules.title: Cointegration, stationarity and half-life diagnostics
modules.subtitle: Use statistical diagnostics as conditional evidence rather than a guarantee of spread stability.
modules.objective: Use statistical diagnostics as conditional evidence rather than a guarantee of spread stability.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 10 minutes of original explanation and primary-source reading, 8 minutes of calculations, and 12 minutes of research notebook or project work. Longer independent experiments and exam time are additional.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

High return correlation does not establish that a price-level spread is stationary. Two integrated price series can share short-run movements while their difference wanders. An Engle–Granger cointegration test assesses a particular residual relationship under stated assumptions; its null is no cointegration. Check the integration assumptions, deterministic terms, lag selection and sample size before interpreting the result.

Testing many candidate pairs creates selection bias even when each individual p-value is correctly computed. Reserve later windows to examine persistence and record every pair considered. A discrete AR(1) approximation can summarize local mean-reversion speed when its coefficient lies strictly between zero and one. Coefficients near one imply long, uncertain half-lives; structural changes can invalidate both the estimate and the trading horizon.

$$
h=-\log(2)/\log(\phi),\qquad 0<\phi<1
$$

## A worked example

For a spread deviation following x[t+1] = 0.8x[t] with no new shock, an initial deviation of 10 becomes 5.12 after three steps and 4.096 after four. Its model half-life lies between three and four observations. This conditional decay calculation says nothing about new shocks, changing coefficients or actual execution costs.

## Put the idea into practice

Read the cointegration test's assumptions and write the null in words. Use the [Financial econometrics & factor models](/curriculum/econometrics) for estimation and diagnostics, then design a formation/validation split and a pair-search ledger before ranking p-values.

### Research notebook evidence

Reproduce the worksheet, change the stated assumption, and save your calculation and interpretation with the assignment. Record what information was available, what was estimated, and what would invalidate the conclusion. The browser worksheet stays in cash: its price chart does not backtest this lesson's strategy. Use the downloadable Strategy Lab project for multi-asset simulations, trade ledgers and report exports. All supplied companies, prices and results are fictional teaching cases.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Cointegration describes the gap this lesson points to. Engle and Granger call series co-integrated when each needs differencing to become stationary but some linear combination does not, so deviations from equilibrium have finite variance although the series themselves do not. Economic closeness does not guarantee the property: in their examples consumption and income were co-integrated, but wages and prices were not.

Graziano's single-pair study of PepsiCo and Coca-Cola shows the lesson's steps in order. Over 2013–2018 the two daily return series had a sample correlation of 0.66, yet augmented Dickey–Fuller tests could not reject a unit root in either log-price. An Engle–Granger test with critical values adjusted for the estimated hedge ratio then rejected the null of no cointegration (p = 0.033), and an AR(1) coefficient of 0.9785 on the spread implied a half-life of about 31.9 trading days, matching the lesson's formula. On the later out-of-sample window, re-estimating the hedge ratio gave −0.2376 against 1.6618, and the test no longer rejected (p = 0.12). One pair is an illustration, not a base rate.

Half-lives near φ = 1 are fragile. Yu notes that standard estimators of the mean-reversion parameter are biased in finite samples, and that a simple bias formula works poorly when reversion is slow, a case he calls empirically realistic for financial series. By our arithmetic, φ = 0.99 instead of 0.9785 more than doubles the half-life, to about 69 days, while the lesson's toy φ = 0.8 gives only 3.1.

Exercise: estimate φ on the formation window and again on the validation window. If the half-life more than doubles, or exceeds your maximum holding time, treat the pair as unproven.

### Sources for this section

- [Engle & Granger (1987) · Co-Integration and Error Correction: Representation, Estimation, and Testing](https://doi.org/10.2307/1913236) — *Research paper.* Defines co-integration and develops the residual-based tests; its examples show that economically related series can fail the test.
- [Yu (2012) · Bias in the estimation of the mean reversion parameter in continuous time models](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeconom.2012.01.004) — *Research paper.* Shows that standard estimators of the mean-reversion speed are biased, and that slow reversion (the near-unit-root case) is the hard one.
- [Graziano (2026) · From Cointegration to Out-of-Sample Failure: A Pairs-Trading Case Study on PEP-KO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35359) — *arXiv 2609.35359.* A recent single-author, single-pair case study that walks through ADF, Engle–Granger and AR(1) half-life steps and then tests them out of sample.

modules.title: Borrow, two-leg execution and asynchronous risk
modules.subtitle: Price the full pair trade and handle the case where only one leg fills.
modules.objective: Price the full pair trade and handle the case where only one leg fills.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 10 minutes of original explanation and primary-source reading, 8 minutes of calculations, and 12 minutes of research notebook or project work. Longer independent experiments and exam time are additional.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A statistical spread is not an atomic exchange order unless a specific execution mechanism makes it so. One leg may fill while the other is rejected or delayed, leaving directional exposure. Record order identifiers, partial fills, residual hedge, timeout, cancel and unwind policies. An attractive close-to-close spread change cannot reveal whether the two legs were available at those prices.

Short exposure needs borrow availability, a fee convention, collateral and recall handling. Borrow rates and shares available can change during the holding period. Charge commissions and spread on both legs and use gross capital or a clearly stated margin convention when reporting returns. Dividing a long-short profit by near-zero net notional creates a meaningless return denominator.

$$
\Pi_{\mathrm{net}}=\Pi_{\mathrm{gross}}-\sum_{\mathrm{legs}}\mathrm{fees}-N_{\mathrm{short}}r_b d/D
$$

## A worked example

A pair has 10,000 long and 10,000 short. A 0.1% fee on each of four entry/exit legs costs about 40 if notionals stay constant. Borrow at 6% annually on 10,000 for 30/360 of a year adds 50 under the declared simple convention. A 120 gross gain leaves only 30 before spread, impact and financing.

## Put the idea into practice

Write a state table for both filled, long-only filled, short-only filled, rejected borrow and recall. Define a maximum unhedged interval and a cash-reserved unwind action. These are design exercises; the supplied long-only engine does not pretend to simulate short borrow or atomic pair fills.

### Research notebook evidence

Reproduce the worksheet, change the stated assumption, and save your calculation and interpretation with the assignment. Record what information was available, what was estimated, and what would invalidate the conclusion. The browser worksheet stays in cash: its price chart does not backtest this lesson's strategy. Use the downloadable Strategy Lab project for multi-asset simulations, trade ledgers and report exports. All supplied companies, prices and results are fictional teaching cases.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

The short leg is where a pair stops being symmetric. Under SEC Regulation SHO a broker-dealer needs reasonable grounds to believe a stock can be borrowed before it effects a short sale, and a stock that falls at least 10 percent in one day triggers a price test on short-sale prices for the rest of that day and the following day. Our inference: a long leg can fill while the short leg is refused or delayed.

Borrowing can also change after entry. Engelberg and co-authors describe two risks peculiar to short sellers, that stock loans become expensive and that they are recalled, and find that stocks with greater exposure to this risk earn lower returns, are priced less efficiently and are shorted less. Glover and Hulley model recall risk alongside margin risk, where a short seller who cannot fund a margin call is forced out, and find that realistic constraints cost a substantial amount of value. In our reading, that supports a cash-reserved unwind rule.

Do and Faff charged commissions, market impact and short selling fees on U.S. pairs trading from 1963 to 2009. Well-matched pairs stayed profitable at about 30 basis points a month, risk-adjusted, but pairs trading was largely unprofitable after 2002.

Check the lesson's example. Net profit is 120 − 40 − 50 = 30. With the 120 gross gain and 40 of fees held fixed, the pair breaks even at a borrow rate of 9.6% a year, because 80 of borrow cost on 10,000 for 30/360 of a year is 9.6% annualised (our arithmetic). Then trace a recall on day 10: which leg is left open, and which cash reserve pays to close it?

### Sources for this section

- [U.S. SEC · Key Points About Regulation SHO](https://www.sec.gov/investor/pubs/regsho.htm) — *Official source.* Regulator's summary of the locate requirement, close-out rule and the price test that applies after a 10 percent one-day fall.
- [Engelberg, Reed & Ringgenberg (2018) · Short-Selling Risk](https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.12601) — *Research paper.* Shows that the risk of loans becoming expensive or being recalled is priced across stocks, which is the borrow risk the lesson asks you to record.
- [Glover & Hulley (2019) · Short Selling with Margin Risk and Recall Risk](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.11804) — *arXiv 1903.11804.* Optimal-stopping model of a short seller who can be forced out by margin calls or stock recalls, with the value lost to each friction.
- [Do & Faff (2012) · Are Pairs Trading Profits Robust to Trading Costs?](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1475-6803.2012.01317.x) — *Research paper.* U.S. evidence, 1963 to 2009, that pairs trading survives commissions, market impact and short selling fees only at modest levels.

modules.title: Relationship breaks and pairs research capstone
modules.subtitle: Decide when new information invalidates a spread and design an auditable pair experiment.
modules.objective: Decide when new information invalidates a spread and design an auditable pair experiment.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 10 minutes of original explanation and primary-source reading, 8 minutes of calculations, and 12 minutes of research notebook or project work. Longer independent experiments and exam time are additional.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A spread relationship can break after a merger, a capital-structure change, a business divestiture or a persistent shift in input economics. A widening z-score may therefore reflect a new equilibrium rather than a larger bargain. Monitor both statistical behavior and the economic link. Define observation windows and stop rules before looking at the most dramatic historical episode.

Separate a trading stop from model re-estimation. A stop bounds a particular position under imperfect execution; it does not prove the model is wrong or cap loss through every gap. Re-estimation changes the model and needs later validation. Averaging down increases exposure to the same unverified relationship. Record a maximum holding time and borrow/hedge limits even if the original statistical fit was strong.

$$
\mathrm{exit\ reason}\in\{\mathrm{convergence},\mathrm{risk},\mathrm{time},\mathrm{borrow},\mathrm{thesis\ break}\}
$$

## A worked example

A spread enters at z = 2, has a planned exit at 0.5 and a risk exit at 3.5. A structural announcement moves it from 3.2 to 4.2 overnight. The strategy cannot assume execution at 3.5 through the gap; the actual next executable prices determine the loss on both legs.

## Put the idea into practice

Complete a pair research protocol with formation sample, hedge units, diagnostics, entry/exit policy, two-leg costs and a break scenario. Compare it with the single-asset engine contract and list the additional events needed before a pairs extension could be considered implemented.

### Research notebook evidence

Reproduce the worksheet, change the stated assumption, and save your calculation and interpretation with the assignment. Record what information was available, what was estimated, and what would invalidate the conclusion. The browser worksheet stays in cash: its price chart does not backtest this lesson's strategy. Use the downloadable Strategy Lab project for multi-asset simulations, trade ledgers and report exports. All supplied companies, prices and results are fictional teaching cases.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

A widening spread is ambiguous, and tests alone cannot settle it. Gregory and Hansen built residual-based cointegration tests that allow one break of unknown timing in the intercept or slope. In their limited experiments the tests detected cointegration across such a break, while the conventional ADF test, which allows no regime shift, lost power sharply. Our inference: after a merger or divestiture, a failed standard re-test fits both a broken link and a shifted but intact one, so the economic evidence must decide, and a re-estimated model still needs later data.

A stop is a separate design choice. Leung and Li model the spread as an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process and show that, with a stop-loss, the entry region is a bounded interval strictly above the stop level, and that raising the stop level always lowers the optimal take-profit level. Their stop sits below a long position, so for the lesson's short spread our mirror-image reading is that a nearer stop pairs with a nearer profit target, making the 0.5 exit and 3.5 stop one design. We infer that Ornstein–Uhlenbeck paths do not jump, so that model can fill at the stop while the lesson's overnight gap cannot.

Do and Faff found that pairs-trading profits kept trending down, yet the strategy did well in long stretches of market turmoil, the global financial crisis among them. Our inference: outcomes differ by regime, so recheck stops and holding limits on another stretch.

Exercise: with entry at 2, exit at 0.5 and stop at 3.5, planned gain and planned loss are both 1.5 z-units. A fill at 4.2 after the gap loses 2.2, about 47% more than planned. Repeat for gaps ending at 5 and 6.

### Sources for this section

- [Gregory & Hansen (1996) · Residual-based tests for cointegration in models with regime shifts](https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-4076%2869%2941685-7) — *Research paper.* Cointegration tests that allow one break of unknown timing, and a simulation showing the conventional ADF test loses power when the relationship shifts.
- [Leung & Li (2014) · Optimal Mean Reversion Trading with Transaction Costs and Stop-Loss Exit](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.5062) — *arXiv 1411.5062.* Optimal entry and exit for an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck spread, and how a stop-loss level changes the entry region and the take-profit level.
- [Do & Faff (2010) · Does Simple Pairs Trading Still Work?](https://doi.org/10.2469/faj.v66.n4.1) — *Research paper.* U.S. evidence of a long decline in pairs-trading profitability alongside strong results in prolonged turbulence, so regimes matter.

modules.objective: Turn time-valid predictions into a researchable allocation with a simple baseline.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 10 minutes of original explanation and primary-source reading, 8 minutes of calculations, and 12 minutes of research notebook or project work. Longer independent experiments and exam time are additional.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

A prediction becomes part of a strategy only after you decide how it changes holdings. A model may rank stocks or estimate a return, but the portfolio also needs sizing, constraints, timing, and costs. In this unit, follow the prediction through those decisions. Evaluate the complete process on later data and compare it with simpler rules.

## Understand the idea

A stock-prediction model is one component in a strategy. Define the observable features, tradable target, training dates, refit schedule, prediction output and rule converting predictions to positions. A lower prediction error does not by itself establish better portfolio returns: ranking, turnover, costs and constraints mediate the economic outcome. Begin with a simple factor rank and a regularized linear model before adding flexible alternatives.

Fit imputation, scaling, feature selection and model parameters within training data. Keep all stocks from a date together and purge overlapping forward labels. A cross-sectional ranking at a decision time can use the available cross-section, but a learned preprocessing pipeline cannot learn from the future test distribution. Record model and feature versions alongside every prediction so an execution audit can identify what was actually used.

$$
\widehat\beta=\arg\min_\beta\{\|y-X\beta\|_2^2+\lambda\|\beta\|_2^2\}
$$

## A worked example

A single-feature ridge fit without an intercept has sum(xy) = 6 and sum(x²) = 4. With penalty 2, the coefficient is 1 rather than the unpenalized 1.5. This arithmetic illustrates shrinkage; choosing the penalty after seeing the holdout would still contaminate evaluation, and the example is not a complete trained stock model.

## Put the idea into practice

Write the prediction-to-position contract and compare a frozen rank baseline. Continue to the [Machine learning for stocks](/curriculum/stock-machine-learning) for fitted pipelines, training and evaluation; return here to audit timing, sizing and after-cost portfolio evidence.

### Research notebook evidence

Reproduce the worksheet, change the stated assumption, and save your calculation and interpretation with the assignment. Record what information was available, what was estimated, and what would invalidate the conclusion. The browser worksheet stays in cash: its price chart does not backtest this lesson's strategy. Use the downloadable Strategy Lab project for multi-asset simulations, trade ledgers and report exports. All supplied companies, prices and results are fictional teaching cases.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Gu and co-authors give a large-scale template for this lesson's contract. They fit models on 1957–1974, tuned hyperparameters on 1975–1986 and tested on 1987–2016, refitting once a year with the training sample growing by one year. Their baselines matter. Ordinary least squares on all 920 features scored a monthly out-of-sample R² of −3.46%, worse than forecasting zero, while least squares on size, value and momentum alone scored 0.16% and an elastic net 0.11%. In our reading, that is the lesson's ridge shrinkage (a penalty of 2 cutting 1.5 to 1) at scale. Trees and neural networks did best, with gains traced to nonlinear interactions, and a value-weighted long-short decile strategy built on neural-network forecasts earned an annualized out-of-sample Sharpe ratio of 1.35.

The economic layer can change the verdict. Avramov and co-authors report that deep-learning profits come from difficult-to-arbitrage stocks and high limits-to-arbitrage states. Removing microcaps, distressed stocks or turbulent periods shrinks the profits a lot, and realistic trading costs cut them further because the strategies turn over heavily and hold extreme positions.

Chen and co-authors fit a deep network to individual stock returns using the no-arbitrage condition as the training criterion, and report that it beats every benchmark they tried out of sample on Sharpe ratio, explained variation and pricing errors. Our contrast: the training objective, not only the model class, is a design choice.

Exercise: on your held-out dates, report the top-minus-bottom spread three ways: all stocks, without the smallest and least liquid, and after your cost per traded notional. If the edge vanishes in the last two, the allocation rule is the weak link, not the model.

- [Gu, Kelly & Xiu (2020) · Empirical Asset Pricing via Machine Learning](https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhaa009) — *Research paper.* Time-ordered training, validation and test design for stock-level return forecasts, with linear baselines, flexible models and long-short portfolio results.
- [Avramov, Cheng & Metzker (2023) · Machine Learning vs. Economic Restrictions: Evidence from Stock Return Predictability](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2022.4449) — *Research paper.* Shows that deep-learning profits shrink once microcaps, distressed stocks, volatile episodes and trading costs are handled.
- [Chen, Pelger & Zhu (2019) · Deep Learning in Asset Pricing](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.00745) — *arXiv 1904.00745.* Neural-network asset pricing model for individual stocks that uses the no-arbitrage condition as its training criterion.

modules.title: Walk-forward model selection and nested validation
modules.subtitle: Separate hyperparameter selection from evaluation of the selected training procedure.
modules.objective: Separate hyperparameter selection from evaluation of the selected training procedure.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 10 minutes of original explanation and primary-source reading, 8 minutes of calculations, and 12 minutes of research notebook or project work. Longer independent experiments and exam time are additional.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A walk-forward experiment repeatedly fits on past information and evaluates on a later block. If hyperparameters are selected within that process, use inner training/validation splits restricted to the outer training history. The outer block then evaluates the whole selection procedure rather than a model chosen with knowledge of that block. Purge label overlaps at every relevant boundary, not just the final split.

Specify expanding versus rolling history, training-window length, retraining frequency and what happens when too little valid data remain. A model can use earlier evaluation observations once they become past data in a later live-like refit, but the original evaluation prediction must remain frozen. Chronology determines admissible information; it does not guarantee stationarity or sufficient effective sample size.

$$
\theta_k=\operatorname{select}(D_{\mathrm{outer\ train},k}),\qquad \widehat y_{\mathrm{outer\ test},k}=f_{\theta_k}(X_{\mathrm{outer\ test},k})
$$

## A worked example

An outer fit uses sessions 1–120 and evaluates 121–140. Hyperparameter selection may compare inner fits ending before 120, with their own purges. It cannot choose penalty strength from 121–140. The next outer refit can extend to 140, but it must not overwrite the predictions previously made for that block.

## Put the idea into practice

Draw two outer folds and their inner splits, including label-end dates. Record one prediction file per outer evaluation block and merge those frozen files for portfolio evaluation. Use the stock-ML project for executable fitting; the Strategy Lab project demonstrates a simpler fixed candidate selection protocol.

### Research notebook evidence

Reproduce the worksheet, change the stated assumption, and save your calculation and interpretation with the assignment. Record what information was available, what was estimated, and what would invalidate the conclusion. The browser worksheet stays in cash: its price chart does not backtest this lesson's strategy. Use the downloadable Strategy Lab project for multi-asset simulations, trade ledgers and report exports. All supplied companies, prices and results are fictional teaching cases.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Varma and Simon show why the outer block must stay out of selection. They generated classification datasets in which the two classes did not differ, tuned each classifier by minimizing cross-validated error, and read that same error as its performance. The estimate was below 30% on 18.5% of datasets for shrunken centroids and on 38% for support vector machines, yet on independent data both were no better than chance. A nested procedure, tuning in an inner loop and scoring in an outer one, cut the bias substantially. Cawley and Talbot add that over-fitting the selection criterion is often comparable in size to the performance gaps between learning algorithms. Our inference: a flexible model with more knobs can win by selection alone.

The outer score has limits too. Bates and co-authors prove, for least squares, that cross-validation measures how a procedure performs on average across fresh training sets, not how the one fitted model will do, and that standard intervals can cover the true error far less often than claimed because fold accuracies are correlated. Bergmeir and co-authors show that ordinary K-fold cross-validation is valid for purely autoregressive models whose errors are uncorrelated. Overlapping forward labels, as in the lesson, produce correlated errors, so our inference is that purging stays necessary.

Exercise: replace your features with random noise, keep the real labels and the lesson's 1–120 and 121–140 split, and run the whole inner selection. The winning inner score is the optimistic number; the frozen 121–140 score should show no skill.

### Sources for this section

- [Varma & Simon (2006) · Bias in error estimation when using cross-validation for model selection](https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2105-7-91) — *Research paper.* Null-data simulations showing that a tuned classifier's own cross-validated error is badly optimistic, while nested cross-validation comes close to independent test error.
- [Cawley & Talbot (2010) · On Over-fitting in Model Selection and Subsequent Selection Bias in Performance Evaluation](https://jmlr.org/papers/v11/cawley10a.html) — *Research paper.* Shows that over-fitting the model-selection criterion can be as large as the differences between algorithms, making some evaluation practices unreliable.
- [Bates, Hastie & Tibshirani (2021) · Cross-validation: what does it estimate and how well does it do it?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.00673) — *arXiv 2104.00673.* Proves what cross-validation actually estimates and why its usual confidence intervals are too narrow, and proposes a nested scheme for the variance.
- [Bergmeir, Hyndman & Koo (2018) · A note on the validity of cross-validation for evaluating autoregressive time series prediction](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.csda.2017.11.003) — *Research paper.* Gives the conditions under which ordinary K-fold cross-validation is valid for autoregressive forecasting, a counterpoint to always using forward chaining.

modules.title: Ranking diagnostics and economic usefulness
modules.subtitle: Relate information coefficients and portfolio spreads to costs and concentration.
modules.objective: Relate information coefficients and portfolio spreads to costs and concentration.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 10 minutes of original explanation and primary-source reading, 8 minutes of calculations, and 12 minutes of research notebook or project work. Longer independent experiments and exam time are additional.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A cross-sectional information coefficient measures association between predicted scores and later outcomes at a date. Rank correlation emphasizes ordering rather than return calibration. Compute diagnostics by date and inspect their distribution rather than pooling every stock-date into one impressive number. Observations share market shocks and overlapping labels, so a naive count of rows can overstate independent evidence.

Rank buckets and top-minus-bottom returns help explain the shape of a signal, but a long-short diagnostic is not the same as an implementable long-only portfolio. Compare the actual selected names, turnover, sector exposures and capacity. A weak global rank correlation can coexist with useful tail separation, while a positive correlation can disappear after implementation costs. Keep both the statistical and economic views visible.

$$
\rho_s=1-\frac{6\sum_i d_i^2}{n(n^2-1)}\quad\mathrm{(no\ ties)}
$$

## A worked example

Across three assets, predicted ranks [1,2,3] and realized ranks [2,1,3] have squared rank differences totaling 2. With no ties, Spearman correlation is 1 − 6×2/(3×(3²−1)) = 0.5. This tiny fictional cross-section provides a calculation check, not evidence of a persistent signal.

## Put the idea into practice

Reproduce the rank coefficient, then write a dated diagnostic table with bucket returns, selected-name concentration and traded notional. State how ties are ranked. Link every claimed net return to the engine's holdings and ledger, rather than applying an IC directly to capital.

### Research notebook evidence

Reproduce the worksheet, change the stated assumption, and save your calculation and interpretation with the assignment. Record what information was available, what was estimated, and what would invalidate the conclusion. The browser worksheet stays in cash: its price chart does not backtest this lesson's strategy. Use the downloadable Strategy Lab project for multi-asset simulations, trade ledgers and report exports. All supplied companies, prices and results are fictional teaching cases.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

The bridge from rank correlation to money is the fundamental law of active management: the information ratio (IR, excess return divided by its volatility) depends on IC and on breadth, roughly the number of independent bets. Zhang and co-authors extend that classic relationship with IC volatility and turnover cost. Through derivations and simulations, for mean-variance and quintile portfolios alike, they find a turnover-adjusted IR always lower than one that ignores cost, and that limiting turnover may raise IR, contrary to the law's implication. Our reading: an IC table needs a turnover column, since a higher-IC model that trades far more can still lose.

Constraints separate score from holdings. Clarke and co-authors note that short and turnover limits are common and materially restrictive, and derive an ex post split of performance into the success of return prediction and the noise that constraints add, illustrated with equity portfolios benchmarked to the S&P 500. A long-only top bucket need not capture everything a long-short spread shows.

Statistical fit and profit can diverge. Leitch and Tanner asked why firms buy professional forecasts when a naive model looks about as good on root-mean-squared or mean absolute error. They argued such statistics may not be closely related to profits, and found only very weak relationships. Rank IC is another summary statistic, so the same caution applies (our inference).

Check the lesson's numbers: of the six possible orderings of three assets, three score 0.5 or better, so a random ranking does at least as well as the worked example half the time. For your own run, tabulate IC by date (mean, standard deviation, share positive) beside traded notional and the net return of the holdings actually held.

### Sources for this section

- [Zhang, Wang & Cao (2021) · Turnover-Adjusted Information Ratio](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.10306) — *arXiv 2105.10306.* Extends the fundamental law's IC-and-breadth relationship with IC volatility and turnover cost; a turnover-adjusted IR is always lower, and limiting turnover can raise IR.
- [Clarke, de Silva & Thorley (2002) · Portfolio Constraints and the Fundamental Law of Active Management](https://doi.org/10.2469/faj.v58.n5.2468) — *Research paper.* Derives ex ante and ex post relationships for constrained portfolios, separating the success of return prediction from the noise that short and turnover limits add.
- [Leitch & Tanner (1991) · Economic Forecast Evaluation: Profits versus the Conventional Error Measures](https://ideas.repec.org/a/aea/aecrev/v81y1991i3p580-90.html) — *Research paper.* Finds only very weak links between RMSE-type error statistics and forecast profits, a precedent for judging rank IC by economic value as well.

modules.title: Ablations, negative controls and model failure analysis
modules.subtitle: Test whether added complexity contributes evidence and detect suspiciously good results.
modules.objective: Test whether added complexity contributes evidence and detect suspiciously good results.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 10 minutes of original explanation and primary-source reading, 8 minutes of calculations, and 12 minutes of research notebook or project work. Longer independent experiments and exam time are additional.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

An ablation removes or simplifies a component while preserving the surrounding experiment. Compare value-only with value-plus-quality, a fixed rank with a trained model, and the same signal under slower execution. Match sample, costs and constraints so a difference has an interpretable cause. An ablation is another trial; do not report only the one that favors the preferred model.

Negative controls probe the research machinery. Random labels or deliberately uninformative features should not reliably produce exceptional independent predictions. If they do, investigate leakage, selection and evaluation code before celebrating the original signal. Shuffling must respect the question and dependence structure; indiscriminate row shuffling can remove time dependence and create an unrealistically easy null. Controls diagnose problems, but passing them does not prove a real economic advantage.

$$
\Delta_{\mathrm{ablation}}=M(\mathrm{full\ rule})-M(\mathrm{matched\ simpler\ rule})
$$

## A worked example

A baseline has validation net return 4%, an added feature raises it to 4.1%, and doubling modeled costs reduces the new rule to 1%. If the feature also triples turnover, the incremental prediction result may have little implementation value. A random-label run that appears excellent warrants an audit of label timing and the full search count.

## Put the idea into practice

Create an ablation matrix with one changed element per row and retain losses. Use a fixed seed for controls and record their construction. For a failed experiment, write whether the mechanism, data, model, portfolio or execution assumption was challenged.

### Research notebook evidence

Reproduce the worksheet, change the stated assumption, and save your calculation and interpretation with the assignment. Record what information was available, what was estimated, and what would invalidate the conclusion. The browser worksheet stays in cash: its price chart does not backtest this lesson's strategy. Use the downloadable Strategy Lab project for multi-asset simulations, trade ledgers and report exports. All supplied companies, prices and results are fictional teaching cases.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

An ablation is only as fair as the effort behind its simpler arm. Melis and co-authors re-evaluated popular neural language-model architectures under large-scale automatic hyperparameter tuning and found that standard LSTM architectures, when properly regularised, outperform more recent models. Earlier comparisons had used differing code bases and limited computing, uncontrolled sources of variation. If the full rule gets a tuning search and the matched simpler rule does not, the gap in the lesson's formula may measure search effort, not information. A 0.1-point gain (4.1% against 4%) could be exactly that (our inference).

Negative controls are a laboratory staple that Lipsitch and co-authors argue epidemiology should use more often. They distinguish exposure controls from outcome controls, which can detect suspected and unsuspected sources of spurious causal inference, yet they conclude that more work is needed to specify when controls sensitively detect other errors. A control reassures only about the failure it was built to expose. A forecasting analogue (our inference): shuffle scores within each date, so market-wide moves survive and stock-level information does not; its rank-IC distribution should centre on zero.

Data leakage is widespread enough to be the first suspect when a control looks too good. Kapoor and Narayanan found 17 research fields with reported errors, affecting 329 papers, and proposed a taxonomy of 8 leakage types. In civil-war prediction, every paper claiming that complex machine-learning models beat logistic regression failed to reproduce because of leakage, and the complex models did not perform substantively better.

Exercise: give the baseline the same tuning budget, run a shuffled-score control under several fixed seeds, and repeat every row at doubled costs. Report each paired difference, including losses, and the number of rows tried.

### Sources for this section

- [Melis, Dyer & Blunsom (2017) · On the State of the Art of Evaluation in Neural Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.05589) — *arXiv 1707.05589.* Re-tuning older architectures under the same large-scale search made standard LSTMs beat newer models, a warning that ablations need matched tuning effort.
- [Lipsitch, Tchetgen Tchetgen & Cohen (2010) · Negative Controls](https://doi.org/10.1097/EDE.0b013e3181d61eeb) — *Research paper.* Explains exposure and outcome negative controls and how they detect spurious inference, while noting that their sensitivity to other errors still needs study.
- [Kapoor & Narayanan (2022) · Leakage and the Reproducibility Crisis in ML-based Science](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.07048) — *arXiv 2207.07048.* Surveys leakage across 17 fields, gives a taxonomy of 8 types, and shows complex models losing their edge over logistic regression once leakage is fixed.
