modules.title: Position sizing, exposure caps and volatility targets
modules.subtitle: Translate a score into bounded exposure while treating risk estimates as uncertain.
modules.objective: Translate a score into bounded exposure while treating risk estimates as uncertain.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 10 minutes of original explanation and primary-source reading, 8 minutes of calculations, and 12 minutes of research notebook or project work. Longer independent experiments and exam time are additional.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

Several attractive signals can still produce a concentrated or unaffordable portfolio. Portfolio construction decides how much to hold and how the positions interact. Start with a small set of proposed weights, then check cash, exposure limits, and the effect of trading costs. Accounting for the resulting trades lets you verify that the strategy you measured is the one you intended.

## Understand the idea

A signal says which exposure is preferred; sizing determines how much risk reaches the portfolio. Start with equal weights, a single-name cap, a gross exposure limit and a cash rule. Integer shares, lot sizes and next-open gaps mean realized weights differ from target weights. Record requested and filled quantities so a cash constraint cannot silently appear as a better signal.

Volatility targeting scales exposure using a past estimate of risk. Specify the return horizon, estimator, floor, rebalance frequency and leverage cap. A low recent estimate can otherwise produce excessive leverage just before a shock. Volatility is not a complete loss model: gaps, correlation changes and illiquidity remain possible. Use stress scenarios and capital constraints alongside the estimate rather than interpreting a target as a guaranteed realized volatility.

$$
g_t=\min(g_{\max},\sigma_{\mathrm{target}}/\max(\widehat\sigma_t,\sigma_{\min}))
$$

## A worked example

A 10% target divided by a 20% annualized estimate suggests 0.5 times exposure. If the estimate falls to 4%, the raw multiplier is 2.5; a declared 1.2 cap limits it to 1.2. The resulting future volatility can still exceed 10% if conditions change.

## Put the idea into practice

Calculate target and capped exposure, then convert a 40% weight on 10,000 equity at a 103 close into 38 whole shares. Explain how a next-open gap and fees can reduce the actual purchase. The lab uses long-only caps without volatility leverage; targeting is a tested extension assignment.

### Research notebook evidence

Reproduce the worksheet, change the stated assumption, and save your calculation and interpretation with the assignment. Record what information was available, what was estimated, and what would invalidate the conclusion. The browser worksheet stays in cash: its price chart does not backtest this lesson's strategy. Use the downloadable Strategy Lab project for multi-asset simulations, trade ledgers and report exports. All supplied companies, prices and results are fictional teaching cases.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Volatility targeting rests on volatility clustering: high volatility in the recent past tends to be followed by high volatility soon after. Published tests disagree on whether scaling by inverse volatility still pays when traded in real time. Moreira and Muir found that portfolios taking less risk when volatility is high earned large alphas and higher Sharpe ratios across equity factors and the currency carry trade, because volatility swings are not offset by proportional swings in expected returns. Cederburg and co-authors, using 103 equity strategies, found that volatility-managed portfolios do not systematically beat their unmanaged counterparts in direct comparisons. The strategies implied by spanning-regression alphas cannot be traded in real time, and reasonable out-of-sample versions generally earned lower certainty-equivalent returns and Sharpe ratios, mainly because of structural instability in those regressions.

Harvey and co-authors, covering more than 60 assets, with US equity data from 1926, found higher Sharpe ratios for equities and credit but negligible effects for bonds, currencies and commodities, and fewer extreme returns across assets. Our inference: the stronger case for a target is tail control, not extra return.

Leverage and turnover matter too. Bianco and Bernardi report that smoothing volatility forecasts reduces excess leverage and turnover and improves risk-adjusted returns after transaction costs, and that superior forecasting accuracy does not guarantee superior portfolio performance.

Apply it to the lesson's numbers. With no floor, a 1.2 cap binds whenever the estimate is below 10% / 1.2 ≈ 8.3%, and a floor at or above that level would make the cap redundant (our arithmetic). Replay your prices with two estimator windows and report how often the cap binds, the multiplier's turnover and the worst day, not just a Sharpe ratio.

- [Cederburg, O'Doherty, Wang & Yan (2020) · On the performance of volatility-managed portfolios](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2020.04.015) — *Research paper.* Tests 103 equity strategies as a real-time investor would; the strategies implied by spanning-regression alphas are not implementable and out-of-sample volatility management often earns less.
- [Harvey et al. (2018) · The Impact of Volatility Targeting](https://doi.org/10.3905/jpm.2018.45.1.014) — *Research paper.* More than 60 assets, with US equities back to 1926: scaling lifts Sharpe ratios for equities and credit, not for bonds, currencies or commodities, and reduces extreme returns.
- [Bianco & Bernardi (2022) · Flexible variational approximations for stochastic volatility-managed portfolios](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.07288) — *arXiv 2212.07288.* Shows that smoothing volatility forecasts cuts excess leverage and turnover and improves after-cost results, and that forecast accuracy alone does not ensure better portfolios.

modules.title: Covariance, diversification and portfolio constraints
modules.subtitle: Evaluate joint exposures rather than treating several strategies as independent bets.
modules.objective: Evaluate joint exposures rather than treating several strategies as independent bets.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 10 minutes of original explanation and primary-source reading, 8 minutes of calculations, and 12 minutes of research notebook or project work. Longer independent experiments and exam time are additional.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Combining strategies changes the portfolio through weights and covariance, not through the number of names alone. Two individually attractive signals may own the same stocks or respond to the same macro factor. Inspect holdings overlap, sector and factor exposures, and correlations of aligned net returns. Correlations estimated in quiet periods may rise during stress, exactly when diversification is most valuable.

A minimum-variance or risk-budget allocation depends on uncertain covariance estimates. Small samples and nearly duplicate strategies can make unconstrained solutions unstable. Compare a simple equal-weight allocation with constrained alternatives, regularize estimates when justified, and report sensitivity. Exposure limits and cash reserves express the mandate; an optimizer should not silently violate them to produce an attractive historical objective.

$$
\sigma_p^2=w_A^2\sigma_A^2+w_B^2\sigma_B^2+2w_Aw_B\rho\sigma_A\sigma_B
$$

## A worked example

Two sleeves each have 20% volatility and receive 50% weights. At correlation zero, portfolio variance is 0.02 and volatility about 14.14%. At correlation one, volatility becomes 20%. Merely labeling the sleeves 'value' and 'AI' does not establish the zero-correlation assumption.

## Put the idea into practice

Reproduce both covariance cases and build a holdings-overlap table. Add a correlation-one stress to the research notebook, and compare equal weights with a capped candidate allocation using the same net-return calendar.

### Research notebook evidence

Reproduce the worksheet, change the stated assumption, and save your calculation and interpretation with the assignment. Record what information was available, what was estimated, and what would invalidate the conclusion. The browser worksheet stays in cash: its price chart does not backtest this lesson's strategy. Use the downloadable Strategy Lab project for multi-asset simulations, trade ledgers and report exports. All supplied companies, prices and results are fictional teaching cases.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

The lesson's algebra generalises to N sleeves, and the result is a floor on diversification. With N equally weighted sleeves of volatility σ and the same pairwise correlation ρ, portfolio variance is

$$
\sigma_p^2=\sigma^2\left[\rho+\frac{1-\rho}{N}\right],
$$

so volatility cannot fall below σ√ρ however many sleeves you add (our algebra). At σ = 20% and ρ = 0.5 that floor is 14.14%, the figure the lesson reaches with two uncorrelated sleeves. Polakow and Gebbie make a related point about breadth, the number of independent bets. Applying a singular value decomposition to the return correlation matrix, they estimated South African breadth as considerably lower than anticipated, and suggest concentration and commodity-cycle and currency exposure as possible causes.

Estimating the inputs is the next hazard. Ledoit and Wolf averaged the sample covariance matrix with a single-index matrix using optimal weights; for NYSE and AMEX stocks from 1972 to 1995 this selected portfolios with significantly lower out-of-sample variance than existing estimators, including multifactor models. Bun and co-authors review random-matrix tools for estimating large covariance matrices and report that, in a financial application, their rotationally invariant estimator was superior to all previously proposed methods. Jagannathan and Ma add a twist: requiring non-negative weights can reduce risk in estimated optimal portfolios even when the constraint is wrong, and with it the sample covariance matrix did as well as factor-model, shrinkage and daily-data estimates. Our inference: a long-only run already imposes that constraint, so test whether a fancier estimator changes your allocation at all.

Exercise: estimate your sleeves' correlation over the full sample and over your weakest months, then compare equal weights with the capped allocation under both matrices and under correlation one.

### Sources for this section

- [Polakow & Gebbie (2006) · How many independent bets are there?](https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0601166) — *arXiv physics/0601166.* Separates the number of bets from independent breadth using the correlation matrix, finding South African breadth well below the naive count.
- [Ledoit & Wolf (2003) · Improved estimation of the covariance matrix of stock returns with an application to portfolio selection](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0927-5398%2803%2900007-0) — *Research paper.* Shrinks the sample covariance matrix toward a single-index matrix and reports lower out-of-sample portfolio variance for NYSE and AMEX stocks, 1972 to 1995.
- [Jagannathan & Ma (2003) · Risk Reduction in Large Portfolios: Why Imposing the Wrong Constraints Helps](https://doi.org/10.1111/1540-6261.00580) — *Research paper.* Explains why non-negative-weight constraints can cut the risk of estimated optimal portfolios even when wrong, leaving the sample covariance matrix competitive.
- [Bun, Bouchaud & Potters (2016) · Cleaning large correlation matrices: tools from random matrix theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.08104) — *arXiv 1610.08104.* Reviews random-matrix methods for estimating large covariance matrices and reports that a rotationally invariant estimator beat earlier methods in a financial application.

modules.title: Turnover, transaction costs and strategy capacity
modules.subtitle: State turnover conventions and test whether proposed orders fit plausible liquidity.
modules.objective: State turnover conventions and test whether proposed orders fit plausible liquidity.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 10 minutes of original explanation and primary-source reading, 8 minutes of calculations, and 12 minutes of research notebook or project work. Longer independent experiments and exam time are additional.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Turnover measures trading activity, but conventions differ. The sum of absolute weight changes counts both purchases and sales; half that sum is often called one-way turnover for a fully invested rebalance. Fees assessed per traded notional apply to the full traded amount. Mixing these conventions can understate cost by a factor of two. Keep cash changes and drift assumptions explicit.

Capacity asks whether more capital changes the execution economics. Measure order size relative to an observable liquidity estimate, then consider spread, impact, urgency and participation limits. A fixed fee does not capture market impact, and current-session total volume is unknown at the open. The teaching engine uses a fraction of prior-session volume as a quantity cap; this is a transparent approximation, not a claim about actual opening liquidity.

$$
T_{\mathrm{traded}}=\sum_i|w_i^*-w_i|,\qquad C/E\approx cT_{\mathrm{traded}}
$$

## A worked example

Weights move from [0.6,0.4] to [0.4,0.6]. Absolute changes total 0.4; one-way turnover is 0.2. At 20 basis points per traded notional, approximate fee drag is 0.0008 of equity. A desired 300-share order with a 5% cap on prior volume of 2,000 can fill at most 100 shares under the lab policy.

## Put the idea into practice

Reconcile both turnover conventions, double costs and reduce the participation cap. Compare unfilled quantities and cash across runs. Record that a prior-volume proxy cannot determine the actual order book or spread available at the opening event.

### Research notebook evidence

Reproduce the worksheet, change the stated assumption, and save your calculation and interpretation with the assignment. Record what information was available, what was estimated, and what would invalidate the conclusion. The browser worksheet stays in cash: its price chart does not backtest this lesson's strategy. Use the downloadable Strategy Lab project for multi-asset simulations, trade ledgers and report exports. All supplied companies, prices and results are fictional teaching cases.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

A flat fee per traded dollar is a placeholder, and measurement shows why. Frazzini and co-authors analysed 1.7 trillion dollars of live executions by one large institutional manager across 21 developed equity markets over 19 years. Actual trading costs were an order of magnitude smaller than earlier studies suggested, and they varied with trade type, stock characteristics, trade size, time and exchange. The lesson's 20 basis points is therefore an assumption about who trades and how, not a measurement (our inference).

Size matters, but the shape of its effect is contested. Almgren and co-authors, using Citigroup US equity trading data, rejected the common square-root model of temporary impact against trade rate in favour of a 3/5 power law across the order sizes considered. Zarinelli and co-authors studied large orders executed in U.S. equities between 2007 and 2009 and found that the square-root formula fits well across only about two orders of magnitude in size, while a logarithmic form fits across almost five. Capacity estimates are most fragile where they extrapolate beyond observed sizes (our inference).

Apply it to the lesson. A 300-share order against a 100-share cap (5% of 2,000) fills one-third; at double the capital, 600 desired shares fill one-sixth, so unfilled quantity is already a capacity signal before any impact is charged. As an illustration only, a 3/5 law raises per-share impact about 1.5 times when the trade rate doubles (our arithmetic; it was fitted to other data, not to a prior-volume cap). Exercise: run one, two and four times the capital, log fill ratio, unfilled shares and net result, and declare beforehand the fill ratio or net advantage at which the strategy counts as full.

### Sources for this section

- [Frazzini, Israel & Moskowitz (2018) · Trading Costs](https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.3229719) — *Research paper.* Live execution data from 21 developed equity markets over 19 years: real trading costs far below earlier estimates, varying with trade size, stock traits, time and exchange.
- [Almgren, Thum, Hauptmann & Li (2005) · Direct Estimation of Equity Market Impact](https://www.cis.upenn.edu/~mkearns/finread/costestim.pdf) — *Research paper.* Analyses Citigroup US equity executions and rejects the square-root model of temporary impact against trade rate in favour of a 3/5 power law.
- [Zarinelli, Treccani, Farmer & Lillo (2014) · Beyond the square root: Evidence for logarithmic dependence of market impact on size and participation rate](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.2152) — *arXiv 1412.2152.* Large U.S. equity orders, 2007 to 2009: the square-root law fits only about two orders of magnitude of size, while a logarithmic form fits almost five.

modules.title: Portfolio accounting and independent engine checks
modules.subtitle: Reconcile cash, holdings, fees and wealth with a hand-calculated event ledger.
modules.objective: Reconcile cash, holdings, fees and wealth with a hand-calculated event ledger.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 10 minutes of original explanation and primary-source reading, 8 minutes of calculations, and 12 minutes of research notebook or project work. Longer independent experiments and exam time are additional.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Before interpreting performance, prove that the engine accounts for its own events. Each fill changes shares and cash once, fees are charged once, and wealth equals cash plus marked holdings. Process sells before buys if that is the declared rebalance convention, maintain deterministic allocation when cash is scarce, and record partial fills. A correct signal with incorrect accounting produces an invalid research result.

Use tiny independent fixtures with obvious expected answers: constant prices, an overnight gap, one profitable round trip, one losing round trip, insufficient cash and a final unexecuted signal. Compare event-ledger arithmetic with the wealth path. Tests that simply repeat the implementation's formula are weaker than a separately worked cash ledger. Mark remaining holdings at the end and disclose whether liquidation costs are included.

$$
E_t=C_t+\sum_i q_{i,t}P_{i,t},\qquad \Pi_{\mathrm{net}}=\Pi_{\mathrm{gross}}-\mathrm{fees}
$$

## A worked example

Start with 1,000. Buy two shares at the next open of 100 with a 1% fee: cash becomes 798. Sell both at a later open of 110 with a 1% fee: proceeds are 217.8 and final cash is 1,015.8. Gross gain is 20, fees total 4.2 and net gain is 15.8.

## Put the idea into practice

Run the archive's unit tests and reconcile the fixed trade fixture without reading the implementation first. Inspect positions.csv and verify cash plus closing market value equals equity on every row. Confirm the first signal cannot earn a return before its next-open fill.

### Research notebook evidence

Reproduce the worksheet, change the stated assumption, and save your calculation and interpretation with the assignment. Record what information was available, what was estimated, and what would invalidate the conclusion. The browser worksheet stays in cash: its price chart does not backtest this lesson's strategy. Use the downloadable Strategy Lab project for multi-asset simulations, trade ledgers and report exports. All supplied companies, prices and results are fictional teaching cases.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Weyuker called a program non-testable when no oracle, a reliable way to judge its output, exists or checking takes extraordinary effort, and concluded that assuming an oracle is often unrealistic. A multi-asset backtest is plausibly non-testable in that sense (our inference); the two-share round trip is not, so it can serve as your oracle.

A second engine is the usual substitute. In a 2026 preprint, Yin and co-authors ran 15 benchmark strategies through five independent open-source engines on 180 S&P 500 stocks. With costs set to zero, all five agreed exactly, so cost handling was the only possible source of disagreement. With costs switched on they diverged: by under 0.75 percentage points for most strategies but 3.71% for high-turnover rotations, and reading the source code exposed seven defects nobody had documented. One engine processed its order queue in sequence and rejected purchases that depended on cash from sales queued after them, the case a declared sells-before-buys convention is meant to settle.

Two cautions follow (our inference). Give every fixture a nonzero fee and one purchase that only a sale can fund. And a second implementation is less independent than it sounds: Knight and Leveson had 27 versions written from one specification at two universities and ran one million tests, and the individually extremely reliable versions failed together substantially more often than expected. A ledger and an engine built from the same reading of the rules can share a misreading, so Yin and co-authors recommend validators chosen for implementation diversity.

Try it on the round trip. If the sell fee is computed from the entry price of 100 instead of the exit price of 110, final cash is 1,016.0 rather than 1,015.8. Set your test tolerance below that 0.2 gap, then predict each variant's result before running it.

### Sources for this section

- [Weyuker (1982) · On Testing Non-Testable Programs](https://doi.org/10.1093/comjnl/25.4.465) — *Research paper.* Defines non-testable programs, where no oracle exists or checking output is impractical, and questions the routine assumption that a tester can recognise the correct answer.
- [Knight & Leveson (1986) · An experimental evaluation of the assumption of independence in multiversion programming](https://doi.org/10.1109/TSE.1986.6312924) — *Research paper.* Twenty-seven versions written independently from one specification failed together more often than independence predicts, a limit on any second-implementation check.
- [Yin, Miki, Lesnichenko & Gural (2026) · Implementation Risk in Portfolio Backtesting: A Previously Unquantified Source of Error](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.20319) — *arXiv 2603.20319.* Runs the same strategies through five open-source backtest engines: exact agreement at zero cost, cost-driven divergence otherwise, and seven undocumented defects found by source inspection.

modules.title: Chronological validation and untouched evaluation
modules.subtitle: Select a candidate on validation data and evaluate its frozen rule on a later segment.
modules.objective: Select a candidate on validation data and evaluate its frozen rule on a later segment.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 10 minutes of original explanation and primary-source reading, 8 minutes of calculations, and 12 minutes of research notebook or project work. Longer independent experiments and exam time are additional.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

The final research stage asks whether the selected strategy deserves further work. Keep the evaluation period separate from the trials used to choose it. Then challenge the result with reasonable changes to assumptions, parameters, and execution conditions. A defensible conclusion explains what passed, what failed, and which parts of the idea remain untested.

## Understand the idea

A research comparison needs a selection protocol, not only a train/test label. Fix the candidate list, development period, validation objective, tie-break and final evaluation window. Use development fixtures to find implementation errors, then select the candidate using validation outcomes only. Freeze the specification before revealing the final segment and record that the segment has now been consumed.

A reset evaluation and a continuous walk-forward simulation answer different questions. The supplied project starts each validation and test account in cash at the preceding decision close, with historical observations available only for indicator warm-up. No earlier holdings are imported. A continuous strategy would carry holdings and accounting state across the boundary; implement and disclose that separately. Short synthetic segments exercise this procedure but cannot provide convincing market evidence.

$$
j^*=\arg\max_j R_{j,\mathrm{validation}},\qquad R_{\mathrm{reported}}=R_{j^*,\mathrm{test}}
$$

## A worked example

Validation net returns for equal-weight, value-quality and momentum are 2%, 3% and 1%. The predeclared highest-return rule selects value-quality. If the later test returns −4%, the result remains −4%; selecting equal-weight after seeing test outcomes would turn that segment into another selection sample.

## Put the idea into practice

Run strategy_lab.py and inspect experiments.json. Confirm the winner depends only on validation rows. Open the selected strategy's test export after writing your prediction in the notebook. The program evaluates only the selected candidate on the final segment; repeated manual trials still need disclosure.

Record what information was available, what was estimated, and what would invalidate the conclusion. The browser worksheet stays in cash: its price chart does not backtest this lesson's strategy. Use the downloadable Strategy Lab project for multi-asset simulations, trade ledgers and report exports. All supplied companies, prices and results are fictional teaching cases.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Each look at a held-back segment spends some of its independence. Dwork and co-authors point out that classical inference presumes the analysis plan was settled before anyone looked at the data, whereas real analysis is adaptive: each step is shaped by exploration and by what earlier steps showed on the same data. Opening the test export, reacting and rerunning therefore makes the segment part of selection, even if no code trains on it (our reading). Their reusable holdout lets analysts query one holdout many times, drawing on privacy-preserving data analysis. The lab relies on disclosure instead, so your count of looks is the control.

Finance shows the cost too. Wiecki and co-authors studied 888 Quantopian strategies that had at least six months of out-of-sample performance. Backtest Sharpe ratios were poor predictors of that performance (R² < 0.025), and strategies that had been backtested more showed a bigger gap between backtest and out-of-sample results.

Not every drop is selection, though. Recht and co-authors built fresh CIFAR-10 and ImageNet test sets after almost a decade of heavy reuse and found accuracy drops of 3% to 15% and 11% to 14%. Their results suggest the drops did not come from adaptivity but from slightly harder images, and gains on the old test sets still carried over. A later market segment is likewise a new draw, perhaps under different conditions, so a gap like the lesson's 3% validation return and −4% test return, seven points, cannot alone separate overfitting from a changed market (our inference; their evidence comes from image classification).

Before opening the test export, write down the sign and rough size of that gap you expect, and log every look. A second look after any tweak consumes the segment: report that result as exploratory.

modules.objective: Interpret a selected backtest in light of search effort and dependent observations.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 10 minutes of original explanation and primary-source reading, 8 minutes of calculations, and 12 minutes of research notebook or project work. Longer independent experiments and exam time are additional.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

The best result among many noisy trials tends to look better than its underlying process. Count families, features, windows, costs, benchmarks and informal revisions, not just the final grid. A nominal p-value or Sharpe estimate for the selected winner does not automatically account for that search. The probability-of-backtest-overfitting literature formalizes aspects of selection; citing it is not the same as implementing its procedure.

Returns also exhibit dependence and changing regimes. A row-wise bootstrap may break serial structure, while a block bootstrap preserves some local dependence under its own stationarity and block-length assumptions. Uncertainty intervals from one selected series remain conditional on selection unless the procedure explicitly models the search. Use descriptive intervals, independent periods and economic reasoning together, and distinguish a failed rejection from proof that no effect exists.

$$
\Pr(\mathrm{at\ least\ one\ false\ positive})=1-(1-\alpha)^m\quad\mathrm{(independent\ nulls)}
$$

## A worked example

If twenty independent null tests each have a 5% false-positive probability, the chance of at least one false positive is 1 − 0.95²⁰, about 64.15%. Real strategy trials are usually dependent, so this is an illustrative independence calculation rather than the exact probability for a research grid.

## Put the idea into practice

Record the complete trial count and identify dependencies among settings. Use the final reporting course's block-uncertainty tool for a descriptive interval, explicitly retaining its selection caveat. Do not label a simple count or bootstrap as a computed PBO estimate.

### Research notebook evidence

Reproduce the worksheet, change the stated assumption, and save your calculation and interpretation with the assignment. Record what information was available, what was estimated, and what would invalidate the conclusion. The browser worksheet stays in cash: its price chart does not backtest this lesson's strategy. Use the downloadable Strategy Lab project for multi-asset simulations, trade ledgers and report exports. All supplied companies, prices and results are fictional teaching cases.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Bailey and López de Prado argue that the number of trials attempted is the key missing fact in nearly every published backtest. Their deflated Sharpe ratio uses it to correct for selection under multiple testing and for non-normal returns. Trials are rarely independent, so they shrink M dependent trials to an implied number of independent ones using the average correlation between trials. That makes the lesson's request to identify dependencies concrete: it needs each trial's return series, not only the winner's (our inference).

How large is the selection effect? For twenty independent strategies with no true edge, the expected best z-score is about 1.87 (our calculation, in standard-error units rather than Sharpe units), already above the one-sided 5% cutoff of 1.645. The lesson's 64.15% is the same selection effect stated as a probability.

Dependence also matters for intervals. Ledoit and Wolf point out that the classic test for a Sharpe-ratio difference is not valid for heavy-tailed or time-series returns, and propose a studentized time-series bootstrap interval for the difference, declaring two ratios different only if zero lies outside it. That suits comparing the selected rule with its benchmark, but it still ignores how the rule was chosen (our inference). Neither a count nor a bootstrap is a deflated Sharpe ratio.

Nor is a failed rejection proof of no effect. Chen and Dim mined 136,000 long-short strategies built from accounting ratios, past returns and ticker symbols, and found that the multiple-testing procedures common in finance miss most of the strategies that went on to perform out of sample. Report the trial count, an effective count and a benchmark-difference interval, and word a null result as "not distinguished from luck".

### Sources for this section

- [Bailey & López de Prado (2014) · The Deflated Sharpe Ratio: Correcting for Selection Bias, Backtest Overfitting, and Non-Normality](https://doi.org/10.3905/jpm.2014.40.5.094) — *Research paper.* Argues the number of trials is the missing number in most backtests, deflates the Sharpe ratio for selection and non-normality, and converts dependent trials into an implied number of independent ones.
- [Ledoit & Wolf (2008) · Robust performance hypothesis testing with the Sharpe ratio](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jempfin.2008.03.002) — *Research paper.* Shows the standard Sharpe-difference test fails for heavy tails and time-series returns, and proposes a studentized time-series bootstrap confidence interval instead.
- [Chen & Dim (2023) · High-Throughput Asset Pricing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.10685) — *arXiv 2311.10685.* Mines 136,000 long-short strategies and finds that popular multiple-testing methods miss most out-of-sample performers, a reminder that a failed rejection is not proof of no effect.

modules.objective: Challenge a frozen strategy with adverse costs, delays, liquidity and concentration.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 10 minutes of original explanation and primary-source reading, 8 minutes of calculations, and 12 minutes of research notebook or project work. Longer independent experiments and exam time are additional.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Stress tests ask how the proposed rule behaves when an assumption becomes less favorable. Keep the candidate fixed while increasing costs, tightening a prior-volume participation cap, delaying execution, removing a feature or imposing a concentration shock. Preserve the base input identity when testing one changed assumption so the comparison remains interpretable. A stress is a scenario, not a prediction of its probability.

Separate implementation readiness from expected profitability. Correct accounting, deterministic replay and clean inputs support engineering confidence. Later independent performance, an economic mechanism and robust implementation assumptions support a research argument. Paper execution adds evidence about data freshness, order handling and reconciliation without proving that live fills will match. Set concrete pause conditions such as stale inputs, irreconcilable holdings or an unexplained model-version change.

$$
\mathrm{stress\ impact}=M(\mathrm{fixed\ rule},\mathrm{adverse\ assumption})-M(\mathrm{fixed\ rule},\mathrm{base})
$$

## A worked example

A fixed strategy returns 5% at base costs, 1% at doubled costs and −2% under a tighter liquidity cap. The appropriate conclusion identifies execution sensitivity rather than averaging the three into a guaranteed return. If a replay changes earlier fills after only future data are edited, that is a causality defect requiring repair before any performance claim.

## Put the idea into practice

Run the download's cost and liquidity stress modes on the selected rule, retain every output and label them as post-selection diagnostics. Propose a one-event execution delay as an extension. Use the Python bot or C/HPC track for subsequent operational implementation.

### Research notebook evidence

Reproduce the worksheet, change the stated assumption, and save your calculation and interpretation with the assignment. Record what information was available, what was estimated, and what would invalidate the conclusion. The browser worksheet stays in cash: its price chart does not backtest this lesson's strategy. Use the downloadable Strategy Lab project for multi-asset simulations, trade ledgers and report exports. All supplied companies, prices and results are fictional teaching cases.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Chen and Velikov stripped three adverse effects from the returns of 204 published stock anomalies at once: effective spreads, post-publication effects and the modern era of trading technology. The average anomaly's expected return fell to 4 bps per month, and even the strongest netted at most 10 bps once data mining was controlled for, with price impact still left out.

Stacking suggests that one-at-a-time stresses can understate the damage (our inference). Saltelli and co-authors found that many analyses vary one factor at a time, along what they call one-dimensional corridors, and that 42% of the highly cited papers they analysed failed to explore the input space properly. A 2026 preprint by Deo warns that hand-chosen scenarios can miss the truly dangerous combinations or dwell on shocks too unlikely to matter.

With the lesson's numbers, doubled costs lose 4 points (5% to 1%) and the tighter cap 7 points (5% to −2%). If the effects simply added, both together would give −6%; run the combination and compare. If the return fell linearly with costs, it would hit zero at 2.25 times base costs (our inference); test that break-even directly.

On readiness, the SEC found that Knight Capital's router sent more than 4 million orders in the first 45 minutes to fill 212 customer orders, and the firm lost more than $460 million. It lacked adequate controls, including a check of outgoing orders against the customer orders entered, and 97 automated emails flagging a router error before the open went unheeded. That is more than 18,800 orders per customer order. Put a trigger like that, and an owner for it, into your pause rules.

Check the fixture too: doubling the 1% fee in the 1,015.8 round trip must cut final cash by exactly the 4.2 of base fees, to 1,011.6.

### Sources for this section

- [Chen & Velikov (2022) · Zeroing In on the Expected Returns of Anomalies](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022109022000874) — *Research paper.* Nets spreads, post-publication effects and the modern trading era out of 204 anomalies at once; expected returns shrink to a few basis points a month, with price impact still omitted.
- [Saltelli et al. (2019) · Why so many published sensitivity analyses are false: A systematic review of sensitivity analysis practices](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envsoft.2019.01.012) — *Research paper.* Systematic review finding that many highly cited analyses vary one input at a time and leave most of the input space unexplored.
- [Deo (2026) · Generating Plausible Stress Scenarios via Large Deviations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.31122) — *arXiv 2606.31122.* Warns that handpicked stress scenarios can miss dangerous configurations or dwell on implausible shocks, and proposes generating scenarios systematically from the loss itself.
- [U.S. SEC (2013) · SEC Charges Knight Capital With Violations of Market Access Rule](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2013-222) — *Official source.* The SEC's account of Knight Capital's 2012 incident: millions of erroneous orders, missing pre-submission controls and unheeded automated warnings.

modules.content:
## Understand the idea

The capstone combines the strategy contract, data audit, experiment ledger, selected rule, order and position records, net wealth path, benchmark and limitations. Reproduce the supplied engine's independent fixtures before studying its fictional results. Then complete one predeclared research extension and show what changed, what remained fixed and what evidence challenged the original idea. A careful negative result is a successful research deliverable.

The downloadable engine runs equal-weight, value-quality and momentum portfolios with available filings, next-open fills, fees, whole shares, cash and prior-volume caps. It selects on a validation segment, evaluates the frozen choice on a later synthetic segment, and exports two post-selection stresses. Pairs execution, fitted ML, corporate actions and real market adapters are explicit extension work. Do not describe them as implemented merely because their design appears in the course.

$$
\mathrm{dossier}=\mathrm{specification}+\mathrm{audited\ data}+\mathrm{tested\ execution}+\mathrm{independent\ evaluation}+\mathrm{limitations}
$$

## A worked example

Your engine fixture must finish the two-share round trip at 1,015.8 with 4.2 of fees. The 100-point dossier rubric allocates 20 to hypothesis/data, 25 to timing/accounting, 20 to comparison/selection, 20 to stress/limitations and 15 to reproducibility/communication. Unresolved look-ahead or unreconciled cash requires revision regardless of score.

## Put the idea into practice

Run the archive tests and project, complete research-notebook.md and inspect the exported CSV/JSON files. Send the base test equity.csv and manifest.json to [Algorithm evaluation & results reporting](/curriculum/algorithm-evaluation) for the final report, charts and written decision. Continue operational implementation in [Algorithmic & AI stock bots](/curriculum/stock-bots) or [Algorithmic trading II: C & high-performance computing](/curriculum/c-hpc-trading) with the same research contract.

### Research notebook evidence

Reproduce the worksheet, change the stated assumption, and save your calculation and interpretation with the assignment. Record what information was available, what was estimated, and what would invalidate the conclusion. The browser worksheet stays in cash: its price chart does not backtest this lesson's strategy. Use the downloadable Strategy Lab project for multi-asset simulations, trade ledgers and report exports. All supplied companies, prices and results are fictional teaching cases.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

A dossier needs two defences that do not substitute for each other. In a 2026 preprint, Gençay built a strategy-discovery system whose tools make look-ahead impossible and which logs every strategy it tries, so reported results can be discounted by the number of trials. A deliberately leaky "oracle" strategy with a Sharpe ratio of 35 passed the deflated Sharpe ratio and probability-of-backtest-overfitting tests untouched, while honest evaluation rejected every strategy the language models discovered, which the paper lists among its main findings: a negative result as the deliverable. Our reading: statistical corrections cannot stand in for the lesson's mechanical checks, which is why unresolved look-ahead or unreconciled cash forces revision regardless of score.

Sums also hide holes. The rubric gives 25 of 100 points to timing and accounting, so a dossier that earned every other point would still total 75. Breck and co-authors' ML Test Score takes the minimum of its four section scores, choosing it because all four sections are important. Because your sections carry different maximums, report each as a share of its own maximum and flag the lowest share, not only the total.

Expect the headline to shrink. McLean and Pontiff examined 97 published return predictors and found their portfolio returns 26% lower out of sample and 58% lower once the papers appeared, reading the first drop as an upper bound on data-mining effects. State the shrinkage your dossier assumes, and remember that the fictional segments here exercise the protocol, not the market idea.

Last, rerun everything. The same ML paper lists reproducible training as a test: training twice on the same data should ideally produce identical models. Rerun the engine from a clean copy and confirm that the two-share fixture still ends at 1,015.8 and that equity.csv and the manifest figures match before you hand over the bundle.

### Sources for this section

- [Gençay (2026) · What survives honest evaluation? Leakage-safe, search-aware assessment of LLM-driven trading strategy discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27734) — *arXiv 2608.27734.* Pairs structural look-ahead guardrails with trial-count deflation, shows that a planted leaky strategy passes the statistical tests, and reports that honest evaluation rejects every discovered strategy.
- [Breck et al. (2017) · The ML test score: A rubric for ML production readiness and technical debt reduction](https://doi.org/10.1109/BigData.2017.8258038) — *Research paper.* A 28-test readiness rubric whose overall score is the minimum across four sections, so strength in one area cannot hide a weak one; also lists reproducible training as a test.
- [McLean & Pontiff (2016) · Does Academic Research Destroy Stock Return Predictability?](https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.12365) — *Research paper.* Documents how returns on 97 published predictors fall out of sample and after publication, the shrinkage a dossier should expect for a published idea.

Deliver a reproducible research dossier and export results to the final evaluation/reporting course.
readingGuide:
An investment idea becomes a strategy only when another person could follow its rules and reach the same decisions. This course takes you through that translation: define the idea, choose data that was available at the time, create a signal, decide what to hold, and record how trades change the portfolio.

For each strategy family, start with the reason it might work and the reason it might fail. Follow the worked calculation, then use the project to inspect individual holdings, trades, and costs. Compare the result with a simple alternative over the same period. A useful research result may be a clear reason to reject an idea; the goal is to reach a conclusion you can explain and reproduce.

32 lessons × 30 minutes = 16 hours of planned study across eight units; exam time is additional. Includes 64 practice questions, eight four-question checkpoints, a 32-question final, a downloadable Python research project and a separately self-assessed capstone.

Original fictional cases teach research methods; they do not establish real-market profitability. The local engine implements equal-weight, value-quality and momentum portfolios.

Pairs and ML receive guided design/calculation labs; their full engines are extension assignments linked to the econometrics and stock-ML courses.

exams.title: Unit 1: Specify the research
exams.description: Four original transfer questions. Use your notes, show calculations, and review the explanations after submitting. This checkpoint samples the preceding unit; the final covers every module.

questions.question: Which artifact most clearly fixes the proposed signal before evaluation?
options: A dated specification with data timing and rejection rules
questions.explanation: A specification makes the intended decisions inspectable independently of their outcome.

questions.question: Selecting the weakest benchmark after evaluation introduces:
options: A correction for all factor exposures
questions.explanation: Benchmark selection is another degree of freedom that must be disclosed.

questions.question: An overnight gap makes the target unaffordable. The engine should:
options: Use the previous close as its fill
Apply a declared cash constraint and record the partial fill
questions.explanation: Execution must respect available cash under the documented allocation policy.

questions.question: Which missing artifact most prevents reproduction of a winning backtest?
options: The exact input and configuration manifest
questions.explanation: Exact inputs and decisions are necessary to reproduce the computation.

exams.title: Unit 2: Build trustworthy data
exams.description: Four original transfer questions. Use your notes, show calculations, and review the explanations after submitting. This checkpoint samples the preceding unit; the final covers every module.

questions.question: What should happen when a late amendment concerns an older reporting period?
options: Apply the documented period-and-revision selection policy
questions.explanation: Preserving period identity prevents late old-period revisions from silently replacing newer accounts.

questions.question: Cash dividends added to an already dividend-adjusted total-return path cause:
questions.explanation: The same distribution must enter the wealth calculation only once.

questions.question: Two equal scores compete for one portfolio slot. A reproducible rule needs:
options: The stock with the best future return
questions.explanation: A stable tie rule prevents hidden dependence on row ordering or future outcomes.

questions.question: What determines an appropriate purge or embargo policy?
options: Label intervals and the design's information overlap
questions.explanation: The required separation follows actual information horizons, not a favorable test outcome.

exams.title: Unit 3: Value and quality strategies
exams.description: Four original transfer questions. Use your notes, show calculations, and review the explanations after submitting. This checkpoint samples the preceding unit; the final covers every module.

questions.question: Using current liabilities alone in a net-net screen generally:
options: Eliminates the need for share counts
Overstates equity's residual claim when other liabilities exist
questions.explanation: Long-term creditors and other senior claims also reduce the residual available to common equity.

questions.question: Pooled quality ranks select nearly one sector. A useful diagnostic is:
options: Compare sector exposures and within-sector ranks
Assume the sector is inherently superior
questions.explanation: Sector analysis separates intended company selection from broad industry exposure.

questions.question: What is the strongest reason to invalidate an asset-value thesis?
options: Evidence that expected recoverable assets have materially deteriorated
questions.explanation: Disconfirmation should challenge the mechanism or valuation assumptions directly.

questions.question: What reveals where a fundamental rule loses most of its universe?
options: An eligibility waterfall with exclusion reasons
questions.explanation: Counts after each filter expose coverage and selection effects.

exams.title: Unit 4: Trend, momentum and reversal
exams.description: Four original transfer questions. Use your notes, show calculations, and review the explanations after submitting. This checkpoint samples the preceding unit; the final covers every module.

questions.question: Repeated small reversals around a trend threshold primarily create:
questions.explanation: Frequent entries and exits can lose money even without a large directional move.

questions.question: Adding a positive-score gate to a relative ranking changes:
options: Nothing when every asset is falling
The allocation and potentially its cash exposure
questions.explanation: The gate can exclude relative winners and leave cash when their absolute returns are negative.

questions.question: What cannot daily bars establish for an intraday reversal order?
options: The number of supplied daily rows
Its queue position and executable quote sequence
That a daily close was recorded
questions.explanation: OHLC aggregation omits the order-book and event sequence needed for precise fill claims.

questions.question: Which tie-break can be fixed before the final test?
questions.explanation: A predeclared selection rule avoids using the final result to choose the candidate.

exams.title: Unit 5: Pairs and relative value
exams.description: Four original transfer questions. Use your notes, show calculations, and review the explanations after submitting. This checkpoint samples the preceding unit; the final covers every module.

questions.question: A z-score threshold by itself establishes:
options: A standardized deviation under the fitted reference distribution
questions.explanation: Standardization describes the observed deviation but does not prove an executable profitable trade.

questions.question: High return correlation alone proves a stationary price spread:
options: Yes if both prices are positive
questions.explanation: Correlated returns do not ensure a stable linear relationship between price levels.

questions.question: What must a short strategy do when borrow is unavailable?
options: Follow the declared rejection or alternative-position policy
questions.explanation: Borrow is an implementation constraint and failed availability belongs in the event record.

questions.question: A complete pairs protocol needs which exit reasons beyond convergence?
options: Risk, time, borrow and thesis invalidation
questions.explanation: Operational and economic failures can require exit even without mean reversion.

exams.title: Unit 6: Machine learning as a signal
exams.description: Four original transfer questions. Use your notes, show calculations, and review the explanations after submitting. This checkpoint samples the preceding unit; the final covers every module.

questions.question: What is a useful first comparator for a complex cross-sectional model?
options: An unrelated asset with a different calendar
A time-valid simple factor rank under the same portfolio rule
Only the weakest random test result
questions.explanation: A matched simple baseline tests whether model complexity contributes useful evidence.

questions.question: Purging overlapping labels belongs at:
options: Every split boundary where labels cross information sets
No boundary when data are chronological
questions.explanation: Chronological ordering alone does not remove forward-label overlap at inner or outer boundaries.

questions.question: Why report IC by date rather than only pooling all stock rows?
options: To inspect time variation and shared-date dependence
questions.explanation: Date-level diagnostics expose instability obscured by a single pooled correlation.

questions.question: Passing a negative-control check establishes:
options: Freedom from every possible implementation error
Only that this diagnostic did not reveal the tested failure
questions.explanation: A diagnostic has a defined scope and cannot certify all assumptions.

exams.title: Unit 7: Portfolio and implementation
exams.description: Four original transfer questions. Use your notes, show calculations, and review the explanations after submitting. This checkpoint samples the preceding unit; the final covers every module.

questions.question: Realized portfolio volatility above its target is:
options: Possible because the estimate and future conditions differ
Proof that transaction costs are zero
questions.explanation: A target uses past estimates and cannot control all future shocks.

questions.question: Why stress correlations upward?
options: To prove every strategy always loses together
To remove the need for a benchmark
Diversification can weaken during common shocks
questions.explanation: A stressed joint-risk case challenges reliance on quiet-period diversification.

questions.question: A fixed commission rate alone models strategy capacity adequately:
options: Only if gross returns are high
No; liquidity and market impact also matter
questions.explanation: Trading more capital can change fill prices and available size beyond fixed fees.

questions.question: Open positions at the final mark should be described as:
options: Marked holdings with liquidation costs omitted unless explicitly modeled
Realized cash profits regardless of sales
questions.explanation: A closing mark and an executed liquidation are different economic events.

exams.title: Unit 8: Validate and defend a strategy
exams.description: Four original transfer questions. Use your notes, show calculations, and review the explanations after submitting. This checkpoint samples the preceding unit; the final covers every module.

questions.question: Indicator warm-up before a test boundary may use:
options: Historical observations available before each decision
questions.explanation: Past data can initialize indicators without allowing future evaluation information into decisions.

questions.question: Citing a PBO paper allows a report to claim it computed PBO:
options: Whenever there are at least two trials
Only if the stated procedure was actually implemented and validated
questions.explanation: Method attribution does not substitute for performing and checking the claimed analysis.

questions.question: Successful deterministic replay establishes:
options: Reproducibility under the tested inputs and implementation
questions.explanation: Replay checks engineering consistency rather than the economic value of the strategy.

questions.question: What should be handed to the final reporting course?
options: Invented holdings for an unimplemented pairs engine
Aligned net valuations, benchmark, manifest and supporting research evidence
questions.explanation: The report needs traceable data and assumptions rather than an isolated or fabricated performance claim.

exams.title: The strategy lab final exam
exams.description: Open-book, untimed assessment with new cases from every module. Budget about three minutes per question. Answers and explanations appear after submission. Pass at 80%; retries remain available. The written capstone is self-assessed separately.

questions.question: A researcher changes the rule after inspecting the final result. The changed rule is:
options: Proof that the original hypothesis passed
A new exploratory specification requiring new evidence
questions.explanation: Outcome-driven revisions must be logged and evaluated as new research choices.

questions.question: A net strategy is compared with a costless index. What belongs in the report?
options: The benchmark cost convention and a matched-cost sensitivity
A claim that the cost basis is identical
questions.explanation: A costless index can be useful, but it does not isolate selection under identical costs.

questions.question: What happens to a new signal on the dataset's final close?
options: It fills at an invented next open
It is moved backward one day
It has no modeled fill without a later bar
questions.explanation: Missing future execution data cannot be replaced by a favorable assumption.

questions.question: A viewed test segment is reused to choose a parameter. It is now:
options: Equivalent to a new future sample
Part of the research selection process
questions.explanation: Once outcomes influence decisions, the segment has participated in selection.

questions.question: A date-only feed lacks publication time. A defensible lab convention is:
options: Delay use until a later session and document it
Assume every release preceded the open
questions.explanation: A conservative explicit delay avoids claiming intraday knowledge the data cannot establish.

questions.question: Dropping a −80% delisted stock from a +20%/−80% equal-weight pair changes the record through:
questions.explanation: Removing failed securities conditions the universe on future survival.

questions.question: A contemporaneous cross-sectional rank uses:
options: Only the universe and values available at that decision
questions.explanation: Ranking is causal only when its membership and inputs are available at the decision time.

questions.question: Why keep stocks from the same date together in a chronological split?
options: They share time information and market shocks
questions.explanation: Random stock-row splitting can expose evaluation-period structure to training.

questions.question: A stock passes raw NCAV but fails after conservative inventory haircuts. The analyst should:
options: Delete the haircut to preserve the purchase
Claim the raw screen guarantees liquidation proceeds
Retain the sensitivity and investigate realizable asset values
questions.explanation: The discrepancy exposes dependence on asset-recovery assumptions.

questions.question: A candidate fails a mandatory coverage floor but has exceptional earnings yield. It should:
options: Have its debt removed from the data
Remain excluded under the predeclared rule
Automatically pass because the composite is high
questions.explanation: Hard eligibility constraints are applied before compensating composite scores.

questions.question: A known earnings date provides advance knowledge of:
options: The scheduled event, not the eventual earnings surprise
questions.explanation: Event timing and event content are different information sets.

questions.question: Only one name qualifies under a fixed 40% cap. The allocation should:
questions.explanation: A shortage of candidates does not justify changing the predeclared concentration rule.

questions.question: A close-based trend rule signals at 105 before an open of 110. Its modeled entry uses:
questions.explanation: The next-open convention cannot choose an earlier or retrospectively favorable price.

questions.question: A top-two long-only daily rule and the French momentum factor are:
options: Different constructions whose calendars and exposures must be disclosed
Identical because both use past returns
questions.explanation: A common broad idea does not make the universe, horizon or long-short construction identical.

questions.question: A permanent earnings impairment should prompt a reversal researcher to:
options: Remove the bad announcement from the sample
Reassess whether the previous reference level remains valid
questions.explanation: A permanent information change differs from temporary price pressure.

questions.question: A single excellent parameter surrounded by poor validation results suggests:
options: No need to count attempted settings
questions.explanation: An isolated optimum may depend on noise or fragile implementation assumptions.

questions.question: A log-price hedge coefficient can be used directly as a fixed share ratio:
options: Only after a justified conversion; not automatically
Only when the test return is positive
questions.explanation: Log-price exposure and share quantities have different units and need an explicit sizing conversion.

questions.question: Choosing the smallest p-value among hundreds of pairs requires disclosure of:
options: The full search and independent stability evidence
questions.explanation: Multiple searched hypotheses change the interpretation of the selected result.

questions.question: A long-short profit divided by nearly zero net notional is:
options: Equivalent to return on gross exposure
An unsuitable return measure without an economic capital basis
questions.explanation: Offsetting notionals do not eliminate the capital, collateral or risk supporting the trade.

questions.question: Re-estimating the hedge after a break should be treated as:
options: A revised model needing later validation
Proof the old model never failed
A reason to remove the loss
questions.explanation: New parameters change the hypothesis and cannot retroactively repair its historical trade.

questions.question: Which record allows a fill to be linked to the model that requested it?
options: Versioned predictions with decision and model timestamps
questions.explanation: Prediction provenance connects trained artifacts to the resulting orders.

questions.question: A later refit learns from an earlier completed evaluation block. What must stay unchanged?
options: The predictions originally issued for that earlier block
questions.explanation: Live-like refitting can use newly historical data while preserving past prediction provenance.

questions.question: A long-short bucket spread can be labeled as a long-only strategy return:
options: Only after constructing and evaluating the actual long-only allocation
questions.explanation: Diagnostic portfolios and implemented holdings have different exposures and costs.

questions.question: Excellent independent-looking performance on random labels should first trigger:
options: An audit of leakage, selection and evaluation code
questions.explanation: An uninformative target performing exceptionally can reveal a broken research process.

questions.question: A 40% target on 10000 equity at price 103 requests how many whole shares?
questions.explanation: Flooring 4000/103 gives 38 shares before next-open execution constraints.

questions.question: A covariance optimizer assigns extreme weights after a tiny data change. This suggests:
options: Estimation sensitivity requiring constraints and diagnostics
questions.explanation: Unstable weights can amplify noisy covariance estimates.

questions.question: Using today's total volume to size an opening fill introduces:
options: Information unavailable at that opening event
questions.explanation: The session's eventual total volume is future information at its open.

questions.question: Which invariant should hold on every valuation row?
options: Fees are added back to cash
Equity equals cash plus marked holdings
questions.explanation: Portfolio wealth reconciles the cash account and current value of all holdings.

questions.question: A reset test account differs from a continuous simulation because:
options: It starts in cash instead of carrying prior holdings
It can use future prices freely
questions.explanation: Boundary state affects trades and returns and must be part of the evaluation contract.

questions.question: A block interval computed on a selected winner automatically corrects all strategy search:
options: Only if the chart has confidence bands
No; selection must be addressed explicitly
questions.explanation: Resampling one selected path does not reproduce the process that selected it.

questions.question: Editing only future prices changes earlier fills. This indicates:
questions.explanation: Decisions and fills in the past must not depend on later observations.

questions.question: A high concept-exam score with unreconciled cash means the project:
options: Still requires revision before its results are credible
questions.explanation: Concept knowledge does not repair a broken accounting result.

modules.title: Specify a bot before writing a loop
modules.subtitle: Turn an investment idea into a testable decision contract with explicit data, execution, and failure assumptions.
modules.objective: Turn an investment idea into a testable decision contract with explicit data, execution, and failure assumptions.
modules.reading: Start here. Deliverable: a bot decision contract. Read the project guide, then complete the data and event units before designing a trading rule.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

Before writing the bot's loop, describe one complete decision in words. Which data arrives, what rule uses it, what checks can reject a trade, and what record proves what happened? Those details are the specification. This first unit connects the research idea to an event-driven system, where each new event can update state or trigger a carefully defined action.

## Define the operation

A bot is a process that turns observations into state changes. Start with a decision contract: eligible instruments, information cutoff, signal rule, target holdings, rebalance frequency, execution convention, risk budget, and conditions for doing nothing. A slogan such as buy strong companies leaves almost every engineering choice unresolved.

Distinguish an alpha model from an execution algorithm. The first proposes which exposure might be useful. The second tries to obtain an already chosen exposure under trading constraints. A good execution algorithm does not establish predictive edge; a useful signal does not guarantee affordable fills.

The course follows a fictional Harbor research team building a long-only paper system. Dollar amounts, thresholds, and model outputs are stipulated teaching inputs. Each lesson produces one artifact for the final design dossier. Small calculations run in the in-app sandbox; the downloadable Python project runs an offline event and ledger simulation.

$$
\text{Net edge}_{bps}=\text{gross edge}-\text{spread}-\text{fees}-\text{slippage}
$$

## A worked example

Harbor proposes a daily strategy in a $100,000 paper portfolio. It may allocate at most 10% to one eligible stock, observes completed daily bars, and places a target order at the next eligible open. An estimate of 12 basis points of gross benefit faces 4 basis points of spread cost, 2 of fees, and 3 of slippage. The rough expected net benefit is only 3 basis points.

A second analyst assumes 6 basis points of slippage. That consumes the entire gross estimate. Before building a faster bot, the team must decide whether the underlying idea survives a plausible cost range. An estimate is not a realized return, and these cost components must not overlap.

### Connect the specification to the cost estimate

A 10% single-stock limit in a $100,000 paper portfolio allows at most $10,000 for that stock under the stated rule. It does not require the bot to use that entire amount. The timing rule is another separate condition: the signal uses completed daily bars and the target order is placed at the next eligible open.

Now examine the claimed benefit. One basis point is 0.01 percentage points. The estimated costs total 4 + 2 + 3 = 9 basis points. Subtracting them from 12 basis points of gross benefit leaves only 3 basis points, or 0.03 percentage points, under those assumptions.

If slippage rises to 6 basis points, the costs become 4 + 2 + 6 = 12 basis points. That uses up the entire estimated gross benefit. Writing this down before building the bot helps the team see which assumption matters and what needs stronger evidence. Faster execution code alone does not settle whether the research idea survives its costs.

## Acceptance evidence

Write observable requirements: duplicate delivery does not duplicate exposure; missing features produce no new order; a fill changes cash exactly once; a restart recovers a halted state. Pair each requirement with a normal and adverse example. Define success in terms of reconciliation and sound evaluation before looking at a profit chart.

Keep research permission, paper execution, and any later live release as separate stages. Completing this course produces a tested educational prototype and a review packet. It does not silently connect credentials or authorize a brokerage trade.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

A decision contract should state how many alternatives will be tried, because that count changes what a good result means. Bailey, Borwein, López de Prado and Zhu make the point with a random walk. They generated 1,000 daily prices, about four years, searched a mesh of 8,800 combinations of entry day, holding period, stop loss and side, and the best combination showed an annualized Sharpe ratio of 1.27 even though the series contains no pattern. Their rule of thumb is that five years of data supports no more than 45 independent configurations before a skill-less winner with a Sharpe ratio near 1 becomes almost guaranteed, and they describe that length as necessary but not sufficient.

Edges also fade once they are known. McLean and Pontiff studied 97 predictors taken from published papers and found portfolio returns 26% lower out of sample and 58% lower after publication. As an illustration of our own, not a forecast, a 58% haircut on Harbor's 12 basis points of gross benefit leaves about 5, already below the 9 basis points of assumed costs.

The cost line is an assumption about a particular trader. Frazzini, Israel and Moskowitz used nearly a trillion dollars of one large manager's live trades across 19 developed equity markets from 1998 to 2011 and found actual costs under a tenth of earlier estimates. They attribute the gap to two things: earlier studies priced the average investor, and the portfolios they tested were not designed with costs in mind. That manager is far larger and more sophisticated than a paper bot, so its numbers are not a template for Harbor. They do show that 9 basis points needs a named trader, size and portfolio design behind it.

Exercise: add three lines to Harbor's contract before any code exists. State the maximum number of variants you will compare, the history length that supports that number, and a pessimistic case that combines a decay haircut with 6 basis points of slippage. If the idea fails the pessimistic case, do not write the loop.

### Sources for this section

- [Bailey, Borwein, López de Prado & Zhu (2014) · Pseudo-Mathematics and Financial Charlatanism: The Effects of Backtest Overfitting on Out-of-Sample Performance](https://doi.org/10.1090/noti1105) — *Research paper.* Shows with a random-walk experiment and a minimum-backtest-length rule how the number of configurations tried inflates in-sample Sharpe ratios.
- [McLean & Pontiff (2016) · Does Academic Research Destroy Stock Return Predictability?](https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.12365) — *Research paper.* Measures how much the returns of 97 published predictors fall out of sample and after publication.
- [Frazzini, Israel & Moskowitz (2012) · Trading Costs of Asset Pricing Anomalies](https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.2294498) — *Research paper.* Live institutional trade data showing actual costs far below earlier estimates, and why estimates depend on who trades and how portfolios are built.
