modules.title: Event-driven bot architecture
modules.subtitle: Separate market events, targets, orders, and fills so repeated or delayed messages cannot silently change the strategy.
modules.objective: Separate market events, targets, orders, and fills so repeated or delayed messages cannot silently change the strategy.
modules.reading: Deliverable: event schema and architecture diagram. Broker reference: stable client identifiers and order lookup; implementation semantics must be verified per adapter.
modules.content:
## Design a pipeline with explicit boundaries

Market ingestion records an observation. Feature computation produces a dated input set. Strategy logic proposes a target. Risk logic permits, resizes, or rejects that target. An order manager tracks instructions, and a fill handler updates the ledger. These steps can live in one process initially while retaining separate interfaces.

A vectorized research calculation is useful for rapid experiments; an event-driven replay is useful for modeling chronology and operational state. Neither architecture automatically prevents look-ahead. Both require correct timestamps and information boundaries.

Give each event a stable identity, source, event time, receipt time, and schema version. Event time describes the underlying observation; receipt time describes when the bot learned about it. A late event should follow a documented policy rather than revise a decision as if the data had arrived earlier.

$$
\text{Observation}\rightarrow\text{Features}\rightarrow\text{Target}\rightarrow\text{Risk}\rightarrow\text{Order}\rightarrow\text{Fill}
$$

## A worked example

The feed delivers event E101 twice, followed by E102. The strategy intends one rebalance per completed event, so the expected count is two distinct intents. If each delivery creates a fresh random order ID, the bot can accidentally produce three orders. A deterministic intent key such as strategy-version plus symbol plus decision timestamp ties retries to the same decision.

Now crash after a broker accepts E101's order but before acknowledgement is stored. Local absence of confirmation means unknown external state, not rejection. Reconcile using the stable client identifier and broker records before deciding whether another submission is permissible. Identifier support and retry semantics are adapter-specific; verify the actual broker contract.

## Make replay a first-class tool

Keep an immutable input log and enough state to reconstruct what each component believed. Test duplicate events, a missing sequence number, late data, an out-of-order acknowledgement, and a fill arriving during cancellation. Record the transition and the reason for every rejected action.

A single owner of account mutations makes reasoning easier. If multiple workers are introduced, use a durable transactional boundary and uniqueness constraints. An in-memory set alone does not survive a crash or coordinate two processes.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Two clocks sit behind every event a bot receives. Akidau and co-authors, describing a model for processing unbounded and out-of-order data, define event time as when an event actually occurred and processing time as when the pipeline observes it. They stress that the skew between the two is inherent and keeps changing, and that a system usually lacks the knowledge to build a fully correct watermark, its running estimate of how complete the data is. A bot faces the same problem with a sharper edge, because a dashboard can quietly revise a late number but an order cannot be retracted. Our inference is that the late-event rule belongs in the specification: say in advance what happens to an event that arrives after the decision it should have informed.

Identity needs the same discipline. The FIX standard for electronic order messages requires a client order ID to be unique within a single trading day and advises firms that trade across days to embed a date in it. A separate PossResend field marks a message that may carry information already sent under another sequence number. Harbor's key of strategy version, symbol and decision timestamp fits that pattern, but each broker's guarantee has its own scope, so read the adapter's contract.

Replay and live trading also differ more than the pipeline diagram suggests. QuantConnect's LEAN documentation says algorithm events fire synchronously in backtests, while in live trading order events fire immediately from the brokerage thread, asynchronously. Its own example is a limit order on hourly data that fills between bars. The ABIDES simulator of Byrd and co-authors makes such timing visible instead: every agent talks to the exchange through messages with configurable network latencies, in a design modelled on Nasdaq's ITCH and OUCH protocols.

Exercise: replay the feed E101, E101, E102 three ways. Run it in order, with the duplicate delayed until after E102, and with a simulated crash between broker acceptance and the stored acknowledgement. Each run should end with exactly two intents and the same ledger. Any difference exposes a hidden dependence on arrival order or on in-memory state.

### Sources for this section

- [Akidau et al. (2015) · The Dataflow Model](https://doi.org/10.14778/2824032.2824076) — *Research paper.* Defines event time versus processing time for out-of-order streams and explains why completeness estimates (watermarks) are heuristic.
- [FIX Trading Community · ClOrdID field definition, FIX Latest](https://fiximate.fixtrading.org/en/FIX.Latest/tag11.html) — *Technical documentation.* Standard definition of the client order ID, including the day-level uniqueness requirement and the advice to embed a date.
- [QuantConnect · Algorithm Engine](https://www.quantconnect.com/docs/v2/writing-algorithms/key-concepts/algorithm-engine) — *Technical documentation.* Documents how one engine triggers events synchronously in backtests but fires order events asynchronously in live trading.
- [Byrd, Hybinette & Balch (2019) · ABIDES: Towards High-Fidelity Market Simulation for AI Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.12066) — *arXiv 1904.12066.* A discrete-event market simulator in which agents interact only through messages with configurable latencies, modelled on Nasdaq protocols.

modules.subtitle: Reject stale or historically unavailable inputs and make sessions, adjustments, and missing data explicit.
modules.objective: Reject stale or historically unavailable inputs and make sessions, adjustments, and missing data explicit.
modules.reading: Deliverable: point-in-time data contract and six bad-data fixtures. Reuse the data-provenance methods from Quantitative Investment Analysis.
modules.content:
## A timestamp is part of the value

A price needs an instrument, venue or source, currency, event timestamp, receipt timestamp, and adjustment convention. A financial statement also needs its publication timestamp and revision identity. Calendar dates alone are insufficient when a decision depends on intraday availability.

Store a consistent clock representation and convert to the exchange's session schedule at the boundary. Daylight-saving changes, holidays, half-days, and trading halts should come from a maintained calendar or broker session interface. Never equate a weekday with an open market. The offline project uses a supplied session-open flag rather than pretending to implement an exchange calendar.

Distinguish a missing bar from a genuine zero return. Mixing adjusted historical closes with raw order prices can fabricate a signal around splits. Keep corporate actions and total-return assumptions separate from executable quotes.

$$
\text{Age}=t_{decision}-t_{event};\quad 0\leq\text{Age}\leq\text{limit}
$$

## A worked example

A quote event is timestamped 10:00:00.000 and arrives at 10:00:00.400. At a decision time of 10:00:00.900, its age from the event clock is 900 ms. Under a stipulated 750 ms freshness limit, the bot rejects a new entry even though network transport took only 400 ms.

A second quote carries a timestamp after the decision time because of clock skew. It must not pass merely because the computed age is negative. Validate both clock ordering and a maximum age. These thresholds are policy examples, not universal trading standards.

## Reconstruct the information set

For each decision, retain the exact quote or bar ID and the latest eligible filing version. A March release describing December cannot enter a February historical decision. Reject unsupported instruments and nonfinite or nonpositive prices before computing exposure.

The assignment should include fixtures for stale data, future timestamps, duplicate bars, missing volume, a split, and a closed session. Explain whether each causes an abstention, a delayed decision, or a research-only adjustment. Avoid filling a data gap with generated prices while labeling the result historical.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Treat the trading clock as data. The NYSE's published calendar lists Friday 3 July 2026 as a holiday (Independence Day observed) and early 1:00 p.m. Eastern closes on Friday 27 November and Thursday 24 December 2026. Sessions also differ by venue: the core session runs from 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., but NYSE Arca's early session starts at 4:00 a.m. and late trading runs until 8:00 p.m. Our inference for Harbor: on an early-close day a completed daily bar exists three hours sooner than usual, so a calendar that assumes a 4:00 p.m. close delays the signal, and one that assumes a session on 3 July may mistake a missing bar for a zero return.

Feeds also stamp events with more than one clock. Bartlett and McCrary used the microsecond timestamps recorded by the two centralized processors that consolidate U.S. exchange quotes and trades. In a sample running from August 2015 to June 2016 they found average reporting latencies of 1.13 milliseconds for quotes and 22.84 milliseconds for trades, and they note that the exchanges' own participant timestamps were recorded only in milliseconds. Which clock a freshness limit such as the lesson's 750 milliseconds uses is therefore part of the data contract.

Documents have the same problem. Under the SEC's Regulation S-T, an electronic filing submitted after 5:30 p.m. Eastern is deemed filed on the next business day, although some insider and ownership forms get a 10 p.m. cutoff. A filing date is a legal label, not a clock reading, so a bot that stores only the date cannot say whether the document was readable at 10:00 a.m. that day. Our suggestion: store the acceptance time when the source provides one, and otherwise treat the document as usable only after the full filing date has passed.

Exercise: extend Harbor's fixtures with a bar on Friday 27 November 2026 that completes at 1:00 p.m., a Friday 3 July 2026 with no session, and a filing accepted at 6:00 p.m. Eastern. For each, write down whether the bot abstains, delays or labels the result research-only, and which timestamp it used.

### Sources for this section

- [NYSE · Holidays & Trading Hours](https://www.nyse.com/trade/hours-calendars) — *Official source.* The exchange's own 2026 to 2028 holiday and early-close schedule, with session windows for each NYSE venue.
- [Bartlett & McCrary (2016) · How Rigged Are Stock Markets?: Evidence From Microsecond Timestamps](https://doi.org/10.3386/w22551) — *Research paper.* Uses the SIPs' microsecond timestamps to measure how late consolidated quotes and trades are reported compared with exchange direct feeds.
- [U.S. SEC · eCFR · 17 CFR 232.13: Date of filing; adjustment of filing date](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-17/chapter-II/part-232/section-232.13) — *Official source.* The rule that fixes when an electronic EDGAR filing counts as filed, including the 5:30 p.m. Eastern cutoff and its exceptions.

modules.title: Feature engineering and reproducible signals
modules.subtitle: Build past-only features with explicit warm-up, scale, and version rules shared by research and execution.
modules.objective: Build past-only features with explicit warm-up, scale, and version rules shared by research and execution.
modules.reading: Deliverable: a feature dictionary and exact input/output fixtures. Read the preprocessing consistency reference linked from the course plan.
modules.content:
## Treat features as versioned computations

Define each feature with its input field, window, lag, adjustment basis, missing-data rule, and units. A twenty-bar return and a twenty-calendar-day return need not be identical. A trailing average that includes the current completed bar is available only after that bar completes.

Warm-up is a state, not a zero. If a feature needs twenty valid observations and only twelve exist, the model should see an unavailable input or abstain under a documented rule. Filling the missing feature with zero can change a model's meaning and create unexpected orders.

Use the same transformations in training and inference. Fitted preprocessing belongs to the training artifact, while rolling calculations require a defined historical window. A price-level feature can drift with splits or nominal scale; return, ratio, or normalized features can be more interpretable but do not automatically become stationary.

$$
Momentum_t=P_t/P_{t-L}-1
$$

## A worked example

Completed closes are 100, 102, 101, and 104. A three-period simple return at the final close is 104/100 − 1 = 4%. The three most recent completed closes average (102 + 101 + 104)/3 = 102.333. The final close is about 1.63% above that average.

This is a feature calculation, not proof of trend profitability. If the decision instead occurs before the final close, 104 is unavailable and both inputs must be recomputed from earlier data. Feature timing determines the earliest possible execution.

## A reproducibility check

Save a tiny input fixture and expected feature values. Compare research and running-bot outputs on identical data, including a missing observation and the first eligible warm-up point. Record model and feature versions together so an old model cannot silently consume a reordered feature vector.

When a new feature is proposed, document the economic hypothesis before tuning its window. Log rejected variants and retain a baseline. A precise calculation can still be an overfit research choice.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Start with what a window counts. The pandas documentation says a rolling window given as an offset, such as twenty days, defaults to a minimum of 1 observation, while an integer window defaults to its full size. Both can be called a twenty-day average, but by default only the integer version has a warm-up state: the offset version returns a one-close "average" on the first day. The default window also includes its last point, the current bar. Our inference is that a feature specification should state the minimum observations and whether the current bar is inside the window.

Kaufman and co-authors define leakage as information about the prediction target entering the data when it should not legitimately be there, and they propose a data-management approach they call learn-predict separation. For a bot, "legitimately" means stamped before the decision time, so the lesson's final close of 104 is off limits to an earlier decision. A prefix test follows (our suggestion): compute each feature on the full history, then again on the history cut at the decision time. Any difference signals leakage or a revised past.

Research and live code can also drift apart. Google's Rules of Machine Learning define training-serving skew as a difference between performance during training and during serving, and list three causes: different data handling in the two pipelines, a change in the data between training and serving, and a feedback loop. Rule #29 says to save the features used at serving time and log them for training. Rule #37 says the same example at training and at serving should give exactly the same result, so a discrepancy probably indicates an engineering error. Pineau and co-authors, reporting on the NeurIPS 2019 reproducibility program, define reproducibility as obtaining similar results from the same code and data; the lesson's fixture applies that definition to a single feature.

Exercise: log Harbor's live feature vector with its version, replay the same closes through the research function, and require identical values, including a missing day and the first warm-up bar.

### Sources for this section

- [pandas · pandas.DataFrame.rolling](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.rolling.html) — *Technical documentation.* Documents the min_periods defaults for offset and integer windows and the closed argument that decides whether the current bar is inside a rolling window.
- [Kaufman, Rosset, Perlich & Stitelman (2012) · Leakage in data mining](https://doi.org/10.1145/2382577.2382579) — *Research paper.* Defines leakage as information that should not be legitimately available and proposes a learn-predict separation in data management.
- [Google · Rules of Machine Learning: Best Practices for ML Engineering](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/guides/rules-of-ml) — *Technical documentation.* Defines training-serving skew, recommends logging serving-time features for training (Rule #29) and treats a train/serve mismatch as an engineering error (Rule #37).
- [Pineau et al. (2020) · Improving Reproducibility in Machine Learning Research (A Report from the NeurIPS 2019 Reproducibility Program)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.12206) — *arXiv 2003.12206.* Defines reproducibility as similar results from the same code and data and reports a code policy, community challenge and checklist used to promote it.

modules.title: Rule-based strategy bots
modules.subtitle: Convert a signal into a target position and reconcile that target with holdings and outstanding orders.
modules.objective: Convert a signal into a target position and reconcile that target with holdings and outstanding orders.
modules.reading: Unit 2 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

A rule-based bot makes decisions from explicit conditions. Its simplicity can make the behavior easier to inspect, but the rule still needs evidence and realistic execution assumptions. Work through one signal at a time and record when it becomes known. Then examine how turnover, costs, and the chosen comparison affect the research result.

## Design and reasoning

Separate the desired end state from the instruction sent now. A binary signal can mean a target weight of 0% or 10%; it does not mean buy another 10% on every iteration. Convert weight to shares using a dated equity estimate and an executable price convention. Specify rounding, minimum lot size, cash reserves, and when a target expires.

Outstanding orders are commitments. A pending buy contributes positive shares and a pending sell contributes negative shares to the projected holding. Ignoring them causes repeated rebalancing to overshoot. A cancellation request does not remove that commitment until its result is known.

$$
q_{new}=q_{target}-q_{held}-q_{pending,buy}+q_{pending,sell}
$$

## A worked example

Harbor targets 200 shares and holds 120. With no open orders the buy requirement is 80 shares. With a previously accepted buy of 50 shares still outstanding, the residual is only 30. If 20 of that order fill, holdings become 140 and remaining commitments become 30; the residual stays 30. This invariance is a useful test of the accounting.

If the signal disappears, first reconcile or cancel the existing buy. Do not immediately submit a 120-share sell while assuming the buy vanished. Treat conflicting instructions as an order-management problem.

## Implementation and review

Implement target calculation as a pure function of a versioned snapshot. The order manager, not the signal function, owns retries. Introduce a no-trade band so negligible target changes do not create excessive turnover. Record the raw target, rounded target, existing holdings, commitments, and final permitted instruction. Compare the same rule against cash and a declared passive benchmark using identical costs and dates.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Treat the broker's open quantity as the pending term in the lesson's formula. The FIX standard defines CumQty as the total quantity filled and LeavesQty as the quantity open for further execution, equal to OrderQty minus CumQty unless the order has reached a state that ends it: Canceled, DoneForTheDay, Expired, Calculated or Rejected. For Harbor's 50-share buy with 20 filled, that is 30. A cancel request still awaiting an answer is not on that list, so our inference is that its open quantity stays until the broker reports Canceled. Test it: held plus open quantity is 170 before and after the partial fill, and only a confirmed cancel moves the shortfall from 30 to 60.

A rule-based bot also needs conditions that a program can evaluate, and the research record shows why. Lo and co-authors observed that chart patterns are often in the eye of the beholder, so they replaced chart reading with nonparametric kernel regression and applied it to U.S. stocks from 1962 to 1996. They compared the unconditional distribution of daily returns with the distribution conditioned on indicators such as head-and-shoulders and double bottoms, and found that over the 31-year sample several indicators provided incremental information and might have some practical value. Our inference is that Harbor's benchmark should follow the same design (returns after the rule fires against returns on all dates, under identical costs), and that information in a return distribution must still survive turnover.

Turnover is where that is decided. Gerhold and co-authors study a long-horizon investor facing small proportional costs and show that, to first order, the liquidity premium, the model's measure of what illiquidity costs the investor, equals the spread times share turnover times a universal constant. Our inference is that a no-trade band acts on the turnover factor, so its width belongs in the specification, fixed before any results are seen.

Exercise: replay the 200/120/50/20 sequence with a delayed cancel confirmation, and assert that the projected holding changes only when a broker report arrives.

### Sources for this section

- [FIX Trading Community · LeavesQty field definition, FIX Latest](https://fiximate.fixtrading.org/en/FIX.Latest/tag151.html) — *Technical documentation.* Standard definition of open order quantity as OrderQty minus CumQty, with the list of terminal order states in which it may be zero.
- [Lo, Mamaysky & Wang (2000) · Foundations of Technical Analysis: Computational Algorithms, Statistical Inference, and Empirical Implementation](https://doi.org/10.1111/0022-1082.00265) — *Research paper.* Turns subjective chart patterns into an algorithm and compares conditional with unconditional return distributions for U.S. stocks over 1962 to 1996.
- [Gerhold, Guasoni, Muhle-Karbe & Schachermayer (2011) · Transaction Costs, Trading Volume, and the Liquidity Premium](https://arxiv.org/abs/1108.1167) — *arXiv 1108.1167.* Shows that, to first order, the cost of illiquidity in a small-cost model equals the spread times share turnover times a universal constant.

modules.title: Trend rules, breakouts, and turnover
modules.subtitle: Specify an executable trend rule with entry, exit, warm-up, and turnover controls.
modules.objective: Specify an executable trend rule with entry, exit, warm-up, and turnover controls.
modules.reading: Unit 2 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

A rule must define the information window precisely. For a breakout observed at today's completed close, compare that close with an earlier high window that excludes today. Including today's high changes the question and can make a strict close-above-high test impossible. A moving-average rule instead compares levels computed from a declared window.

Use separate entry and exit thresholds when a small fluctuation would otherwise churn the portfolio. This hysteresis is a design choice with a trade-off: less turnover can delay an exit. Do not select the band after inspecting the final evaluation period.

$$
\text{Entry threshold}=\max(H_{t-L},\ldots,H_{t-1})(1+b)
$$

## A worked example

Earlier highs are 100, 102, and 101. A completed close of 103 exceeds the prior maximum of 102. Under an illustrative rule requiring a 0.5% breakout, the entry threshold is 102.51, so the signal qualifies. A 1.5% band would require 103.53 and would not qualify. Execution occurs on a later eligible event, whose price need not equal 103.

A backtest earns 1.2% gross while turning the portfolio over six one-way notional equivalents. At 15 bps per equivalent, estimated trading costs are 0.9%, leaving 0.3% before other omitted costs.

## Implementation and review

Build a fixture for a flat market, a gap, a missing close, and a split-adjustment mismatch. Evaluate a small preregistered parameter grid on training and validation windows, then freeze it. Report return, drawdown, time in market, turnover, and sensitivity to costs. A trend indicator is a descriptive transformation; the ability to compute it does not establish an economic edge.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Breakouts have a long evidence trail and a long list of ways to fool yourself. Brock and co-authors tested a moving-average rule and a trading-range break, the breakout in this lesson, on the Dow Jones index from 1897 to 1986. They judged both against bootstrapped null models (a random walk, an AR(1), GARCH-M and exponential GARCH), found that buy signals produced higher returns than sell signals, and reported negative returns after sell signals. Two habits are worth copying: split outcomes by signal state, and measure a rule against simulated series that contain no edge.

George and Hwang found that nearness to the 52-week high explains a large portion of the profits from momentum investing in stocks and dominates past returns as a forecaster, without long-run reversal. Their variable is a distance, whereas the lesson's rule keeps one bit: above or below the prior maximum times (1 + b). Our inference is that a bot should log the distance as well, then test whether a banded or sized response beats the yes-or-no one at equal turnover.

Potters and Bouchaud solved a simple trend-following model exactly. Its profit per trade has an asymmetric, option-like distribution, the average gain per trade is exactly zero, and the fraction of winning trades falls from one half at low volatility to zero at high volatility. They conclude that win rate indicates trading style, not reliability. Our inference is that a win rate under one half is not a defect by itself, and that a good-looking payoff needs a null to beat.

Exercise: simulate driftless random-walk prices at a low and a high volatility, run the 0.5% and 1.5% breakouts, and record average gross gain per trade, win fraction and turnover. Then charge 15 bps per notional equivalent and compare the result with the real-data run.

### Sources for this section

- [Brock, Lakonishok & LeBaron (1992) · Simple Technical Trading Rules and the Stochastic Properties of Stock Returns](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1992.tb04681.x) — *Research paper.* Tests moving-average and trading-range-break rules on the Dow Jones index from 1897 to 1986 against four bootstrapped null models, comparing returns after buy and sell signals.
- [George & Hwang (2004) · The 52-Week High and Momentum Investing](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.2004.00695.x) — *Research paper.* Shows that nearness to the 52-week high explains much of momentum profit and dominates past returns, with no long-run reversal; a distance-based cousin of the lesson's prior-high breakout.
- [Potters & Bouchaud (2005) · Trend followers lose more often than they gain](https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0508104) — *arXiv physics/0508104.* Solves a simple trend-following model exactly: asymmetric profit per trade, zero average gain, and a win fraction that reflects trading style rather than reliability.

modules.title: Mean reversion and pairs hypotheses
modules.subtitle: Distinguish a normalized deviation from evidence of reversion and account for both legs of a spread.
modules.objective: Distinguish a normalized deviation from evidence of reversion and account for both legs of a spread.
modules.reading: Unit 2 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

A z-score describes deviation relative to an estimated mean and scale. It is not a guarantee that price will return to a historical level. Structural changes can move both the mean and variance. Specify the estimation window, fit the relationship using past data, and explain why a temporary displacement might close.

For pairs, define a spread such as A minus beta times B. Correlation of returns does not prove that this price spread is stationary. A fitted hedge ratio, a stationarity diagnostic, and an economic relationship answer different questions. Check sensitivity to sample choice and corporate changes before treating a spread as tradable.

$$
z_t=(s_t-\mu_{train})/\sigma_{train}
$$

## A worked example

A spread of 14 has a training mean of 10 and standard deviation 2, giving a z-score of 2. Harbor's paper research rule considers selling the spread above 1.5. That requires short A and long beta units of B under the stated sign convention; the current in-app long/cash sandbox cannot express both legs.

If the planned legs are $10,000 long and $10,000 short, net dollar exposure is zero but gross exposure is $20,000. Fees, stock borrow, asymmetric fills, beta mismatch, and abrupt divergence can still produce a loss.

## Implementation and review

Keep pairs work as a research worksheet unless the execution engine explicitly supports borrow availability, short margin, and two-leg state. Test a one-leg fill, a borrow recall, and a spread that never reverts. Define an exit based on elapsed time or invalidated evidence as well as the signal. Zero estimated net exposure must never bypass gross and concentration limits.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Why would a displacement close? Nagel gives one answer for short-term equity reversals: their returns proxy for the pay from supplying liquidity, and that pay is highly predictable from the VIX, with expected returns and conditional Sharpe ratios spiking in market turmoil. Our inference is that part of what a stretched-spread trade earns is a fee for standing in when liquidity is scarce, and that the spread that keeps stretching is likeliest to appear in the same periods. Tag every entry with a volatility regime and report results by regime as well as in total.

A z-score also inherits the error of the estimates behind it. Elliott and co-authors modelled a pair's spread as a mean-reverting Gaussian Markov chain observed in Gaussian noise, and compared the calibrated model's predictions with later observations to decide trades; our inference is that a raw z-score treats the noisy observation as the true state. Holý and Černý add that the parameters of a mean-reverting spread are never known exactly and are estimated from finite samples, and they quantify the loss against a trader who knows them. With the lesson's numbers, a training mean of 11 instead of 10 puts a spread of 14 at a z-score of 1.5, exactly on Harbor's threshold, so a half-standard-deviation error is enough to remove the signal.

Exercise: simulate a mean-reverting spread with a known mean, estimate the mean and scale from short, medium and long windows, and trade the 1.5 rule with estimated and true parameters; record how the gap in net result shrinks with window length. Then shift the true mean by two standard deviations halfway through and record how long the position stays open without a time stop.

### Sources for this section

- [Nagel (2012) · Evaporating Liquidity](https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhs066) — *Research paper.* Interprets short-term reversal returns as pay for liquidity provision and shows that this pay is predictable from the VIX and spikes in turmoil.
- [Elliott, van der Hoek & Malcolm (2005) · Pairs trading](https://doi.org/10.1080/14697680500149370) — *Research paper.* Models a pair's spread as a mean-reverting Gaussian Markov chain observed in noise and compares model predictions with later observations to decide trades.
- [Holý & Černý (2021) · Bertram's Pairs Trading Strategy with Bounded Risk](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.04160) — *arXiv 2102.04160.* Treats estimation error in the parameters of a mean-reverting spread as critical in practice and quantifies the loss against a trader who knows them exactly.

modules.title: Backtests that respect costs and chronology
modules.subtitle: Evaluate a frozen trading rule using a declared information cutoff, execution delay, benchmark, and cost model.
modules.objective: Evaluate a frozen trading rule using a declared information cutoff, execution delay, benchmark, and cost model.
modules.reading: Unit 2 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

Separate signal time, order time, and fill time. A strategy computed from a completed closing bar cannot assume it entered earlier at that bar's open. An OHLC bar also does not reveal whether its high preceded its low. Any intrabar stop or limit convention is an assumption that needs documentation.

Keep research selection distinct from final evaluation. Changing a window after seeing the holdout makes that period part of development. Record every tried variant, fit preprocessing on training data, and keep an untouched later segment for the final frozen rule. Corporate actions, delistings, and availability timestamps belong in the data audit.

$$
\Pi=q(P_{exit}-P_{entry})-f q(P_{entry}+P_{exit})
$$

## A worked example

Harbor signals at a close of 100 and buys 10 shares at the next open of 102. Later it sells at 104. At 5 bps commission on each notional, entry commission is $0.51 and exit commission $0.52. Net P&L is $18.97. Pretending entry occurred at the signal close would overstate the gross profit by $20.

If slippage is modeled in the fill price, do not subtract the same slippage again as a separate ledger fee. Compare with a passive position using the same timestamps, capital, and cost convention.

## Implementation and review

Review an order-by-order trace in addition to aggregate statistics. Report drawdown, turnover, exposure, number of independent decisions, and a cost stress. A smooth curve from few trades does not support a precise Sharpe claim. Use the sandbox to demonstrate timing and costs; use the offline project for event and ledger failure tests. Neither establishes a live execution advantage.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

An engine's timing convention is a documented assumption, and Backtrader states its own. The current data has already happened, so a rule that tests an examined close cannot expect a fill at that close; a market order executes at the next bar's opening price. That is the lesson's 100 signal and 102 fill. Its slippage page shows a cost silently vanishing: in the sample run, a 1.5% slippage setting changed no fill price until slip_open was switched on, and even then a buy on a bar whose open equalled its high could not be pushed above that high. Our inference is that a bot should assert, for each simulated market buy, that fill price minus the raw next open equals the declared slippage unless the bar's high caps it, and that the ledger fee is commission alone. A failure exposes skipped or doubled costs, and the cap makes simulated slippage smaller than declared on such bars.

Holdout discipline needs a count as well as a rule. Dwork and co-authors describe analysis as adaptive: hypotheses and parameters are chosen after seeing earlier results, and they warn that a holdout consulted again and again, each choice informed by the last answer, can easily end up overfit itself. Their algorithm lets a large number of adaptively chosen hypotheses be validated while provably avoiding overfitting. For a bot, our suggestion is a ledger of every look at the final segment, with the segment reclassified as development data once the declared budget is spent.

Park and Irwin surveyed technical trading studies: of 95 modern ones, 56 reported positive results, 20 negative and 19 mixed, with profits documented at least until the early 1990s. They also note that most studies suffer from data snooping, hindsight selection of rules, and weak estimates of risk and transaction costs. A majority-positive tally says little when the weaknesses are shared (our inference).

Exercise: rerun Harbor's trade three ways, filled at the 100 signal close, at the 102 next open, and one bar later, with slippage counted once, and report which line of the order trace each change moves.

### Sources for this section

- [Backtrader · Orders - Creation/Execution](https://www.backtrader.com/docu/order-creation-execution/order-creation-execution/) — *Technical documentation.* Documents that a backtest cannot fill an order at the close it just examined and that market orders use the next bar's opening price.
- [Backtrader · Broker - Slippage](https://www.backtrader.com/docu/slippage/slippage/) — *Technical documentation.* Shows in a sample run that a slippage setting moved no next-open fills until slip_open was switched on, and that slipped prices are capped at the bar's high or low unless slip_out is set.
- [Dwork et al. (2015) · Generalization in Adaptive Data Analysis and Holdout Reuse](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.02629) — *arXiv 1506.02629.* Shows that adaptively reusing a holdout set overfits it and gives an algorithm that validates many adaptively chosen hypotheses while provably avoiding overfitting.
- [Park & Irwin (2007) · What Do We Know About the Profitability of Technical Analysis?](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-6419.2007.00519.x) — *Research paper.* Surveys 95 modern technical-trading studies and lists the shared testing problems: data snooping, ex post rule selection and weak risk and cost estimates.

## Start with a simple picture

Submitting an order and receiving a fill are separate events. Between them, quotes may change, quantities may run out, and cancellation requests may race with execution. This unit follows the life of an order and the cash it commits. Use a small paper ledger to check that every accepted fill changes balances exactly once.

## Design and reasoning

A quote is an indication at a particular time, size, and venue. The midpoint is useful as a benchmark but is not necessarily executable. A marketable buy typically consumes offered liquidity; a resting limit may fail to fill or fill when the market moves against it. Better price and greater fill certainty are competing objectives.

Implementation shortfall compares execution with a decision benchmark, adjusted for trade direction. Explicit fees can be added separately. Spread, market impact, and delay are explanatory components whose estimates may overlap; avoid presenting a precise causal decomposition without the necessary data.

$$
IS_{bps}=10^4 d(P_{fill}/P_{decision}-1),\quad d\in\{+1,-1\}
$$

## A worked example

The bid is 99.90 and the ask 100.10, so the midpoint is 100 and the quoted spread is 20 bps. A buy filling at 100.12 costs 12 bps relative to that midpoint before commission. Half the quoted spread accounts for 10 bps in a simple interpretation; the extra 2 bps cannot be confidently called permanent impact from this single observation.

A sell at 99.88 also has 12 bps adverse shortfall under a direction-adjusted convention. Use consistent signs so a worse sell is not accidentally reported as a benefit.

## Implementation and review

Store the benchmark's source, timestamp, and size with each decision. Report fill rate and unfilled opportunity cost alongside the average cost of completed trades; measuring only successful fills can flatter passive strategies. Paper fills do not reproduce queue priority, hidden liquidity, or adverse selection. The course uses explicit toy assumptions that should be challenged before interpreting results.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Perold defined implementation shortfall as the profit on a paper portfolio, which trades at benchmark prices, minus the profit on the real one. Against the bid-ask midpoint it is what Hasbrouck's lecture notes call the effective cost: for Harbor's buy, the lesson's 12 bps. The notes define price improvement for a buy as the offer minus the fill price, so a 100.12 fill against a 100.10 offer scores −0.02. Our inference: the extra 2 bps came from a quote that moved before arrival or from depth that ran out, and only an arrival-time quote and the book's size can tell which.

Impact needs a second quote. Realized cost uses the midpoint five minutes after the trade, and price impact is effective cost minus realized cost, the midpoint's move in the trade's direction. If Harbor's midpoint is still 100.00 five minutes later, all 12 bps is realized cost; if it has reached 100.12, all 12 bps is impact. Bouchaud, Farmer and Lillo define market impact as the average response of prices to trades and review evidence that it decays slowly. Our inference: five minutes is a convention, not the line between temporary and permanent. Overlap distorts it. In the notes' example, three quick trades that each move the midpoint by $0.10, all measured against the same later midpoint, show impacts of $0.30, $0.20 and $0.10.

Unfilled orders need the same care. In the notes' experiment, market buys pay the $0.05 half-spread while the limit buys that fill show −$0.05, so limits seem to win. Complete each unfilled limit at the final offer and the notes' eight-path random walk gives an average of 10.00 for a limit one cent below the offer, the same as a market order.

Exercise: replay a path where each fill moves the midpoint by one basis point, with three fills seconds apart. A naive markout reports an average of 2 basis points; make it return 1, then reproduce the eight-path result as a unit test.

### Sources for this section

- [Perold (1988) · The implementation shortfall](https://doi.org/10.3905/jpm.1988.409150) — *Research paper.* Origin of implementation shortfall: the gap between a paper portfolio traded at benchmark prices and the portfolio actually implemented.
- [Hasbrouck (2015) · Securities Trading: Principles and Procedures, Chapter 8: Transaction costs (lecture notes)](https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~jhasbrou/Teaching/POST%202015%20Spring/classNotes/STPPTradingCosts.pdf) — *Technical documentation.* Lecture notes defining effective cost, realized cost, price impact and price improvement, with worked examples of overlapping markouts and of limit orders that fail to fill.
- [Bouchaud, Farmer & Lillo (2008) · How markets slowly digest changes in supply and demand](https://arxiv.org/abs/0809.0822) — *arXiv 0809.0822.* Review of theory and evidence on market impact, including its slow decay with time, which limits what any single markout horizon can reveal.

modules.title: Order state machines and cancellation races
modules.subtitle: Handle acknowledgements, partial fills, cancellations, rejections, and ambiguous submissions without losing commitments.
modules.objective: Handle acknowledgements, partial fills, cancellations, rejections, and ambiguous submissions without losing commitments.
modules.reading: Unit 3 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

Model submission, acknowledgement, partial fill, complete fill, cancellation, and rejection as explicit states with legal transitions. A timeout is an observation about communication, not necessarily an order state. Broker messages can arrive twice or out of order, so deduplicate by durable identity and reconcile cumulative quantities.

Separate an intent ID from an external order ID and a fill ID. One intent may have a documented cancel-and-replace sequence, while one order may have many fills. Track original quantity, cumulative filled quantity, remaining quantity, and cancellation status. Do not assume a cancellation acknowledgement erases earlier fills.

$$
q_{remaining}=q_{original}-\sum_i q_{fill,i}
$$

## A worked example

An order buys 100 shares. Forty fill, leaving 60. The bot requests cancellation, but 15 more fill before the cancellation completes. The ledger must contain 55 bought shares; the successful cancellation removes only the remaining 45. If the 15-share fill message is replayed, holdings remain 55.

If the broker reports cumulative filled quantity of 55, do not treat it as 55 additional shares after already booking 40. Distinguish incremental fill messages from cumulative order updates in the adapter contract.

## Implementation and review

Build a transition table and test every terminal state. Preserve unknown orders as risk commitments until reconciliation resolves them. Record rejected transitions for investigation instead of forcing state to match the latest message blindly. The offline lab demonstrates partial fills and idempotent fill records; a real asynchronous adapter additionally needs broker-specific cancel races and sequencing behavior.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

The FIX Trading Community's order-state document tabulates the lesson's cancellation race. Scenario B.1.b follows a 10,000-share order: 2,000 fill, a cancel request goes out, 3,000 more fill while it is in flight, the broker confirms Pending Cancel, another 1,000 fill, and the final report is Canceled with 6,000 filled. ExecType gives the reason a report was sent; OrdStatus gives the order's status after that event. When an order is in several states at once, the highest-precedence state is reported, and Pending Cancel outranks Filled even though the standard stresses that it does not indicate cancellation.

That precedence rule is the trap. In scenario B.1.c the last 5,000 shares fill while the cancel is pending, so the report carrying them shows Pending Cancel, not Filled, and a Cancel Reject with reason 0, too late to cancel, follows. Our inference: an adapter that books shares when it sees a Filled or Partially Filled status will lose that fill, so book from the trade reports and treat a too-late reject as an ordinary outcome. Scenario B.1.d adds a second surprise: a cancel request may name an order the broker has not yet acknowledged, so Pending Cancel can arrive before New, and a transition table that insists on New first would reject legal traffic.

These races are common. Aquilina, Budish and O'Neill used exchange message data, which, unlike limit order book data, include failed attempts to trade or cancel. They found latency-arbitrage races about once a minute per symbol for FTSE 100 stocks, a modal race lasting 5 to 10 millionths of a second, and about 20% of trading volume involved. Cartea and co-authors, modelling marketable orders under latency, note that delay leaves a liquidity provider with no guarantee of withdrawing a stale quote before it is picked off. A one-millisecond round trip is 100 to 200 times the modal race, so a bot cannot count on its cancel arriving first.

Exercise: scale B.1.b, B.1.c and B.1.d to 100 shares and replay each three ways: in order, with one fill delivered twice, and with the cancel reject ahead of the last fill. Every variant should end with the same position and no open commitment.

### Sources for this section

- [FIX Trading Community (2023) · Order State Changes, FIX Latest as of EP284](https://www.fixtrading.org/wp-content/uploads/download-manager-files/FIX-Latest-as-of-EP284-Order-State-Changes.pdf) — *Technical documentation.* The standard's own scenario tables for cancels that cross fills, with the OrdStatus precedence rule and the cancel-for-unacknowledged-order case.
- [Aquilina, Budish & O'Neill (2021) · Quantifying the High-Frequency Trading “Arms Race”](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjab032) — *Research paper.* Exchange message data that include failed trades and cancels, used to measure how often and how fast latency races for stale quotes occur.
- [Cartea, Jaimungal & Sánchez-Betancourt (2019) · Latency and Liquidity Risk](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.03281) — *arXiv 1908.03281.* Models how exchange latency removes any guarantee that an order, or the withdrawal of a stale quote, lands before the book changes.

modules.title: Execution schedules: TWAP, VWAP, and participation
modules.subtitle: Choose and evaluate a slicing policy with explicit urgency, liquidity, and completion constraints.
modules.objective: Choose and evaluate a slicing policy with explicit urgency, liquidity, and completion constraints.
modules.reading: Unit 3 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

TWAP distributes quantity over time; VWAP schedules against an estimated volume profile; a participation policy sizes child orders relative to observed or estimated market volume. Each needs a remaining-quantity cap, eligibility rules, and an end-of-window policy. Naming the algorithm does not define its actual fill mechanics.

Fast execution reduces waiting exposure but can consume expensive liquidity. Slow execution may reduce immediate pressure while risking price movement or an unfinished parent order. Models that optimize this trade-off rely on assumptions about volatility, impact, and constraints; there is no universally optimal schedule.

$$
q_{child}\leq\min(q_{remaining},\rho V_{eligible})
$$

## A worked example

A 1,000-share parent has four equal time buckets. TWAP requests 250 per bucket. A forecast volume profile of 10%, 20%, 40%, and 30% suggests VWAP child targets of 100, 200, 400, and 300. Under a 5% participation cap, a bucket with 4,000 shares of eligible volume permits at most 200 shares, even when the schedule asks for 400.

The remaining 200 cannot simply disappear from the report. The parent needs a documented carry-forward, cancellation, or urgency change, with risk approval. Do not use a bucket's eventual full volume for an order placed before that volume was known.

## Implementation and review

Simulate sparse volume, a missed bucket, a session ending early, and a late cancellation. Report both shortfall and completion percentage. A schedule should preserve parent quantity after partial fills and retries. Cap each child by remaining authorized quantity as well as participation; otherwise a catch-up rule can overfill the original decision.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

TWAP and VWAP differ in which clock they follow, and Kato makes the link precise. Adding an explicit trading-volume process to the Almgren–Chriss execution model, he shows that a risk-neutral trader's optimal schedule is VWAP, trading in proportion to volume, when the day's total volume is known in advance. He calls that case unrealistic but a useful benchmark, and with constant volume it reduces to equal slices, which is TWAP. For a schedule fixed in advance, his optimum weights each interval by the harmonic mean of volume, 1/E[1/v], rather than the average. Our inference: in that model an erratic bucket earns a smaller share than its average volume implies. A bucket equally likely to trade 2,000 or 6,000 shares averages 4,000 but has a harmonic mean of 3,000.

Białkowski, Darolles and Le Fol attack the forecast itself. They split intraday volume into a part that follows the market's evolution and a stock-specific pattern, applied the model to CAC 40 stocks, and let the VWAP strategy adjust during the day to track the end-of-day VWAP better. For Harbor, recompute the remaining targets from volume already seen, never from volume yet to come.

Participation rules have their own failure mode. On 6 May 2010 a 75,000-contract E-Mini sell program ran through an algorithm that targeted 9% of the previous minute's volume, without regard to price or time. The same trader's earlier program of that size took more than 5 hours; this one finished in 20 minutes. In the 14 seconds from 2:45:13, high-frequency traders traded over 27,000 contracts, about 49 percent of volume, while adding only about 200 net. Our inference: a rule of ρ times observed volume speeds up exactly when observed volume is least informative. A 5% cap on a bucket that suddenly prints 8,000 shares allows 400, so add an absolute cap and a price limit.

Exercise: if the lesson's 4,000-share bucket is its 40% bucket, the day trades 10,000 shares and a 5% cap can complete only 500 of the 1,000. Check that feasibility first, then replay a bucket with doubled volume.

### Sources for this section

- [Kato (2014) · VWAP Execution as an Optimal Strategy](https://arxiv.org/abs/1408.6118) — *arXiv 1408.6118.* Adds a trading-volume process to the Almgren–Chriss model and shows when VWAP is optimal, why exact VWAP needs future volume, and how forecast volume enters a fixed schedule.
- [Białkowski, Darolles & Le Fol (2008) · Improving VWAP strategies: A dynamic volume approach](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jbankfin.2007.09.023) — *Research paper.* Decomposes intraday volume into a market-wide and a stock-specific part so that a VWAP schedule can be adjusted during the day to track the closing VWAP.
- [U.S. CFTC & SEC staffs (2010) · Findings Regarding the Market Events of May 6, 2010](https://www.cftc.gov/sites/default/files/idc/groups/public/%40otherif/documents/ifdocs/staff-findings050610.pdf) — *Official source.* The joint staff report on how a sell algorithm that targeted a share of recent volume, with no price or time limit, interacted with recycled volume.

modules.title: Mock broker and paper accounting
modules.subtitle: Reconcile cash, inventory, fees, reservations, and marked equity from a durable fill ledger.
modules.objective: Reconcile cash, inventory, fees, reservations, and marked equity from a durable fill ledger.
modules.reading: Unit 3 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

An order does not itself change owned inventory. Accepted orders reserve resources; fills change cash and holdings; cancellations release only unfilled commitments. Keep available cash distinct from settled or total ledger cash. The educational lab uses immediate settlement, long-only integer shares, and one symbol, so its simplicity remains visible.

Use a stable fill ID and an atomic transaction to book cash, shares, and fill history together. Money should have an explicit precision policy. The downloadable project uses integer cents for prices and a deterministic commission rounding rule; a production adapter must match the broker's actual currency and settlement semantics.

$$
E_t=C_t+q_tP_{mark,t}
$$

## A worked example

Harbor starts with $10,000. Buying 40 shares at $100 with a $2 fee leaves $5,998 cash and 40 shares. Marking at $101 produces equity of $10,038: $5,998 plus $4,040. The $38 gain combines $40 unrealized appreciation with the $2 entry fee.

A pending order for 60 additional shares is not a holding. It reserves buying power using its price cap and a fee buffer. Canceling that remainder releases the reserve without undoing the 40-share fill.

## Implementation and review

Test cash and share conservation after every transition, not just at the final report. Reconcile independent order and fill records after restart. Compare paper outcomes with the documented simulation model; vendor paper environments can differ from live conditions, and the offline lab does not model queue position, market impact, borrow, or settlement delays. Treat correct arithmetic as evidence of ledger correctness, not a forecast of execution quality.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Start with the number type. The Python documentation shows that 0.1 + 0.1 + 0.1 − 0.3 is exactly zero in decimal arithmetic but about 5.55 × 10⁻¹⁷ in binary floating point, that such residues block reliable equality tests and can accumulate, and that decimal is therefore preferred in accounting applications with strict equality invariants. Harbor's checks are equalities: $5,998 plus $4,040 must equal $10,038 to the cent. Integer cents or Decimal remove the residue but not the rounding policy. The module offers eight rounding modes and defaults to half-even, so a half-cent-per-share fee on a 41-share fill is $0.205, booked as $0.20 under half-even and $0.21 under half-up. One cent per tie is enough to break reconciliation with a broker statement, so name the mode in the adapter contract.

Next, test the equalities after every transition by letting a tool choose the sequences. Hypothesis's rule-based state machines take primitive actions, search for sequences that fail, and run invariants after every step. Useful invariants for Harbor: cash and shares each equal their opening balance plus the signed fill flows, with fees deducted from cash; reserved cash covers the price cap times the open quantity plus the fee buffer; replaying any fill changes nothing. A failing sequence it finds is a ready-made replay.

A correct ledger can still hold an unrealistic fill rule. Huang, Lehalle and Rosenbaum treat the book as a queueing system whose order-flow intensities depend only on its current state, and use it to compute execution probabilities of passive orders and as a market simulator. Our inference: a mock that fills Harbor's pending 60 shares whenever a trade prints at its price ignores the queue ahead. Add a property test that the fill probability never rises as the queue ahead grows.

Exercise: write the three invariants and the monotonicity property as one state machine, run it over many generated sequences, then kill the process between booking cash and booking shares and check that the ledger still balances.

### Sources for this section

- [Python Software Foundation · decimal: Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic](https://docs.python.org/3/library/decimal.html) — *Technical documentation.* Documents why binary floats break equality tests in accounting code, the eight rounding modes and the half-even default.
- [Hypothesis · Stateful tests](https://hypothesis.readthedocs.io/en/latest/stateful.html) — *Technical documentation.* Rule-based state machines that generate sequences of actions and check invariants after every step.
- [Huang, Lehalle & Rosenbaum (2013) · Simulating and analyzing order book data: The queue-reactive model](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.0563) — *arXiv 1312.0563.* Models the order book as a state-dependent queueing system, used for execution probabilities of passive orders and as a market simulator.

modules.title: Position sizing and circuit breakers
modules.subtitle: Translate uncertain return assumptions into constrained position sizes and explicit loss-control states.
modules.objective: Translate uncertain return assumptions into constrained position sizes and explicit loss-control states.
modules.reading: Unit 4 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

A trading system needs rules for when it must refuse an otherwise valid signal. Those rules depend on positions, cash, outstanding orders, data quality, and operating limits. Begin by writing the condition that must always hold, then test a case that tries to break it. Later lessons explain how to halt and resume without losing track of existing commitments.

## Design and reasoning

Kelly sizing maximizes expected log growth in a specified repeated-bet model; it does not supply reliable probabilities or eliminate drawdowns. The binary-bet expression assumes a known win probability, a fixed payoff ratio, and losses bounded by the staked fraction. Stock gaps, changing payoffs, correlated bets, and estimation error break a literal mapping.

Fractional Kelly reduces the output of that model, but remains sensitive to its inputs. Practical sizing also needs capital, exposure, liquidity, and loss limits. A stop distance is a planned trigger distance, not a guaranteed maximum loss: a gap or unavailable market can execute beyond it.

$$
f^*=p-(1-p)/b;\quad q_{risk}=\lfloor B/|P_{entry}-P_{stop}|\rfloor
$$

## A worked example

For a hypothetical even-money bet with win probability 0.55, full Kelly is 0.55−0.45 = 10%; half Kelly is 5%. If the true probability is 0.51, full Kelly is only 2%. The original estimate therefore matters more than the apparent precision of the arithmetic.

Under a separate stop-risk rule, a $200 loss budget and $2 distance suggest 100 shares before other caps. If an entry gaps from a $50 assumption to $55 while the stop remains $48, the $7 distance suggests at most 28 integer shares. Recompute at the executable price.

## Implementation and review

Keep the position-size function deterministic and place it after the model proposal. Validate positive distances and finite inputs before division. Combine the resulting cap with cash, single-name, and portfolio constraints. Define which events halt new risk and who can resume. A halt blocks new exposure; cancellation and risk reduction require their own reconciled procedures.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

MacLean, Thorp and Ziemba summarise the trade-off in Kelly sizing: the criterion maximises the limiting exponential growth rate of wealth, but its suggested wagers may be very large, so it can be very risky in the short term. For processes well approximated in continuous time, growth drops to the risk-free rate at exactly twice the Kelly wager and keeps falling beyond it. For the lesson's even-money bet with a true probability of 0.51, true Kelly is 2%. Our calculation of expected log growth per bet gives +0.020% at a 2% stake, about zero at 4%, −0.025% at 5% and −0.30% at 10%. Half Kelly sized from the 0.55 estimate is a 5% stake, already past break-even.

A halt is a drawdown rule, and Busseti, Ryu and Boyd treat drawdown directly, measured from starting wealth. They bound by β the probability that wealth ever falls to a fraction α of its start. The bound holds when the expected value of the growth factor raised to the power −λ is at most 1, with λ = log β / log α; in their simulations such bets beat fractional Kelly at the same drawdown risk. For a halt 30% below starting equity (α = 0.7) tolerated with probability 0.1, applying that bound to Harbor's even-money bet gives a stake cap of about 2.7% when p = 0.55 and about 0.5% when p = 0.51. In our simulation of 4,000 bets per path at p = 0.55, that halt was touched on about 9% of paths at 2.7%, 32% at 5% and 66% at 10%; a halt measured from the running peak fires at least as often.

Market-wide circuit breakers trigger at 7%, 13% and 20% declines in the S&P 500; the first two pause trading for 15 minutes before 3:25 p.m., the third ends the day. A single stock pauses for five minutes if it stays at its price band for 15 seconds, and no trade can occur outside the band. Our inference: copy the graded thresholds and fixed pauses for Harbor's halts, name who may resume, and do not assume a stop fills beyond a band.

Exercise: simulate the three stakes at p = 0.55 and p = 0.51 and count how often the halt fires.

### Sources for this section

- [MacLean, Thorp & Ziemba (2011) · Good and Bad Properties of the Kelly Criterion](https://doi.org/10.1142/9789814293501_0039) — *Book.* Summarises why Kelly maximises long-run growth yet can be very risky in the short term, and what happens to growth when stakes exceed the Kelly wager.
- [Busseti, Ryu & Boyd (2016) · Risk-Constrained Kelly Gambling](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.06183) — *arXiv 1603.06183.* Turns a drawdown limit into a bet-size constraint, with a bound on the probability that wealth ever falls to a given fraction of its starting value.
- [U.S. SEC · Investor.gov · Stock Market Circuit Breakers](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/glossary/stock-market-circuit-breakers) — *Official source.* The SEC's plain-language summary of market-wide and single-stock circuit breakers: trigger levels, pause lengths and price bands.

modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

A collection of individually acceptable orders can violate the account's overall limits. Calculate projected cash and holdings after outstanding commitments, then test gross exposure, net exposure, single-name concentration, sector concentration, and any factor budgets supported by reliable estimates. Different measures detect different failure modes.

For a long-only account, net and gross dollar exposure coincide, but sector and name concentration still differ. A future long/short extension cannot assume that netting removes liquidity or margin risk. An exposure estimate also needs a declared mark and stale-price policy.

$$
w_{projected}=(N_{held}+N_{pending}+N_{new})/E
$$

## A worked example

Harbor's $100,000 account holds $12,000 in one name and has an accepted $5,000 buy outstanding. A proposed additional $4,000 would produce $21,000 projected exposure. It breaches a stipulated 20% name limit even though the current holding is only 12%. The maximum extra notional under this cap is $3,000 before fee and price buffers.

Two $10,000 positions in different companies may still create $20,000 exposure to the same industry. Splitting orders across names does not necessarily diversify the underlying economic risk.

## Implementation and review

Recompute reservations atomically with acceptance, so two simultaneous proposals cannot both consume the same remaining budget. Revalue after material price changes; a limit that held at submission can be exceeded by the market without any new order. Such a breach should trigger the declared review or reduction policy, not rewrite historical acceptance records. Test concurrent buys, opposite-side commitments, and a stale mark.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

The SEC's market access rule is explicit about what counts. Its adopting release says brokers should measure credit and capital thresholds against orders entered, counting the exposure of open orders that have not yet executed. That exposure may be discounted for the chance of execution only where sound risk models back the discount, and a firm relying on them should monitor their accuracy. Harbor has no such model, so its $5,000 pending buy counts at face value. Illustration: a 50% discount lifts the room for a new buy from $3,000 to $5,500, and if everything filled the name would end at 22.5%. The release also splits an aggregate limit: $1,000,000 across five venues may become $200,000 each, provided each assumes the others are full. Our inference: fixed slices of Harbor's 20% name limit, one per strategy, avoid a shared counter at the price of idle budget.

Shared counters invite races. Berenson and co-authors describe write skew: one transaction reads x and y, which satisfy a constraint, a second reads both and writes x, then the first writes y, and the constraint may break. Their bank example lets balances go negative while the joint sum stays non-negative, and snapshot isolation allows the anomaly. Our inference: two $2,000 buys, each leaving the name at 19%, can both pass checks made on separate order rows and sit at 21% together. Under first-committer-wins, a shared reservation row that every acceptance updates makes the second commit abort.

Exercise: submit both buys concurrently a thousand times; exactly one must be accepted every time. Then revalue the name 23% higher after the pending buy fills; the breach should raise a review, not rewrite the acceptance record.

### Sources for this section

- [U.S. SEC (2010) · Risk Management Controls for Brokers or Dealers with Market Access](https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/final/2010/34-63241.pdf) — *Official source.* Adopting release for Rule 15c3-5: thresholds are measured on orders entered including open orders, execution-likelihood discounts need monitored models, and an aggregate limit may be split into venue sub-limits.
- [Berenson et al. (2007) · A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels](https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0701157) — *arXiv cs/0701157.* Defines read skew and write skew, the way two transactions that each respect a constraint can jointly break it, and shows that snapshot isolation still admits write skew.

modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

A risk gate evaluates a typed proposal against a consistent account and market snapshot. Validate the schema first: known instrument, supported side, positive integer quantity, finite positive price, and an allowed order type. Then validate freshness and session eligibility, followed by cash, shares, exposure, and halt policy. A malformed number must never participate in arithmetic as if it were valid.

Collect explicit rejection reasons rather than replacing invalid input with zero. The exact evaluation order is an implementation choice, but every mandatory condition must hold. Keep model confidence outside this permission boundary: confidence can influence a proposed target, while the gate owns hard limits.

$$
qP_{cap}+Fee(q,P_{cap})\leq C_{available}
$$

## A worked example

Available cash is $1,000, a buy price cap is $100, and commission is 10 bps. Ten shares require $1,001, so the order fails cash validation. Nine require $900.90 and fit that constraint. They still need to pass all other gates.

A quote can have an acceptable price and insufficient freshness. An order can fit the name limit and exceed the sector limit. Passing one gate is not a general approval.

## Implementation and review

Write assertions over all accepted orders: projected cash never becomes negative under the fill-price cap; cumulative fills never exceed authorized quantity; sell reservations never exceed owned shares. Mutate one input at a time to test each rejection. The lab's market-event flag and price cap are explicit simplifications, with no exchange calendar or broker connection. Keep an invariant failure visible and halt further mutations until the state is reconciled.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

The CFTC's 2013 concept release, which asks questions rather than imposing rules, lists pre-trade controls as separate layers. A price collar stops orders priced outside an acceptable band from reaching the book or trading at extreme levels, and collars can be dynamic, following prices and volatility. A maximum order size caps quantity at a preset "fat finger" limit. The release also asks about reasonability checks on incoming market data. Harbor's price cap makes its cash arithmetic safe, but cash alone would still accept a typo the account can afford, so quantity needs its own bound (our inference).

Bailis and co-authors ask when an invariant survives concurrent updates without coordination. For counters, a greater-than threshold survives increments but not decrements, and a less-than threshold survives decrements but not increments. Our reading: Harbor's three invariants sit on the unsafe side: cash ≥ 0 under buy reservations, fills ≤ authorized quantity under new fills, and sell reservations ≤ owned shares under new reservations. So only steps that move a counter toward its bound need serialized handling; cancels and deposits do not.

Claessen and Hughes describe QuickCheck properties as functions tested on random input, with custom generators and pitfalls to avoid. Our inference: a gate's pitfall is vacuity, because uniform random orders are mostly rejected. Exercise: generate thousands of boundary orders, assert that every accepted one keeps cash ≥ 0, and count rejections by reason; a reason that never fires is untested. Nine shares at the $100 cap with 10 bps commission cost $900.90, yet 9 × 100 × (1 + 10/10000) evaluates to 900.8999999999999 in Python floats, so keep money in integer cents or Decimal with a stated rounding rule.

### Sources for this section

- [U.S. CFTC (2013) · Concept Release on Risk Controls and System Safeguards for Automated Trading Environments](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2013/09/12/2013-22185/concept-release-on-risk-controls-and-system-safeguards-for-automated-trading-environments) — *Official source.* Describes price collars, maximum order sizes and market-data reasonability checks as distinct pre-trade controls for automated trading, and poses questions about each.
- [Bailis et al. (2014) · Coordination Avoidance in Database Systems (Extended Version)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1402.2237) — *arXiv 1402.2237.* Invariant confluence decides which application invariants need coordination; for counter thresholds, the update direction decides the answer.
- [Claessen & Hughes (2000) · QuickCheck](https://doi.org/10.1145/351240.351266) — *Research paper.* Introduces property-based testing: properties are functions checked on automatically generated random inputs, with custom generators for constrained data.
