modules.title: Halts, loss limits, and controlled resumption
modules.subtitle: Design a persistent operating-state machine that separates stopping new risk from managing existing exposure.
modules.objective: Design a persistent operating-state machine that separates stopping new risk from managing existing exposure.
modules.reading: Unit 4 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

Define states such as running, new-risk halted, reconciling, and disabled. A loss threshold, stale feed, ledger mismatch, or unknown external order may require different actions, but each transition needs a recorded reason. A halt must survive restart; otherwise reboot becomes an accidental permission reset.

Stopping new risk does not guarantee that all orders disappeared or that positions are flat. Cancel outstanding entries through the order manager and reconcile their actual results. A reduction order still needs valid quantity, price, session, and execution controls; an emergency label is not a license to corrupt the ledger.

$$
L_{session}=1-E_t/E_{start}
$$

## A worked example

A session begins with equity $100,000 and later marks at $97,400. The session loss is 2.6%, crossing Harbor's illustrative 2.5% halt threshold. Peak-to-trough drawdown would use a different denominator if equity had first risen above $100,000. Decide which measure the policy means.

If equity rebounds to $98,000, a latched halt remains active until an explicit review and resume event. Automatic oscillation around the boundary can produce repeated stop-and-start trading.

## Implementation and review

Write a resumption checklist tied to evidence: current balances reconcile, unknown orders are resolved, input freshness is restored, the triggering defect is understood, and a permitted reviewer records the release. Test restart while halted, a fill arriving during the halt, and an attempted unreviewed resume. The educational project offers an explicit resume method for experiments; it is not a multi-user approval system.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

A halt is a state with its own traffic, not silence. Corwin and Lipson found that on the NYSE, order submissions and cancellations rise markedly during halts, that much of the reopening book consists of orders entered during the halt, and that quoted depth is unusually thin around halts. Our inference: Harbor's halted state must keep processing acknowledgements, cancels and late fills, and a resume should wait for a fresh quote.

Xu and co-authors followed 203 Shanghai-listed stocks from August 2009 to August 2011. Absolute return, trading volume and, around intraday halts, the bid-ask spread all peaked after a halt and then relaxed along a power law. Our inference: add spread normalization to the resumption checklist, and restart with reduced size caps rather than full limits.

The lesson's trigger is a fixed floor 2.5% below the session start, at $97,500. Grossman and Zhou study a floor that ratchets with the peak: wealth must stay above a fixed fraction of its running maximum, and for constant relative risk aversion the optimal risky investment is proportional to the surplus above that floor. If equity first rose to $102,000, a 2.5% floor under the peak would sit at $99,450. Our reading: surplus-scaled exposure shrinks smoothly toward the limit in theory; gaps and fees make the latched halt the backstop.

Exercise: replay 100,000 → 97,400 → 98,000. The halt must latch at 2.6%, survive the rebound and a restart, process a fill that arrives while halted, and refuse an unreviewed resume.

### Sources for this section

- [Corwin & Lipson (2000) · Order Flow and Liquidity around NYSE Trading Halts](https://doi.org/10.1111/0022-1082.00267) — *Research paper.* Shows that order submissions and cancellations rise during NYSE halts, that the reopening book is largely built during the halt, and that depth is thin around halts.
- [Xu, Zhang & Liu (2013) · Short-term Market Reaction after Trading Halts in Chinese Stock Market](https://arxiv.org/abs/1309.1138) — *arXiv 1309.1138.* Measures return, volume and spread after 203 stocks' halts on the Shanghai Stock Exchange, finding a sharp peak followed by power-law relaxation.
- [Grossman & Zhou (1993) · Optimal Investment Strategies for Controlling Drawdowns](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9965.1993.tb00044.x) — *Research paper.* Derives the optimal risky investment under a floor tied to the running maximum of wealth, with exposure proportional to the surplus above the floor.

modules.title: Labels, overlapping horizons, and time splits
modules.subtitle: Construct prediction targets without allowing future labels or fitted preprocessing to leak into evaluation.
modules.objective: Construct prediction targets without allowing future labels or fitted preprocessing to leak into evaluation.
modules.reading: Unit 5 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

A model's target describes an outcome that becomes known after the prediction. If a future outcome overlaps the period used for another example, an ordinary data split can accidentally share information. Draw the timeline of each example before fitting a model. This unit connects those time boundaries to baselines, thresholds, and monitoring.

## Design and reasoning

A label has an observation time and an end time: a five-day forward return becomes fully known five days later. Features at a decision time must use only information available then. Training rows whose labels extend into the evaluation interval can carry future information across an apparently chronological boundary.

Use forward validation with a training cutoff that respects label availability. Purge overlapping label intervals when necessary. A fixed gap in a time-series splitter is convenient for fixed horizons, but it does not automatically identify variable event horizons or solve every dependence problem. An embargo is a separate exclusion interval; naming a split purged does not make it so.

$$
\text{Eligible training row }i:\quad t^{label}_{end,i}<t^{validation}_{start}
$$

## A worked example

Validation begins at time index 10. Candidate training labels begin at 4, 6, and 8 and end three steps later at 7, 9, and 11. Under a strict end-before-validation rule, the first two are eligible; the row ending at 11 is excluded. Training data that starts before 10 can still contain a label unavailable at 10.

A scaler is fitted on the eligible training features and then applied unchanged to validation. Fitting it on all dates leaks information even if the labels were properly separated.

## Implementation and review

Save train, validation, and test index manifests with label intervals and data versions. Unit-test boundary cases where a label ends exactly at the cutoff and explicitly declare whether that endpoint is allowed. Tune only on development folds and retain a later frozen evaluation. Report the number of independent time periods, not just the number of overlapping rows.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Overlap costs twice: it leaks across the split and it shrinks the honest sample. A label spanning h steps and sampled every step shares h − 1 steps with its neighbour. In the lesson's split the surviving labels, ending at 7 and 9, still share the step from 6 to 7. Richardson and Stock derived a different asymptotic theory for statistics built on multi-year returns, since the standard approximations behaved badly; it matched finite-sample distributions far better and made the data look much more compatible with no mean reversion. Hodrick's Monte Carlo analysis found the Hansen–Hodrick procedure biased at long horizons while the alternatives did better. Our arithmetic: 250 daily rows with 5-day labels hold only 50 non-overlapping windows, so report 50 beside any corrected statistic, because the corrections themselves have finite-sample problems.

Shuffling rows is no remedy. Roberts and co-authors found that ignoring dependence in cross-validation seriously underestimates predictive error, and recommend block validation wherever dependence exists, even when the residuals look uncorrelated. Rabinowicz and Rosset give a criterion for when standard cross-validation stays suitable under correlation, and a bias-corrected estimator for when it does not. Our inference: in a forward-only split, purging at the cutoff is the whole job; an embargo after the validation block matters only when later rows also train.

Exercise: run the whole pipeline, scaler included, on a simulated random walk. Skill above the training-mean baseline under shuffled folds, but not under purged walk-forward splits, measures the leak; after the fix, scores should sit at or below zero.

### Sources for this section

- [Richardson & Stock (1989) · Drawing inferences from statistics based on multiyear asset returns](https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-405X%2889%2990086-X) — *Research paper.* Develops asymptotic theory for statistics built on multi-year returns, because the usual approximations performed poorly in finite samples.
- [Hodrick (1992) · Dividend Yields and Expected Stock Returns: Alternative Procedures for Inference and Measurement](https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/5.3.351) — *Research paper.* Monte Carlo comparison of inference procedures for long-horizon forecasting, finding the Hansen–Hodrick procedure biased at long horizons.
- [Roberts et al. (2017) · Cross-validation strategies for data with temporal, spatial, hierarchical, or phylogenetic structure](https://doi.org/10.1111/ecog.02881) — *Research paper.* Shows that random cross-validation underestimates predictive error on dependent data and recommends blocked splits wherever dependence exists.
- [Rabinowicz & Rosset (2019) · Cross-Validation for Correlated Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.02438) — *arXiv 1904.02438.* Gives a criterion for when standard cross-validation is suitable under correlation and a bias-corrected estimator for when it is not.

assignment.solution: Only 17 and 19 qualify. The strict rule excludes the endpoint at 20. A random split can train on future outcomes and overlapping intervals relative to an earlier evaluation decision.

modules.title: Baselines and prediction-to-position mapping
modules.subtitle: Compare simple predictive baselines and convert model output into a bounded decision under trading costs.
modules.objective: Compare simple predictive baselines and convert model output into a bounded decision under trading costs.
modules.reading: Unit 5 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

Start with an explicit no-skill baseline: a training mean for regression or a training base rate for classification. A complex model must improve a relevant out-of-sample objective, not merely fit the training data. Compare squared error, calibration where relevant, ranking quality, and eventual cost-aware decisions without conflating them.

A prediction in return units can be compared with estimated trading costs. A rank cannot directly be treated as a return magnitude, and a probability of a positive return does not state the size of wins or losses. Define the mapping from model output to target before evaluating the holdout.

$$
MSE=n^{-1}\sum_i(y_i-\hat y_i)^2
$$

## A worked example

Observed validation returns are 1% and −1%. The zero-return baseline has mean squared error 0.0001. Predictions of 0.8% and −0.6% have MSE 0.00001, improving this tiny illustrative sample. Two rows are insufficient evidence of durable performance.

If a proposed trade has expected benefit 8 bps and estimated nonoverlapping cost 6 bps, only 2 bps remain before model uncertainty. Harbor may require an additional margin or abstain. Position size is capped by deterministic risk logic even if the prediction is large.

## Implementation and review

Log the baseline, prediction units, evaluation dates, costs, turnover, and target mapping. Inspect whether apparent gains come from one outlier or one regime. A ranking model may be assessed with cross-sectional rank correlation, but time-series dependence and universe construction still affect inference. Keep predictive evaluation and portfolio simulation as separate evidence artifacts.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Welch and Goyal found that the proposed predictors of the equity premium had by and large forecast badly for 30 years, judged in sample or out of sample, and looked unstable. The yardstick, as Campbell and Thompson describe it, was a simple forecast based on the historical average return: the lesson's training mean. Campbell and Thompson's working paper found that two output rules improve out-of-sample performance: zero out a regression coefficient whose sign is wrong, and floor negative forecasts at zero.

Scale is the useful part. They judge an out-of-sample R² against the squared Sharpe ratio S². With a monthly S² of 1.2%, an R² of 0.25% for the earnings-price ratio lifts a mean-variance investor's average portfolio return by a proportional 0.25/1.2 = 21%. Harbor's two rows give an R² of 90% against the zero baseline, so they establish nothing. Their stock weight was confined to between 0 and 150%, and predictable variation produces no portfolio gain while an upper limit binds: test the capped policy, not the raw forecast.

Babiak and Baruník score neural-network forecasts against linear regressions by certainty-equivalent return and Sharpe ratio, and report gains that survive transaction costs and borrowing and short-selling constraints. Our reading: climb a ladder of baselines, training mean then linear then nonlinear, and score every rung with the same capped, costed policy.

Exercise: report R² against the training mean, clip negative forecasts, apply the cap, then subtract the 6 bps cost; claim nothing from a step you skipped.

### Sources for this section

- [Welch & Goyal (2008) · A Comprehensive Look at The Empirical Performance of Equity Premium Prediction](https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhm014) — *Research paper.* Re-examines the predictors proposed for the equity premium and finds poor, unstable in-sample and out-of-sample performance against simple benchmarks.
- [Campbell & Thompson (2005) · Predicting the Equity Premium Out of Sample: Can Anything Beat the Historical Average?](https://doi.org/10.3386/w11468) — *Research paper.* NBER working paper: sign restrictions on coefficients and forecasts, an out-of-sample R² judged against the squared Sharpe ratio, and portfolio weights bounded between 0 and 150%.
- [Babiak & Baruník (2020) · Deep Learning, Predictability, and Optimal Portfolio Returns](https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.03394) — *arXiv 2009.03394.* Scores deep-learning return forecasts against linear regressions by certainty-equivalent return and Sharpe ratio, with transaction costs and portfolio constraints.

modules.title: Boosted trees and defensible constraints
modules.subtitle: Develop a nonlinear model with controlled complexity, time-aware selection, and documented feature assumptions.
modules.objective: Develop a nonlinear model with controlled complexity, time-aware selection, and documented feature assumptions.
modules.reading: Unit 5 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

Boosting adds learners that correct the current model under a specified loss. Depth, learning rate, number of rounds, minimum leaf support, and regularization influence complexity. More rounds can improve training loss while degrading later performance. Use a chronologically valid validation set for early stopping and preserve the chosen iteration with the model artifact.

A monotonic constraint imposes a direction on a model's response to a selected feature while other inputs are held fixed. It expresses a modeling assumption. It does not prove that a financial relationship is universally monotonic, causal, or stable across regimes. Forcing an unjustified relationship can reduce accuracy.

$$
m^*=\arg\min_m L_{validation}(m)
$$

## A worked example

Validation losses over five training checkpoints are 0.90, 0.75, 0.71, 0.73, and 0.78. Under this illustrative selection rule, checkpoint three is preferred. Choosing checkpoint five merely because it trained longest ignores the validation evidence. The final test set must not become another tuning input.

Harbor considers a positive constraint on a quality score. Before adopting it, the team documents the score's definition, tests an unconstrained baseline, and checks whether the same feature meaning survives revisions. A renamed or rescaled feature is not automatically compatible with an old constraint vector.

## Implementation and review

The in-app worksheet illustrates model selection arithmetic; it does not train XGBoost. For an optional external extension, pin a supported library version, save feature order and constraints, inspect that version's early-stopping prediction behavior, and reproduce the result from a clean environment. Report the validation manifest and rejected variants. The later standard-library project trains a small ridge model to make the fit/evaluate boundary runnable without extra dependencies.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Early stopping is where the lesson's checkpoint rule meets library behavior, and XGBoost's API reference lists several traps. Its native training function stops once the validation metric has gone the stated number of rounds without improving, uses the last entry of the evaluation list, and returns the model from the last iteration, not the best one. With the lesson's losses and a patience of two, training halts after checkpoint five, and a plain call to the booster's predict uses all five rounds, including the two that made validation worse. The documented remedies are a save_best option that drops the rounds after the best one, or slicing the model, but slicing removes the best_iteration attribute, so Harbor's own manifest must record the chosen round. Because the last evaluation entry decides stopping, a test set appended for monitoring would become the stopping criterion, which breaks the lesson's rule that the final test never tunes anything.

Constraints deserve similar suspicion. LightGBM's documentation says the monotone-constraint vector must list every feature in order, so a reordered or inserted column can move a constraint onto a different feature (our inference), and it describes the default method as over-constraining the predictions. The wider case for boosted trees has limits too. Grinsztajn and co-authors found tree-based models still state of the art on medium-sized tabular data, about ten thousand samples, across a 45-dataset benchmark, but they removed stream-like data and time series, so the result cannot vouch for a market model by itself.

Exercise: save the chosen round, feature order and constraint vector beside the model, reload it in a clean process, and require predictions to equal those of the first three rounds. Then sweep the quality score across its observed range with the other inputs fixed and assert that predictions never fall.

### Sources for this section

- [XGBoost contributors · XGBoost Python API Reference](https://xgboost.readthedocs.io/en/stable/python/python_api.html) — *Technical documentation.* Version 3.4.2 documentation: native early stopping uses the last evaluation set and returns the last-iteration model; slicing a booster drops best_iteration; the save_best option keeps only rounds up to the best one.
- [LightGBM contributors · LightGBM Parameters](https://lightgbm.readthedocs.io/en/stable/Parameters.html) — *Technical documentation.* Version 4.7.0 documentation: the monotone-constraint vector must cover all features in order, and the default constraint method over-constrains predictions.
- [Grinsztajn, Oyallon & Varoquaux (2022) · Why do tree-based models still outperform deep learning on tabular data?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.08815) — *arXiv 2207.08815.* A 45-dataset benchmark of tree models against neural networks, with an analysis of why trees do well and an explicit exclusion of time series.

modules.title: Calibration, thresholds, and drift
modules.subtitle: Evaluate probability quality and monitor changes in data, predictions, and delayed outcomes.
modules.objective: Evaluate probability quality and monitor changes in data, predictions, and delayed outcomes.
modules.reading: Unit 5 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

Calibration asks whether predicted probabilities agree with observed frequencies in comparable cases. Discrimination asks whether the model separates outcomes. A proper score such as Brier loss reflects more than calibration alone, so a lower score is not a pure proof of better calibration. Inspect reliability bins with counts and uncertainty as well as aggregate scores.

Fit a calibration transform using development data separate from the base model's fitting observations, under a valid time design. Never calibrate on the final holdout and then report that same holdout as untouched. A calibrated probability still needs a payoff and cost model before becoming a trading decision.

$$
BS=n^{-1}\sum_i(p_i-y_i)^2
$$

## A worked example

Predictions 0.8 and 0.3 face outcomes 1 and 0. The Brier score is ((0.8−1)² + (0.3−0)²)/2 = 0.065. A constant 0.5 forecast scores 0.25 on these two observations. This is an arithmetic comparison, not enough data to establish calibration.

If a winning trade gains 1 unit and a losing trade loses 1, expected gross payoff is 2p−1. With a cost of 0.1 units per trade, break-even requires p above 0.55 under those stipulated payoffs. Different loss sizes change the threshold.

## Implementation and review

Monitor feature missingness, schema changes, prediction distribution, abstention frequency, and eventually realized label quality. Covariate drift does not necessarily imply performance failure; stable inputs do not prove stable outcomes either. Outcomes arrive late, so distinguish immediate operational alerts from delayed predictive monitoring. A drift alert should trigger a declared review or fallback; it should not silently retrain and promote a model.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

The lesson's 0.55 threshold treats a model score as a probability, and the calibration literature says to check that for boosted trees. Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana compared learning methods on eight binary problems and found that maximum-margin methods such as boosted trees and stumps push probability mass away from 0 and 1, a sigmoid-shaped distortion; after calibration, boosted trees, random forests and SVMs gave the best probabilities. Whether a current log-loss library shows the same distortion is something a reliability table must answer (our inference). They also explain why a calibrator needs its own data: a model that separates its training cases perfectly teaches a sigmoid that outputs just a 0,1 function. Calibration-set size matters too: below roughly 200 to 1000 cases, Platt scaling beat isotonic regression for all nine methods they plotted, because isotonic is less constrained. A bot's calibration window of a few hundred trades may sit in that range (our inference).

Elkan frames the decision step. The best action has the lowest expected cost under the model's probabilities, and any two-class cost matrix has essentially one degree of freedom for decisions, the threshold. He argues that rebalancing training classes has little effect on standard Bayesian and decision-tree learners, and recommends learning from the data as given and then computing decisions explicitly. With the lesson's payoffs of plus and minus 1, the break-even probability is (1 + cost) / 2, so a cost of 0.2 moves 0.55 to 0.60.

Drift alerts need triage as well. Rabanser and co-authors, working mainly on MNIST and CIFAR-10 images, note that distributions shift constantly and often benignly, and that target error cannot be computed without labels. Their best univariate detector tested the classifier's own softmax outputs, the analogue of Harbor's prediction distribution.

Exercise: bin Harbor's validation predictions with counts, fit a Platt sigmoid on a later window, recompute the threshold at costs 0.1 and 0.2, then replay a feature shift and a flipped outcome relationship. Only the first should alert before labels mature.

### Sources for this section

- [Niculescu-Mizil & Caruana (2005) · Predicting good probabilities with supervised learning](https://doi.org/10.1145/1102351.1102430) — *Research paper.* Compares how learning methods distort predicted probabilities, why calibration needs an independent set, and how Platt scaling and isotonic regression behave as calibration data shrinks.
- [Elkan (2001) · The Foundations of Cost-Sensitive Learning](https://cseweb.ucsd.edu/~elkan/rescale.pdf) — *Research paper.* Shows how optimal decisions follow from a cost matrix and probability estimates, and why class rebalancing is a weak substitute for explicit decision thresholds.
- [Rabanser, Günnemann & Lipton (2018) · Failing Loudly: An Empirical Study of Methods for Detecting Dataset Shift](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.11953) — *arXiv 1810.11953.* Benchmarks shift detectors, separates benign from harmful shift, and shows why target error needs labels.

modules.title: AI decision layers and authority boundaries
modules.subtitle: Assign useful research tasks to AI while keeping order permissions and risk limits outside model-generated text.
modules.objective: Assign useful research tasks to AI while keeping order permissions and risk limits outside model-generated text.
modules.reading: Unit 6 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

An AI research tool can summarize or extract information, but the trading system still needs explicit rules for accepting its output. Start with a narrow task and a source the result can be checked against. Distinguish a model's suggestion from the authority to change an account or submit an order. The following lessons make that distinction testable.

## Design and reasoning

An AI component can summarize evidence, extract candidate facts, classify documents, or draft a research rationale. A deterministic controller validates these outputs and decides whether they are usable. Separate a research recommendation from an authorized target, and keep both separate from broker submission.

A multi-agent committee can provide different analytical perspectives, but agreement is not independence when agents share the same model, prompt, or source error. More discussion does not convert missing evidence into a fact. Start with a small bounded workflow and add autonomous steps only when their benefit can be evaluated.

$$
q_{accepted}=RiskGate(Proposal,Account,Market,Policy)
$$

## A worked example

An AI analyst proposes a 30% position with a confidence score of 0.9. Harbor's fixed single-name cap is 10%. The proposal is rejected or resized under the declared deterministic policy. The model's explanation cannot override the cap, and confidence is not an authenticated permission.

A second proposal includes a plausible conclusion but no source identifier for its revenue figure. The research controller marks the required evidence missing and abstains. Passing numeric risk checks does not repair an unsupported premise.

## Implementation and review

Define a narrow input/output contract: task, document identifiers, allowed fields, uncertainty or missing status, and an explanation linked to evidence. Keep API secrets and trading tools out of document-analysis context. Evaluate correctness, unsupported claims, abstentions, latency, and cost against a deterministic or human-reviewed baseline. The downloadable AI lab uses fixed fictional responses to test validation; it does not call an AI provider or imply measured model accuracy.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Parasuraman and co-authors give the lesson's three-way split a standard vocabulary. They divide automation into four function types, information acquisition, information analysis, decision and action selection, and action implementation, each of which can be set anywhere from fully manual to fully automatic, and they name automation reliability and the costs of decision and action consequences among their secondary criteria for judging a design. Mapped onto Harbor (our inference), a model can sit high on analysis, a proposal is decision selection, and the broker call is action implementation, which only the risk gate may reach.

The 0.9 attached to the 30% proposal deserves scrutiny of its own. Xiong and co-authors benchmarked ways of eliciting confidence from five language models on five types of datasets and found that verbalized confidence tends to be overconfident, with every method struggling on tasks that need professional knowledge. NIST's generative AI profile defines confabulation as confidently stated but erroneous content, and warns that automation bias, meaning excessive deference to automated systems, can exacerbate it. That is a reason to distrust a human reviewer who waves through whatever clears the gate (our inference).

A committee does not fix this by voting. Kim and co-authors evaluated over 350 language models and found that on one leaderboard dataset two models agree 60% of the time when both are wrong, and that larger, more accurate models have highly correlated errors even across providers. NIST names the broader hazard algorithmic monocultures. Our suggestion is to count a committee as one opinion and to require independent evidence, such as a source identifier, before anything is accepted.

Exercise: replay the 30% proposal with the model's confidence low, at 0.9 and near certainty, and with one, three and five agreeing agents; the gate's output must not change. Then delete the revenue source identifier and require an abstention.

### Sources for this section

- [Parasuraman, Sheridan & Wickens (2000) · A model for types and levels of human interaction with automation](https://doi.org/10.1109/3468.844354) — *Research paper.* Four automation function types and a continuum of levels, with reliability and the cost of wrong decisions or actions as criteria; a vocabulary for what the AI may do versus what code must control.
- [Xiong et al. (2023) · Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? An Empirical Evaluation of Confidence Elicitation in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.13063) — *arXiv 2306.13063.* Benchmarks verbalized, sampled and aggregated confidence from five LLMs on five dataset types, finding overconfidence in verbalized confidence.
- [NIST (2024) · Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile (NIST AI 600-1)](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.600-1.pdf) — *Official source.* Defines confabulation, automation bias and algorithmic monocultures among generative AI risks.
- [Kim, Garg, Peng & Garg (2025) · Correlated Errors in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07962) — *arXiv 2506.07962.* Measures how often over 350 LLMs make the same mistakes, including models from different providers.

modules.reading: Unit 6 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

Retrieval selects candidate evidence; generation interprets it. Store each document's issuer, filing type, reporting period, publication timestamp, revision identity, and retrieval provenance. A semantic match does not establish that a passage answers the question or was available at a historical decision time.

Chunk boundaries should retain headings and table context. A revenue number without currency, scale, period, or scope can be materially misleading. Keep the original document pointer and local source identifier so a reviewer can trace the candidate fact. Access and redistribution rights for stored documents remain separate from their usefulness as evidence.

$$
Value_{base}=Value_{reported}\times UnitMultiplier
$$

## A worked example

A fictional Harbor filing published on March 15 reports prior-year revenue of 120 million currency units. It is eligible for an April 1 research decision but not a March 1 historical decision. An amended filing published April 20 cannot silently replace it in the April 1 record.

The analyst extracts 120 and tags the unit as millions. A controller normalizes it to 120,000,000 for a ratio calculation. If the accompanying text said thousands, the same digits would mean a thousandfold smaller amount. Preserve both the reported and normalized value.

## Implementation and review

Test missing pages, conflicting revisions, ambiguous table headers, and a relevant-looking passage about the wrong issuer. Require an explicit not-found outcome. An evidence packet should include the question, allowed as-of time, candidate documents, supported fields, unresolved disagreements, and reviewer disposition. A citation points to a source; it does not prove that the generated claim follows from it.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

EDGAR's own API documentation shows where a research packet can leak the future. Its frames endpoint returns, for each company, the fact that was last filed and best fits the requested calendar period. A query run after Harbor's April 20 amendment would therefore serve the amended figure to an April 1 decision (our inference), so facts must be selected by filing date, not by period alone. The submissions endpoint holds at least a year of filings or the 1,000 most recent, whichever is more, and lists older filings in extra files, so a retriever that reads only the first object can call an old filing missing (our inference). The company-concept endpoint keeps a separate array of facts for each unit of measure, which turns a currency check into a lookup.

Index vintage matters just as much. Lewis and co-authors swapped the Wikipedia index behind a retrieval-augmented model between December 2016 and December 2018 and asked about 82 world leaders who had changed in between. The model answered 70% correctly with the 2016 index on 2016 leaders and 68% with the 2018 index on 2018 leaders, but only 12% and 4% when index and question disagreed. Answers followed the index, so the index snapshot belongs in the evidence record (our inference).

A citation needs its own test. Gao and co-authors' ALCE benchmark scores citation recall, whether the output is fully supported by the passages it cites, and citation precision, whether each citation is relevant, judging support with a natural-language-inference model. On ELI5 even the best models lacked complete citation support 50% of the time. Those are open-domain questions, not filings, but the check ports (our inference): test that each cited passage entails its claim.

Exercise: freeze the index as of March 1, April 1 and just after the April 20 amendment, and ask for prior-year revenue. Expect not found, the original 120 million, and the amendment as a separate later record. Then require every cited passage to entail its claim and to name the right issuer and period.

### Sources for this section

- [U.S. SEC · EDGAR Application Programming Interfaces (APIs)](https://www.sec.gov/search-filings/edgar-application-programming-interfaces) — *Official source.* Describes the submissions and XBRL endpoints: filing-history limits and extra files, per-unit fact arrays, last-filed frames and typical update delays.
- [Lewis et al. (2020) · Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401) — *arXiv 2005.11401.* Introduces retrieval-augmented generation and shows by swapping a 2016 and a 2018 index that a model's answers follow the index it retrieves from.
- [Gao, Yen, Yu & Chen (2023) · Enabling Large Language Models to Generate Text with Citations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14627) — *arXiv 2305.14627.* Benchmark that scores citation recall and precision with an entailment model; reports how often the best systems fail to fully support their answers with their citations.

modules.title: Structured extraction and numeric validation
modules.subtitle: Validate AI-extracted facts beyond JSON syntax by checking provenance, units, scope, and arithmetic.
modules.objective: Validate AI-extracted facts beyond JSON syntax by checking provenance, units, scope, and arithmetic.
modules.reading: Unit 6 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

A schema can require fields and restrict types; it cannot guarantee that a value is true. Validate source membership, instrument identity, reporting period, allowed units, numeric finiteness, and consistency with the supplied evidence. Reject unknown fields when they could be interpreted as instructions or unauthorized actions.

Keep reported facts separate from derived ratios and judgment. Let deterministic code compute ratios from validated inputs, with explicit zero-denominator and missing-value behavior. Avoid using a generated ratio when the underlying numerator and denominator are available for verification.

$$
g=Revenue_{current}/Revenue_{prior}-1
$$

## A worked example

A fictional evidence record states current revenue 120 million and prior revenue 100 million. The computed growth is 20%. A generated response of 200% has valid numeric syntax but fails arithmetic reconciliation. A response saying 120 thousand fails its unit contract even though its raw number matches.

If prior revenue is zero, percentage growth under this formula is undefined. The controller should return a missing or not-applicable result with a reason instead of producing an infinite score that might dominate position sizing.

## Implementation and review

Build accepted and rejected fixtures before connecting a provider. Include a fabricated source ID, mixed currencies, a future filing, an omitted field, a zero denominator, and unsupported instructions embedded in a note. Measure false acceptance as well as extraction completeness. The offline fixture project demonstrates strict comparison against supplied records; general document interpretation still requires a separately evaluated extraction system.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Units are where a valid-looking number most often goes wrong, and the Inline XBRL specification shows how filings encode them. In financial statements a figure is commonly scaled for display in thousands, millions or billions, so the tagged element carries a scale attribute written as an exponent of ten: a value shown in thousands must be multiplied by 1,000 to give the stored fact, which is scale 3. A percentage shown as an integer is often stored as a decimal, and negative values are flagged by a separate sign attribute. For filings that carry these tags, the lesson's unit contract can be checked against the filing's own machine-readable scale and sign instead of the model's reading of a table header (our inference).

Syntax is a weaker guarantee than it sounds. Willard and Louf describe guided generation that constrains output with regular expressions and context-free grammars and guarantees the structure of the generated text. A grammar can force some number into the revenue field, so the schema also needs an explicit not-found branch (our inference).

Right answers can hide wrong inputs. Chen and co-authors built FinQA, 8,281 expert-annotated questions over S&P 500 earnings reports, and note that execution accuracy tends to overestimate performance because a model sometimes hits the correct answer by chance. In their 2021 baselines, generating the final number directly with the same architecture scored near zero, which they took as evidence that generating an executable reasoning program is necessary. By analogy (our inference), 20% growth should pass only if both revenue inputs trace to the filing, because 240 over 200 gives the same 20%.

Exercise: add that coincidence fixture, a pair of wrong-issuer inputs that still yields 20%, and require rejection on provenance rather than arithmetic. Then report false acceptances next to completeness.

### Sources for this section

- [XBRL International (2013) · Inline XBRL Part 1: Specification 1.1](https://www.xbrl.org/Specification/inlineXBRL-part1/REC-2013-11-18/inlineXBRL-part1-REC-2013-11-18.html) — *Technical documentation.* Defines the scale and sign attributes that connect a figure displayed in thousands or millions to its stored value, the machine-readable counterpart of the lesson's unit multiplier.
- [Willard & Louf (2023) · Efficient Guided Generation for Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.09702) — *arXiv 2307.09702.* Constrains generation with regular expressions and grammars so the output structure is guaranteed, which fixes syntax but says nothing about whether a value is true.
- [Chen et al. (2021) · FinQA: A Dataset of Numerical Reasoning over Financial Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.00122) — *arXiv 2109.00122.* Expert-annotated numerical questions over earnings reports with gold reasoning programs; scores both execution and program accuracy because a right number can be a coincidence.

modules.title: Agent tools, prompt injection, and evaluation
modules.subtitle: Keep untrusted retrieved text from changing tool permissions and test bounded AI workflows against adversarial fixtures.
modules.objective: Keep untrusted retrieved text from changing tool permissions and test bounded AI workflows against adversarial fixtures.
modules.reading: Unit 6 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

A retrieved filing, webpage, tool response, or agent message is data, even when it contains imperative language. A passage that says ignore the risk policy does not acquire authority because it appears in a source document. Enforce allowed operations in application code, with narrow tool arguments and task-scoped permissions.

Use a bounded workflow: retrieve approved documents, extract candidate facts, validate evidence, draft a memo, and submit for review. Set maximum calls, elapsed time, and output size. A recursive agent loop without a budget can fail operationally even if every individual response is harmless. Secrets and broker capabilities do not belong in a read-only research worker.

$$
Cost_{budget}=N_{calls,max}\times Cost_{call,assumed}
$$

## A worked example

Harbor budgets four analysis calls at an illustrative $0.03 each, for $0.12 maximum modeled call cost. A fifth requested call is stopped by the controller. An embedded source instruction requesting a cash transfer is recorded as untrusted content and has no corresponding allowed tool.

The evaluation suite includes supported extraction, missing evidence, fabricated citations, conflicting filings, prompt injection, malformed output, and provider timeout. Score whether the workflow produces the expected decision and evidence, not whether its prose sounds confident.

## Implementation and review

Test defenses outside the prompt: reject disallowed tool names, constrain schemas, preserve a permission boundary, and verify that rejected requests create no state changes. Prompt instructions can help the model behave but are not an access-control mechanism. A timeout should lead to a declared fallback or abstention, never a stale recommendation promoted as fresh. Track false acceptance, unsupported claims, correct abstention, latency, and cost separately.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Debenedetti and co-authors built AgentDojo to measure agents that call tools over untrusted data: 97 tasks and 629 security test cases. Its simple tool filter, in which the model first restricts itself to the tools a task needs, lowered the attack success rate to 7.5%. It works when the user task needs only read access and the attack needs write access, which describes Harbor's research worker: with no transfer tool in its list, the cash-transfer instruction has nothing to call. It fails when the tools a task needs also suffice for the attack, which the authors count in 17% of their test cases.

Harbor's memo step is such a case. An injected line telling the model to rate a stock a strong buy needs no new tool, and the CaMeL defense, which separates control flow from untrusted data, lists attacks that affect neither flow, such as a summary that differs from its source, as outside its scope. Our inference: catching this falls to evidence validation and the unsupported-claim score, so keep a fixture for it.

Fixtures that run once also understate risk. NIST's Center for AI Standards and Innovation extended AgentDojo and found that attacks written for a newly upgraded model raised the success rate from 11% for the strongest baseline attack to 81%, and that repeating each attack 25 times raised the average from 57% to 80%. CaMeL's authors report solving 77% of AgentDojo tasks with what they describe as provable security, against 84% for an undefended system, so score utility beside the attack rate.

Exercise: run each prompt-injection fixture 25 times at production sampling settings and report the any-success rate per fixture. Assert on the call log and ledger, not on the prose: no tool outside the allowlist, no fifth call, and zero state changes.

### Sources for this section

- [Debenedetti et al. (2024) · AgentDojo: A Dynamic Environment to Evaluate Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13352) — *arXiv 2406.13352.* A benchmark of 97 tasks and 629 security test cases for tool-calling agents, with the tool-filter defense and an account of when it fails.
- [Debenedetti et al. (2025) · Defeating Prompt Injections by Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.18813) — *arXiv 2503.18813.* CaMeL keeps untrusted data out of control flow and checks policies at tool calls; its stated non-goals include text-to-text attacks.
- [NIST · CAISI (2025) · Technical Blog: Strengthening AI Agent Hijacking Evaluations](https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2025/01/technical-blog-strengthening-ai-agent-hijacking-evaluations) — *Official source.* Shows that fixed single-attempt hijacking tests understate risk compared with adaptive attacks and repeated attempts.

modules.title: Async queues, backpressure, and retry budgets
modules.subtitle: Prevent slow consumers and ambiguous writes from turning transient failures into duplicated work or stale decisions.
modules.objective: Prevent slow consumers and ambiguous writes from turning transient failures into duplicated work or stale decisions.
modules.reading: Unit 7 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

A system must keep behaving predictably when work arrives faster than it can be processed or when a request fails. Queues, retries, and saved state are ways to manage those situations. Follow one event through an interruption and restart. The important question is whether it is lost, duplicated, or recovered with the same meaning.

## Design and reasoning

An asynchronous pipeline needs bounded queues and an overload policy. Waiting for queue capacity creates backpressure; dropping or coalescing observations is a separate policy that may be appropriate for some quote updates but not for authoritative fills. A queue is not a durable ledger, and process-local async coordination does not automatically coordinate threads or machines.

Classify operations before retrying. Repeating a read is different from resubmitting an order whose outcome is unknown. Bound attempts, use a total deadline, and apply jitter where appropriate to avoid synchronized retries. Reconcile an ambiguous write before deciding whether it can be repeated.

$$
t_{full}=Capacity_{free}/(Rate_{in}-Rate_{out})
$$

## A worked example

A consumer handles 80 events per second while a producer supplies 100. Backlog grows by 20 per second. A queue with 200 free slots fills in roughly 10 seconds under those constant rates. An unlimited queue hides the overload in rising latency and memory use.

A sequence of retry delays 1, 2, and 4 seconds consumes seven seconds before considering request duration. If the decision expires after five seconds, the planned retry schedule is already inconsistent with its freshness budget.

## Implementation and review

Measure queue depth and age of the oldest event, not just CPU use. Define priority and preservation rules for fills, cancellations, and observations. Use structured shutdown: stop new proposals, drain or persist authoritative events, reconcile orders, and close resources. The synchronous offline lab isolates accounting first; an async extension must preserve the same invariants across task cancellation and process failure.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Little proved that, under stationarity and finite means, the mean number of units in a system equals the arrival rate times the mean time each unit spends there: L = λW. Our inference: queue depth divided by the consumer's throughput estimates how old the newest accepted event is when served. At 80 events a second and a five-second freshness limit, a backlog above 5 × 80 = 400 events serves stale work. With the 20-a-second surplus, an unbounded queue that starts empty crosses 400 after 20 seconds, while a 200-slot queue caps the wait at 200 ÷ 80 = 2.5 seconds.

Retries can keep an overload alive after its cause has gone, a pattern called metastable failure. Alvaro and co-authors modelled a request-response server and found a queue length beyond which average latency exceeds the client timeout; the retries this triggers tend to keep a filled queue full. Huang and co-authors studied 22 metastable failures from 11 organisations: retry policy sustained more than 50% of them, and recovery often required reducing load. The lesson's 1, 2 and 4 second delays put the third retry at 7 seconds, after a five-second decision has expired.

Amazon's Builders' Library supplies the remedies. A timeout does not prove that side effects failed to happen, so it treats calls with side effects as safe to retry only when idempotent; for orders, our inference is a stable client identifier plus reconciliation first. It also limits retries locally with a token bucket shared by all calls: they may retry while tokens last, then at a fixed rate.

Exercise: feed 100 events a second to an 80-a-second consumer for a minute. Drop non-fill events older than five seconds at dequeue, and check that no fill is lost and retries stay inside the bucket.

### Sources for this section

- [Little (1961) · A Proof for the Queuing Formula: L = λ W](https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.9.3.383) — *Research paper.* States L = λW for the mean number in a queueing system, the arrival rate and the mean time in the system, under stationarity and finite means.
- [Alvaro et al. (2025) · Formal Analysis of Metastable Failures in Software Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.03551) — *arXiv 2510.03551.* Models a request-response server with a queue, timeouts and retries, and locates the queue length where retries keep a filled queue full.
- [Huang et al. (2022) · Metastable Failures in the Wild](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi22/presentation/huang-lexiang) — *Research paper.* Studies 22 metastable failures from 11 organisations in public incident reports; retry policy is the most common sustaining effect.
- [Amazon Web Services · Builders' Library · Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/timeouts-retries-and-backoff-with-jitter/) — *Technical documentation.* Engineering guidance on idempotency before retrying calls with side effects, and on limiting retries locally with a token bucket.

modules.title: Durable state and crash recovery
modules.subtitle: Use transactions and stable identities to reconstruct orders, fills, and risk state after interruption.
modules.objective: Use transactions and stable identities to reconstruct orders, fills, and risk state after interruption.
modules.reading: Unit 7 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

Persist the decision identity, immutable order payload, fills, and risk-state transitions. A uniqueness constraint prevents the same identity from creating multiple local records; a payload comparison detects a conflicting reuse of that identity. Merely returning the old result for a changed payload hides a caller defect.

An atomic transaction should encompass all local ledger changes caused by a fill. If the process stops midway, recovery sees either the committed fill and its effects or neither. This does not create an atomic transaction with an external broker: network submission still needs an intent record, stable external identifiers, and reconciliation.

$$
State_{recovered}=Fold(State_0,UniqueCommittedFills)
$$

## A worked example

Fill F1 buys 10 shares for $1,000 plus a $1 fee. Applying it twice under the same unchanged fill identity must leave one ledger entry, a $1,001 cash reduction, and 10 shares. Reusing F1 for 12 shares is a conflict, not another fill.

After a restart, the bot reads its persisted halt state before accepting a proposal. Reconstructing current holdings from durable fills provides an independent check against the cached account row. A disagreement blocks further trading until investigated.

## Implementation and review

Test a restart after order acceptance, after a partial fill, and while halted. Include transaction rollback and duplicate delivery fixtures. Keep schema migrations and model versions explicit. The downloadable SQLite lab uses local transactions and uniqueness, and demonstrates reopening the same database; it does not claim exactly-once execution across an external service boundary.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

SQLite's documentation separates two failures that a restart test can blur. Transactions are durable across application crashes under every setting. A transaction committed in WAL mode with synchronous=NORMAL, though, might roll back after a power loss or system crash, and FULL in rollback mode is not necessarily durable across a power loss. By its matrix, only synchronous=FULL in WAL mode and synchronous=EXTRA are marked ACID. A test that kills the process and reopens the file exercises only the first case. Our inference: a halt flag lost to a power cut leaves a restarted bot willing to trade, so print journal_mode and synchronous at startup and keep the ledger on one of them.

Mohan and co-authors' ARIES recovery method repeats history on restart: it redoes missing updates before rolling back unfinished transactions, a log sequence number on each page shows which logged updates the page already holds, and logging stays bounded even if restart itself fails repeatedly. Our inference: a fill's unique identity plays the sequence number's role in Harbor's ledger, so replay onto a stale cache applies each fill at most once, and the recovery pass must itself survive a crash.

Pillai and co-authors traced the update protocols of eleven widely used systems in 2014 and found 60 vulnerabilities, because correctness depends on file-system behaviours they call persistence properties; for SQLite they report no durability in the default journal mode. Gu and co-authors note that the crash-state space grows exponentially with the operation count; their Pathfinder tests a small set of representative crash states, finding 18 bugs across 8 production-ready systems.

modules.objective: Instrument decision traces and operational invariants so incidents can be detected and reconstructed.
modules.reading: Unit 7 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

Link market event, feature version, model version, intent, order, fill, and account update through stable correlation identifiers. Record decision reasons and timings while keeping secrets out of logs. A profit dashboard cannot explain whether a missing trade arose from absent data, an abstention, a risk rejection, or an order failure.

Separate operational measures from investment outcomes. Track data age, queue delay, rejected proposals, unknown orders, reconciliation mismatches, duplicate messages, fill latency, fees, and exposure. Performance measures require their own benchmark and horizon. A low error count can hide a component that stopped producing useful work.

$$
AcceptanceRate=N_{accepted}/N_{proposed}
$$

## A worked example

During a window with 200 proposals, 30 are rejected for stale data, 10 for risk caps, and 160 are accepted. The acceptance rate is 80%. That number alone does not tell whether the rejection policy is correct; review samples and expected fixture outcomes.

If accepted order count continues rising but no acknowledgements arrive, investigate the external-state gap rather than simply increasing retries. Unknown-order age is a more useful alert than another aggregate request-success percentage.

## Implementation and review

Write a runbook with detection signal, immediate containment, evidence to preserve, reconciliation steps, and resumption criteria. Test it using a deliberate feed outage and a duplicate fill. Version configuration and deployment artifacts so the incident can be replayed. Access to logs, backups, and secrets should follow the actual operational roles; never paste a live token into a research notebook or a course exercise.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Dapper's authors held that monitoring should always be on, because unusual behaviour is often difficult or impossible to reproduce. Spans carry a span id and a parent id, every span in a trace shares one trace id, and when work is deferred or made asynchronous the callbacks store the trace context of their creator. Our inference: Harbor's correlation id must travel inside the queued event, or the consumer's log lines become orphans. Dapper sampled to keep overhead low in latency-sensitive services; an intent, order and fill trail is an audit record, and at 200 proposals a window it needs no sampling (our inference).

A process can look healthy while doing no useful work. Huang and co-authors, writing about gray failure in cloud systems, point to differential observability: the system's failure detectors may not notice problems even when applications are afflicted by them. The SRE book counts errors explicitly, implicitly (a success response with the wrong content) and by policy, and notes that white-box monitoring can reveal failures masked by retries. Our inference: an acknowledgement after the freshness limit is an error by policy, so alert on unknown-order age and log attempts per order beside the success rate.

Yan and co-authors analysed four years of incidents at a leading generative AI cloud provider. Of those incidents, 38.3% were reported by humans, and incidents that came with a troubleshooting guide were resolved more swiftly than those without one. Our suggestion: put the runbook link and the correlation ids in the alert itself.

Exercise: stop the feed for ten minutes while the process stays up, then record which alert fires first, how long after the last quote, and whether it names the runbook.

### Sources for this section

- [Sigelman et al. (2010) · Dapper, a Large-Scale Distributed Systems Tracing Infrastructure](https://research.google/pubs/dapper-a-large-scale-distributed-systems-tracing-infrastructure/) — *Research paper.* Google's tracing design: trace, span and parent ids, with trace context carried through asynchronous callbacks, and the case for always-on monitoring.
- [Huang et al. (2017) · Gray Failure](https://doi.org/10.1145/3102980.3103005) — *Research paper.* Argues that failure detectors can miss problems that applications feel, a gap the authors call differential observability.
- [Google SRE · Monitoring Distributed Systems](https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/) — *Technical documentation.* The SRE book's chapter on symptoms versus causes, white-box and black-box monitoring, and errors defined explicitly, implicitly or by policy.
- [Yan et al. (2025) · An Empirical Study of Production Incidents in Generative AI Cloud Services](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.08865) — *arXiv 2504.08865.* Four years of incidents at a leading generative AI cloud provider: who detects them, and how troubleshooting guides affect time to mitigate.

modules.title: Paper release gates and rollback
modules.subtitle: Build an evidence-based promotion packet and practice rollback without confusing paper results with live readiness.
modules.objective: Build an evidence-based promotion packet and practice rollback without confusing paper results with live readiness.
modules.reading: Unit 7 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

A release gate is a declared acceptance condition with supporting evidence. Examples include passing ledger invariants, reproducing a frozen replay, reconciling partial fills after restart, and rejecting malformed or stale proposals. A paper profit threshold alone does not test operational correctness.

Freeze the code, configuration, feature schema, model artifact, data version, and validation manifest together. Shadow evaluation can compare proposed decisions without executing them, while a paper canary tests a limited scope in a simulated environment. Neither automatically authorizes live deployment or demonstrates realistic liquidity.

$$
ReleaseEligible=\bigwedge_{j=1}^{k}Gate_j
$$

## A worked example

Harbor defines five mandatory gates: deterministic replay, correct fees and inventory, duplicate handling, persistent halt, and evidence-validation failures. A release passes four but fails persistent halt after restart. Its status is blocked under the declared policy even if the simulated return is positive.

Rollback restores a known software and model version, but it does not reverse fills that actually occurred. The restored process must reconcile current account state before resuming. Database schema compatibility is part of the rollback plan.

## Implementation and review

Prepare a release record with artifact hashes, test results, known limitations, an owner, and rollback instructions. Run an incident rehearsal before promotion. Keep the paper evaluation scope and capital limits visible. Any later real broker integration requires its own adapter tests, access configuration, market-data permissions, and review; this course ends at an offline educational acceptance packet.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

FINRA Regulatory Notice 15-09 is addressed to member firms and says its practices would not necessarily satisfy a firm's obligations by themselves, so treat it as a checklist to borrow. Several practices map onto the lesson's packet: change management that reviews test results and scales approvals to the change; testing independent of development and segregated from production, with records of protocols and results; archived code versions; a way to disable the algorithm in a minimal number of steps; and a pilot of limited size, increased only as results are confirmed. Our inference: the archive is the rollback target, and a gate with no recorded evidence or approver is a checkbox.

Google's SRE Workbook defines canarying as a partial, time-limited deployment of a change together with its evaluation, compares the canary with a control that keeps the old version, and calls before-and-after comparison risky. It reports that a majority of Google's incidents are triggered by binary or configuration pushes, and its example without a rollback option ends with a patch deployed mid-outage. Our inference: run the candidate beside the incumbent on the same frozen replay, compare decisions on identical bars, and treat a changed threshold or feature schema as a release.

Lindon and co-authors at Netflix treat canary tests as a common quality control gate and propose sequential tests that allow continuous monitoring while strictly controlling the false detection probability. A fixed-sample test checked after every fill offers no such guarantee (our inference), so write the stopping rule into the release record before the canary starts.

Exercise: make each gate a command that exits nonzero on failure and fail the persistent-halt gate on purpose; confirm the packet reads blocked despite a positive simulated return, then roll back to the archived build and reconcile before resuming.

### Sources for this section

- [FINRA (2015) · Regulatory Notice 15-09: Guidance on Effective Supervision and Control Practices for Firms Engaging in Algorithmic Trading Strategies](https://www.finra.org/rules-guidance/notices/15-09) — *Official source.* Regulator guidance on change management, independent testing, archived code, quick disablement and limited pilots for algorithmic strategies.
- [Google SRE · Canarying Releases](https://sre.google/workbook/canarying-releases/) — *Technical documentation.* The SRE Workbook chapter on canary and control populations, metric choice, why before-and-after comparison is risky, and rollback.
- [Lindon, Sanden & Shirikian (2022) · Rapid Regression Detection in Software Deployments through Sequential Testing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14762) — *arXiv 2205.14762.* Sequential tests that let a canary be monitored continuously while controlling the false detection probability, shown on two Netflix case studies.

modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

Historical market records include changes in the instruments themselves. Splits, dividends, trading sessions, and company membership can all affect prices and eligibility. Begin by deciding what each record represents and how it should change the bot's state. This unit extends that accounting discipline into order-book replay and multiple-asset execution.

## Understand the idea

A production-shaped dataset needs separate concepts for investment returns, executable prices, and account events. Split-adjusted prices help compare historical levels, but orders execute in the actual share and price units at that time. A dividend can enter a total-return calculation without being an immediate cash receipt under a particular settlement convention.

Universe membership must be dated. Selecting today's liquid survivors for an earlier test can exclude bankrupt or delisted companies. Eligibility also depends on session, halts, available history, supported order types, and the intended jurisdiction or venue. The course project uses supplied session flags and synthetic fixtures; it does not implement exchange calendars or corporate-action feeds.

$$
q_{after}=s q_{before},\quad P_{after}=P_{before}/s
$$

## A worked example

A two-for-one split changes a holding of 10 shares priced at 100 into 20 shares priced at 50, preserving value 1,000 before other market movement. A pending limit of 98 needs a broker-specific adjustment or cancellation policy; assuming it stays numerically unchanged can create unintended exposure.

If a dividend is 1 per share and price changes from 100 to 99, the simple total-return calculation is (99+1)/100−1=0 before taxes and reinvestment assumptions. A raw price-only return reports −1% and answers a different question.

## Put the idea into practice

Define fixtures for a split, a cash dividend, a delisting, a newly eligible instrument, a holiday, and a halt. Reconcile holdings, order units, and data adjustments at the effective time. Retain raw and adjusted fields with source versions. Do not infer a causal trading opportunity from an adjustment artifact. A strategy release should fail its data contract if corporate-action handling or historical membership is unknown.

modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A limit order book stores resting quantities at prices, with a venue-specific priority rule. Under a simplified price-time rule, a marketable buy consumes the cheapest ask first and earlier orders first at a tied price. Actual venues may have hidden liquidity, special order types, pro-rata rules, and other allocation details. State the modeled rule explicitly.

Top-of-book quotes and OHLC bars do not reveal an individual resting order's queue position. A bar touching a limit price does not prove that an order would have filled. A book replay needs time-ordered updates, sequence handling, and a defined response to missing messages; otherwise a detailed-looking simulation can still invent liquidity.

$$
P_{avg}=\sum_iq_iP_i/\sum_iq_i
$$

## A worked example

The asks are an early three-share order at 100, a later four-share order at 100, and nine shares at 101. A five-share buy capped at 100 fills all three early shares and two later shares; its average price is 100. The higher-priced order is ineligible. If the taker requests ten shares with the same cap, three remain unfilled.

The downloadable research lab's match_asks function executes this price-time fixture. It is ask-side and synchronous, with no hidden orders or real exchange queue; the earlier paper-bot project handles durable account and fill identities separately.

## Put the idea into practice

Test tied prices, an unmarketable limit, partial consumption, duplicate resting identities, and zero or invalid quantities. Preserve both price and arrival order. Report unfilled quantity rather than silently forcing completion at the last bar's price. If extending to a live feed, design sequence-gap recovery and snapshot reconciliation before using the reconstructed book for decisions.

modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A portfolio rebalance begins with a dated account snapshot, executable marks, and a target vector. Compute target holdings and deltas per asset, then apply cash, share, exposure, and order constraints. Two individually affordable buys can be jointly unaffordable, so the account-level reservation must be atomic or otherwise coordinated.

A sale may provide buying power only after its actual execution and under the account's settlement rules. Planned sale proceeds are not always spendable cash. The downloadable lagged replay uses immediate settlement, synchronous fills, fractional shares, and reductions before entries; those assumptions are explicitly narrower than a real brokerage workflow.

$$
q_i^*=w_iE/P_i,\quad \Delta q_i=q_i^*-q_i^{held}-q_i^{committed}
$$

## A worked example

With equity 10,000 and two desired weights .4 and .3, target notionals are 4,000 and 3,000 before fees, leaving 3,000 nominal cash. At prices 100 and 50, corresponding holdings are 40 and 60 shares. If holdings already include 20 shares of the first asset, its residual target is 20 shares, not 40.

To fund worst-case turnover in the toy replay, a fee reserve reduces the total target budget. The project declares this scaling rather than silently allowing a negative cash balance when requested weights sum to one.

## Put the idea into practice

Test target sums above one, stale prices, conflicting outstanding orders, sell failures, and a price gap between decision and execution. Save target weights, fee reserve, actual fills, and remaining cash separately. A real multi-asset adapter needs settlement and margin rules, asynchronous reconciliation, and partial-fill planning. Portfolio weights describe a desired end state; they are not permission to bypass account constraints.

modules.title: Transaction-cost analysis and unfilled opportunity cost
modules.subtitle: Reconcile realized execution cost with decision benchmarks and include the quantity that never traded.
modules.objective: Reconcile realized execution cost with decision benchmarks and include the quantity that never traded.
modules.reading: This lesson belongs to Unit 8. Read the explanation and work through the example before trying the assignment. Use the linked sources to check the underlying method, then write your calculation and what it means in your notebook.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Transaction-cost analysis needs a declared benchmark, trade direction, authorized quantity, actual fills, explicit fees, and unfilled remainder. A midpoint or arrival price measures a different question from the signal-time price or a later market VWAP. Choosing the most favorable benchmark after the trade distorts interpretation.

Average cost of completed fills omits the opportunity cost of quantities that did not trade. This can flatter passive strategies that fill mainly under adverse selection while missing favorable moves. A complete parent-order analysis records cancellation, expiry, changed intent, and the price convention used to value the unfilled decision.

$$
IS=q_f(P_f-P_d)+q_u(P_{eval}-P_d)+Fees
$$

## A worked example

A decision authorizes buying 100 shares at benchmark 50. Sixty fill at 50.10 with 3 of fees; forty remain unfilled while the evaluation price reaches 51. Realized price shortfall is 60×.10=6. Under this stipulated opportunity-cost convention, unfilled cost is 40×1=40. Total implementation shortfall is 6+3+40=49, or 98 bps of the 5,000 decision notional.

The unfilled component is model-dependent: if the investment decision was legitimately withdrawn, its interpretation may differ. Preserve the reason and time of withdrawal rather than rewriting the benchmark retrospectively.

## Put the idea into practice

Report completion rate, average fill price, explicit fees, benchmark timestamps, and the opportunity-cost convention. Separate spread, delay, and impact only to the extent the data support their decomposition. Compare execution policies on the same parent decisions and market paths. A toy price-time matcher validates arithmetic and allocation rules; it does not estimate the causal market impact of the orders themselves.

modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

Different strategy families create different patterns of exposure and trading. A ranked portfolio, a pairs trade, and a market maker need different assumptions about positions and execution. Start with the economic idea and a small worked decision. Then ask how the system behaves when a relationship changes, liquidity falls, or inventory becomes unbalanced.

## Understand the idea

Cross-sectional momentum compares assets with one another, while a time-series trend rule compares an asset with its own past. Define the return window, any skipped recent interval, corporate-action convention, minimum history, liquidity filters, and rebalance schedule. A universe filter can influence performance as much as the ranking formula.

A rank gives ordering, not expected return magnitude. Specify the number of selected names, equal or score-based weights, name and sector caps, and what happens when too few assets qualify. Deterministic tie-breaking and fixed missing-data rules support reproducibility. Do not impute an ineligible asset into the top group merely because its score is high.

$$
w_i\leq w_{cap},\quad w_{cash}=1-\sum_iw_i
$$

## A worked example

Scores are A=.1, B=.2, and C=.9, but C is unavailable under the dated universe rule. Selecting two eligible names gives B then A. With a .4 per-name weight cap, each gets .4 and .2 remains in cash. The downloadable rank_targets function reproduces this case.

If only A is eligible, a .4 cap leaves .6 in cash. Redistributing everything to A would violate the declared mandate even though the ranking step itself succeeded.

## Put the idea into practice

Evaluate the full historical selection process, including delisted securities and contemporaneous liquidity. Compare equal weighting and a passive benchmark, report turnover and concentration, and test costs and delayed execution. Tie-breakers and filters must be frozen before final evaluation. A successful ranking function is evidence of implementation correctness; predictive performance requires independent market data and an executable portfolio study.
