modules.title: Robustness: parameter neighborhoods, regimes, and stress
modules.subtitle: Challenge the mechanism with predeclared perturbations and preserve unsuccessful results.
modules.objective: Challenge the mechanism with predeclared perturbations and preserve unsuccessful results.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 10 minutes reading primary references, 8 minutes reproducing calculations, and 12 minutes assembling or challenging report evidence. All supplied company, return and timing examples are fictional. Evaluate algorithms written in Python, C or other languages through a documented result-export contract.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Robustness asks whether a conclusion survives reasonable changes to assumptions and conditions. Examine neighboring parameters, different chronological regimes, delayed execution, higher costs, data gaps and relevant market shocks. Choose perturbations because they challenge the proposed mechanism, not because they produce attractive plots. A broad stable region can be more credible than one isolated best setting, but it is not proof of future profitability.

Keep separate base, sensitivity and stress cases. A sensitivity changes one assumption to explain direction; a scenario combines related changes into a coherent environment; a stress probes an adverse condition. Some scenarios require a rerun of the algorithm because positions and compounding change. Linear subtraction from final profit may be only a rough labeled approximation. The reporting tool summarizes supplied paths; it does not automatically execute every robustness experiment.

$$
\mathrm{sensitivity}\approx\frac{f(\theta+\Delta)-f(\theta-\Delta)}{2\Delta}
$$

## A worked example

Neighboring windows 19, 20 and 21 show net returns 2%, 18% and 1%. That sharp peak deserves investigation of data selection, event timing and parameter sensitivity. It does not justify reporting only window 20 as representative performance.

## Put the idea into practice

Prepare a robustness matrix with scenario, mechanism, changed input, expected direction, actual result and interpretation. Link every executed case to its output hash. Preserve scenarios that invalidate the initial hypothesis and define a review trigger for new data.

### Build your evaluation dossier

Reproduce the small worksheet before applying the idea to a full run. Save the input, calculation, interpretation and limitation in your notebook. Add the corresponding evidence to the downloadable report notebook. The in-browser Python worksheet remains in cash and is an arithmetic aid; it does not execute the evaluated trading algorithm. Run the downloadable reporting project locally for actual metrics, files and figures. A clear negative result is a valid finding: never remove a losing period or failed experiment to improve the story.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

The lesson's central difference cannot see the spike. At window 20 it gives (1% − 2%) ÷ 2 = −0.5 points per step, nearly flat, though both neighbors are far lower. The second difference, 2% − 2 × 18% + 1% = −33 points, does show it (our arithmetic). A central slope misses any peak whose neighbors are alike, so judge a peak by its drop to them.

Bailey and co-authors define the probability of backtest overfitting as the chance that the best in-sample strategy underperforms the out-of-sample median. In their example, 1,000 daily random-walk prices were searched over 8,800 parameter combinations; the best reached an annualized Sharpe ratio of 1.27, yet the probability was as high as 55%. A plateau shows smoothness, not persistence (our inference). Lezmi and co-authors generate artificial multi-asset histories that keep return distribution, asset dependence and serial correlation, and read backtest statistics off the resulting distribution. That probes sampling luck, not unseen regimes (our inference).

Stress cases may exceed your sample and need a full rerun. The Bank of England reported that in September 2022 the 30-year gilt yield rose 130 basis points in three days, three times larger than any earlier move over a similar span, as forced selling by levered funds fed fire-sale dynamics; the bid-ask spread widened from about 0.5 basis points on 22 September to 2.5 by 11 October. Positions, margin and costs changed along the path, so a linear subtraction from final profit misses them (our analogy).

Exercise: state the break condition first, such as net return below cash, then find the smallest cost multiple, delay or removed sub-period that triggers it, and keep that row even if it ends the hypothesis.

### Sources for this section

- [Bailey, Borwein, López de Prado & Zhu (2017) · The probability of backtest overfitting](https://doi.org/10.21314/JCF.2016.322) — *Research paper.* Defines the probability that the in-sample best strategy ranks below the out-of-sample median, with a random-walk example where a 1.27 Sharpe ratio came with a 55% probability.
- [Lezmi, Roche, Roncalli & Xu (2020) · Improving the Robustness of Trading Strategy Backtesting with Boltzmann Machines and Generative Adversarial Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.04838) — *arXiv 2007.04838.* Proposes synthetic multi-asset histories that preserve return distributions, cross-asset dependence and autocorrelation, to estimate the distribution of backtest statistics.
- [Bank of England (2023) · Financial stability buy/sell tools: a gilt market case study](https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/quarterly-bulletin/2023/2023/financial-stability-buy-sell-tools-a-gilt-market-case-study) — *Official source.* Records the September 2022 gilt shock: a 130 basis point three-day yield rise, margin calls, forced selling and wider spreads that changed positions and costs along the path.

modules.title: Evaluate computing performance alongside trading results
modules.subtitle: Report C/HPC speed, correctness parity, and operational latency as separate evidence.
modules.objective: Report C/HPC speed, correctness parity, and operational latency as separate evidence.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 10 minutes reading primary references, 8 minutes reproducing calculations, and 12 minutes assembling or challenging report evidence. All supplied company, return and timing examples are fictional. Evaluate algorithms written in Python, C or other languages through a documented result-export contract.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A complete algorithm report distinguishes financial behavior from computing behavior. Document workload size, input identity, parameter count, worker count, compiler/version, flags, hardware, operating system, timing boundaries and output equality. A faster candidate with changed fills is not an equivalent implementation speedup until the discrepancy is explained.

Use repeated paired runs and show both elapsed times and speedup. The median of paired speedup ratios can differ from the ratio of elapsed-time medians; label the statistic you actually calculate. Tiny workloads may be dominated by thread setup. A batch research benchmark does not measure gateway tail latency. For operations, define the event population and include queueing, stale data, risk checks, network uncertainty and failure recovery.

$$
S_i=T_{\mathrm{serial},i}/T_{\mathrm{parallel},i},\qquad \widetilde{S}=\mathrm{median}(S_i)
$$

## A worked example

Five paired serial/parallel timings are (30,10), (31,11), (29,9), (32,12), (30,10) milliseconds. Median serial time is 30, median parallel is 10, and the median paired speedup is 3×. These are illustrative fixture values, not a measurement of your own machine.

## Put the idea into practice

Transfer the C/HPC lab's actual paired timing rows into the reporting timing CSV and retain all equal=yes evidence. Run the evaluator with --timings, inspect the summary and write a separate interpretation of workload scaling and observed variability.

### Build your evaluation dossier

Reproduce the small worksheet before applying the idea to a full run. Save the input, calculation, interpretation and limitation in your notebook. Add the corresponding evidence to the downloadable report notebook. The in-browser Python worksheet remains in cash and is an arithmetic aid; it does not execute the evaluated trading algorithm. Run the downloadable reporting project locally for actual metrics, files and figures. A clear negative result is a valid finding: never remove a losing period or failed experiment to improve the story.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Hoefler and Belli reviewed how HPC papers report performance. Among papers from three top HPC conferences, 39 reported speedups and 15 (38%) of those omitted the absolute performance of the base case. Their rules: state whether the base is a single parallel process or the best serial execution, never report ratios without absolute values, and avoid summarizing ratios; summarize the underlying costs instead, using a geometric mean of ratios only when costs are unavailable.

On the lesson's five pairs, the median of the ratios and the ratio of median times are both 3.00. The ratio of mean times is 152 ÷ 52 ≈ 2.92 and the geometric mean of the ratios is ≈ 2.94 (computed): a small spread here, though not necessarily on skewed timings. Chen and Revels designed a timing strategy for the highly nonideal statistics of timing measurements and implemented it in Julia's BenchmarkTools. The package manual argues that machine noise is, in some sense, inherently positive, so timings are right-skewed: the minimum is a robust location estimate, the median tolerates outliers, and the mean is pulled upward. Our reading: the minimum asks what the code can do, while medians and tail percentiles describe what a run experiences.

Tails need separate evidence. In Dean and Barroso's hypothetical service, each server has a 99th-percentile latency of one second, so a request waiting on 100 of them in parallel exceeds a second 63% of the time. In a Google service they measured, the 99th-percentile latency was 10 ms for a single request but 140 ms for all requests to finish. Five timings cannot see a 1% tail: the chance that none falls in the slowest 1% is 0.99⁵ ≈ 95% (computed).

Exercise: compute all four summaries for your own paired timings, print the serial base time beside them, and state whether serial means the best serial code or the parallel code on one worker. For gateway latency, define the event population, log every event, and report the median, 99th percentile and maximum with the count.

### Sources for this section

- [Hoefler & Belli (2015) · Scientific benchmarking of parallel computing systems](https://doi.org/10.1145/2807591.2807644) — *Research paper.* Reviews speedup reporting in HPC papers and gives rules on the base case, absolute values and summarizing ratios.
- [Chen & Revels (2016) · Robust benchmarking in noisy environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.04295) — *arXiv 1608.04295.* Designs a timing strategy that tolerates timer error, OS jitter and the highly nonideal statistics of timing measurements; implemented in BenchmarkTools.
- [JuliaCI · BenchmarkTools.jl · BenchmarkTools.jl manual: which estimator should I use?](https://juliaci.github.io/BenchmarkTools.jl/stable/manual/) — *Technical documentation.* Explains why timing noise is positive and right-skewed, and what the minimum, median and mean each estimate.
- [Dean & Barroso (2013) · The tail at scale](https://doi.org/10.1145/2408776.2408794) — *Research paper.* Shows how rare slow components dominate a request that waits on many of them, with a hypothetical case and a measured Google service.

modules.title: Build clear result tables and honest charts
modules.subtitle: Turn calculations into readable, traceable visuals without concealing unfavorable periods.
modules.objective: Turn calculations into readable, traceable visuals without concealing unfavorable periods.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 10 minutes reading primary references, 8 minutes reproducing calculations, and 12 minutes assembling or challenging report evidence. All supplied company, return and timing examples are fictional. Evaluate algorithms written in Python, C or other languages through a documented result-export contract.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

A clear report helps a reader move from evidence to a decision. Choose tables and charts according to the question they answer, then label their units, periods, and assumptions. The final lessons connect those displays to attribution and a written conclusion. Explain which findings are well supported and which still require further investigation.

## Understand the idea

A figure should answer a specific question. Use a common date axis and normalized starting wealth for strategy/benchmark comparison, a separate drawdown panel for losses, and tables with units, sample length, cost basis and undefined-value explanations. Keep the complete evaluation period visible; a selectively cropped winning segment is a different sample and must be identified as such.

Avoid visual choices that imply more precision than the evidence supports. A dense legend, misleading axis, unmarked log scale or unexplained annualization makes scrutiny harder. Include a caption describing the data and interpretation. For export, use standard plotting software and save standalone files with readable fonts. The project creates PNG and SVG figures plus printable HTML and Markdown that reference those artifacts.

$$
W_t^{\mathrm{index}}=100\frac{E_t}{E_0}
$$

## A worked example

Two portfolios both start at index 100. One reaches 110 after a deep drawdown, while the other reaches 108 smoothly. A final-value bar chart misses the path distinction; aligned wealth and drawdown panels show both terminal return and the route taken.

## Put the idea into practice

Install the project requirements and generate the sample report with charts. Open report.html, compare its table with metrics.json, and inspect the exported PNG/SVG. Retain the report folder so relative image links work when shared.

### Build your evaluation dossier

Reproduce the small worksheet before applying the idea to a full run. Save the input, calculation, interpretation and limitation in your notebook. Add the corresponding evidence to the downloadable report notebook. The in-browser Python worksheet remains in cash and is an arithmetic aid; it does not execute the evaluated trading algorithm. Run the downloadable reporting project locally for actual metrics, files and figures. A clear negative result is a valid finding: never remove a losing period or failed experiment to improve the story.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Weissgerber and co-authors reviewed 703 articles in top physiology journals and found continuous data mostly shown as bar and line graphs, which is problematic because many different data distributions can lead to the same bar or line graph and the full data may suggest different conclusions from the summary statistics. The lesson's portfolios are a case in point: bars at 110 and 108 look alike, yet the path behind one of them includes a deep drawdown. By our inference, any single summary (final wealth, annualized return, a Sharpe ratio) shares this blind spot, so a path panel belongs beside it.

Axes then decide how large an edge looks. Correll and co-authors report that bar charts whose y-axes do not begin at zero can visually exaggerate effect sizes, while for other chart types truncation can be beneficial or harmful depending on intent. In their crowd-sourced experiments the impact of truncation persisted across designs, even with explicit visual cues that truncation had occurred. A wealth index plotted from about 100 rather than 0 is already truncated, so choose its range by the size of the effect you mean to show and print the end values on the chart.

Scale type matters too. Romano and co-authors showed COVID-19 deaths on logarithmic or linear axes: log-scale viewers understood the pandemic's course less accurately, predicted its evolution less accurately and held different policy preferences, and the authors recommend a linear default for the general public. A log axis gives equal heights to equal percentage changes, which suits compounding, so label it in the caption and keep a table beside it.

Exercise: plot your strategy and comparator wealth index three ways (range from zero, tight range, log scale) and ask a colleague who has not seen the table to estimate how much larger the strategy's final wealth is than the comparator's in each. Keep the version whose answers come closest to the table, state the scale in the caption, and show the drawdown panel beneath it.

### Sources for this section

- [Weissgerber, Milic, Winham & Garovic (2015) · Beyond Bar and Line Graphs: Time for a New Data Presentation Paradigm](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.1002128) — *Research paper.* Systematic review showing that bar and line graphs of summary values can hide very different underlying distributions.
- [Correll, Bertini & Franconeri (2019) · Truncating the Y-Axis: Threat or Menace?](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.02035) — *arXiv 1907.02035.* Crowd-sourced experiments on how y-axis truncation changes perceived effect size across chart types, including designs that flag the truncation.
- [Romano, Sotis, Dominioni & Guidi (2020) · The scale of COVID-19 graphs affects understanding, attitudes, and policy preferences](https://doi.org/10.1002/hec.4143) — *Research paper.* Shows that log versus linear axes change how accurately people read a growth series and what they conclude from it.

modules.subtitle: Explain performance by exposures, periods, decisions and costs without overstating causality.
modules.objective: Explain performance by exposures, periods, decisions and costs without overstating causality.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 10 minutes reading primary references, 8 minutes reproducing calculations, and 12 minutes assembling or challenging report evidence. ## Understand the idea

After measuring the outcome, ask what generated it. Break results down by time period, instrument, sector, direction, signal family, market exposure and execution cost when the underlying data supports that partition. An attribution table should reconcile to a declared total under its accounting method. Simply adding compounded period returns does not generally reconcile to the multi-period wealth change.

Distinguish explanation from causal proof. A positive correlation with a factor can describe exposure; a regression intercept is conditional on the chosen model and sample. Strategy-minus-benchmark return is not automatically alpha. Concentration in a single instrument or regime can weaken the claim that a broad mechanism is working. The report generator does not fit factor models; bring those estimates and diagnostics from the quantitative/econometric projects and cite the exact specification.

$$
\Pi_{\mathrm{total}}=\sum_j\Pi_j\quad\text{under consistent PnL accounting}
$$

## A worked example

A total net gain of 900 is decomposed into 700 from one asset, 300 from another and −100 from a hedge under a consistent PnL ledger. The sum reconciles, but 700/900 ≈ 77.8% comes from one asset, which is important context for robustness.

## Put the idea into practice

Create a reconciled PnL contribution table using consistent units and an explicit treatment of costs. Add relevant exposure or regression evidence only if available. Identify the concentration, alternative explanations and missing diagnostics in the written interpretation.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Brinson and co-authors split returns into investment policy, market timing and security selection by comparing a passive policy portfolio with actual returns. For 91 large U.S. pension plans over 1974–83, policy explained on average 93.6% of the variation in total plan return. Yet the average plan earned 9.01% against 10.11% for the policy benchmark, so active management cost 1.10% a year. A high explained share and a negative active contribution coexisted, because the 93.6% describes variation, not the level of return.

Ibbotson and Kaplan traced the controversy to different questions. Policy explained about 90% of a typical fund's variability over time, about 40% of the variation among funds, and on average about 100% of the return level. A share means little until its denominator is named. The lesson's 700 ÷ 900 ≈ 77.8% is a share of the PnL level. A sleeve's share of PnL variance is a separate answer and can differ sharply, because a sleeve with little PnL can still move the total a great deal (our inference).

Risk can be attributed in the same additive way. Tasche describes the Euler principle, which many financial institutions use to allocate capital to business units and sub-portfolios, and how Euler risk contributions are estimated for some important risk measures. For variance, a sleeve's contribution is its covariance with total PnL divided by the variance of total PnL, and these shares sum to 100% by construction. Setting each sleeve's PnL share beside its risk share shows whether concentration sits in the result, in the risk, or both (our reading).

Exercise: from daily PnL per sleeve, tabulate both shares for the lesson's three lines. Then rerun with the signal removed, or the parameters moved to a neighborhood median, and report how much of the net gain survives. Label each sentence of the interpretation as measured or conjectured.

### Sources for this section

- [Brinson, Hood & Beebower (1986) · Determinants of Portfolio Performance](https://doi.org/10.2469/faj.v42.n4.39) — *Research paper.* Attributes plan returns to policy, timing and selection; policy explains 93.6% of return variation, yet active management cost the average plan 1.10% a year.
- [Ibbotson & Kaplan (2000) · Does Asset Allocation Policy Explain 40, 90, or 100 Percent of Performance?](https://doi.org/10.2469/faj.v56.n1.2327) — *Research paper.* Resolves the disagreement over attribution shares by showing that variability over time, variation among funds and return level are three different questions.
- [Tasche (2007) · Capital Allocation to Business Units and Sub-Portfolios: the Euler Principle](https://arxiv.org/abs/0708.2542) — *arXiv 0708.2542.* Describes Euler allocation, widely used to split a portfolio's capital into contributions of its sub-portfolios, and how Euler risk contributions are estimated.

modules.content:
## Understand the idea

The executive page should make the reader's decision easier. State the question and evaluated version, summarize the strongest supporting and contrary evidence, explain uncertainty and scope, and choose reject, revise or a bounded next paper study. Link each factual assertion to its supporting artifact. A report can be complete even when the algorithm is rejected.

Use precise language: the observed sample showed a result under specified costs and timing; it does not guarantee future returns. Distinguish measured behavior from an untested explanation or proposed next step. Explain benchmark weaknesses, selection history, small samples and omitted execution costs near the conclusion rather than burying them in an appendix. The generator deliberately leaves a REVIEW REQUIRED section so a descriptive metric table is not mistaken for an automatic investment decision.

$$
\mathrm{claim}\longleftrightarrow\mathrm{evidence}\longleftrightarrow\mathrm{limitation}
$$

## A worked example

A report finds 10% sample return versus 8% benchmark, a 6.67% drawdown, only twelve synthetic monthly observations and sixty-four tried configurations. A defensible conclusion treats this as a successful reporting fixture, not independent evidence that the algorithm should trade real capital.

## Put the idea into practice

Complete the one-page conclusion in report-notebook.md. Make a claim/evidence/limitation table, then ask another reader to locate each cited artifact. Define a concrete next test that could disprove the mechanism instead of promising to find better parameters.

### Build your evaluation dossier

Reproduce the small worksheet before applying the idea to a full run. Save the input, calculation, interpretation and limitation in your notebook. Add the corresponding evidence to the downloadable report notebook. The in-browser Python worksheet remains in cash and is an arithmetic aid; it does not execute the evaluated trading algorithm. Run the downloadable reporting project locally for actual metrics, files and figures. A clear negative result is a valid finding: never remove a losing period or failed experiment to improve the story.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Boutron and co-authors examined what happens to conclusions when the primary result disappoints. From 616 reports of randomized trials published in December 2006, they appraised the 72 with a clearly identified, statistically nonsignificant primary outcome. Spin, meaning reporting that highlights benefit anyway or distracts the reader from the nonsignificant result, appeared in 18.0% of titles and 37.5% of abstract results sections, but in 58.3% of abstract conclusions and 50.0% of main-text conclusions. Our inference: the conclusion is where the pull is strongest, so it is where an executive page needs the guard. The setting is clinical, so this is an analogy. In the lesson's example, whatever criterion the contract predeclared, such as net return against the comparator, should lead the conclusion even if a favorable subperiod or gross metric looks better.

Lipton and Steinhardt, writing about machine learning, list among four patterns they see trending the failure to distinguish explanation from speculation and the misuse of language, such as terms of art with colloquial connotations. In a strategy report, words like significant, robust or alpha should each carry the meaning actually computed (our examples), and every sentence can be marked measured or conjectured.

Stating limits need not cost credibility. In five experiments (total n = 5,780), van der Bles and co-authors found that people perceived greater uncertainty when it was communicated, yet trust in the numbers and the source fell only slightly, and mostly for verbal expressions. By our inference, a numeric range is a safer way to state uncertainty than hedging adjectives, and facts such as twelve months of data and sixty-four tried configurations belong beside it.

Exercise: write the first sentence of your conclusion so that it reports the contract's primary criterion as pass or fail, with sample size, period and cost basis. Then add one numeric statement of uncertainty, one measured limitation, and one test that could disprove the mechanism.

### Sources for this section

- [Boutron, Dutton, Ravaud & Altman (2010) · Reporting and Interpretation of Randomized Controlled Trials With Statistically Nonsignificant Results for Primary Outcomes](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2010.651) — *Research paper.* In 72 trials with nonsignificant primary outcomes, spin appeared in 18.0% of titles and 37.5% of abstract results but 58.3% of abstract conclusions; a clinical analogy for conclusions.
- [Lipton & Steinhardt (2018) · Troubling Trends in Machine Learning Scholarship](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.03341) — *arXiv 1807.03341.* Names failing to separate explanation from speculation, and misusing language, as recurring faults in how empirical results are reported.
- [van der Bles, van der Linden, Freeman & Spiegelhalter (2020) · The effects of communicating uncertainty on public trust in facts and numbers](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1913678117) — *Research paper.* Five experiments found only a small drop in trust when uncertainty was communicated, mostly for verbal rather than numeric expressions.

modules.content:
## Understand the idea

The final course deliverable is a report bundle that another researcher can inspect and rerun. Include the evaluated algorithm/source identity, input data and manifest, calculation code, JSON metrics, full-period wealth/drawdown charts, readable report, notebook interpretation and references. Add execution diagnostics, robustness outputs and computing measurements when those claims are part of your conclusion.

First validate the supplied fixture, then replace it with your documented algorithm outputs. Do not silently invent a path from a C sweep's terminal values or relabel illustrative timing rows as measurements. The reporting project accepts aligned no-flow net valuations; other account conventions need an explicit adapter. Audit all claims against available evidence and leave unimplemented analyses labeled as proposals. The concept final and the report rubric assess different work.

$$
\mathrm{report}=\mathrm{reproducible\ inputs}+\mathrm{validated\ results}+\mathrm{balanced\ interpretation}
$$

## A worked example

The supplied twelve-month fixture must produce 10% net strategy return, 8% benchmark return, a two-percentage-point difference, and a maximum drawdown of 1 − 9,800/10,500 = 6.6667%. Its timing fixture has a median paired speedup of 3×. All values are fictional and serve as independent report checks.

## Put the idea into practice

Run the project tests, then generate HTML, Markdown, JSON, PNG and SVG output. Review the report in a browser and reconcile its table to the JSON. Complete the 100-point rubric and executive conclusion, retain the archive's source hashes, then submit the final concept exam.

### Build your evaluation dossier

Reproduce the small worksheet before applying the idea to a full run. Save the input, calculation, interpretation and limitation in your notebook. Add the corresponding evidence to the downloadable report notebook. The in-browser Python worksheet remains in cash and is an arithmetic aid; it does not execute the evaluated trading algorithm. Run the downloadable reporting project locally for actual metrics, files and figures. A clear negative result is a valid finding: never remove a losing period or failed experiment to improve the story.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Reproducibility is easy to promise and hard to deliver. Stodden and co-authors drew a random sample of 204 computational articles from Science, published after the journal began requiring authors to supply data and code on request. They obtained artifacts for 44% and were able to reproduce the findings for 26%. They called on-request sharing an improvement over no policy but insufficient, and recommended that the journal verify deposit of the artifacts as a condition of publication. By inference, your bundle should be rerun from a clean copy before it ships, not after someone asks.

Wilson and co-authors give the matching practice: provide a simple example or test data set that anyone, yourself included, can run to learn whether the program works and returns a known correct output for a simple known input. Such a smoke test helps when supposedly innocent changes are made or the code moves between machines, and dependencies should be explicit. The lesson's fixture is that test, with known answers: a 10% net return, an 8% benchmark, a 6.6667% drawdown and a 3× median speedup.

A passing fixture has limited reach. GIPS 2020 distinguishes verification, a voluntary firm-wide test of a firm's policies and procedures, from a performance examination, a further optional test of one particular composite. By analogy (our inference), the fixture is assurance about the pipeline, and only reconciling your own run's table to its JSON and its input valuations is assurance about your numbers.

Exercise: copy the bundle to an empty directory, run only the commands in its README, and compare the regenerated metrics.json and input hashes with the shipped ones. Log every failure as a missing item, such as an undeclared dependency, an absolute path or an unrecorded seed.

### Sources for this section

- [Stodden, Seiler & Ma (2018) · An empirical analysis of journal policy effectiveness for computational reproducibility](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1708290115) — *Research paper.* Random sample of 204 Science articles: artifacts obtained for 44%, findings reproduced for 26%; on-request sharing judged insufficient.
- [Wilson et al. (2016) · Good Enough Practices in Scientific Computing](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.00037) — *arXiv 1609.00037.* Practical rules for research projects, including a simple example or test data set with known output and explicit dependencies.
- [CFA Institute · GIPS Standards (2020) · 2020 GIPS Standards for Firms](https://www.gipsstandards.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/03/2020_gips_standards_firms.pdf) — *Official source.* Describes verification (firm-wide testing of policies and procedures) and the optional performance examination of a particular composite.

readingGuide:
A result is useful only when a reader can understand how it was produced and what it supports. This final course helps you turn a completed algorithm project into a report that another person can check. Begin with the question, the data period, the comparison, and the rules you promised to use.

Next, reconcile the exported cash and portfolio values before calculating performance. Work through returns, drawdowns, costs, and uncertainty, then choose tables and charts that make those findings clear. Finish by explaining the strongest evidence, the main weaknesses, and what further work is needed. Treat the report as an argument supported by records, rather than a collection of attractive numbers.

The final learning track has 16 lessons × 30 minutes = 8 hours of planned study across four units: 10 minutes reading, 8 minutes calculations and 12 minutes report work per lesson; exam time is additional. Includes 32 practice questions, four four-question checkpoints, a 16-question final, a real downloadable reporting project and a separately self-assessed capstone dossier.

Generated metrics and figures require analyst interpretation; sample prices and timings are fictional. The reporting program does not automatically certify strategies, execute all robustness proposals, or claim regulatory/GIPS compliance.

Only after the best chart is selected

questions.question: For two independent 5% false-positive tests, at least one false positive has probability:
questions.explanation: One minus 0.95 squared equals 0.0975 under the stated independence assumption.

questions.question: A base net gain of 900 with an additional assumed 500 cost gives a first-order sensitivity of:
questions.explanation: Subtract the additional assumed cost once, while labeling the approximation's limits.

questions.question: A paired run takes 24 ms serial and 8 ms parallel. Its speedup is:
questions.explanation: The paired speedup divides baseline elapsed time by candidate elapsed time.

questions.question: Starting equity 5,000 and current equity 5,500 give a wealth index of:
questions.explanation: Normalize as 100 × 5,500 / 5,000 to get an index level of 110.

questions.question: Contributions 500, 200 and −100 sum to:
questions.explanation: The net total retains the negative contribution: 500 + 200 − 100.
